Alfred de Musset's third volume of The Confession of a Child of the Century deepens Octave's torment over Brigitte. After dinner she feels the air would do her good and asks whether they shall walk to the opera. Octave refuses to go, staying home while she takes Smith's arm and leaves. He remains alone all evening, paper before him, trying in vain to collect his thoughts for writing.

As a lonely lover draws a mistress's letter from his bosom and loses himself in reverie, so Octave shuts himself in solitude. He yields to the sweet allurement of doubt. Before him stand the two empty seats Brigitte and Smith just occupied, which he scrutinizes anxiously as if they could tell him something. Readers who like Musset's jealousy study will find a volume of watching, waiting, and self torture.
39411-henry-of-guise-or-the-states-of-bl:
Henry of Guise, volume one of three, is a historical novel by James. Longman issued it in London in 1839. Its subtitle names the States of Blois. James also wrote The Robber and other tales. A dedication to Francis Scott opens the book. In it James explains his course of writing. Great persons are praised and blamed in their own day, he says. Time blows the mists of prejudice away.

The greater facts stay clear when the mists lift, he holds. Some characters, though, stay obscure through all ages. Their acts cannot be fully accounted for. Guise is one such doubtful figure, the preface implies. The novel is set amid the French wars of religion. Blois saw the States-General and Guise's murder. James wrote history in the manner of Scott. His many novels taught the past as drama.
39412-henry-of-guise-or-the-states-of-bl:
Henry of Guise, or The States of Blois, volume two of three, is a historical novel by G P R James, printed at London in 1839. The first chapter opens at the little inn of Montigny, where all is bustle. Twenty or thirty horses employ as many grooms and stable-boys. Sixty or seventy citizens stand in knots outside, talking over matters more important than the horses.

The sign of the inn is the Croix de Lorraine, and the name of the Duke of Guise is heard in every group. One man calls it a great pity that his Highness does not stay the night. Another says the King's troops are pursuing him, and a third wonders how an open town could be defended. He has not twenty men behind him, the talk runs.
3945-monsieur-de-camors-volume-3:
Octave Feuillet's third volume of Monsieur de Camors turns on a wife's terrible revelation. A young countess tells Madame de Tecle, in a low voice and without once looking up, what has been revealed to her and confirmed by her husband's avowal. Madame de Tecle does not interrupt once during the cruel recital, and only imprints a kiss on her hair from time to time.

The countess, ashamed as if of another's crime, fears she has exaggerated her misfortune, since her mother receives the confidence with such calmness. But Madame de Tecle's calm is that of the martyrs, the narrator says, for all Christians suffered under the tiger's claws. Readers who like Feuillet's dramas of honor will find a volume of confession, shame, and maternal steadiness.
3949-cinq-mars-volume-3:
Alfred de Vigny's third volume of Cinq Mars pauses on a king surveying his battlefield. The cannon has ceased to roar when broken columns of infantry fall back into Perpignan, and the remainder already stands within the walls. On the plain no living man is seen save the glittering squadrons of the king, who follow him and form ranks as they go.

He returns at a slow walk and contemplates with satisfaction a field swept clear of enemies. He passes haughtily under the very fire of Spanish guns. They send only a few balls after him, whether from lack of skill, secret agreement with the prime minister, or shame at killing a king of France. Readers who like Vigny's history will find a volume of war, pride, and a monarch caught between minister and crown.
3956-l-abbe-constantin-volume-3:
Ludovic Halevy's third volume of L'Abbe Constantin turns on a young woman's heart and an older woman's reading of it. Susie guards her feelings as a miser guards and caresses the first coins of his treasure, waiting for the day she sees clearly into her own heart and is sure she loves. On that day she would speak, and how happy she would be to tell all to Susie herself, the narrator's confidante.

Mrs Scott, meanwhile, attributes Jean's growing melancholy to herself, flattered by the thought of being beloved and vexed at the same time. She holds Jean in great esteem and affection, but is distressed that his sadness might come from her, while Susie remains conscious of her own innocence. Readers who like Halevy's comedy will find a volume of misunderstanding, affection, and hearts not yet spoken.
3960-a-romance-of-youth-volume-3:
Paris in the late nineteenth century gives the backdrop for the third part of Francois Coppee's novel about a young poet named Amedee. The volume picks up his story after his first steps in print, when cafes and small journals begin to notice his work.

Amedee's sonnets win praise in La Guepe, and writers who meet at the Cafe de Seville start to talk about the rising poet. The chapters follow his growing fame, the friends and rivals it brings, and the strain that success puts on his hopes and his heart. Readers get a warm, street-level view of a young writer learning how praise, pride, and love can pull in different ways.
39611-mortomley-s-estate-a-novel-vol-1-o:
Mrs Riddell opens a three-volume novel of money and property in volume one. Tinsley Brothers issued it at London in 1874. She dedicates the tale to Emma Martin of Wadesmill.

Chapter one presents Mr Asherill to the reader. The city around him is changing fast. New blocks of offices rise across the old precincts, built by city men and held by companies. Later chapters bring a very wet Saturday and summer days. Mrs Mortomley gets advice meant for her good. A dead faint, plain speech from Rupert, and the first mutterings of the storm close the list. Riddell wrote knowing novels of business life. Her city scenes draw on a world of clerks, shares, and sudden loss.
3965-cosmopolis-volume-3:
Paul Bourget's third volume of Cosmopolis turns from plot to the code of honor itself. The narrator asks how women can admit the inflexible rigor that founds manly relations, when they allow no similar rigor in their arguments with men or their discussions among themselves. Accustomed to appeal from convention to instinct and from reason to sentiment, women face laws of justice or honor in a state of incomprehension worse than ignorance.

A duel, for example, appears to them like an arbitrary drama, which the wish of one concerned can change at fancy. Ninety nine women out of a hundred would think like Lydia Maitland, the novel's American heroine, and treat a point of honor as a quarrel to be talked away. Readers who like Bourget's moral psychology will find a volume of duels, scruples, and two worlds misunderstanding each other.
39661-mortomley-s-estate-a-novel-vol-3-o:
Mortomley's Estate, volume three, closes Mrs Riddell's novel of a ruined house. Tinsley Brothers of London published the three volumes in 1874. Mrs Riddell had already written George Geith and Too Much Alone, and she dedicates the story to Emma Martin of Wadesmill.

The final volume opens at a meeting of creditors in the matter of Archibald Mortomley. Mr Swanland, junior partner to Mr Asherill, presides with a judicial calm that no creditor dares question, holding the scales, as the narrator insists, with strict impartiality between debtor and creditor. The chapters carry the wreck to its settlement: Mortomley's blue, sauve qui peut, and Mortomley understands at last. Mr Werner asks a favour, two unwelcome visitors call, and Mrs Mortomley breaks the news. What Rupert had done is confessed, Mr Asherill is persuaded, and a conclusion winds up the estate and the family.
39692-mildred-arkell-a-novel-vol-1-of-3:
Mildred Arkell, volume one, opens a three-volume novel by Mrs Henry Wood, the author of East Lynne. Tinsley Brothers published it in London in 1865.

The narrator promises a story of real life, of a kind common enough in fact but hidden, so that told in full it reads like romance. The scene is Westerbury, a fair midland city where a great cathedral stands apart from the busy manufacturing town below. Clergy and old families on one side, trade on the other, do not mix. Chapters introduce the Miss Hughes's home and the coming of Charlotte Travice. A flight, a miserable mistake, and a seared heart follow. Mildred goes out as a lady's maid, and an offer from Mr Carr changes her course. Two more volumes complete the tale.
3970-jacqueline-volume-3:
Th. Bentzon's novel reaches a darker turn in its third volume, as Jacqueline feels for the first time how poverty and a lack of protection expose her to insult. A man named Talbrun treats her as a plaything, and the slight cuts her pride deeply.

Jacqueline faces the hurt with a mix of anger and shame, asking what right any man has to use her so. Her womanly instincts rebel, yet she has few shields and fewer allies. The volume is the novel's painful middle passage, showing a young woman who must find her own strength when the adults around her fail to guard her.
3974-the-ink-stain-tache-d-encre-volume-:
Rene Bazin's diary novel continues into summer in its third volume, with a fishing trip and the return of an old friend. A letter from Jupille gives minute directions for the meeting, and the diarist walks from Sceaux across woods toward the forts.

The July entries keep the book's easy mix of travel, talk, and study, as the young scholar steps out of his books into fields and water. Old ties renew and new plans take shape along the way. Readers get the warmest stretch of the novel so far, where nature and friendship offer a break from family pressure and scholarly worry.
3978-fromont-and-risler-volume-3:
Alphonse Daudet's third volume turns to Desiree, called Mam'zelle Zizi, whose mornings brighten when Frantz comes to sit at her feet as in old days. He no longer comes to talk of Sidonie, and the change gives her a quiet, daily joy.

Around that tender center, the novel keeps its Paris business world in motion, with the house of Fromont, its workers, and its tangled marriages. Daudet writes with warmth for the overlooked and sharp eyes for pride and gain. The volume offers a softer passage in a hard story, where small kindnesses count for a great deal.
3983-gerfaut-volume-3:
Charles de Bernard's novel deepens its central struggle in the third volume, as Madame de Bergenheim fights love with the help of falsehood. Virtue, doubting its own strength, turns to deceit as a shield, while Octave tries to stir her jealousy.

The volume is a study in defense and attack within a marriage-bound world, where honor demands concealment and feeling demands truth. Bernard follows each move with care, showing how a plan built on deceit can wound the very duty it means to guard. Readers who like courtly intrigue and moral tension will find this the novel's most tightly wound part.
39878-miser-farebrother-a-novel-vol-2-of: Miser Farebrother is a novel by Farjeon, printed at London by Ward and Downey. The work runs to three volumes, and the hosted copy is the second of them. Farjeon also wrote Great Porter Square, Grif, In a Silver Sea and The House of White Shadows. The evidence in the hosted text is the title page alone, so the tale itself cannot be summed up from it.
3988-conscience-volume-3:
Hector Malot's novel tightens in its third volume around testimony and a doctor's attempt to shape it. Saniel insists on seeing Nougarede, not to falsify what Phillis said, but hoping his medical voice can show that a paralytic witness counts for no more than a confused one.

At the first words of excuse, Nougarede stops him, and the plan fails. Malot uses that blocked move to show how guilt narrows a man's choices, turning each clever step into a new trap. The volume keeps the crime story grounded in talk, sickrooms, and law, with Saniel's conscience pressing harder as the net draws close.
3993-madame-chrysantheme-volume-3:
Pierre Loti's Japan novel continues in its third volume aboard ship and ashore in late August. The Triomphante leaves its dock between the mountains and takes up old moorings in the harbor, under a clear sky swept clean as if by a cyclone.

Loti notes duty hours, harbor hills, and the strange clarity of light, keeping his sailor's eye on both ship routine and shore life. The volume carries the story of his brief Japanese marriage forward through festivals and farewells. Readers get vivid, firsthand scenes of a port world that feels at once near and far from home.
3998-an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-volum:
Emile Souvestre's Paris journal continues in its third volume into autumn, when nights grow cold and long and the sun no longer wakes the writer before work. Warm under his counterpane, he argues each morning between activity and idleness, waiting like the Gascon for the dispute to settle.

The volume keeps the journal's mix of season notes and short essays, this time turning to country, home, and the duties of a citizen. Souvestre writes from his attic perch with mild humor and plain sense. Readers get a calm, companionable book, best read a little at a time, like letters from a thoughtful neighbor.
40054-margaret-capel-a-novel-vol-3-of-3:
Margaret Capel, volume three of three, closes a novel by the author of The Clandestine Marriage. Bentley published the set in London in eighteen forty six. Chapter one opens with verses from Coleridge on patience and stolen self knowledge. Margaret has lived over a year in deep retirement at a widow's cottage.

Mrs Fitzpatrick's quiet house suits her grief better than Ashdale's solitude did before. The two women, both much tried by sorrow, grow fond without speaking of it. Margaret's cough and side pain at first alarm her hostess with sad memories. Her lost daughter's illness is recalled by each pause on the stairs. The doctor calls the cough nervous, and the sea air soon mends her. The name of Haveloc still strikes her heart like a dagger's plunge.
40097-the-world-as-will-and-idea-vol-2-o:
Arthur Schopenhauer's supplements to his great work fill volume two of three in English dress. R B Haldane and J Kemp turned the German into English. Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner and Company issued this sixth edition at London in 1909.

An appendix gives his long criticism of the Kantian philosophy. Supplements to the first book treat perception, the senses, and knowledge got before experience. Other chapters weigh logic, rhetoric, and the methods of mathematics. One chapter treats the ludicrous. Another asks how the thing in itself can be known at all. A long chapter gives the will the first place in self-knowledge. Schopenhauer wrote these pieces to shore up his system. They let a reader enter his thought by many doors.
40332-a-rich-man-s-relatives-vol-2-of-3:
A Rich Man's Relatives, volume two, is the middle volume of a novel by Cleland, author of Inchbracken. The volume's front matter reprints the press notices of that earlier novel, which the Westminster Review praised in 1883 as a clever sketch of Scottish life at the Disruption.

Inchbracken, as the reviewers explain, is set in a remote northern parish at the great secession from the Church of Scotland. Its young Free Church minister, Roderick Brown, rescues a baby from a shipwreck and is ruined by gossip for his charity to a fallen parishioner. The Academy admired the portraiture of elders, gossips and village notables, and the broadest Scotch dialogue. A Rich Man's Relatives continues Cleland's world of Scottish parish and family intrigue across three volumes, of which this is the second.
40333-a-rich-man-s-relatives-vol-3-of-3: A Rich Man's Relatives, volume three, is the closing part of a novel whose hosted opening gives press notices for the author's earlier book instead of this volume's first pages. Those notices praise Inchbracken, a novel of Scottish life at the Disruption, for its humour and its Free Church minister's story. On that evidence this is the third and final volume of a three volume novel by the same hand, Cleland.
40405-mary-seaham-a-novel-volume-1-of-3:
Mrs Grey, who wrote The Gambler's Wife, stands behind this novel in three volumes. Colburn printed the first volume of Mary Seaham in London in 1852. A verse from Watts heads chapter one: she left her home with a bounding heart.

The wedding feast is cleared away as the tale opens. Guests have gone, and the last joy peal rings from the old church tower. Cannons crash their salute over the mountain valley of Glan Pennant. A strange hush of spent joy lies on the place, the tale notes. Even the servants feel the flat calm after their night of sport. Mary Seaham's own story now starts, in that hush.
40418-it-may-be-true-vol-1-of-3:
The first volume of a three-volume novel by Mrs Wood. T Cautley Newby published it at London in 1865. The title runs simply It May Be True. An epigraph from Keats opens the first chapter. That chapter names its village setting: Ashleigh. Elms, oaks, and beeches embosom the place.

Mountains rise on one side in varied green. Forest clumps on the other side frame peeps of the sea. White sails and fishing boats dot the blue distance. The village has its inn, its ivy-mantled church, and its parsonage. A large brick manor crowns a small eminence. Creepers and ivy soften its plain bulk. Mrs Wood, later famous as Mrs Henry Wood, wrote this before East Lynne made her name.
40437-plato-and-the-other-companions-of-:
George Grote wrote Plato, and the Other Companions of Sokrates. Volume Three of a new edition came from John Murray in London in 1888. The set runs to four volumes in all. Grote also wrote a History of Greece. Chapter Twenty-Six opens this volume. It treats the Phaedrus and the Symposion together.

Those two works are the two erotic dialogues of Plato, the contents say. Eros in Plato's thought fills the chapter's early pages. Love of the good drives men by many paths, the summary notes. Beauty seen in a person starts the mind toward beauty itself. The Symposion sets rival speeches on love side by side. Alkibiades ends the feast with praise of Sokrates, drunk as he is. Scholars of Greek thought can trace Plato's doctrine here in Grote's close, ordered digest.
40682-lulu-s-library-volume-1-of-3:
Lulu's Library, volume one, is a book of children's stories by Louisa Alcott, author of Little Women, published by Roberts Brothers at Boston in 1886. The preface, dated from Concord in August 1885 and signed Aunt Jo, explains how the tales began.

All but three of the stories were told to Alcott's little niece during the quiet hour before bedtime. They became such favourites with her and her friends that Alcott wrote them down in several small blue books. Having nothing else to offer that year, she collected them as a Christmas gift to her boys and girls. The twelve tales include a Christmas dream, the candy country, Naughty Jocko, the skipping shoes, Rosy's journey, the fairy box, the piggy girl, and the three frogs.
40683-lulu-s-library-volume-3-of-3:
Louisa M Alcott published a third volume of Lulu's Library at Boston in 1889, listing her works from Little Women to Aunt Jo's Scrap Bag on the title page. Recollections of My Childhood heads this volume's contents. A Christmas Turkey, and How It Came follows. The Silver Party and The Blind Lark come next.

Music and Macaroni, The Little Red Purse, and Sophie's Secret fill the middle. Dolly's Bedstead and Trudel's Siege close the list. Roberts Brothers issued the set for Alcott's girl readers. The childhood recollections give the volume an autobiographical core rare in her story collections. Alcott wrote the Lulu stories for her niece.
40868-the-world-as-will-and-idea-vol-3-o:
The World as Will and Idea, by Arthur Schopenhauer, in the rendering of Haldane and Kemp, fills three volumes; the third reached a sixth edition in London in 1909. This volume holds the supplements: to part of the second book, and to the third and fourth books. Chapters run from a retrospect and an objective view of the intellect through matter, teleology, and instinct.

The supplements to the third book treat the knowledge of the ideas, the pure subject of knowledge, genius, and madness. Remarks on natural beauty, the inner nature of art, architecture, poetry, history, and the metaphysics of music follow. The fourth book's supplements take up death, heredity, the metaphysics of the love of the sexes, and the vanity and suffering of life. Schopenhauer built the volume as a second storey on his system's frame.
40974-blue-stocking-hall-vol-1-of-3:
Blue-Stocking Hall, in its first volume of three, is a novel in letters published in London in 1827 by Henry Colburn. A verse from Love's Labour's Lost stands at its head. It praises women's eyes as the books and academies of the world. The author, in a preface, owns this is a first book. Strong prejudice against ladies called bas bleus was once his own, he writes. A visit to Blue-stocking Hall cured him of it. He wishes the same cure on any reader who shares his old bias.

The tale is told in letters, the first from Charles Falkland to Arthur Howard at Dover. The hall of the title is a house where learned women gather. Their talk and character are the book's real subject. The novel pleads for respect for the blue-stocking, a tag then used in scorn.
4103-the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1:
Azel Ames's Mayflower history continues in its third volume with the officers and crew of the ship. The pilot John Clarke, hired by Weston and Cushman before a vessel was even found, holds the distinction of being the first man shipped for the voyage.

Ames traces each officer and sailor through records and inference, showing how much the Pilgrim venture owed to seamen as well as saints. The volume suits readers who like maritime detail, from hiring and wages to duties at sea. It adds the crew's story to the better-known tale of the passengers.
41253-history-of-the-reformation-of-the-:
History of the Reformation of the Sixteenth Century, Volume Three, is Merle d'Aubigné's great church history in English dress. D'Aubigné presided over the theological school of Geneva. H White translated the work, and the author revised the translation and added new matter. The American Tract Society printed this volume at New York in 1848.

In his preface d'Aubigné praises the new hunger for original documents in France, Switzerland, Germany, and England. He hopes to add his mite to that work. He admits the need for unpublished papers grew urgent as he neared the twelfth book, on the Reformation in France. The history is told with a preacher's fire and a scholar's care for sources. It remains a landmark of Protestant historiography in English.
41314-my-danish-sweetheart-a-novel-volum:
The second volume of a sea novel by W Clark Russell. Methuen published the three-volume set at London in 1891. Russell also wrote The Wreck of the Grosvenor. His Danish sweetheart is Helga, a captain's daughter. This volume follows the ship Early Morn. Nine chapters carry the voyage south.

The narrator has just told his story to the lugger's crew. Their eyes glow in the lamplight as they listen. News of a stove lifeboat at Tintrenale Bay troubles him. The sailors recall the Danish barque Anine from two years past. Her captain had small eyes and a goat-like beard. Helga confirms she sailed aboard her father's ship. A sailor's death and the end of the Early Morn await in later chapters.
41329-mrs-dorriman-a-novel-volume-1-of-3:
Mrs Dorriman is the first volume of a three-volume novel by the Honourable Mrs Henry Chetwynd, published in London by Chapman and Hall in 1886. The author had earlier written Life in a German Village, The Dutch Cousin, and A March Violet. Three-volume form was the standard dress of the Victorian circulating-library novel.

The heroine is introduced as a woman in a settled attitude of bewilderment. The problems of life weigh on her, from household gas bills to shooting stars. She is content, with some wisdom, to remain unenlightened about most of them. Her present trouble begins with a letter from her brother, lying on her lap as the chapter opens. The novel builds its comedy and its plot on a mind overwhelmed by a complex world.
41330-mrs-dorriman-a-novel-volume-2-of-3:
Chetwynd wrote a three volume novel that Chapman and Hall published in London in 1886. The second volume opens at an inn. A servant named John comes to bear his master's wishes to the keeper, Macrae, a portly man whose waistcoats have taken to riding up in front.

His wife steps in before he can go. If Sir Albert wants a little talk, she will go herself, for her husband cannot leave the bar at the busiest hour. She answers his protest with strong scorn: she will do better in both ways. What does he know of the diet Sir Albert may wish to discuss? The scene sets the pair in a page: a keen, slight wife and a slow man under her rule.
41331-mrs-dorriman-a-novel-volume-3-of-3:
Dorriman, a novel by Chetwynd, closes with this third volume, printed in London in 1886. Chapman and Hall issued the set, and the author had written Life in a German Village before it. The volume opens on spring fighting through smoke and fog in a city garden.

Dorriman watches sparrows tug at one long straw and reads her own life in the scene. Alone, none of the birds can lift it, and they will not join forces, so the wind takes it. Her youth, marked by injustice and a want of affection, left lines that age makes plain. Sweetness of temper alone kept her from fretfulness, the tale says. Her brother Sandford, mending at his writing-table, has changed since his attack. He shows her in small ways how much he has learned to value her.
41339-mount-royal-a-novel-volume-1-of-3:
Volume one of a three-volume novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret opens at Mount Royal in 1882, from the London house of John and Robert Maxwell. Nine chapters carry titles drawn from verse, most of them about love.

The first chapter, The Days That Are No More, sets Christabel kneeling in firelight at her Aunt Diana's knee. She hears the tale of the aunt's own life, told as calmly as a plot. Christabel balks at one point: the man in the tale was a widower, and she cannot see caring for a man who cared for someone else first. A third voice, Jessie, lays down the law of lovers from the twilight. The scene sets up the book's ground: old love retold, young love listening, and pride in the way of both.
41340-mount-royal-a-novel-volume-2-of-3:
Mount Royal, volume two, is the middle part of a novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret. Maxwell published it in London in 1882 in three volumes. The contents list twelve chapters with verse lines as titles. Let Me and My Passionate Love Go By opens this volume. Alas for me then, my good days are done, follows. Grief a fixed star, and joy a vane that veers, gives the third title. Love Will Have His Day stands fourth in the list. 

The first chapter opens in the second week of July. That week was not altogether peerless weather, the narrator says. A sultry tropical Tuesday gave way to a chilly Wednesday wind. Such sudden changes try humanity more than winter, she holds. The novel is a sensation story of love and loss. Quotation titles give each chapter a mourning tone.
41341-mount-royal-a-novel-volume-3-of-3:
Mount Royal is a novel in three volumes by the author of Lady Audleys Secret. The hosted text holds the third and last volume of the three. The book came out in London in the year eighteen eighty two. Verse heads in the list lend each part a grim tag from the poets.

Swift fresh woes lead the list, then a vow made and a grave side part. A duel or a murder is asked in one stark head of the last book. No mercy, a toast to a road girl, and old days mocked fill the turns. Love bears a dead fruit ere tears and plots are done at last. The tale trades in the lush shock mode its author made famed.
41374-mohawks-a-novel-volume-1-of-3:
Mohawks is a novel in three volumes by the author of Lady Audley's Secret, Mary Elizabeth Braddon. Volume one was published in London by John and Robert Maxwell. Its twelve chapters bear quoted lines as their titles, from poets and plays. The story opens on a heathery knoll with a farmer and his spaniels.

A bundle of dirty papers is found on a dead wayfarer in that opening scene. A small baby lies asleep beside the dead man on the grass. The year is that of the battle of Malplaquet, one hundred seventy seven years before. That battle had just been fought at a cost of twenty thousand slain. Talk turns to Marlborough, whose glory some now thought to be waning. Fears grow that he might seek to make himself a dictator.
41375-mohawks-a-novel-volume-2-of-3:
Mohawks is a novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret, in three volumes. The hosted text is volume two, issued at London. Contents of this volume run to twelve chapters. Their heads are quotations in verse. The first reads, in opposition against fate and hell. The second stands upon the ground of the speaker's own honour.

Later heads speak of folk born poor who lived poor and died poor. Ladies who must needs be rooks and a speaker yet in love fill the middle. Chapter one opens next day in an abbey hall. The room is half armoury, half picture gallery, the tale says. Damascened steel of Damascus and Toledo hangs beside early Italian saints and virgins. A man named Lavendale turns suddenly to his friend Herrick there.
41376-mohawks-a-novel-volume-3-of-3:
The author of Lady Audley's Secret, Vixen, and Ishmael wrote a novel in three volumes, with volume three printed at London. Quoted lines head every chapter: You called me, and I came home to your heart, opens the last book. O, to what end, except a jealous one, and all your honour in a whisper lost follow. Smite his hard heart and shake his reptile soul comes fourth.

Another turn of the social wheel starts the text. Summer was over, and Twickenham, Richmond, Bath, and Tunbridge Wells stood deserted for the new squares between Soho and Hyde Park Corner. The king had only one objection to London, the tale notes, and it reached to all his British dominions: he would rather have been in Hanover. Court and season intrigue close in this final volume.
41564-mabel-a-novel-vol-1-of-3:
Mabel, a novel by Emma Warburton, opens with this first of three volumes. Newby printed the set in London in 1854. Warburton inscribes the work to Emma Tylney Long as a slight token of grateful esteem.

A morning hymn by Keble stands at the head of the first chapter. The scene is Aston, a village in a pretty Gloucestershire valley, early in August. Sunlight lingers on the ivy-covered church tower, then floods the rectory and the old manor house. A single figure walks the steep path from the rectory in the latest fashion. Captain Clair has quit his regiment in India and come home to rebuild his health. Service abroad had worn it down, and the slow pace of his stroll betrays his fatigue.
42095-the-eve-of-all-hallows-or-adelaide:
The Eve of All-Hallows, or Adelaide of Tyrconnel, volume two of three, is a romance by Matthew Weld Hartstonge, published at London in 1825. A motto from Virgil's Aeneid stands on the title page. The volume opens on a famous morning: the first of July 1690, by the river Boyne. Trumpets sound, drums beat to arms, and hearts throb high.

The signal gun announces the march of the Prince of Orange's troops toward the stream the narrator calls the rubicon of empire. The plan of attack has three parts. Count Schomberg, son of the field marshal, leads the right wing toward the fords by the bridge of Slane, with ten thousand men, chiefly horse. The volume carries the Irish war story forward.
42145-the-world-before-them-a-novel-volu:
The World Before Them, volume two, was written by Mrs Moodie. Bentley published the novel in London in 1868. The full tale runs to three volumes. Moodie had won fame with Roughing It in the Bush. Chapter one of this volume treats the Martins. Their cottage stands by the churchyard of a small Gothic church. Old elms shade long rows of nameless graves. A public-house sits at the centre of the hamlet. Sailors and smugglers gather there to drink and gamble. Jonathan Sly, the landlord, reads the weekly paper aloud.

Dorothy avoids the main road on her walks to the parsonage. Half-drunken sailors have scared her with rough looks and praise. Her mother lies buried under a dark yew by the chancel window. No sunbeam reaches that grave. Dorothy clears its weeds and plants flowers there.
42167-the-pit-town-coronet-a-family-myst:
Charles J Wills wrote The Pit Town Coronet, a family mystery in three volumes. Ward and Downey issued volume one in London in eighteen hundred eighty eight. Wills gave the book to Edmund Yates, the famed editor. The Warrender clan of Essex stands at the heart of the tale.

Four hundred years the Warrenders have held The Warren and its fat acres. Squire and parson rule the parish of King’s Warren side by side. Big Reginald Haggard courts the elder of two fair Warrender girls. Georgina weighs the man in her mind and finds him wanting. Her book of grave social thought lies face down, unread, in the rose garden. A croquet party, a wedding, and Lord Mayor’s Day fill the first span. Rome and the Villa Lambert wait in the last long chapters.
42168-the-pit-town-coronet-a-family-myst:
Pit Town Coronet, a family mystery, volume two of three, is a novel by Charles Wills. Ward and Downey published the set in London in 1888 from York Street, Covent Garden. Wills is named as author of In the Land of the Lion and Sun. Project Gutenberg holds the first and third volumes beside this middle volume.

Contents of volume two open with A Horrible Scandal at page one of the book. At the Parsonage, How They Came Home, and The Return of the Wanderer follow in the list. The pit town of the title is a mining town, and the coronet hints at hidden rank in the family mystery. The middle volume of a mystery was built to deepen the scandal and delay the answer, and Wills contents promise exactly that pace for his readers.
42169-the-pit-town-coronet-a-family-myst:
The Pit Town Coronet, a family mystery, volume three of three, by Charles J Wills, was printed in London by Ward and Downey in 1888. Wills wrote In the Land of the Lion and Sun.

Chapters open after seventeen years, then at Monte Carlo and an anonymous letter. Pallida Mors, a little red box, and Lucius Haggard is bewildered follow. Enter Mr Brookes, the hollow beech tree, and Mr Capt leaves service close the set. The text opens as seventeen uneventful years streak Georgie Haggard abundant chestnut locks with grey. A lovely woman still, her girlish beauty has grown into sweet matronly dignity. She is still the loving woman of the old happy times, her beauty touched by a dash of sadness. Readers should start at volume one for the full family secret.
42174-the-world-before-them-a-novel-volu:
Mrs Moodie, author of Roughing It in the Bush, wrote a novel in three volumes, of which this third volume was printed at London in 1868. Chapter one is titled Mrs Gilbert Rushmere. A dinner is so well cooked and nicely served that Mrs Rowly and her daughter eat heartily despite the unusual hour. Mrs Rushmere's chair is drawn to the table's head.

Dorothy sits beside her and carves, since Gilbert cannot cut his own food. His injured arm must heal before he can help himself. Dorothy longs to carve for him, seeing how unwillingly his wife does it. Moodie's Canadian fame rested on her bush memoir, but she wrote fiction too.
42493-lady-eureka-or-the-mystery-a-proph:
Lady Eureka, or The Mystery is a speculative novel in three volumes by the author of Mephistopheles in England, published in London by Longman and its partners in 1840. The subtitle calls it a prophecy of the future. This hosted file holds the third volume.

The contents of the final volume turn strange. An Australian colony in Spain appears, then old England and the last of the Englishmen. A chapter gives an account of the decline and fall of old England, and another the death of the last Englishman. The volume opens aboard ship, with a fat cook complaining to the surgeon of a devil of a pain in his stomach. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
42496-miracle-gold-a-novel-vol-2-of-3:
Richard Dowling wrote this novel in three volumes, printed by Ward and Downey of London in 1888. The part held here is volume two. Dowling had written The Mystery of Killard, The Weird Sisters, and Tempest Driven. Front ads list new novels at the libraries, from Marvel by the author of Molly Bawn to One Maid's Mischief by G M Fenn.

Chapters in this volume run from Spirit and Flesh through A Substitute for Gold and Red Herrings. Dinner at Curzon Street, a night in the dark, and Mrs Hanbury fill the middle. A quarter past twelve, an early visitor to Timmons, and Gracedieu in Derbyshire mark the turns. The title's miracle gold hangs over a plot of money, substitutes, and London drawing rooms.
42498-miracle-gold-a-novel-vol-1-of-3:
Richard Dowling wrote Miracle Gold, a novel in three volumes, here in volume one. Ward and Downey put it out at London in 1888. Dowling had written The Mystery of Killard and The Weird Sisters before it. Contents open with Too Late, then Voices of the Unseen. An offer of marriage and a flight follow in the chapter list.

Chapter one opens at a country station, with a young lady in distress. The last train for London has just gone, two or three minutes past. The station woman proves civil and ready to talk with her. A deputy of Leigh, and Oscar Leigh's cave of magic, stand in the contents. A juggler and his last feat, and a chapter called Only a Woman, come next. Stranger than miracle gold, and an omen, point to the mystery ahead.
42499-miracle-gold-a-novel-vol-3-of-3:
Richard Dowling wrote a novel in three volumes, here in its third and last part. Ward and Downey issued the set in London in 1888. Chapters run from Twenty-seven to Forty-two, the end. John Hanbury stands near the heart of the close, with Dora Ashton and Leigh at his bench.

Hanbury comes home to Chester Square at dusk, still stunned by a vast find. A note to his mother calls the news the most strange that ever befell a man. Flight, confession, and a doctor's verdict crowd the last act. Readers who have tracked the long plot gain its full, tense payoff here.
4259-andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-mili:
The third volume of John McElroy's prison narrative picks up inside the Andersonville stockade. Daily life there had settled into grim routine. Chapters describe the difficulty of exercise and the prison marketplace the men called the Rialto. They describe the cursing of the Confederacy and the battle of Spottsylvania Court House as told among prisoners.

McElroy's picture of the camp is unsparing. It shows a crowded mass of men with almost no movement in or out. Sickness and despair grow in that stillness. Read with the earlier volumes, this section shows how prisoners kept some order and talk alive.
42595-the-last-call-a-romance-vol-1-of-3:
Richard Dowling wrote The Last Call, a romance in three volumes, of which this file holds the first, issued at London by Tinsley Brothers in 1884. Dowling had written The Mystery of Killard, The Weird Sisters, and Sweet Inisfail before it. The tale opens at low water in summer, the sun low behind a bank of leaden cloud over a horse shoe cove and a placid bay.

On the ridge of shingle lies a young man of twenty seven or twenty eight, gray tweed suit and straw hat, his eyes on the sea. Far out a small dot moves on the bay, a boat holding a man and a woman. The man in the boat is Dominique Lavirotte, French by descent and birth, and looking like a Greek. Part one bears the book's own name.
42724-the-works-of-christopher-marlowe-v:
A H Bullen edited The Works of Christopher Marlowe, Volume Two, issued at London in 1885. John C Nimmo published the set. One hundred and twenty copies were printed on laid paper. Copy Number Forty Seven is shown here. Four plays fill the volume. The Jew of Malta leads the set.

Edward the Second, The Massacre at Paris, and Dido, Queen of Carthage follow. A note on The Jew of Malta says no edition is older than the quarto of 1633. Thomas Heywood brought that quarto out. Edward Alleyn first played the Jew, the note recalls. Heywood's own prologues for a court show are kept in the text. Greek lines from Pindar head the volume. The set forms part of a series on English dramatists.
42752-tempest-driven-a-romance-vol-3-of-:
Richard Dowling wrote Tempest Driven, a romance in three volumes issued in London by Tinsley Brothers in eighteen eighty six. The hosted text is volume three. Dowling had earlier written The Mystery of Killard and The Weird Sisters. Chapters thirty two to forty seven fill the volume. Chapter thirty two is Salmon and Cows. Luncheon at Carlingford House opens the closing act.

Luncheon that day was a quiet, subdued meal, the tale says. Edith Paulton, small and vivacious, was better looking than Madge and shrewdly discontented. She alone at table tried to be sprightly, though not unsympathetic. Her elder sister Madge radiated amiability, by contrast. Later chapters bring A Fortune Lost and A Telegram from the Mail. Solicitor and Client and The Widow Theory of the Case deepen the plot. At the Whale Mouth, The Red Cave, and A Last Appeal close the romance.
42907-great-porter-square-a-mystery-v-3:
Great Porter Square, a Mystery, volume three, by B L Farjeon, was printed in London by Ward and Downey in 1885, in three volumes. Farjeon had written Grif, London Heart, and The House of White Shadows. This last volume runs from chapter thirty one.

Becky gives a description of her interview with Richard Manx, and tells how Fanny became acquainted with Mrs Lydia Holdfast. Mr Pelham makes his appearance once more, and Fanny discovers who Richard Manx is. Becky and Fanny on the watch, and number 119 Great Porter Square let to a new tenant, pace the mid part. Mrs Holdfast insists on becoming an active partner, and Frederick Holdfast makes the discovery. Mr Holdfast diary fills two chapters, then a caging closes the run. Readers should start at volume one for the full London mystery.
43052-donald-ross-of-heimra-volume-1-of-:
William Black wrote this tale of the Highlands, in three books of which this is the first. It was printed at London in 1891. The list of parts of this book names its world in Gaelic heads: Godiva, Young Donald, the Cave of the Crowing Cock, and a cave of a sea thief. A fight at a place named Ru-Minard closes the book. The tale opens on the rails of the Highland line.

Two folk talk on the stand of the stop at Invershin. One is a tall young maid of grand air and a high hand. She has been given a fine plaything, her mate jests: an estate in the Highlands. No doubt all her fine plans will come right, he says. But she will have to change three things first. Those three are human kind, and the soil and the air of Scotland.
43053-donald-ross-of-heimra-volume-2-of-:
Donald Ross of Heimra, volume two, continues William Black's Highland novel. Sampson Low published the three volumes in London in 1891. The contents of this volume list eight chapters. A crofters' commission sits among them. A revolution that failed closes the list.

The volume opens on a black night by the sea. Two men pace a little wooden quay in the dark. They await the expected steamer. Coinneach Breac falls to telling strange tales of night watchers. He warns that such things are not safe to mention. Some listener may stand at one's shoulder. He tells of his uncle at a lighthouse instead. Fog-bells ringing on clear nights begin the wonders. Gaelic speech flavours the scene throughout.
43054-donald-ross-of-heimra-volume-3-of-:
Donald Ross of Heimra, volume three of three, is a novel by William Black, printed at London in 1891. The first chapter, Smoke and Flame, opens in argument. Fred Stanley tells his friend Frank that there is some trick in an amazing incident. There is some underhand trick in it, and he wants to know what it means.

He urges that they get the keepers and go up the hill at once to see what is going on. Frank answers with good humour that the jugglery has come in very handy. If a riot had been started, who knows what the end might have been? His anxiety was not for the raid into the Glen Orme forest, nor the sheep driven off the hill, but for Stanley's sister. She might have been denounced before an angry meeting.
43188-the-harlequin-opal-a-romance-vol-2:
The Harlequin Opal is a romance by Fergus Hume, who also wrote The Island of Fantasy. The text here is volume two of three. It came out in London in 1893.

A proem in verse tells how the opal got its many hues. Earth, sea, air and fire each gave the stone a shade. A verse at the front sets the scene in a land of old Aztec glory. Serenades, dances and scornful looks fill that tropic world. The opal's bright ray is said to tell the fate of its holder. Love and risk turn on the stone. Hume sets love and pride under a hot southern sun.
43411-life-of-mozart-vol-1-of-3:
Volume one of Otto Jahn's Life of Mozart, in Pauline Townsend's English translation, was published in London in 1882, with a preface by George Grove. The biography runs to three volumes, and this first one carries Mozart from childhood through his early manhood. Its chapters cover his study in Salzburg, his first opera in Vienna, the Italian tour, and his early church and stage works.

Grove's preface calls the book epoch-making, because Jahn asks how the music was made, not only what befell the man. Older lives of composers, he says, gave gossip and outward facts, and left the making of the music untouched. The volume also treats opera seria and opera buffa, sonatas, and the Mannheim journey. It stands as a founding work of modern musical biography, built on documents and close study of the scores.
43412-life-of-mozart-vol-2-of-3:
Volume two of the Life of Mozart, by Otto Jahn, was turned from the German by Pauline Townsend and issued at London in 1881. George Grove wrote a preface to the English edition. The full life ran to three volumes in that form. This middle volume opens with a chapter on French opera.

Paris in 1778 and the return home fill the next long chapters. Court service in Salzburg and the opera Idomeneo follow in the tale. Release from that service and first attempts in Vienna come next. The Abduction from the Serail and Mozart’s courtship stand in the list. Married life and his family and friends close the view given here. Jahn built the first great life of Mozart from letters and records.
43413-life-of-mozart-vol-3-of-3:
Life of Mozart, volume three, is the closing volume of Otto Jahn's biography of the composer. Jahn's German work was translated by Pauline Townsend, and George Grove wrote the preface. The three volumes were printed in London by Novello. This volume carries the life through its final stretch.

A list of facsimiles shows the book's care for documents. One reproduces Mozart's letter to Bullinger from Paris, written after the death of his mother. Another gives the original manuscript of a song. Two more are sketches that show Mozart's method of composing at work. The words of an ode set by Mozart are printed below one sketch. A biography built from letters, manuscripts, and musical drafts lets the reader watch the composer's hand move, and this volume completes that design.
4403-the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-e:
Book Three of George Meredith's Shaving of Shagpat opens on the enchanted sea, where a cockle-shell skims calmly, then pitches on surging foam. The surges boil like savage animals, hissing with anger, as Shibli Bagarag's voyage grows wilder. The lily of the enchanted sea gives the book its first tale.

Later tales tell of Noorna bin Noorka, the genie Karaz, and the princess of Oolb, with the wiles of Rabesqurat and the palace of Aklis. The sons of Aklis and the sword of Aklis complete the book. Meredith's nested fantasies carry Shibli closer to the blade that must shave Shagpat, through marvels told in ornate prose.
44035-systematic-theology-volume-1-of-3:
Systematic Theology, in its first part of three, is a store book of church lore. It was made for students of the priest craft. Its hand was Strong, head of a great school of the faith. He held the chair of the lore of the book there. This form is made new and large.

It came out from a press of his sect in the first years of the last age. Its towns of print span America and Canada. Its theme, told on its title page, is the lore of God. Three quotes stand at its head. A sage of Rome tells that the eye sees just what it brings the power to see. Two lines from the Psalms join it, on eyes oped to the law.
44061-crossed-trails-in-mexico-mexican-m:
Helen Randolph wrote Crossed Trails in Mexico, issued by A L Burt Company in New York and Chicago in nineteen thirty six. The book is the third in the Mexican Mystery Stories for Girls. Earlier books are The Mystery of Carlitos and The Secret of Casa Grande. Jo Ann, Peggy, and Florence are the chief girls. Twenty one chapters carry the hunt.

Chapter one opens on a Texas road, where a sign sets the speed limit at eighty miles. The girls old car, Jitters, can scarce make forty or fifty miles. Florence, who has lived long in Mexico, drives slow and sure. Later chapters promise a hitch hiker, a hidden car, and a mine shaft plunge in the dark. A pottery woman gives a warning, and a secret hides in an olla pot. Girls of the age got travel, risk, and sleuth work in Mexico.
4408-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volum:
George Meredith's third volume of The Ordeal of Richard Feverel carries Richard's story into crisis. Its contents list a summons to town to hear a sermon, the approaches of fever, a crisis in the apple-disease, and the spring primrose and the autumnal. Later chapters record the hero taking a step, his rapid development, and an intercession for the heroine.

The volume opens with Berry, the baronet's man, arriving post-haste from town with orders to conduct Richard thither, and Richard refusing to go. Meredith follows the clash between father and son to its painful point. Readers of the first volumes will find the system's costs now fully counted, in a novel of growing tragic force.
4415-sandra-belloni-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni opens with Wilfrid leading a town life and visiting Stornley. He is not in love with Lady Charlotte Chillingworth, Meredith notes, but he is in harness to her. In love, one has some idea where one would go, while in harness one is pulled along with no say in where the road ends.

The book's chapters promise the return of the sentimentalist into bondage, life at Brookfield, and a walk by Wilming Weir. The return of Mr. Pericles, the pitfall of sentiment, and Wilfrid diplomatizing follow, with Emilia making a move and a farce within a farce. Emilia's singing career and Wilfrid's wavering heart drive the comedy.
4423-rhoda-fleming-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Rhoda Fleming opens with a bet that Mrs. Boulby's ears had not misheard. Robert would have fared badly that day without Mrs. Lovell's winning wager, Meredith notes. What seemed heroism to Warbeach appears in a different light, and the novel's ironies multiply.

The book's chapters glimpse what poor villainies the story contains, follow Edward taking his course, and introduce Major Percy Waring. Warbeach village church, a fearful temptation upon Anthony Hackbut, and his meeting with Dahlia follow. A study of a fool in trouble and Edward's letter close the book, as Rhoda's world darkens.
44252-richelieu-a-tale-of-france-v-1-3:
Richelieu, A Tale of France, volume one of three, is a historical novel printed in London in eighteen twenty nine. Colburn published it, and its author signs no name to the title page. An epigraph from Shakespeare warns of the cardinal's malice and his power. A dedication hides its great man's name until the book's fate is known.

The preface plays a teasing game with the reader about the tale's source. The author claims to have come by a bundle of manuscript notes honestly. Their small crooked hand was hard to read, with strange shaped letters throughout. Yet the tale held him in his chair until he had read it through. Only later did he learn, he says, that every word of it was true. The reader is asked to take that claim on the novelist's bare word.
44253-richelieu-a-tale-of-france-v-2-3:
A tale of France in the days of Cardinal Richelieu fills three books. Volume two came out in London in 1829. A Shakespeare line on the cardinal's spite heads the book. Claude de Blenau is the hero whose spurs ring in part one. He leaves the Palais Cardinal with a light heart here.

Hope lifts him as high as fear once sank him low. That swing of mood is the part's own sly theme. Out of the pan and into the fire is its motto. Court plots, swords, and love press him at each turn. The great cardinal's long arm lies over all the land. Past tale fans get pomp and peril in French dress.
44264-the-eve-of-all-hallows-or-adelaide:
Hartstonge wrote a romance in three volumes, and Whittaker of London published the last of them in 1825. The third volume opens in the wake of a fierce attack by banditti. Those men, drawn from many nations and led by a Spaniard, have been seized in Soignies wood. The tale then turns back to the mansion of Tyrconnel, where all is distress.

A wounded man lies in pain and fever, and two surgeons are called in haste. One is Leach, an English doctor long settled at Brussels. The other is Bourreau, a French surgeon of that city. Their meeting with the house doctor, Sir Patricius Placebo, turns into a comic scene of mixed tongues. The Frenchman holds that ten sword wounds are safer than one gunshot. The talk runs in French and broken English, with snuff passed round. The volume joins romance to stage humor of its day.
4429-evan-harrington-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Evan Harrington opens with the countess describing the field of action. Meredith pauses to clear up a point: readers may think the Comic Muse strains nature in making the countess rush open-eyed into danger. She has seen her brother pointed out as the tailor-fellow, yet she neither casts him off nor flies.

The book's chapters follow a capture, a small skirmish between Rose and Evan, and Evan writing himself tailor, then calling himself gentleman. The countess's campaign for rank meets Evan's honest love for Rose. This volume sharpens the novel's central joke: birth against breeding, and truth against show.
4437-vittoria-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Vittoria opens at the maestro's door, off the Borgo della Stella, where Carlo Ammiani conducts Vittoria to Rocco Ricci. They talk little on the way, and she asks him abruptly whether he is a good swordsman. He answers with the skill of perfect intimacy with the weapon, and she notes his father was a general.

The book's chapters follow Ammiani through the midnight, Countess Ammiani, and the Piazza d'Armi. The night of the fifteenth and the prima donna close the book. Vittoria's singing and the conspiracy draw together, as the revolution's night approaches and her voice becomes its signal.
44391-the-arts-and-crafts-of-older-spain:
Arts and Crafts of Older Spain, volume one of three, is an art survey by Leonard Williams. Williams was a corresponding member of the Royal Spanish academy circle in his field. The World of Art Series carried the three volume study of Spanish craft. A frontispiece shows the great iron reja of the choir in Seville Cathedral.

Goldsmith work, ironwork, and church treasure of old Spain fill such a survey. Williams writes for travellers and collectors who met Spanish art past its golden age. Project Gutenberg holds the companion volumes two and three of the same work. Students of decorative art gain a guided tour of Spain workshops and shrines.
4446-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book Three of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens at a forest inn. Bowls of hot coffee and milk refresh Harry and Temple after a meal. White rolls to dip in them complete the fare. They talk like interchanging puffs of smoke, and the road soon brings a beautiful little lady accosting them in the forest.

The book's chapters promise the statue on the promontory. They promise the moment when Harry's father breathes, moves, and speaks. A delightful evening, a morning vision, and the return homeward follow. News of a fresh conquest of his father's, and a promenade in Bath, close the book. Harry's adventurer father steps fully into the story here.
44493-history-of-civilization-in-england:
Henry Thomas Buckle wrote a history of civilization in England, here Volume One. The Rose-Belford Publishing Company issued the new form at Toronto in 1878. A full analytical contents runs for pages at the front. Buckle argues that human acts obey laws as fixed as those of nature.

Crime, suicide, and marriage counts stay steady year by year, he shows. Climate, food, soil, and the face of nature shape each people's path. Ireland, Hindustan, Egypt, and Mexico serve as his great test cases. Readers gain a bold, system-building classic of Victorian thought.
44494-history-of-civilization-in-england:
Henry Thomas Buckle wrote a history of civilization in England, of which volume two appeared in a Toronto edition of 1878. An analytical table of contents opens the volume. Chapter one outlines the history of the French intellect from the mid sixteenth century to Louis the Fourteenth. Buckle argues the church held greater power in France than in England.

Hence, he says, all French life was more theological, and toleration was impossible. Scepticism appeared at the century's end, first in Montaigne rather than Rabelais, and Charron carried it on. The Edict of Nantes marked toleration's start. Richelieu then humbled the church and backed a secular scheme of government.
44495-history-of-civilization-in-england:
Volume 3 of History of Civilization in England is the last part of that work by Henry Thomas Buckle. This new edition came out at Toronto in 1878 from the Rose-Belfort Publishing Company, in three volumes. An analytical table of contents sets out its plan. The first chapter treats the state of Scotland to the end of the fourteenth century.

The table states the line of the argument. Scotland and Spain are most unlike in loyalty, it says, but most alike in superstition. The Scots join free views in politics with narrow views in religion. That is the largest and most weighty fact in their history, the table holds. The rest of the volume is spent in search of its causes. The sway of the land itself stands first among them, then the invasions of Romans, Irish, Norsemen, and English in turn.
44522-jack-sheppard-a-romance-vol-2-of-3:
W Harrison Ainsworth wrote Jack Sheppard, a romance in three volumes dated eighteen thirty-nine, and this is volume two. The hero is the famed housebreaker Jack Sheppard. Pictures show his theft in Willesden Church and his escapes from cages and prisons.

Chapter thirteen opens in the house of Mr Wood, a worthy carpenter. Two boys have vanished, and the household is in deep distress. Winifred flies to the door at a soft knock, sure her Thames has come. Her father doubts it, since Jack slips in by back door or shop window. Crime, daring, and doom drive the tale toward Newgate.
44523-jack-sheppard-a-romance-vol-3-of-3:
Jack Sheppard, volume three, closes the romance by Harrison Ainsworth, first printed in 1839. The tale follows the famed thief Jack Sheppard and his foe Jonathan Wild, the thief taker. The pictures listed for this volume show escapes from Newgate and Wild seizing Jack at his mother's grave.

The text opens at Dollis Hill, where Winifred watches over a sleeping woman worn thin by grief and fear. Her stillness looks like death itself, broken only by the faint stir of her breast. From such dark rooms the tale moves to its last scenes: the irons knocked off in Newgate, and the grim procession to Tyburn.
4455-beauchamp-s-career-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career opens with Lord Palmet and certain electors, then a day at Itchincope and the question of examining the Whigs. A fine blow struck by Mr. Everard Romfrey follows, with the drive into Bevisham, Tourdestelle, and Beauchamp's holiday. The adventure of canvassing begins.

Nevil's radical candidacy meets the realities of an English borough: electors, landlords, newspapers, and family pressure. Meredith treats the election as comedy and as moral test. This volume shows Beauchamp learning that principle must survive contact with voters, rivals, and his own temper.
44583-a-noble-queen-a-romance-of-indian-:
A Noble Queen, volume two of three, is a romance of Indian history by Meadows Taylor. Kegan Paul published this volume in London in eighteen seventy eight. Taylor had written Seeta and Tara, tales of India, before this longer work. An epigraph from Antony and Cleopatra calls its queen mightily betrayed by fate.

The contents finish book two and run through the whole of book three. Friends in council and a night council open the stretch at a durbar's close. Troops file out in glittering array as the sun breaks through the clouds. Abbas Khan rides home wounded, his name cleared of cowardice by the ordeal. Chapters ahead hold a rapid march, a surprise, and a daring attack. A governor's breakfast cooked by Zuffoora Bee gives the tale a lighter turn.
4463-the-tragic-comedians-a-study-in-a-w:
Book Three of George Meredith's Tragic Comedians opens in a garden, where the heroine runs to the shade of the walls to read alone. Her own letter to the baroness crashes back sentence upon sentence, in retort, with the combative instinct of a beast. Twice she reads the lines with that defensive accompaniment, before they lay octopus limbs on her.

The baroness coldly states she has come to arrange matters, an answer that strikes chill as a glacier cave to a letter of fervid respect and supplication. This volume carries Lassalle's love story toward its fatal turn, as families, honor, and pride close in. Meredith's irony keeps the tragedy human, never merely grand.
4467-diana-of-the-crossways-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways opens with the authoress, as Diana turns her gifts to writing. A drive in sunlight and a drive in moonlight follow, with Diana's night-watch in the chamber of death. The young minister of state appears, and between Diana and Dacier the wind blows east over bleak land.

A visit from one of the world's good women follows, with a soul prepared for desperation, and once more the crossways and a change of turnings. A disappointed lover receives a multitude of lessons. This volume shows Diana at work and in danger, as authorship, politics, and love pull her toward scandal.
4473-one-of-our-conquerors-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's One of Our Conquerors opens on nature and circumstance, and the dissension between them, with a satirist's malignity toward his country. The great assembly at Lakeland follows, with Dartrey Fenellan and the intrusion of Jarniman. A lapdog named Tasso shows how minor causes produce momentous effects.

Nesta's engagement closes the book, as Victor Radnor's daughter steps toward marriage and independence. The conqueror's household, built on love outside the law, faces the world's judgment through his child. This volume mixes high comedy with the novel's moral pressure, as nature, society, and satire contend.
44789-a-noble-queen-a-romance-of-indian-:
A Noble Queen, a romance of Indian history by Meadows Taylor, reaches volume three in the 1878 edition. Kegan Paul published the three volume set at London in that year. A line from Antony and Cleopatra on a queen betrayed stands as its motto. Contents of this volume open with book four of the tale.

The king entry, pardon, trial, and freedom lead the chapters of that book. Proceedings at Goa and a chapter on the Inquisition deepen the Indian court plot. A death, a marriage, and a departure close the fourth book of the romance. Book five brings a siege, an assault, and a bishop embassy in its train. A second siege, a last tragedy, and a conclusion end the tale, with a glossary after.
4479-lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta opens in a punctual household, where Mrs. Lawrence reports a cavalry messenger riding up the street. Weyburn directs a boy to ring the bell, and Lord Ormont goes to meet the day's business. The domestic opening hides the novel's military and marital maneuvers.

The book's chapters promise more of Cuper's boys, war at Olmer, and old lovers meeting new friends. A secret fished without angling follows, with two roads to Steignton. Ormont's past as a soldier and Aminta's present as his wife draw together, as brother, sister, and society press their claims.
4485-the-amazing-marriage-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Amazing Marriage opens with studies in fog, gout, an old seaman, a lovely serpent, and the moral effects of a borrowed shirt. Further glimpses of the wondrous mechanism of the younger man follow, with a right-minded great lady and Dame Gossip in her vein. A kidnapping with no great harm follows.

The philosopher man of action appears, with fencing, a descent into a steamer's engine room, and concessions to Mistress Gossip. Fleetwood's marriage to Carinthia, amazing in its mismatch, proceeds through comedy and crisis. This middle volume keeps Meredith's gossips busy, and his hero's pride under steady pressure.
44996-rank-and-talent-a-novel-vol-2-of-3:
Rank and Talent, volume two, is the middle volume of an anonymous novel published by Henry Colburn in London in 1829. The title page credits only the author of Truckleborough-Hall. The epigraphs, from Shakespeare and Marston, set the theme: rank newly made, and envy wrestling great men's doings into malice.

The volume opens on the London season. Equipages roll in, saloons light up, and cards of invitation shower on old John Martindale, because gossip has discovered him a daughter and made her a sensation. All the world talks of Signora Rivolta as the finest woman living and Clara as a jewel of beauty. Martindale, who read none of the paragraphs, calls his congratulators simpletons. The novel is Regency society satire, built on the gap between reputation and fact.
45283-systematic-theology-volume-3-of-3:
Systematic Theology, volume three, is the closing volume of Augustus Hopkins Strong's compendium for theological students, in the revised edition published at Philadelphia in 1909. Strong was president of Rochester Theological Seminary. This volume is given to the doctrine of salvation, and after it the doctrine of the church.

The contents lay out the Baptist system in its full order. Redemption is applied through election and calling, begun in union with Christ, regeneration, conversion and justification, and continued in sanctification and perseverance. Each head is handled by definition, scripture proof, and answers to false views and objections. The church section then defines the church as set up by God but a free society, proves its government democratic, and fixes its officers at two: pastor and deacon.
4536-sylvia-s-lovers-volume-3:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Sylvia's Lovers closes in this third volume, which runs from chapter thirty to chapter forty-five. Philip Hepburn, once poor and striving, now seems prosperous, with a flourishing business and money beyond his modest wants. Yet the chapter titles warn that ease will not last: happy days give way to evil omens, a rescue from the waves, an apparition, and a reckless recruit.

Later chapters bring mysterious tidings, bereavement, a recognition, confidences, an unexpected messenger, and a closing turn described as saved and lost. Readers who have followed Sylvia, Philip, and their rivals through the first two volumes will find the threads drawn together here. New readers should start earlier, since this volume assumes the loves, lies, and losses already in play.
45818-the-house-on-the-moor-v-3-3:
Mrs Oliphant, the unnamed author of Margaret Maitland and Adam Graeme, wrote this three-volume novel. Hurst and Blackett printed The House on the Moor at London in 1861. This third volume brings the tale toward its close.

Susan opens the volume on the road to Tillington at dawn. Six miles of lone road, a bundle in hand, have tired the girl of nineteen. Shame and anger gave her strength at first; fear and want now weigh her down. Peggy's stern words ring in her ears as she walks. The moor house of the title waits ahead, with the fate of a cast-off girl in the balance, in the grave Scots manner of its author.
45880-a-secret-inheritance-volume-1-of-3:
A Secret Inheritance, volume one of three, is a novel by Farjeon, issued at London in 1887. Farjeon had written Great Porter Square and other tales named on the title page. The first volume is styled the record of Gabriel Carew, its narrator and hero. Its first chapter opens on his earliest clear memories. They are of a mean and common home in London, he says.

There he lived with his parents and a servant named Fortress. She was a young woman of twenty four or five, he recalls. Yet her manners were as sedate as those of a matron who disliked frivolity and tittle tattle. She did her duties quietly and in silence, and seldom spoke unless first addressed. She took no trouble to make herself agreeable to the boy, or to win his love. This was entirely to his liking, he says, being of a retired habit himself.
45881-a-secret-inheritance-volume-2-of-3:
A Secret Inheritance, volume two of three, is a novel by B L Farjeon, printed at London in 1887. Farjeon also wrote Great Porter Square and The House of White Shadows. This volume continues the record of Gabriel Carew. Chapter fourteen opens with his travels: I travelled for many months alone.

He made acquaintances which never ripened into friendships. Seldom did twenty-four hours pass without his thoughts wandering to Silvain. Thinking it not unlikely that one or both of the twin brothers had returned to their home in Germany, he wrote several letters there without receiving an answer. The silence increased rather than diminished his interest in the man he loved as a brother. Family circumstances left him free to go wherever his inclination led. But he had no clue to guide him in search of his friend.
45882-a-secret-inheritance-volume-3-of-3:
A Secret Inheritance, volume three of three, is the closing volume of a novel by B L Farjeon. It was published in London in eighteen eighty seven by Ward and Downey. Farjeon's other tales, including Great Porter Square, are listed on the title page. The secret of the inheritance is revealed in this volume, its own part title states.

That reveal is told in a series of letters from Abraham Sandival in England to a friend in California. The letters concern Gabriel Carew, to whom the secret was passed. A novel that ends by letters lets the truth arrive voice by voice. Readers of the first two volumes get the payoff the whole plot has withheld here.
46280-james-s-account-of-s-h-long-s-expe:
Edwin James's Account of S H Long's Expedition of 1819-1820 stands here in its third part. Reuben Gold Thwaites edited the reprint for his Early Western Travels series. The Arthur H Clark Company published it at Cleveland in 1905, as volume sixteen of the set. The original page and chapter numbers are kept in braces. The first chapter here takes an excursion to the summit of the Peak. Mineral springs and an encampment on the Arkansa follow.

A detachment ascends the Arkansa to the mountains, past Bell's Springs. A grizzly bear livens the descent. Natural mounds and preparations to divide the party come next. The sandstones of the high plains south of the river get their notes. The fourth chapter records sufferings from stormy weather and want of provisions. An inscribed rock and signs of settlements close it.
46492-the-death-of-the-gods-christ-and-a:
Dmitri Merejkowski wrote The Death of the Gods, first part of his Christ and Antichrist trilogy. Herbert Trench turned the book into English for G P Putnam’s Sons. The firm issued it in New York and London in nineteen hundred one. A tale of Leonardo and one of Peter the Great complete the set.

One master thought runs through all Merejkowski’s work, the front note says. Flesh and soul, pagan and Christian, war in each human breast. God made man and man made god pull in two ways at once. Full manhood joins both cults in fair balance, he holds. Julian the Apostate fills this first great tale of the clash. That fourth century emperor strove to wake the old gods. Constantine had set Christ’s faith on the throne before him. Europe was born of that vast fight, the novelist claims.
46846-mysteries-of-police-and-crime-vol-:
Mysteries of Police and Crime is a study of crime and its chase by Arthur Griffiths. The author once held a post as a crown jail inspector in Britain. Past works by his hand treat two famed jails of London in depth. The hosted text holds the first of three volumes of the work.

A print shows a watch house and its men from a full age past. The first part scans crime kinds, from slayings to thefts, in broad view. Small clues, hand marks, and body counts earn praise as the new craft. Press aid in famed cases is cited to show how the hunt has grown. The work stands as a chief guide to the sleuth age in print.
46858-george-crabbe-poems-volume-1-of-3:
Poems by George Crabbe, the first of three volumes, gathers the verse of a poet who lived from 1754 to 1832. The Cambridge edition of 1905 was edited by a master of Peterhouse, whose note sets out the plan. Poems are arranged in the order of their first publication, as far as that can be known.

One early poem, called Midnight, is placed at a guessed date among the juvenile poems of 1772 to 1780. Poems never printed before are held back in the set. They will follow the published poems in the order of their making, so far as that can be traced. The editor's care in dating gives readers a life in verse, step by step. This first volume opens that long span of Crabbe's writing.
47086-cradock-nowell-a-tale-of-the-new-f:
Cradock Nowell is a tale of the New Forest by Richard Doddridge Blackmore, who also wrote Clara Vaughan. The novel came out in London in 1866 in three volumes. The text here is volume three, the last of the set.

The volume opens on Christmas morning in a forest parish church. Amy and Eoa have decked the church with wreaths and garlands of green. The flock comes in amazed, and old Parson John climbs to the pulpit. Word is spreading that he must soon leave the parish he loves. The scene sets a warm tone of love and loss. Blackmore fills the forest scenes with close, loving detail of woods and folk.
4727-john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-volume:
Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr., closes his memoir of John Lothrop Motley in this third volume, opening in 1874, when Motley was sixty. Chapter twenty-two takes up the Life of John of Barneveld, with criticisms and Groen van Prinsterer. The full title of Motley's next and last work, Holmes notes, is The Life and Death of John of Barneveld, Advocate of Holland.

This volume therefore treats Motley as historian at the height of his powers, defending and explaining a Dutch statesman of an earlier age. It follows his later years, his writing, and his standing among critics, after the diplomatic and historical work of earlier volumes. Readers should start with volumes one and two, since this volume assumes Motley's life, friendships, and quarrels already known, and it brings his story to its close.
47303-historical-parallels-vol-2-of-3:
Historical Parallels, volume two of three, is a history reader issued at London in 1846. Its plan is in its title: great deeds of the past are set side by side, age against age, so that each lights the other. The contents of this volume open with Marathon matched against the battle of Tours, a Spanish epic poem, and the siege of Vienna by the Turks in 1683.

Swiss battles for freedom stand in the same chapter. Thermopylae is then paired with a Swiss last stand near Basle, the siege of Malta in 1565, and a Greek sacred band destroyed in a war of freedom. Salamis is matched with the siege of Leyden and the Spanish Armada. Later chapters follow the after lives of the Greek captains. The set was made for the improving reading of its century.
47304-historical-parallels-vol-3-of-3:
Historical Parallels, volume three of three, was published in London in eighteen forty-six by Charles Knight and Company. The work sets events from different ages side by side so each explains the other, and this final volume also carries the index for the set.

Its chapters compare great sieges from Plataea, Tyre, and Syracuse to Ostend, Magdeburg, and Zaragoza, tracing what gunpowder changed. Other chapters pair the Corcyrean sedition with the civil wars of Rome and the September massacres of seventeen ninety-two, and the Athenian Cleon with Titus Oates of the Popish Plot. The Sicilian expedition is matched against later disastrous retreats, including Ney's in Russia. The parallels teach history by rhyme rather than by chronology.
47316-new-witnesses-for-god-volume-2-of-:
New Witnesses for God, volume two, is a defence of the Book of Mormon by Roberts, printed at Salt Lake City in 1909 by the Deseret News. The set runs to three volumes, and Roberts also wrote The Gospel and Outlines of Ecclesiastical History. His preface traces the work back twenty-two years, to his days as a missionary editor in England.

Roberts had first planned this treatise on the Book of Mormon as the opening volume, then set it aside to write first on Joseph Smith as a witness. The material served in 1903 to 1905 as manuals for senior classes of the Young Men's Mutual Improvement Associations. He holds that the whole work of God in the last days may be said to stand or fall with the book.
47338-kate-vernon-a-tale-vol-1-of-3:
Kate Vernon, a tale in three volumes, of which this is the first, was published by Thomas Cautley Newby of London in 1854. The narrator is an officer of a regiment of Light Dragoons. The Horse Guards, he complains, banished the regiment at the start of the grouse season to a smoky town in the west of England, which he calls Carrington.

The autumn of the tale is gloomy: commerce and crops look down, and starving mechanics raise riots. The rich manufacturers give the officers enormous dinners, and their daughters are pretty enough. Yet talk fails, since the girls hold sporting a loss of time and miss every allusion. The first chapter is headed The Ball. The narrator's dry regimental humour carries the social war of the garrison town.
47433-babylon-volume-3:
Babylon is a novel in three volumes by Grant Allen, writing as Cecil Power. The hosted text is volume three, issued at London in eighteen eighty five with twelve pictures by P Macnab. Allen is billed as author of Philistia and Strange Stories. The volume opens deep in the tale, at chapter twenty nine.

That chapter gives a view of Rome through the eyes of Hiram Winthrop. The modern city crouches, in his telling, within its huge old walls. A broad skirt of empty hillocks and stunted vineyards rings the shrunken town. Along a dull muddy river the real city huddles under the ruins of a nobler age. Dingy tile roofed houses crowd into a maze of alleys. Beggars fill the streets in his harsh sketch.
47529-oliver-twist-vol-1-of-3:
