Volume one of Oliver Twist, in a second edition of eighteen thirty nine from Richard Bentley of London, opens Charles Dickens's second novel. Dickens, still signing himself Boz after the Pickwick Papers, begins in a workhouse in an unnamed town. A pauper child is born to a dying mother there, and the parish must decide his fate.

The first chapter is mostly irony about that birth. He gives us a parish surgeon who attends by contract, an old woman misty with beer, and a baby who nearly fails to breathe. Dickens adds that workhouse birth was, in this one case, the best thing that could have happened to Oliver. The three volume format was the standard dress for a new novel of the day. The volume starts the foundling toward London, Fagin's gang of boy thieves, and the mystery of his birth.
47530-oliver-twist-vol-2-of-3:
Oliver Twist, by Charles Dickens, appears here in volume two of the second edition of 1839. Richard Bentley published the three volume set at London in that year. Dickens is named on the title page as author of The Pickwick Papers. A plate of the burglary, dated January 1838, fronts the volume in this copy.

Chapter twenty opens the portion with Oliver delivered over to William Sikes. Oliver wakes to find new shoes with strong thick soles at his bedside. Hope of release rises in him at that kind gift at first. Breakfast alone with Fagin kills that hope in short order. He learns he is to be taken that night to the house of Bill Sikes. The criminal world closes round the boy again in this famed middle volume.
47531-oliver-twist-vol-3-of-3:
Oliver Twist, volume three, closes Charles Dickens's tale of the workhouse boy, in a second edition printed at London in 1839. Dickens was by then known as the author of The Pickwick Papers. This last volume holds chapters from the thirty-seventh on, as the plots against Oliver draw tight.

The volume opens on a dull, close summer evening of coming storm. Bumble and his wife pick their way to a low colony of ruined houses by the river, the haunt of thieves. There they meet Monks by night, in secret. The scene sets the dark tone of the end, where Oliver's birth and worth are at last brought to light.
47601-illustrations-of-exotic-entomology:
Dru Drury's Illustrations of Exotic Entomology, Volume Three, holds foreign insects. J O Westwood brought this new edition up to date. Henry G Bohn issued it at London in 1837. Six hundred fifty figures crowd the whole work. Each species gets its systematic marks here. Synonyms, indexes, and fresh matter join the plates.

Drury's own preface to the first edition fronts it. Two volumes before this won warm praise, he says. Lovers of natural history gave that welcome. This third and last volume comes late, he admits. Its text and plates were bound apart in some copies. The plates here sit beside their text. Other volumes stand as separate Gutenberg texts today. Hand-colored bugs from every shore taught Georgian collectors the world's insect wealth before cameras shrank it.
47620-at-his-gates-a-novel-vol-3-of-3:
Mrs Oliphant wrote At His Gates, a novel in three volumes. Tinsley Brothers issued Volume Three at London in 1872. Chapter One opens on a country house evening. Light and dark war wildly outside its doors. Music plays at one end of the drawing room. Some guests read, some talk, within.

Flirtations and grave talks share that room. Private yawning spreads through the party, Oliphant notes. Watches get checked in secret all evening. Some guests plead their rooms early for relief. Fancying themselves elsewhere is their sport, she says. A tall stranger sits by the fire in care. Diamond studs mark his subdued evening dress. Ned reads him as Golden at first sight. Clara listens close to that fire-side group. A final volume's slow evening gathers every thread of a country house tale toward its close.
4773-the-letters-of-horace-walpole-earl-:
The Letters of Horace Walpole, Earl of Orford, including letters first published from original manuscripts, runs to four volumes, and this third volume covers 1759 to 1769. Its 1759 contents open with a letter to Montagu on November 17, on Temple's resignation of the privy seal and Lady Carlisle's marriage with Musgrave. A letter to Pitt on November 19 congratulates him on his administration's lustre.

A letter to Sir Horace Mann on November 30 reports Hawke's victory over Conflans and Kinnoul's mission to Portugal. A December 13 letter to Mann has Walpole regretting his ignorance of mathematics and common figures, and reporting Prince Henry's victory. December 23 brings a letter to Montagu on tumults in Ireland and a story of Lyttelton and Shelley, and one to Zouch on Clarendon and Lucan. The year 1760 opens with a visit to Emily and commotions in Ireland. Readers get Walpole's letters from a decade of war and politics.
47772-mirk-abbey-volume-2-of-3:
James Payne opens the second volume of a three-volume novel in mid-conversation at a great house. The London edition dates to 1866. Payne had written Lost Sir Massingberd before it.

Lady Lisgard asks her maid Mary for a serious talk tonight. Let them not be mistress and maid, she says, but only friends. Mary answers with a humility that hides resolve. She knows the question coming, and her answer is already no. The two have known each other more than half their lives without a single quarrel. Mary was not fifteen when she came, as willing and kind a girl as the sun ever shone upon. She still dreams of the storm that cast a sweet innocent creature at their very door by the raging sea. Payne builds his secret from that night.
47773-mirk-abbey-volume-3-of-3:
Mirk Abbey, in its third part of three, is a novel by Payne, author of past tales of a lost knight and of a house on a cliff. It came out at London in the mid eighteen sixties. Its first part here is named for a lady of France.

On the fourth day past the come of her Paris note, the text says, my Lady had to leave the abbey for town. Her work there bore on the affairs of a young man of the house. She could not let his big brother bear the whole weight of the new costs. Her trip was to the house law man. She went lone, save for one maid at her side.
4799-the-complete-poetical-works-of-perc:
The Complete Poetical Works of Percy Bysshe Shelley, volume three, is the Oxford edition of 1914, edited by Thomas Hutchinson. It includes materials never before printed, and this volume gathers Shelley's translations. Its contents open with a Hymn to Mercury, translated from Homer, followed by Homer's hymns to Castor and Pollux, the Moon, the Sun, the Earth, Minerva, and Venus.

The Cyclops, a satyric drama from Euripides, follows, with epigrams from Plato, including To Stella, Kissing Helena, and Circumstance. A fragment of the elegy on the death of Adonis, from the Greek of Bion, appears. A fragment of the elegy on the death of Bion, and Pan, Echo, and the Satyr, come from Moschus. Pieces from Vergil's tenth eclogue and fourth georgic, a sonnet from Dante, and the first canzone of the Convito close the contents. Readers get Shelley as translator of Greek, Latin, and Italian verse.
47997-a-life-for-a-life-volume-1-of-3:
A Life for a Life is a novel by Dinah Maria Craik, who also wrote John Halifax, Gentleman. Volume one of three came out in London in 1859. Two texts from the Bible stand at the front and set the theme of sin and pardon.

The story opens as a journal kept by a woman at Rockmount. She writes with heat about the army camp that has spoiled her quiet moor. Her pages look back to the war in the East two years before. Grief for dead heroes sits close beside her anger at the red coats near her home. Her journal voice is sharp, funny and sad by turns, and it holds the reader close.
48163-the-pennycomequicks-volume-3-of-3:
The Pennycomequicks, in its third part of three, is a novel by Gould, author of famed tales of the moors and coasts. All rights were kept for this form, put out at London in the late eighteen eighties. Its parts here run from the mid tale to its end.

A lone house opens this part. Then come a start, a fall from a post, and a trip on a lake. A great inn, two women, and two men fill the next run. One small cloth, a glove thrown down, a glove cast, and a glove took up play out the code of pride. High Alps, a Greek huntress name, a famed white flower, and a trap lead to the end.
48197-hester-a-story-of-contemporary-lif:
Hester, a story of contemporary life by Oliphant, fills three volumes, the first printed in London in 1883 by Macmillan. A motto from Charles Lamb praises a girl trained in Nature's school, with a waking eye and a prying mind. Sixteen chapters in this volume run from Vernon's and Miss Catherine through first meetings, recollections, and a lover, to walks and talks.

Chapter one presents the banking house of the Vernons. Through all the Home Counties it was held second only to the Bank of England in stability and strength. Business men allowed as much, at least. Its own clients, the shopkeepers of Redborough and the farmers round about, rated it higher still. Oliphant builds her tale on that bank: family pride, money, and a young heroine growing up in its shadow.
48471-foxglove-manor-a-novel-volume-1-of:
Foxglove Manor, a novel by Robert Buchanan, was published at London in 1884 in three volumes. Chatto and Windus issued volume one of the set from Piccadilly. A prefatory note calls the work an attempt at a tragedy in fiction. That tragedy, however, is without a tragic ending, the author promises there.

The note warns that the tale is no attack on the English priesthood in general. In the Reverend Charles Santley he has pictured a type of man that exists, he says. Such men are uncommon, and most clergy are sane and healthy in his account. Chapter one opens at Saint Cuthbert church as the choir sings the closing hymn. Old Gabriel Ware, sexton and doorkeeper, limps to the porch at sermon time.
48473-foxglove-manor-a-novel-volume-3-of:
Foxglove Manor is a novel by Robert Buchanan, printed at London in 1884 in three volumes. The portion here opens at chapter twenty-eight, a monkish tale taken from a note-book. The writer sits at home on a Sunday in September while his wife Ellen goes to church, and the bells ring in the distance.

Writing in his diary, he works through a discovery he has made about his wife. For all her purity and high sense of honour, he judges, she is jealous of the clergyman she admires. He tells how he broke his news to her at breakfast, over an eggshell, and kept back the part of the tale that touched her name.
48482-a-life-for-a-life-volume-2-of-3:
A Life for a Life, volume two, continues Dinah Maria Craik's novel in the hero's own hand. Hurst and Blackett published the three volumes in London in 1859. Craik had earlier written John Halifax, Gentleman. Two verses on repentance head the volume. The wicked man who turns from his sin shall save his soul.

The narrator is Max Urquhart. He had ended his record vowing to write no more. Now he breaks that vow and renounces resolutions altogether. He means to set down events that happened almost without his will. He throws aside his feigned correspondent at last. He knows for whom he writes, though she may never read a line. A dying officer's packet of unsent letters deepens the theme.
48483-a-life-for-a-life-volume-3-of-3:
Volume three of A Life for a Life, a novel by Dinah Maria Craik, was issued at London by Hurst and Blackett in 1859. Craik was the author of John Halifax, Gentleman, as the title page notes. The work ran to three volumes in the standard form. This last volume opens a chapter called Her Story, in a woman’s own voice.

The narrator takes up her journal again after many weeks away. She sits at the open window in her old attitude, her lips on a ring. Max gave her that ring, and now Max and she are not to be married. Great and miserable changes have befallen them both, she writes. Penelope’s marriage enters the tangle of the plot. The volume drives a tale of love, guilt, and sacrifice to its close.
49107-a-history-of-matrimonial-instituti:
George Elliott Howard, professorial lecturer at the University of Chicago, wrote this history of matrimonial institutions chiefly in England and the United States. The university press with Callaghan and Company published it at Chicago in 1904, and Fisher Unwin in London. He dedicates it to his wife Alice Frost Howard. This is the first of three volumes.

Part one analyses the literature and theories of primitive marriage. It covers the patriarchal theory, answered by Spencer and McLennan, and Bachofen's theory of the horde and mother-right. Morgan's and McLennan's constructive theories, and the original pairing family, follow. A chapter traces the rise of the marriage contract through wife-capture and wife-purchase to free marriage, and another the early history of divorce. Part two opens England's story, where old English wife-purchase yields to free marriage and the church accepts the lay contract.
4911-wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-cons:
John Richardson's Wacousta continues in this third volume aboard a schooner where superstitious mariners fear their silent steersman. The crew, worn by anxiety, whispers that the steersman is a spirit sent to warn them of evil, and Fuller's repeated warnings through a sleepless night deepen their dread.

The volume carries the Pontiac conspiracy tale toward its close, with frontier sieges, disguised enemies, and personal revenge still driving the plot. Richardson keeps the lake and fort country vivid throughout. Readers who followed the first volumes get the payoff here: mystery resolved through action rather than explanation alone.
49247-a-history-of-matrimonial-instituti:
George Elliott Howard, a lecturer at the University of Chicago, wrote this history of marriage in three volumes. The Chicago press issued volume two in 1904. Its ground is matrimonial institutions in England and the United States.

Howard gives the set to his wife, Alice Frost Howard, in a plain dedication. The first volume weighed the tales and theories of primitive marriage and the family. This second walks the law's long road: church courts, common law, and the American states. Howard wrote as a trained historian of institutions, with notes thick as text. Marriage here is no private tale but a public machine, built by law and custom across a thousand years. Scholars still cite the set.
49276-a-history-of-matrimonial-instituti:
A History of Matrimonial Institutions, volume three, was written by George Elliott Howard. The University of Chicago Press issued the work in 1904. Callaghan shared the Chicago imprint, and Fisher Unwin took London. Howard lectured at the University of Chicago. He gives the book to his wife, Alice Frost Howard, for her aid. The full work treats marriage chiefly in England and the United States. An opening part weighs the literature and the theories of primitive marriage. Patriarchal theory, mother-right, and the pairing family each get a chapter.

Wife-capture, wife-purchase, and the rise of the marriage contract follow. Early divorce is traced by right, form, and effect. The contents survey all three volumes in fine detail. Howard writes as a sociologist: marriage is an institution with a history, not a fixed gift of nature.
49305-princess-napraxine-volume-1-of-3:
Ouida wrote a novel in three volumes, with volume one printed at London in 1884. The book is given to two perfectly wise and happy people, her friends Pierre and Emilie de Tchihatch eff, and she calls it a story of people neither happy nor wise. Ads for new three volume novels head the front pages. Thirteen chapters make the first volume.

A blue sea, palms with their heads bound up, hedges of cactus and aloes, and thickets of high rose laurel open the scene. A long marble terrace shines in the sun over huge groups of geraniums not yet frost bitten. A low white house with green shutters and wooden balconies stands by an orange orchard and an olive wood. A princess, a coast villa, and fine folk at their games fill Ouida's rich pages.
49792-personal-sketches-of-his-own-times:
Personal Sketches of His Own Times is a memoir by Sir Jonah Barrington, an Irish admiralty judge, in three volumes. Barrington dedicates the book to Chief Justice Bushe as the pastime of a winter's evening. The contents promise family history, Irish customs and a gallery of anecdotes from the age of the Irish gentry.

The first chapter describes the family mansion, its library and garden, and the state of landlord and tenant in 1760. Among its stories is Barrington's great-grandfather, Colonel John Barrington, hanged on his own gate but saved by a trooper of King James. Later chapters cover his great-aunt besieged in her castle and his own schooling. The book is valued as a witness's picture of eighteenth-century Ireland, told with a raconteur's relish.
49793-personal-sketches-of-his-own-times:
Personal Sketches of His Own Times, volume two, is a memoir by Sir Jonah Barrington, a judge of the High Court of Admiralty in Ireland. The work fills three volumes. This second edition, revised and improved, was printed in London in 1830.

Barrington dedicates the volume to Lord Stowell. His letter of dedication is a small essay on praise. The general approval of the public, he writes, gratifies any author. But the warm approval of one eminent man, whose grave judgment and deep learning give weight to his opinions, gratifies in a higher order. Stowell had suggested a third volume of sketches composed of similar materials. To have amused such a reader gave Barrington pleasure, and to have informed him touched his vanity. The sketches themselves gather the people, scenes, and stories of his Irish world.
49794-personal-sketches-of-his-own-times:
Sir Jonah Barrington closes his sketches of Irish life with volume three. Henry Colburn and Richard Bentley issued it at London in 1832. He dedicates the book to Lord Stowell.

His letter to Stowell glows with pride. The first two volumes won the public's praise. Stowell told him the sketches were read with general avidity in England. They gave, he said, much insight into the original character of the Irish. Barrington began the work to pass a long winter. Three months of leisure hours held the whole writing. The sketches mix courts, duels, elections, and country-house talk. Barrington had been a judge and a member of the Irish Parliament. His loose, funny record remains a first source for old Ireland.
49802-the-death-ship-a-strange-story-vol:
Clark Russell, a famed writer of sea tales, wrote The Death Ship, a strange story in three volumes issued in London in 1888. Ads for other new tales fill the first leaf, then the true title page names the source: papers left by Geoffrey Fenton of Poplar, a master mariner. This first volume holds twenty parts of his cruise.

Fenton sails as second mate in the Saracen, hears tales of the Death Ship from his captain, and is chased at sea. At Table Bay the talk turns back to the ghost ship, the Flying Dutchman of old lore. A wreck throws Fenton aboard her at last, and he meets Vanderdecken and a girl named Imogene Dudley on the doomed deck.
49864-traits-of-american-humour-vol-2-of:
Traits of American Humour, by native authors, here volume two of three, was edited and adapted by the author of Sam Slick. Colburn and Company in London issued the set in eighteen fifty two. The editor Sam Slick books include The Old Judge and The English in America. A preface from volume one heads this volume. It warns British readers against two great popular errors about America.

Most Europeans, the preface says, speak of America as one great country like England or France. They forget it covers more of the globe than all of them collectively. Eastern and western, northern and southern states differ widely in climate, soil, and produce, it notes. Their folk share a language and institutions but have few features in common. Yankee, a sectional nickname, is wrongly used for all Americans. Tales and sketches then show humour state by state.
49899-the-death-ship-a-strange-story-vol:
The Death Ship is a strange sea tale by W Clark Russell in three volumes. The hosted text holds the second volume of the three. Its full title claims the tale was drawn from the papers of a dead master mariner. The book came out in London in the year eighteen eighty eight.

The hero sails as guest on the ghost ship of the Flying Dutchman tale. Love talks with a girl named Imogene fill long calm parts of the cruise. A gale, a dead helm man, and a wreck boarded at sea raise the dread. The Dutch captain walks in sleep and shows hid gold to his guest. A bid on the hero life near the close lifts the stakes once more.
49975-the-death-ship-a-strange-story-vol:
Volume 3 of The Death Ship, a strange story by Clark Russell, was published in London in 1888. The tale claims to be drawn from the papers of Geoffrey Fenton of Poplar, a master mariner, and tells of a cruise in the Flying Dutchman. Russell was famed for The Wreck of the Grosvenor and other sea tales.

Twelve chapters close the story: love told again, a sail sighted, a pirate boarding, a tempest, and a leak. Imogene fears for Fenton as the death ship brings up in a bay and weather aids his scheme. At last he is alone, as the final sad heads show. Russell's rich sea prose, full of azure water and foam, carries the ghost-ship romance.
50213-encyclopedia-of-diet-a-treatise-on:
Eugene Christian's Encyclopedia of Diet, a five-volume treatise on the food question, reached its third volume with the Christian Dietetic Society at New York in 1914. The title page promises the chemistry of food and of the human body. They are joined in the act of eating so as to set digestion right and clear away the causes of stomach and bowel disorders.

Volume three opens with Lesson Twelve, on which foods go well together, with tables of food pairings that agree or clash, and the changes cooking makes in food. Lesson Thirteen sorts foods by their chief food values and weighs how well cereals and vegetables are digested. Lesson Fourteen sets out the Vieno plan of food measure against the old plan. Lesson Fifteen gives set menus meant to cure sour stomach, constipation, gastritis, and other troubles, with recipes from coddled egg to sassafras tea.
50238-stormy-voyage-sandy-steele-adventu:
Stormy Voyage is a boys sea tale by Barlow, third in a run of risks of a lad of the coast. A list at its front names that whole run: a black hoard, a risk at a west ford, fire at a red lake, and more. It came out at New York in the late age of the big cars.

Its rights were held that year by a great house of the day, with all rights kept. This is its first print. The run sends its lad and his pals to sea and to far shores in each book, in the crisp form of its age. Storm, wreck risk, and the pull of the sea drive this part of the set.
50849-princess-napraxine-volume-3-of-3:
Princess Napraxine, volume three, is the final part of a novel by Ouida. Chatto and Windus published it in London in 1884. The contents list chapters thirty four to fifty five. A short envoi closes the whole novel at the end. Chapter thirty four opens after a crisis at Amyot. Yseulte had recovered enough to travel by then. He took her to the Italian lakes for a while. That was to restore her health and distract her thoughts. With winter they returned to Paris hotels.

They made their home in a great hotel on the Boulevard Saint Germain. He hated that hotel and meant to stay briefly. The chapter heads give only numbers, no titles, in this volume. Ouida's tale of a Russian princess ends across these chapters. Society, love, and ruin are her standing materials here.
51003-george-crabbe-poems-volume-2-of-3:
Poems by George Crabbe, volume two, presents the poet's tales in a scholarly edition. Ward edited the three volumes. Cambridge University Press published them in 1906. Crabbe lived from 1754 to 1832. This volume prints the whole of the Tales. It adds the first eleven Tales of the Hall.

A preface explains the texts in detail. The poems follow the edition of 1823. That was the last edition printed in Crabbe's lifetime. Variants come from the first editions of 1812 and 1819. Manuscript readings come from the poet's son's edition. Press manuscripts and a private collection add more. The editor even lists Crabbe's faulty Shakespeare quotations among the errata. Some, he grants, may be wilful changes.
511-the-purcell-papers-volume-3:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu gathers Irish tales in this third volume of the Purcell Papers, framed as extracts from a parish priest's legacy. Jim Sulivan's adventures in the great snow open the book, with a Tyrone family history, a royalist captain's adventure, the Quare Gander, and Billy Malowney's taste of love and glory.

Le Fanu writes in rich Irish dialect, mixing humor, ghostly hints, and country talk. A memoir by Alfred Perceval Graves fronts the set. The volume preserves Le Fanu's early gift for Irish story, where a singer's luck, a wife's tongue, and a snowbound night can turn a life.
51489-church-history-volume-1-of-3:
Professor Kurtz wrote a Church History in three volumes, here in its first volume, in an authorized English rendering by the Reverend Macpherson. The work stands as the fourth item of the Foreign Biblical Library, a set of twelve volumes shaped by Robertson Nicoll and issued by Hodder and Stoughton at London. Sister volumes hold Delitzsch on the Psalms and on Isaiah, Weiss on the New Testament, Rothe's Still Hours, and sermons of Schleiermacher.

Kurtz was a leading German church historian, and his history was a standard text of its day. The translation was made from his latest revised edition, with his leave. Church histories of this school trace the faith from its first ages through councils, empires, and reformations in close order. This first volume opens that long account for English readers who could not use the German text.
51490-church-history-volume-2-of-3:
Church History volume two of three is a past of the church by Kurtz. John Macpherson turned this last changed form in to the English tongue. A Hodder and Stoughton house of London brought it out in eighteen ninety two. This is the second print of that turn in its run. Part two of the scheme heads the page list of this book.

Notes run through all three books in one count in this set form. Adds from the part two back leaves stand in the main text here. Name forms vary in the old text, so one chief form stands in marks. Speech marks and print have been made one in this clean text. Old spell forms stand as writ save where a note marks a fix.
51491-church-history-volumes-1-3:
Church History, by Professor Kurtz, is a three-volume work in the Foreign Biblical Library, published by Hodder and Stoughton of London. The library was edited by Robertson Nicoll and ran to twelve volumes at seven shillings and sixpence each. Macpherson's authorised translation follows the latest revised edition.

The set stands fourth in the library's list, after Rothe's Still Hours and Delitzsch on the Psalms. Neighbours include an introduction to the New Testament by Weiss and sermons of Schleiermacher. Delitzsch also contributes the library's commentary on Isaiah, in two volumes. In this text, a dagger mark beside a date appears to mean an approximate year of death. The transcriber warns that spelling had not been standardised, and variants are left unchanged.
51617-the-sorceress-v-1-of-3:
The Sorceress is a tale in three parts by Mrs Oliphant, of which this is the first. It came out at London in eighteen ninety-three. Oliphant was known for a famed set of tales of a small town and its church folk. The first part opens on the most keen event that had yet struck one young house.

That house is gay and young in feel, with a wife past forty and young of one and twenty and of nineteen at its head. The wife, a weak one, roams from spa to spa with her girls in train and loves the roam. She has not danced this trip, and a turn with her son brought on a flutter of the heart. The girls laugh off her talk that her dance days are done. That light tone sets the calm past the storm the tale brings.
51630-delaware-or-the-ruined-family-vol-:
Delaware, or The Ruined Family, is a tale in three books printed at Edinburgh in 1833. Book three is the part held here, from the press of Cadell in that town and Whittaker in London. The tale had set its cast in deep straits in the first two books. Its teller opens this book with a sly, frank aside.

He says the best way out for all his folk would be to end at book two. The world could then settle their fates as it liked, he jokes. But his aim is truth, and no reader could guess that truth by force of mind. So he must go on and tell what became of each of them. He asks the reader to call back the end of part four of the last book.
51635-hegel-s-lectures-on-the-history-of:
The first of three volumes of Hegel's lectures on the history of philosophy. E S Haldane translated them from the German. Kegan Paul first published the English edition in 1892. Routledge and Kegan Paul reprinted it in 1955. A translator's note explains the book's strange making. Hegel lectured on the subject nine times in all.

He first taught it at Jena in 1805 and 1806. Heidelberg courses followed, then six more at Berlin. Only the Jena course was fully written out. Later teaching relied on notes and margin additions. His pupil Michelet built the German edition from every surviving source. Students' notebooks supplied much of the text. This volume opens Hegel's grand march through Greek and later thought.
51636-hegel-s-lectures-on-the-history-of:
Hegels Lectures on the History of Philosophy holds talks by the great German thinker. Two scholars turned the talks from German into English for this set. The hosted text is the second of three volumes of the work. This set first came out in England in eighteen ninety four.

Greek thought fills the bulk of this book, led by Plato and his great pupil. Talks treat their talk craft, world views, and views of mind in turn. Stoic schools and doubt schools form the next age in the chain. Lists in the front map each talk to its theme and page. The set stands as the root text for the study of thought lore.
51816-the-sorceress-v-2-of-3:
The Sorceress is a novel by Oliphant, issued in three volumes by White of London in 1893. This text is the second volume. Oliphant had written The Chronicles of Carlingford and The Cuckoo in the Nest.

The volume opens on Bee, whose mother lies ill, in a moment of private collapse. Her fabric of happiness has crumbled like a house of cards, with an earthquake's noise. Even in the hushed sick room she hears the falling walls and flying rafters. The cause is Aubrey, who deserted her without warning or object. His letter's ink was barely dry, and her name was still upon his lips. Oliphant reflects that a great infidelity, like a great faith, is always something: it is tragic.
52136-wanda-vol-2-of-3:
Wanda, in its second volume of three, is a novel of a princess and her great house in the hills. The Princess has come home to Hohenszalras, her seat, wrapped in winter white. The scent of white lilac, and the thought of the man who gave it, pursue her. She tells herself she is as content as ever. Next morning she sees all her people and walks her schools and her stables. A doctor for the ear comes out from Paris to see her.

He soothes her: her slight deafness at times comes from cold, he says. She takes the word with triumph. In this land of rain and snow, she says, it is a wonder to keep one's five senses whole. Her man Greswold had once said deafness was a tax of age, not of climate. The Paris man knew better how to earn his fee.
5236-the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-:
Charles James Lever's Harry Lorrequer continues in this third volume, covering chapters eighteen through twenty-three. Harry takes up detachment duty in an assize town, spends a day in Dublin, passes a night at Howth. Harry journeys on toward Calais, with Fitzgerald's fear of prosecution for abduction hanging over the opening scenes.

The volume holds only this middle stretch of Harry's confessions, told in the same comic, anecdotal voice as the first. Readers following the novel in order will find assize courts, Irish towns. Cross-channel travel follows, all filtered through a young soldier's talent for getting into scrapes.
52375-blue-stocking-hall-vol-2-of-3:
Blue Stocking Hall, volume two of three, is a novel in letters printed in London in eighteen twenty seven. Colburn published it, with a motto from Love's Labour's Lost on its title page. The tale is told through letters between friends in England and abroad. Letter twelve, from Otway to General Douglas, opens this second volume.

Otway accepts a trust from the general, who longs to come home from abroad. The absentee, Otway argues, does wrong to spend his wealth away from his own people. A splendid Hampshire mansion with fine grounds is on sale just then. Its owner, Sir Reginald Barnes, has tired of the place he made princely. Otway treats with the agent Snubb to buy it in the general's name. News of the general's brothers and their fortunes fills out the letter.
52505-daughters-of-belgravia-vol-2-of-3:
Daughters of Belgravia, volume two of three, is a novel by Mrs. Alexander Fraser, printed at London in 1887. Fraser also wrote The Last Drawing-Room and A Fatal Passion. Belgravia was the rich, smart quarter of London, and the tale moves among its balls, drawing rooms, and love affairs.

The chapter heads tell of a state ball, flirtation at the Bagatelle Theatre, and nights at Caryllon House. One head quotes the line about simple faith and Norman blood. Volume two keeps the love plots and social games of volume one in play, with pride, rank, and wealth shaping each choice the young women make.
52568-arminell-a-social-romance-vol-3:
Arminell is a tale of town rank in three parts, of which this is the last. It came out at London in eighteen ninety. Its hand is named past two past tales of note. The first part of this book is named for the turn of the tide. In it a young man races by fast train into the west.

He takes no pass for the near stop, but hires a trap at the next town and walks the last half mile. He means to see his mother in haste, then show his face in the town. Past a turn he comes on an old lame man and a girl, arm in arm. That mean old man is his true father, not the lord he was raised past. A new charge falls on him, to keep that man with no hint of the bond.
52941-amadis-of-gaul-vol-3:
Amadis of Gaul, volume three, is the third book of the famed romance of chivalry. Longman and Rees of London printed this four volume English version in 1803. The title page names Vasco Lobeira as the old author of the tale. Book three opens with King Lisuarte healed knights and royal anger in court.

Angriote and his nephew, healed of their wounds, are bid quit the kingdom at their peril. Don Grumedan, Don Brian of Monjaste, and Gavarte hear their loud complaints in the scene. The king, they say, has forgotten their past services to his crown in war. Knights, courts, and giants fill the prose that Cervantes loved and mocked.
53182-the-sorceress-v-3-of-3:
Mrs Oliphant wrote a novel in three volumes, here the third and last. F V White and Company issued The Sorceress in London in 1893. Oliphant had written The Chronicles of Carlingford, as the title page notes. Chapter One of the volume opens with a young man's flight from Oxford.

Charlie Kingsward flees half mad with misery after a cruel refusal. Sweet-seeming kindness masked the deepest scorn in the woman's reply, Oliphant writes. Mockery, shame, and wasted youth whip him like the Furies' lashes. Readers gain the stormy close of a tale of love and a sorceress's sway.
53305-a-system-of-practical-medicine-by-:
William Pepper edited A System of Practical Medicine by American Authors, volume three, for Lea Brothers in 1885. Louis Starr assisted him in the work, at Philadelphia. Pepper taught the theory and practice of medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. This volume treats diseases of the respiratory, circulatory, and blood-making systems. Each disease gets its own essay by a named hand, with page marks in the contents.

Seiler writes on the throat mirror, Allen on the nasal passages, and Johnson on neuroses of the larynx. Jacobi treats croup in two forms, and Lefferts treats the cutting of the windpipe. Davis writes on the bronchi, and Geddings on bronchial and hay asthma. Later parts treat widened bronchial tubes, collapse of the lung, and congestion of the lung. The book gives ward knowledge of 1885 in one thick, sourced tome.
53356-kate-vernon-a-tale-vol-2-of-3:
Kate Vernon, a tale in three volumes, reaches its second volume here, published in London in 1854 by Newby of Welbeck Street. The volume opens under the head Clouds on the Horizon. Captain Egerton has gone, and the narrator warns that it would give a false idea of Kate's character to say his going left no blank in her quiet routine.

Kate finds, to her own surprise, how closely the captain had linked himself with the pleasures and work of the small secluded circle where chance had thrown him. She misses his ready companionship. The chapter sets a slow, inward tone for the middle volume of a Victorian tale of feeling, duty, and the stirrings of love in a narrow world.
53455-rank-and-talent-a-novel-vol-1-of-3:
Rank and Talent, a novel in three volumes, was written by the author of Truckleborough-Hall. Henry Colburn published the first volume at London in 1829. The tale opens at the summer assizes of a county town. An action rouses more than the usual sensation. Poor old Richard Smith has brought suit against Philip Martindale for assault and false imprisonment. Every carriage that could be hired was engaged to carry the curious to the trial.

Martindale was by no means popular at Brigland. The injury done to Smith was held peculiarly hard and oppressive. The common wish ran that the defendant pay heavy damages. People hoped to hear home truths from the plaintiff's counsel, to mortify his pride. A young counsel's first appearance on the circuit adds a second draw. The novel sets rank against talent in the law courts.
53668-kate-vernon-a-tale-vol-3-of-3:
Kate Vernon, volume three of three, closes a tale of the Vernon family. The hosted text opens with a publisher's list of sporting books. Harry Hieover's works on horses fill those first pages. Prices and press praise crowd the advertisements. Such lists were bound into novels of the day. The tale itself then takes up its final movement. Miss Vernon stands at the centre of the close.

In the closing scenes Colonel Vernon is taken gravely ill. Kate, pale but calm, sends for the doctor at once. She forbids the word death to be spoken near him. Her firmness under shock marks her character. Three-volume tales built to a late crisis of this kind. The last volume held the illness, the parting, or the wedding. Kate Vernon ends a story of a soldier's household. Its end turns on a daughter's strength.
53687-melmoth-the-wanderer-vol-3:
Melmoth the Wanderer, Volume Three, continues the Gothic tale issued at Edinburgh by Archibald Constable and Company in 1820. The title page names no author, only the author of Bertram. The work runs to four volumes, and this is the third. Chapter twelve opens in the middle of an inset tale.

What the room holds suspends even the narrator's terror for a moment. He takes it wisely for a book of magic and closes it with horror. It happens to be a copy of the Hebrew Bible, marked with the Samaritan points. A knife lies there too, and a cock is fastened to the table leg, crowing with impatience. A Latin note explains the rite: the bird is a substitute offered for the man's own life.
54067-a-colonial-reformer-vol-1-of-3:
Rolf Boldrewood, author of Robbery Under Arms, wrote a novel in three volumes, of which this is the first, published in London in 1890. Ernest Neuchamp the younger leaves the ancient home of his race in Buckinghamshire. He goes to a far land for a deliberate conflict with fortune. A purpose steadies him against doubt and depression.

Boldrewood calls him a crusader rather than a colonist. Neuchamp scorns the sordid struggle he expects from half speculator colonists. He means to spread sweetness and light in an uncultured community. He holds that colonisation is heroic work and that he is among its heroes. The gap between his aims and colonial life drives the tale.
54108-squire-arden-volume-1-of-3:
Squire Arden, a novel by Oliphant, is shown here in its first volume of three. Hurst and Blackett published it at London in 1871. Oliphant had already won fame with the Chronicles of Carlingford and Salem Chapel. The tale opens in the pretty village of Arden on a pleasant morning of early summer, with all the leaves young.

Joy bells are ringing, and an old woman asks the clerk Simon what they are for. There is no wedding she knows of, and it is not Whitsuntide or fair day. It's the young Squire, stupid, says Simon, gruffly, leaning on the garden paling: he's come home. The author begs the reader to take Simon's broad Lancashire speech as read, rather than spell out its vowels. A young heir's return to a great house, and a village watching him, set the tale in motion.
54122-squire-arden-volume-2-of-3:
Squire Arden, volume two, is the middle part of a novel by Mrs Oliphant. Oliphant also wrote the Chronicles of Carlingford and Salem Chapel. Hurst and Blackett published the three volume novel in London in 1871. This volume opens with a shift between brother and sister. Clare Arden has long made herself anxious about her brother Edgar. She worried over his ways, his words, and his unlike mind. Edgar took her anxiety with amusement rather than concern.

Now their positions reverse, and he grows anxious about Clare. The matter becomes far more serious in his eyes. Edgar feels slights and censures of fortune but lightly for himself. But his easy mind forsakes him when his duties are in question. He takes those duties seriously, as those around him know. The volume continues a family story of temperament and obligation.
54169-a-history-of-north-american-birds-:
The third volume of a history of North American birds. S F Baird, T M Brewer, and R Ridgway wrote the work. Little, Brown first published it at Boston in 1874. This printing is from 1905. Sixty-four plates and five hundred ninety-three woodcuts illustrate the set. The Carolina parakeet, now extinct, plates this volume's front.

Land birds fill all three volumes. This one opens with the raptores, the birds of prey. Owls take the first hundred pages. Falcons, vultures, pigeons, and curassows follow. Turkeys, grouse, and partridges close the systematic text. Appendices explain terms for describing a bird's external form. A glossary and three indexes serve the working ornithologist. Baird ran the Smithsonian, and Ridgway became America's leading bird taxonomist.
54310-kitty-alone-a-story-of-three-fires:
Baring Gould, author of Mehalah and In the Roar of the Sea, wrote this story of three fires in three volumes, and Methuen published the first volume at London in 1894. Eighteen chapters run from The Philosopher's Stone through The Atmospheric Railway and A Capture to a final chapter called Insured and one called Brazil Nuts.

Chapter one brings Jason Quarm riding in his donkey-cart to Coombe Cellars, singing like a crow with full lungs. Jason is short and stout, somewhat lame, with shaggy sandy hair under a battered beaver hat. He drives seated cross-legged on a wisp of straw that keeps scattering under him. Coombe Cellars stands on a promontory in the estuary of the Teign in south Devon. It is farmhouse, goods depot, eating-house, ferry-house, and wharf in one, where barges load corn and hay for Teignmouth and Dawlish.
54366-a-colonial-reformer-vol-3-of-3:
Volume three of A Colonial Reformer is a novel by Rolf Boldrewood, published in 1890. Macmillan issued the three volume set at London and New York. Boldrewood had written Robbery Under Arms and The Squatter's Dream. This volume opens at chapter twenty four, deep in the story. Its first pages reflect on the friend in need. Under dread and perplexity, some visitors are always welcome, the narrator says.

Helpfulness, sympathy, and decision mark that welcome friend. Weak condolence and mild pity avail nothing, he argues. The friend's judgement, favourable or not, lets in the light. It separates real danger from undefined terror. Project Gutenberg holds the first two volumes as companion files. Boldrewood's fiction drew on his years in colonial Australia. The closing volume brings his reformer's trials toward their end.
54463-john-herring-a-west-of-england-rom:
John Herring is a tale of the west of England by Sabine Baring-Gould, the hand of a famed tale of a maid of the marsh. The host text is the first of three parts. It was put out at London in eighteen eighty three. A first word stands at its front, spoke to those who are not of the west land. That word treats the speech of the folk of the tale.

In a tale of that land, the word says, some of the most low kinds of its folk are brought in. The use of their own speech can not be shun in such a tale. That speech has been made soft, as much as could be, to be plain to all. It has not been turn to the speech of the schools.
54465-john-herring-a-west-of-england-rom:
Volume three of John Herring, a West of England romance, is a novel by Sabine Baring-Gould. Smith, Elder published the three volume set at London in 1883. Baring-Gould had written Mehalah before it. Twenty chapters, numbered forty one to sixty, complete the tale. White Favours opens this volume with a wedding. The marriage has been performed in the chapel of Trecarrel. Eight days have passed, and snow whirls over a white world.

The Captain, indisposed in bed, missed the ceremony. A carriage waits to carry bride and bridegroom to Welltown. The journey is long, over fresh snow on an exposed road. Mirelle descends the stairs slowly, her face marked by weeping and prayer. The Snow Bride, hunting the devil, and a bar of ice follow. Nemesis, an arrest, and dividing the spoils close the contents.
54510-the-athelings-or-the-three-gifts-v:
The Athelings, or The Three Gifts is a novel by Margaret Oliphant, first run in Blackwood's Magazine and printed in book form at Edinburgh and London in 1857. This is volume one of three, and a verse from Cymbeline stands at the front. The first book is named Bellevue, and the tale opens in a street with two young women walking together.

One is eighteen and very pretty, with the sweetest girl's face imaginable under a simple bonnet. The other is twenty, taller and paler, and far from commonplace. They are dressed entirely alike, down to the pink rosebuds in their bonnets, with paper parcels in their hands. Oliphant sets their likeness and their deep difference of mind side by side from the first page.
5463-the-sisters-volume-3:
A feast runs late in a vast peristyle in the third volume of Georg Ebers's The Sisters, as cups empty and carousers grow merrier and noisier. Elsewhere, a Roman and his friend Lysias walk up and down in their tent in violent agitation, speaking low. The contrast between revelry and worry drives the volume's opening.

The chapters move between banquet halls and private tents, where public celebration hides private plans. Ebers keeps Greek and Roman figures close together in Ptolemaic Egypt. Readers get a dramatic stretch of the romance, where a party's noise cannot drown out the trouble brewing beside it.
5469-joshua-volume-3:
Under a sycamore, only Miriam's low moans and a warrior's impatient footsteps break the quiet in the third volume of Georg Ebers's Joshua. The warrior struggles for composure and does not dare disturb her, unable to grasp what has risen like a mountain between him and the object of his love. He has learned from Hur that his father and Moses reject all mediation, yet he still bears promises.

The volume turns on love blocked by authority and divided loyalty among the Hebrews, with Moses and family elders standing firm. Ebers writes the personal conflict against the larger Exodus story. Readers get an emotional stretch of the romance, where private feeling meets unyielding leadership.
54855-the-new-abelard-a-romance-volume-1:
The New Abelard is a romance in three volumes by Robert Buchanan, printed at London by Chatto and Windus in 1884. Buchanan also wrote The Shadow of the Sword and God and the Man. He dedicated the novel to his late father, a socialist lecturer, reformer and poet. This hosted text is the first volume.

The prefatory note explains the hero. The leading character resembles, in strength and weakness, the great Abelard of history. He is not meant for an ideal hero. He is an ardent intellectual man, hopelessly biased against veracity by temperament and hereditary superstition. A verse proem of shipwreck opens the tale: the ship grinds on gnawing rocks, and the drowning man swims toward a lighthouse gleam. The romance plays Abelard's pattern of love and intellect in a modern key.
54856-the-new-abelard-a-romance-volume-2:
Robert Buchanan, who wrote The Shadow of the Sword, stands behind this romance in three volumes. Chatto and Windus printed the second volume at London in 1884. Chapter eleven, An Actress at Home, opens this part of the tale.

A year has passed since the letters of the part before. Young George Craik sits in the Travellers' Club with Cholmondeley, a hand of the Charing Cross Chronicle. The newsman puffs a new church, open a month and fast growing the fashion. Tyndall, Huxley, Carlyle, and Mill were seen at its last service, he boasts. George, glum, swears he wants no new faith, and the talk turns sharp.
54857-the-new-abelard-a-romance-volume-3:
Robert Buchanan wrote The New Abelard, a romance in three volumes, issued in London by Chatto and Windus in eighteen eighty four. The hosted text is volume three, the last part of the tale. Buchanan had earlier written The Shadow of the Sword and God and the Man. Chapter twenty two, From the Post Bag, opens this part in letter form. Alma Craik is the heroine in distress.

Sir George Craik writes to his niece Alma that her letter, dated Lucerne but postmarked Geneva, has eased his mind. He thanks Heaven she is safe and well and bears her suffering with Christian resignation. Her secret, he says, is still safe in family custody. The man to whom she owes all this misery still preaches, and his utterances grow more extraordinary, Sir George warns. Readers get the close of a tale of love, faith, and shame in letters and scenes.
54864-rank-and-talent-a-novel-vol-3-of-3:
Rank and Talent closes in its third volume, a novel issued in London in 1829. Henry Colburn brought out the set, whose author had written Truckleborough-Hall. Two short quotes at the front mock pride of rank and envy of the great. The tale picks up threads left loose in the prior volumes.

Dr Crack, deep in love with Miss Henderson, waits at the side as the tale turns. Quiet Clara Rivolta, not made to shine, bears her trials with calm. Rank, talent, and love pull the cast in opposed ways. Readers who like tales of manners and rank in the old style will follow the end with care.
54901-kitty-alone-a-story-of-three-fires:
S Baring Gould wrote Kitty Alone, a tale of three fires put out in London in 1894. The part held here is book three of three. Gould had won a name with Mehalah. His cast and his fires have been set in the first two books.

Parts here bear names like The Answer of Cain and Wanted at Last. A fear, a hint of guilt, and a cry with a yield of wool raise the heat. The third fire gives the book its crest. A plea in court, the tale of Jason, and a priest cure for a sick soul follow. One man in the tale frets on a trip to Tavistock for the grave rites of his uncle. He had piled crime on crime to save his name as a man of wealth, all in vain.
54919-the-romance-of-war-or-the-highland:
James Grant, late of the 62nd Regiment, wrote this romance of Highland troops in the Peninsular War. Colburn printed The Romance of War in three volumes in London. This second volume carries a marching song as its motto.

In the garb of old Gaul, with the fire of old Rome, the song runs. From the heath-covered mountains of Scotia we come. Our loud-sounding pipe breathes the true martial strain. And our hearts still the old Scottish valour retain, General Erskine's words promise. Grant knew the ranks from inside, and his tales of Spain mix camp fact with high romance. The Highlanders of his title were the wonder of that war: kilted, piped, and first in every breach.
54920-the-romance-of-war-or-the-highland:
James Grant, late of the 62nd Regiment, closes his Peninsular War novel with volume three. Henry Colburn issued it at London in 1846. The title page quotes a martial song about the garb of old Gaul.

The contents mix love and war. A love letter opens the book. Then come a ball, a bull-fight, and the skirmish of Fuente Duenna. Highland troops besiege Alba de Tormes and fight at the Pass of Maya. The passage of the Nive ends the list. Ronald, the hero, burns to duel Louis over an insult. Yet a voice repeats that Alice's heart never wandered from him. Grant wrote from a soldier's own memory of Spain. His tales of Highland regiments sold well for decades.
54928-history-of-spanish-literature-vol-:
History of Spanish Literature, volume one of three, is the great survey by George Ticknor. Ticknor, a Boston scholar, built the work from years of Spanish travel and reading. Footnotes have been renumbered into a single series in this digital edition. Caesuras in split verses are marked in the transcription for the student reader.

The first volume runs from the earliest Spanish writings through the golden age dawn. Romances, chronicles, and the old epics ground Ticknor account of the literature birth. His history gave English readers their first full map of Spanish letters. It held the field for generations and still stands behind modern surveys.
54940-monica-a-novel-volume-1-of-3:
Monica is a novel by Evelyn Everett-Green, issued in London in 1889. The hosted text is volume one of three. Everett-Green wrote Torwood's Trust and Ruthven of Ruthven. The contents list runs to eleven chapters in this volume. Castle Trevlyn and its family open the tale. Monica's ride and Lord Trevlyn's heir follow in turn.

The first chapter sets a grim, decaying castle scene. Lady Monica waits in a great hall of black oak and old armour. A doctor leaves her with word that a patient rests easy. Later chapters bring a suitor named Conrad Fitzgerald. A Sunday at Trevlyn and a scene of peril come next. A wedding closes the middle of the volume. Mischief-makers then start the little rift of the close. Three-volume novels were the standard form of the day.
54942-monica-a-novel-volume-3-of-3:
Monica, a novel by Evelyn Everett-Green, closes with this third volume, printed in London in 1889. The book opens at chapter twenty three, so it takes up a story already well along. Chapter heads in this volume include Beatrice, Storm, Widowed, and Christmas. The last chapter is simply called The Last. Monica is the calm center of the household at Trevlyn.

The opening scene shows Beatrice sad and pale at Trevlyn. Monica fears the place does not suit her guest. Beatrice begs not to be sent away, saying she would die if she had to go. The scene sets a tone of love, duty, and strain. Readers of the full novel get its final turns and close here.
55191-a-history-of-north-american-birds-:
A History of North American Birds, Land Birds, volume one, by SF Baird, TM Brewer, and R Ridgway, is the first of three volumes describing every known bird of the continent. Little, Brown published the work at Boston; the text was entered in 1874 and this copy is dated 1905. Sixty-four plates and five hundred ninety-three woodcuts fill the volume.

The preface says the book fills a long-felt want. For each bird it gives the form, the range, the habits, the nesting, the eggs, and the popular names. The writers survey their forerunners: the American Ornithology of Alexander Wilson, finished in 1814, and the works of Audubon. A catbird in full detail fronts the volume as a sample of the plates. The set became a standard storehouse of American bird lore.
55192-a-history-of-north-american-birds-:
History of North American Birds, Land Birds volume two, is a classic bird work. Baird, Brewer, and Ridgway wrote the history for Little Brown of Boston. The work was entered in eighteen seventy four, this printing dates nineteen o five. Sixty four plates and five hundred ninety three woodcuts picture the birds.

A red headed woodpecker plate fronts the volume in fine colour here. Contents resume the finch family, then pass to sparrow subfamilies in order. Larks follow, then the oriole family with its blackbird kin group. Latin names, measures, and life notes fill each species account in turn. The three volume land bird set long served as a standard reference.
55294-poetical-works-of-robert-bridges-v:
Volume three of the Poetical Works of Robert Bridges holds two stage works. Smith, Elder and Company issued the book in London in eighteen hundred ninety eight. Horace Hart printed it at Oxford for the whole set run. Nero, first part, and Achilles in Scyros fill its pages.

Nero, a tragedy of history, first saw print in eighteen hundred eighty five. Thrasea bids young Priscus learn silence in the senate halls. Speak with least offence, the Stoic warns, or pay a dire price. Agrippina’s crimes and Nero’s follies strain the young reign here. Seneca, Burrus, Lucan, and Otho crowd the new court scenes. Octavia, wife to Nero, and Poppaea stand in the wings of fate. Achilles in Scyros, a drama in mixed manner, came in eighteen hundred ninety. Notes by the poet close the third book of his works.
55528-bothwell-or-the-days-of-mary-queen:
Bothwell, or The Days of Mary Queen of Scots, is a historical novel by James Grant, shown here in its second volume of three. Parry published it at London in 1851. Grant had written The Romance of War and other Scots tales. The contents open with the earl and the queen, then a weaponshaw and a handkerchief.

The Leith Wynd gate, the Red Lion inn, and the Earl of Morton follow. Chapters bring a conflict in Hermitage Glen and the pit of Hermitage. Bothwell revives an early dream, and four choice spirits plot together. The conference of Craigmillar thickens the plot toward the murder that history knows is coming. Grant dresses his earl in black velvet slashed with red, with a silver horse's head crest and one tall ostrich feather. His novel gives the rough border lord his romance, in the full manner of the Scottish historical tale.
55529-bothwell-or-the-days-of-mary-queen:
James Grant, who wrote The Romance of War, stands behind this tale of Mary Queen of Scots. Parry printed the third volume at London in 1851. Bothwell, the queen's bold and ill-starred lord, gives the book its name.

The Kirk-of-Field opens this last part, the house where the king was slain. A midnight mass, guilt that levels all, and remorse follow fast. The Rescue, the Challenge, and Ainslie's Supper crowd the list. How Bothwell used the bond, love and scorn, and Mary's despair mark the fall. The bridal at Beltane and the whirlpool turn the screw. Malmö and retribution close the tale of a queen undone by love and plot.
55589-history-of-spanish-literature-vol-:
George Ticknor wrote this history of Spanish literature in three volumes, printed by Harper and Brothers of New York in 1849. The part held here is volume two. It carries the second period forward, opening with the theatre in the time of Charles the Fifth and the first part of the reign of Philip the Second. The church opposed the drama, and the Inquisition stepped in.

Contents trace religious plays, secular plays, and names like Castillejo, Oliva, and Juan de Paris. Translations from the ancients, attempts at Valencia, and the court-yards of Madrid follow. Ticknor notes that Spanish drama had no uniform character and that a national drama was demanded. His history, the first of its scope in English, made Spanish letters known to American readers.
55744-the-exclusives-vol-1-of-3:
Volume one of a three-volume novel of high society London came out in a second edition in 1830. Henry Colburn and Richard Bentley published it. Tales of its kind were then called silver fork fiction.

Its first chapter, The Boudoir, opens in Lady Tilney's rooms and sets the tone at once. Her drawing room, the narrator argues, is no private retreat but a seat of power, where the talk and the deals of the state of society pass daily. The talk there mixes dress, rank, and sharp wit, and the book promises a close look at the people who ruled fashion and politics alike. It survives as a sharp sample of the society novel at its height, written before the Victorian age changed the form.
55745-the-exclusives-vol-2-of-3:
The Exclusives, a society tale in three volumes, reaches its mid part here. Henry Colburn and Richard Bentley issued this second edition in London in eighteen hundred thirty. Restormel, a great house, frames the closing scene of volume one. Chess, a faint, and sharp tongues open the new book’s first hour.

Lord Albert tells Lady Ellersby of his set plan to leave at dawn. Mr Foley cries checkmate at the board as a cry breaks the room. Lady Hamlet Vernon swoons dead away and is caught in her fall. Lady Boileau scorns scene makers and their bad taste at once. Feint or faint: the room debates which swoon it has just seen. True feels shown in public mark a roturier, one guest holds. No faint looks well, says another; command yourself at all times. French scraps season the talk of this most polished of sets.
55746-the-exclusives-vol-3-of-3:
Volume three of The Exclusives, a society novel in a second edition, was printed in London in 1830. Lady Delamere returns with her niece Adeline, who is left to sleep, the best of all earthly restoratives. Lady Dunmelraise listens with anxious interest to the tale of her daughter's sudden indisposition at the opera.

Lady Delamere holds it came from witnessing Lord Albert's attentions to Lady Hamlet Vernon all evening in the box opposite. She observed Adeline struggling with her feelings, till at length the girl fainted. For Adeline's sake, she says, she must speak without reserve on the subject of Lord Albert. Rank, opera boxes, and watched glances drive this high society tale of love under code.
56255-all-but-lost-a-novel-vol-2-of-3:
Henty, later famed for boys adventure tales, wrote a society novel in three volumes, with volume two printed in London in 1869. Who will win them, the first chapter asks, as Teddy Drake's answer to Frank's letter arrives. Frank, I am truly glad to see your fist again, and still more so to hear you will come down and see us if invited, the reply runs.

Father, mother, and girls all invite him hereby. The Lively Stunners, a slap in the face, a light in the gloom, losing the gloves, and gathering clouds fill the contents. An announcement in the Times, an intercepted letter, a cut direct, and Stephen Walker doing his worst drive a tale of love, money, and reputation at risk.
56371-the-flower-of-the-flock-volume-1-o:
Pierce Egan wrote a long London novel in three books, of which this is the first. The book came out in London in 1865. Egan also wrote The Poor Girl. A bright June morn in busy London starts the tale. Verse from Shelley and Keats heads the first part.

Sun hits church spires, tall works, and the dome of Saint Paul's. Gilt light bathes roofs and pots in the same warm glow. Yet the part's name speaks of a shadow in the sun. Joy and grief mix in the lives that ensue. Egan paints the great town as both stage and trap.
56433-the-manoeuvring-mother-vol-1-of-3:
The Manoeuvring Mother, volume one of three, is a novel by the author of The History of a Flirt. Colburn published it in London in 1842. The printer was Shoberl, of Rupert Street, printer to Prince Albert.

The first chapter lays out the house of Wetheral with a satirist's hand. Sir John and Lady Wetheral are blessed with four fine little girls. Their forms are perfect, their features faultless, and no thick ankles shock the taste. The girls are born distinguished, and will make matches in time. Noblemen, or county kings richer still, are the mark set for them. Lady Wetheral loves an even number in all things. Four daughters are not alarming, but five would be a vulgar fraction. As the chapter turns, a fifth innocent arrives to crush her hopes.
56435-the-manoeuvring-mother-vol-3-of-3:
The Manoeuvring Mother, volume three of three, is a novel by the author of the History of a Flirt. Henry Colburn printed it in London in 1842. This last volume opens at chapter twenty two, four years on at Fairlee in Scotland.

The text says four years passed rapidly and tranquilly at Fairlee. The waters of Lochleven flowed at the foot of its undulating grounds. The mountains of Glencoe ended the grandly beautiful and distant prospect which Christobelle gazed upon with untired delight. She loved to sit in meditation, or paint its glowing and ever changing tints. Often the forms of Anna Maria and Isabel appear before her as she lingers on the mountain tops. She feels the loss of Sir John Spottiswoode society for months. Readers should start at volume one for the full matchmaking tale.
56490-history-of-spanish-literature-vol-:
George Ticknor wrote a history of Spanish literature in three volumes, printed in New York in 1849. Volume three takes up the second period and carries it on. Satirical poetry, letters, and elegiac verse open the contents. Old romances and tales of chivalry fill many pages.

Writers such as Juan de Flores and Gines Perez de Hita get close study. Hita's Wars of Granada earns a long note, and Ticknor says it found no true followers. Ties with Italy and Algiers shape the prose of the age. Appendices keep Spanish texts as first printed. Scholars and keen readers get a full map of Spain's letters in English.
56614-village-folk-tales-of-ceylon-volum:
Village Folk-Tales of Ceylon, volume one of three, was collected and translated by H. Parker, late of the Irrigation Department in Ceylon. It was printed at London in 1910. The first part holds stories of the cultivating caste and of the Vaedda people. Its tales begin with the making of the great earth and the story of the sun, the moon, and great paddy.

The contents run to dozens of tales: the Glass Princess, the Frog Prince, the White Turtle, and the Golden Tree. Jackals, hares, leopards, and mouse-deer fill the beast tales. Other stories turn on princes, princesses, and the spirits called Yakas. The Kadambawa men appear in a run of comic tales near the end of the volume. Parker's book preserves the oral tales of Ceylon's villages in English dress. It is a rich store for readers of folk tale and custom.
56935-first-love-a-novel-vol-3-of-3:
First Love, volume three of three, closes an anonymous novel published by Saunders and Otley in London in 1830. The volume opens the morning after a masquerade. Sir Archibald's mysterious death has sobered the whole party. So has the attempt on the life of Captain Montgomery. The company speaks in whispers of murders, mysteries, and sudden deaths.

Julia slips into the green-house, and the Marquis follows her. An hour passes, and neither reappears. The Marquis's seat at dinner stands empty, and he has ridden off without explanation. Meanwhile Lord Fitz-Ullin is at sea again, and Captain Montgomery's name shines in every newspaper account of the fleet. The volume mixes the country-house mystery with naval glory, in the high romantic manner of its decade.
57008-the-haunted-hangar-sky-scouts-air-:
Van Powell wrote a boys' air mystery about a haunted hangar. The book came out in 1932 with the Saalfield Publishing Company. It is book three in the Sky Scouts Air Mystery Series. Sandy, Jeff, Dick, and Larry form the Sky Patrol. A front plate shows a man hurt in the hangar.

Early flights bring fog, a chase, and a clue from a swamp. A plane seems cursed, and Larry is seized by foes. Later parts set a trap, stage a race, and spend a night in the hangar. The boys solve the ghost tale by grit and flight. Step by step, the clues point past fear to men with a plan.
57060-london-labour-and-the-london-poor-:
Henry Mayhew catalogues the street life of the capital in volume three of his great survey, first issued in 1851 and enlarged in 1861. The title page sorts Londoners into those that will work, those that cannot work, and those that will not work.

This volume treats the street-folk. Destroyers of vermin open it, with Jack Black, rat-killer to Her Majesty, pictured at his work. Street exhibitors, musicians, and vocalists follow. Trained animals and Punch's showman fill the plates. Skilled and unskilled labour comes next: garret-masters, coal-heavers, ballast-men, and dock-labourers. Cheap lodging-houses and the transit of the metropolis follow. Cab-drivers, carmen, and vagrants close the survey. A meeting of ticket-of-leave men ends the book. Mayhew took his facts from the mouths of the poor themselves.
57294-under-lock-and-key-a-story-volume-:
Under Lock and Key, volume one of three, is a mystery story by Speight, printed in London in eighteen sixty nine. Speight opens with a note defending his plot against a charge of borrowing. His plan was sketched, he says, before Collins's Moonstone had appeared in public. He even denied himself reading that book until his own was done.

Seventeen chapters fill the first volume, from an arrival to a return after seven years. Janet Holme, a schoolgirl of twelve, is sent to Dupley Walls in Midlandshire. Her whole wealth fits in one small box nailed up for the journey. Lady Pollexfen, mistress of that house, waits at the end of the trip. Chapters ahead promise a stolen manuscript, a secret, and a diamond of note. A Scotch express and a house called Bon Repos also figure early.
57295-under-lock-and-key-a-story-volume-:
T W Speight wrote a tale of secrets in three volumes, here in its second part. Tinsley Brothers issued the set in London in 1869. Volume Two holds sixteen chapters, from Janet in a new role to a third report from Madgin Junior. Janet Holme stands at the heart of the plot.

Lady Pollexfen of Dupley Walls offers Janet a post left free by the ill Sister Agnes. Pay of thirty guineas a year stings Janet, who had hoped for trust, not wages. Plots turn on counsel, secret trips, and a small packet from London. Readers who like tales of hidden ties and slow reveals will follow keenly.
57672-a-secret-of-the-sea-a-novel-vol-1-:
Speight wrote A Secret of the Sea, a novel in three volumes, for Bentley at London in 1876. Volume one opens in a lawyer's office on a clear, frosty December morning. Matthew Kelvin, attorney at Pembridge in Hertfordshire, keeps that office. His clock races noisily after the grave old abbey clock outside. A youth of sixteen, Podley Piper, called Pod by all, turns the Times with contempt. Pod mutters that the paper is dry reading, with one suicide and no murder in it.

Contents promise Miss Bellamy, the story of the murder, and a broken life. Gerald appears at Pembridge and at Stammars, and a cry of that's the man rings out. Miss Deane finds a new home, and a face in the glass closes the volume. Speight gives a brisk sensation tale of a sea secret, law, and hidden guilt.
57685-griffith-gaunt-or-jealousy-volumes:
Griffith Gaunt, or Jealousy is a tale by Charles Reade, in three parts. The host text holds all three in one pack. The first part was put out at London in eighteen sixty six. Its list of parts is plain: four teen counts with no names. The tale opens in a clash of man and wife in their own house. That clash is the seed of the whole book.

Then I say once for all, says the man, that priest shall not dim my doors once more. Then I say they are my doors and not yours, says the wife. That holy man shall light them when he will, she says. The man and maid who faced each past in this clash were man and wife, the tale says. And they had loved each past well.
57814-a-secret-of-the-sea-a-novel-vol-2-:
Secret of the Sea, volume two of three, is a novel by Speight, published in London in 1876. Richard Bentley and Son issued the set in that year. Speight is named as author of In the Dead of Night and Under Lock and Key. Contents of volume two list twelve chapters for this middle part of the tale.

Miriam Byrne and Floating with the Stream open the volume in order of its chapters. A Secret of the Sea, the title chapter, stands sixth in the contents of the book. Pod Revelation, A Glass of Burgundy, and The Story of the Wreck carry the mystery forward in turn. Speight was a master of the sensation novel in its later years. His middle volumes deal in wrecks, confessions, and recognitions, holding the sea secret back while the tea cups and holiday scenes do their quiet work.
57815-a-secret-of-the-sea-a-novel-vol-3-:
Speight, who wrote In the Dead of Night, closes his sea mystery in this third volume. Bentley printed the end of A Secret of the Sea in London in 1876. Eleanor's Resolve opens the finish, and the tale runs thirteen chapters to its close.

Sir Thomas Dudgeon starts the volume in no hurry to get back to London. The House can get on without him, he hints to his doctor. Pod's stratagem and Van Duren's dream stir the plot. A found letter and Pringle's discovery turn it. Van Duren flees, the strong-room is reached, and the secret is told at last. And You Shall Still Be Lady Clare names the prize: a name, a rank, and a heart all hang on the sea's kept word.
57851-memoirs-of-the-reign-of-king-georg:
Memoirs of the Reign of King George the Second holds court notes of that age. The hosted text is the second of three volumes of the work. Six plates in all dress the set, two in each of its books. Coarse words in the text were cut by the editor and marked with stars.

Cuts and marks in the text show where the editor pruned the raw notes. Court talk, state plots, and great men in their off hours fill the pages. Notes at part ends gloss names and dates for the home reader. The memoir is prized as a tart, close view of a kings whole court. Gossip and state craft share its sharp eye on men of rank.
57945-in-the-dead-of-night-a-novel-volum:
In the Dead of Night, volume one of three, was published in London in eighteen seventy-four by Richard Bentley and Son. The triple-decker format ruled the fiction market of the day. This first volume lists fourteen chapters, from Over the Cliff to At Alder Cottage. New names arrive steadily: Edith West, Kester St George, and Mr Percy Osmond.

The opening chapter is set at a seaside town on a hot, windless August day. Excursionists dance in the Silver Lion while a storm gathers out at sea. Lionel Dering refuses old Ben's advice against the cliff path after dark. Lightning finds him two miles from home, alone on the cliffs. A midnight intruder and the title chapter wait ahead. Sensation fiction begins, as it should, with a man walking into weather and worse.
57946-in-the-dead-of-night-a-novel-volum:
An anonymous novel in three volumes reaches its second volume in a London edition of 1874 from Bentley. Contents open with the eve of the trial, then the trial itself. A bottle of Burgundy and Dr Drayton's suspicions follow. Hide and seek and a chapter called Flown build the suspense. General St George and Cupid at Pincote lighten the middle.

At the Villa Pamphili takes the scene to Rome. Mrs McDermott wants her money in a later chapter. Footsteps in the room and the squire's tribulation close the list. Chapter one finds Mr Cope junior disgusted within a week of Tom Bristow's visit. The dead of night of the title is melodrama's hour.
57947-in-the-dead-of-night-a-novel-volum:
Volume 3 of In the Dead of Night, a novel in three volumes, was published in London in 1874 by Richard Bentley and Son. Contents list eleven chapters, from A Way Out of the Difficulty to Gathered Threads. Heads name Sycamore Walk, Knockley Holt, the Three Crowns Hotel, and a Miss Culpepper who speaks her mind.

The volume opens two hours after a second letter from a widow reaches Squire Culpepper. He sets out, heavy-hearted and slow, for Sugden's bank, though he has never borrowed a farthing since he came into the estate. Shame stings him, and his fine new mansion at Pincote, to be built from Alcazar shares, now stands as a castle in air. Tom finds his tongue and wins his wife, as later heads promise.
5799-life-and-letters-of-thomas-henry-hu:
Volume three of the Life and Letters of Thomas Henry Huxley, edited by his son Leonard Huxley, covers the years 1887 through 1892 and beyond. Chapters run year by year, from 1887 through 1888, 1889, 1890 to 1891, and 1892, tracing Huxley's later career, controversies, and friendships. A portrait from a photograph by Downey in 1890 fronts the volume.

Readers meet the great Victorian biologist in his own words and in his circle's letters, debating evolution, agnosticism, and education. The volume shows Huxley as public champion of science and private correspondent, witty and combative by turns. It suits readers of Darwin's circle, Victorian science, and biography built from letters, offering the closing chapters of a formidable life.
58002-bertha-s-visit-to-her-uncle-in-eng:
Berthas Visit to Her Uncle in England is a journal tale in three volumes. The hosted text holds the first volume of the three. The book came out in London in the year eighteen thirty. A print slip list at its front sets a few place names right.

The front note says the books draw on the diary of a young girl. She had spent her child years at Rio and sails to kin in England. Her sire died on state work in Brazil, and grief broke her dam. The lone child is sent home to friends in the old land for care. Scenes of shore, home, and church life fill her bright young diary.
58003-bertha-s-visit-to-her-uncle-in-eng:
Bertha's Visit to Her Uncle in England, volume two of three, was published by John Murray of London in 1830. The book is cast as a young visitor's journal of her stay. Entries are dated day by day through the winter months. Each day brings some sight, talk, or piece of learning to record.

The entry for December the first gives Colonel Travers describing the pepper vine of the East Indies. Shoots are planted round a tree at the start of the rains and tied to its stem as they climb. Berries picked green and rubbed free of their seeds yield black pepper. Berries left to ripen red yield white pepper, though the vines then tend to die. A good plant gives about thirty two pounds.
5810-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Part three of Mark Twain's Following the Equator covers chapters twenty through twenty-nine, with a Pudd'nhead Wilson maxim on freedom of speech, freedom of conscience, and the prudence never to practice either. A diary note recalls Mr G, unseen since Nauheim in Germany several years earlier, when cholera broke out. From that reunion, the narrative moves through colonial towns and shipboard talk.

Twain gives his sharpest travel satire in compact form, as he weighs empire, race, and respectability against what he actually meets. The part favors anecdote and argument over scenery, letting a chance meeting open a wider reflection. It suits readers tracking Twain's world journey, and it offers some of the book's most quoted jokes about freedom and its limits.
5820-the-gilded-age-part-3:
Part three of The Gilded Age, by Twain and Warner, covers chapters nineteen through twenty-seven, and it opens with Harry Brierly drawing engineer's pay while living at the City Hotel in Hawkeye.
