Thompson kindly says it makes no difference whether Harry is with the corps or not. Harry still protests daily to the Colonel and to Washington Hawkins. He insists he must return at once to superintend the line. The gap between pay and work is the joke.

Readers follow Harry's easy life and the Hawkins family's schemes through Hawkeye and beyond, as railroads, land, and lobbying promise fortunes. The part favors comic character over plot machinery, letting Harry's charm carry scenes of delay and excuse. It suits readers midway through the novel, where satire of western enterprise grows sharper with every unpaid promise.
58320-the-three-brothers-vol-1-3:
Volume one of The Three Brothers is a novel by Mrs Oliphant, published in London in 1870. Hurst and Blackett issued the three volume set. Oliphant had written the Chronicles of Carlingford and Salem Chapel. The first chapter, Their Father, explains the Renton family. The sons were sent into the world in a humble manner. Their father, though, was anything but a poor man.

The Rentons joined active exertion to inherited wealth for centuries. Each heir added by his own efforts to the family store. Pirates stood among their Elizabethan ancestors. The Will and The New Career follow the father's chapter. A magician's cave and the working of the spell turn the plot strange. Bills, rewards, and last interviews fill the later contents. Twenty one chapters complete the first volume.
58322-the-three-brothers-vol-3-3:
The Three Brothers, volume three, is a novel by Mrs Oliphant. Hurst and Blackett issued it in London in 1870. Seventeen chapters bring the tale to its end. Alice's Fate opens the volume. Alice Severn is just over sixteen. Old Welby presses her mother to train her gift. The girl has a clear and marked talent. To leave such a gift unused is folly, he holds.

A struggle, an exchange of regiments, and waters falling follow. The Raven and The Dove mark a paired turn. A will, suspense, and the end of a dream fill the close. What it all meant to Laurie ends the tale. Oliphant wrote tales of family honour and sacrifice. Her Carlingford books had made her name by then.
5838-sketches-new-and-old-part-3:
Part three of Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old opens with Disgraceful Persecution of a Boy, a satire set in San Francisco. A well-dressed boy on his way to Sunday school, the sketch reports, was arrested and thrown into city prison for stoning Chinese men. Twain turns the incident into a commentary on human justice and our disposition to tyrannize the weak, with irony as his weapon.

Twain gives his moral satire at its most pointed, where a small news item exposes a large hypocrisy. The part gathers further sketches in first, second, and third sections, mixing comedy with protest. It suits readers who enjoy Twain as a critic of prejudice, and it shows how humor could carry a serious argument in his hands.
58418-cicero-letters-to-atticus-vol-1-of:
Volume one of Cicero, Letters to Atticus, holds the first six books of that famed set of letters. Winstedt of Magdalen College, Oxford, made the English version for the Loeb Classical Library. Heinemann at London and Putnam at New York put it out, first in 1912 and again in 1919. Latin text and English text face each other, page by page.

Atticus was the close friend to whom Cicero wrote with rare freedom. The first letter deals with his run for high office and the help of friends. Galba is named as a lone canvasser who holds back in the old blunt way. Books one to six run from campaigns to exile and back. Readers get Roman high life in the raw, in the words of its chief actor.
58517-kissing-the-rod-a-novel-vol-1-of-3:
Edmund Yates wrote Kissing the Rod, a novel in three volumes from Tinsley Brothers at London in 1866, inscribed to the Countess of Fife. Yates, author of Broken to Harness and Running the Gauntlet, takes his motto from Proverbs: the heart knoweth its own bitterness. Volume one runs twelve chapters: Dazzled, A Morning Call, Within the Pale, Hester Gould, In Chambers, Katharine Guyon, Investments, Struggle, and Victory among them.

The opening builds the City firm of Streightley and Son at 48 Bullion Lane, money-brokers since the South-Sea bubble, which they survived and even prospered by. Old Sam and his head clerk Fowler kept the house safe; then young Robert joined and chafed at his father's caution. A long bout of gout laid the father up, and he returned to find the business prosperous but wholly changed. The novel turns on money, ambition, and family firm politics.
58519-kissing-the-rod-a-novel-vol-3-of-3:
Kissing the Rod, volume three of three, closes Edmund Yates's novel of that name. Tinsley Brothers published it in London in 1866. Yates was already known for Broken to Harness and Running the Gauntlet. The motto is from Proverbs: the heart knoweth its own bitterness.

The volume opens with Robert Streightley stunned by his wife's letter. Her unexplained absence has thrown the household into suspense. At the same time his father-in-law's death loads him with duties, callers, and letters. The chapters move through deliberation, husband and wife, failure, and a split in the camp. They end with the pledge redeemed, success, and coming home. Yates writes the Victorian domestic crisis at full stretch, with ruin and recovery kept in balance to the last page.
5856-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-vo:
Volume one, part three of Sheridan's Personal Memoirs covers chapters sixteen through twenty-four, at Chattanooga. Headings treat the enemy fortifying Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge, reorganizing the army, removing General Rosecrans, and punishing deserters. Grant arrives at Chattanooga, the fight on Lookout Mountain follows, a brave color bearer stands out, and the Battle of Missionary Ridge crowns the campaign.

It offers a general's account of a turning campaign, written with attention to positions, orders, and morale. Sheridan narrates from inside the army, praising courage and noting command changes without flinching. The part suits Civil War readers who want Chattanooga in a participant's voice, and it forms a key section of Sheridan's larger memoir of the war.
5862-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-:
Part three of Grant's Personal Memoirs covers chapters twenty-seven through thirty-eight, in the western campaigns. Headings move headquarters to Memphis, escape Jackson, handle complaints and requests, and note Halleck appointed commander in chief. A return to Corinth, movements of Bragg, surrender of Clarksville, advance upon Chattanooga, and Sheridan as colonel of a Michigan regiment follow.

Grant gives his account of command in the middle war, balancing logistics, politics, and battle with steady prose. The memoir explains decisions without boasting, letting orders, movements, and results carry the argument. It suits Civil War readers tracing Grant's rise, and it offers a clear, participant's view of the campaigns that shaped the western theater.
58678-a-parisian-sultana-vol-2-of-3:
H Mainwaring Dunstan turns Adolphe Belot's French novel into English in book two of three, subtitled In the Heart of Africa. The volume opens on the Nile at Khartoum.

A little European flotilla rounds Ras-el-Khartoum, where the White and Blue Niles join. Three large mimosas mark the rendezvous for boats bound up the White Nile. Low, flat banks run as far as the eye can see, often flooded like a sea. Snags and dead stumps raise their heads from the river bed. The steamer Khedive tows the party. Her captain, a young Egyptian officer educated in Paris, begs Madame de Guéran to stay aboard. In a few days she will turn up the Gazelle River. Belot's tale mixes river travel with the slave trade's horrors.
58679-a-parisian-sultana-vol-3-of-3:
A Parisian Sultana is an English translation, by Mainwaring Dunstan, of Adolphe Belot's French novel La Sultane parisienne. This file holds the third of its three books, which bears its own title, Venus in Ebony.

The third book opens with a careful recap for readers of the earlier volumes. It will not, the author trusts, have been forgotten that in March 1873 the Count de Pommerelle visited Doctor Desrioux. The young doctor was bowed down with grief at his mother's death. To his affection for her he had sacrificed his love for Madame de Guéran, his plans to travel with her, and his most cherished hopes. In near despair he had begged the Count to take him anywhere out of Paris. The friends meet again at the funeral, and walk together from the house of death to the church and the cemetery of Père La Chaise.
58830-teutonic-mythology-gods-and-goddes:
Viktor Rydberg of the Swedish Academy traces the gods of the north in volume three of a study turned into English by Rasmus B Anderson. The Norrœna Society issued it in 1906. This copy is number ninety-nine of six hundred and fifty sets of the Viking edition.

An etching by Lorenz Frölich shows Thor's journey to Gierrodsgard. Loke, caught in falcon shape, buys his freedom with a promise. He will bring Thor to the giant Geirrod without hammer, belt, or iron gloves. At the river Vimer the waters rise to Thor's shoulders. Gjalp, the giant's daughter, stands astride the stream and swells it. Thor seizes a projecting shrub and drags himself out by main strength. Rydberg reads the myths as a system, not as scattered tales.
58889-village-folk-tales-of-ceylon-volum:
Village Folk-Tales of Ceylon, volume three, gathers tales told by caste and craft. Parker collected and translated them. Luzac of London issued the volume in 1914. Parker had served in Ceylon's irrigation department. The tales are numbered on past two hundred and sixty. Stories of the farming caste open the book. A hare and a parrot show their friendship there. A deer, a jackal, and a crow appear as variants.

Tales of potters and washermen follow in their sections. Tom-tom beaters have a group of their own. Step-mothers, thieves, and foolish princes crowd the pages. Variants are printed side by side for study. Parker was a careful keeper of oral lore. His three volumes remain the great store of Ceylon tales.
5902-journeys-through-bookland-vol-3:
Volume three of Sylvester's Journeys Through Bookland applies a new and original plan for reading to the world's best literature for children. Sylvester, author of English and American literature, presents the volume in a new edition, continuing the series' guided path through stories, poems, and classic tales. Each selection is chosen to lead a young reader onward, from simple delight to deeper reading.

Families get a structured anthology, where famous literature arrives in manageable pieces with context for parents and teachers. The volume favors breadth, mixing fancy, adventure, and moral tales without losing a child's attention. It suits homeschooling, bedtime reading, and anyone building a young reader's library, since the plan itself teaches how to love books.
59204-george-crabbe-poems-volume-3-of-3:
Poems by George Crabbe, volume three of three, closes the Cambridge English Classics edition of his works. Ward edited it, and the Cambridge University Press issued it in 1907. Crabbe was born in 1754 and died in 1832, as the title page records. Ward warns that this last volume's contents are very mixed, needing a long preface.

His remarks chase the sources of Crabbe's earliest verses in the Lady's Magazine of 1770 to 1775. A prize poem called An Essay on Hope stands in the February number for 1773. The six lines the younger Crabbe quoted are not in it, nor in the October poem of 1772. The editor's hunt shows how carefully this edition was made.
59427-gleanings-in-bee-culture-vol-iii-n:
Gleanings in Bee Culture, volume three, number three, is the March 1875 issue of a monthly bee journal. Root and Company published it at Medina in Ohio in that year. Its subtitle promises to show how to realise the most money with the smallest expenditure of capital and labour in the care of bees. A list of bee periodicals consulted stands at its head.

The issue draws on the American Bee Journal, the Bee Keeper Magazine, and the Bee World, among others. Its contents, as sampled in the catalogue, run to short notes on the work of the season. Items named are reports from cold frames, leather for quilts, and straight combs for hives. The number is a practical window on American bee keeping in the 1870s, when the movable frame hive was remaking the craft.
59529-all-but-lost-a-novel-vol-3-of-3:
G A Henty wrote a novel in three volumes, of which this third volume was published in London in 1869. Henty was known for The March to Magdala. The volume opens with Fred Bingham now an important man. He contracts for miles of sewers around London and builds a nobleman's mansion in Sussex. A church in Birmingham, a pier in Cornwall, and a railway in Durham are also in hand.

Casual acquaintances call Bingham a pushing, sharp young fellow. Business men call him cute but hard as nails. At home, his wife and servants know a morose and irritable tyrant. Chapters ahead promise ruin, proffered aid, a clue, and a verdict of not guilty.
5958-the-physiology-of-marriage-part-3:
Honoré de Balzac carries his study of marriage into open civil war between husband and wife. This third part offers meditations on manifestos and on the weapons science can put in a husband's hand. The husband stands single-handed, backed by religion and law, against a wife aided by native craft and social custom.

Balzac states his maxims bluntly, on love, deceit, and the erratic leaps by which women escape pursuit. He cares less for who will be vanquished than for whether resistance is possible at all. The tone is aphoristic and combative, treating wedlock as a contest with rules, allies, and beacons.
5968-what-s-mine-s-mine-volume-3:
George MacDonald opens the third volume with Mercy able to come down to the drawing room again. Evenings pass as never before, and quiet days give her time to think. She finds herself in a region of human life unlike any she has known, where every word and act seems to acknowledge something understood but unspoken.

The volume's chapters include a high school, a terrible discovery, love glooming, a generous dowry, the marches, midnight, the power of darkness, and a flitting to a new village. Alister and his princess figure late in the list.
59720-the-son-of-his-father-vol-1-3:
The Son of His Father opens its first volume with the publisher's list of new novels at all the libraries. That list is itself a shelf of its age: three-volume tales for the lending trade. Caterina, by the author of Lauterdale, heads the roll.

Jacobi's Wife, by Adeline Sergeant, stands at three volumes. On the Scent, by Lady Margaret Majendie, takes one. A Great Platonic Friendship fills three more. The Golden Hope, a romance of the deep by Clark Russell, closes the list. Into that world of subscription shelves and triple-deckers this novel stepped. Its title is a theme in itself: how far a son walks in his father's road, and where he breaks from it.
59721-the-son-of-his-father-vol-2-3:
Mrs Oliphant wrote The Son of His Father, here volume two of three, issued in London by Hurst and Blackett in eighteen eighty seven. Oliphant had earlier written It Was a Lover and His Lass and Agnes. Eighteen chapters fill the volume. Chapter one is Out in the World. John, the hero, leaves home with a mystery about his birth behind him.

Out in the world was not so long a journey as that to Liverpool with the curate, the tale says. But then he had his home to return to, with no need to face the storms of life alone. He had set forth curious, hoping to learn something about himself. He had his natural anchorage, his harbour to sail back to, it adds. London, Susie, and On His Trial follow. A New Influence and The Vita Nuova fill the middle. Novel readers get Oliphant quiet, knowing family tale.
59951-new-witnesses-for-god-volume-3-of-:
B H Roberts wrote New Witnesses for God, here volume three of three, issued by the Deseret News at Salt Lake City in nineteen oh nine. The volume treats the Book of Mormon, in part three on evidences of its truth. Roberts had earlier written The Gospel and Outlines of Ecclesiastical History. Chapters thirty onward fill the volume. Indirect external evidences from American traditions stand first.

Chapter thirty treats signs of Messiah birth and death in native tradition. Chapter thirty one treats Messiah in the western hemisphere, culture heroes, and the Peruvian tradition. Chapter thirty two argues the Hebrew origin of the native American races, with the Pittsfield Hebrew parchment and the Newark Hebrew tablet. Chapter thirty three treats the Cincinnati gold plate and the Kinderhook plates. Latter day Saint readers get a full defence of the Book of Mormon.
60018-the-son-of-his-father-vol-3-3:
Oliphant's novel The Son of His Father closes in this third volume, published in London in eighteen eighty-seven by Hurst and Blackett. The volume's chapters track a family unravelling. John stands on his trial, defeated and wronged, then named the culprit and the convict. A mother faces her son, Susie weighs her lovers, and one chapter is called the darkness that could be felt, another the valley of humiliation.

The opening chapter returns to the great scheme that opens and closes the volume. John's thoughts keep circling back to a strange visitor from the night before. The man's curious sophistries came with a half smile, as if he saw their absurdity himself, and treated morals and reason as things outside his own soul.
60254-cassell-s-book-of-birds-vol-3:
Cassell's Book of Birds, volume three, draws its text from Dr Brehm, the great German naturalist, by way of Thomas Rymer Jones. Cassell, Petter, and Galpin issued the four volumes in London and New York, with upwards of four hundred engravings and a series of coloured plates. A plate of the Blue Grandala, at about two-thirds natural size, opens this volume.

The third volume takes up the climbers and the searchers. Flower birds, blue birds, pitpits, and honeysuckers come first, then spider-eaters, half-bills, oven birds, and bundle-nests. Nuthatches, creepers, and wall creepers round out the survey of birds that climb and probe for a living. Brehm's work was the popular bird book of its century, and Cassell's edition carried it to English parlours.
60965-a-righted-wrong-a-novel-volume-2-o:
Edmund Yates wrote a novel in three books of a wrong set right. Volume two came out in London in 1870. Yates wrote Black Sheep and The Forlorn Hope. Day leads this book, and full pay for the wrong comes next. Three notes and Hayes Meredith's big tell fill the first parts.

A talk of counsel, the come back, and the wed rite mark the turn. Shades fall, kin acts crowd in, and Margaret scents ill ahead. A year's pass closes this book's list of parts. The first page trusts the keen reader to guess a note's gist. House plots and law wrongs drive Yates's tale. Each part ends with a fresh pull.
60966-a-righted-wrong-a-novel-volume-3-o:
Edmund Yates closed a three volume novel for Tinsley Brothers of London in 1870. The last volume opens twenty years after, on a fine day in a fine summer. A grand old mansion, the Deane, stands dressed for a feast, its wide front of grey stone to the sun.

On a garden bench sit a man and a woman, little moved by the sounds of house and nature round them. They speak sadly and slowly. Her tone holds a deference that marks her as below him in rank, though their trust is full. The chapter names promise the rest. An heiress, the first moves in a game, and a mine sprung at last lead to the righting of the wrong.
6097-amelia-volume-3:
Henry Fielding's Amelia, volume three, opens its ninth book looking backwards, then forward, through conversations between Dr. Harrison and others and a dialogue between Booth and Amelia. A surprising accident, perhaps unmatched in history, and a scene of modern wit follow.

Two strangers appear, a curious conversation joins doctor, young clergyman, and the clergyman's father, and the tenth book presses on. Fielding brings Booth's prison past and Amelia's patience toward reckoning. What follows belongs strictly to the closing instalment, so the earlier instalments are not retraced or summarised here. Dr. Harrison's counsel steadies Booth through the final trials.
61093-the-yellow-flag-a-novel-volume-1-o:
The Yellow Flag, a novel by Edmund Yates, was published at London in 1872. Tinsley Brothers issued volume one of three from Catherine Street in the Strand. Yates also wrote A Waiting Race and Broken to Harness, the title page notes. A line from Goldsmith on virtue stands as the motto of the book.

The volume is inscribed to George Augustus Sala, an old friend and fellow worker. Calverley agent opens the contents, and exit Tom Durham follows in chapter two. Home sweet home, Pauline, and a little paradise fill the early chapters. A safe investment and scenes in the City set the money side of the plot. The vicar of Lullington and a hunter on the track close the listed heads.
61122-letters-from-england-volume-1-of-3:
Letters from England, by Don Manuel Alvarez Espriella, was put out as turned from Spanish, in three volumes, with a third edition in London in 1814. The hosted text is volume one. The letters cast a foreign eye on English life in the Napoleonic age.

The first letter treats the arrival at Falmouth, the custom house, and the food and noise of an inn. The road letters praise English inns and roads, yet note the dreariness of the country and the cruelty of travel. Exeter Cathedral, Honiton, and Axminster pass in view. Later letters reach Dorchester, Salisbury, and Old Sarum, with a sharp word on a spoiled cathedral. The set ends toward London. Readers get England seen fresh, with wit, by a supposed Spanish guest.
61137-the-yellow-flag-a-novel-volume-2-o:
Edmund Yates wrote The Yellow Flag, a novel in three books put out in London in 1872. Book two is the part held here, from Tinsley Brothers in the Strand. A line from Goldsmith heads the book, on the hard stop on a road that runs down to ruin. Yates had told tales of a race in wait and of a man broke to the yoke.

Parts bear names like The Act of Telling News and A Charge Kept in Trust. A check, a call to lift her with soft care, and church work speed the plot. A man is run to earth, and a third hand joins the plot in shade. Mrs Calverley loses her spouse in the late parts of the book. The tale opens as Doctor Haughton stares at an old friend in shock.
61180-the-yellow-flag-a-novel-volume-3-o:
The Yellow Flag, volume three, is the final part of a novel by Edmund Yates. Tinsley Brothers published it in London in 1872. Yates also wrote A Waiting Race and Broken to Harness. A Goldsmith motto about stopping in the downhill path fronts the volume. The contents list twelve chapters to the story's end. Rose Cottage to Let opens this final volume. John Calverley had fixed upon Hendon for his second home. There he took the pretty trusting girl who believed herself his wife.

Humphrey Statham Grows Uneasy and Martin Gurwood's Reckoning follow. An Explosion and Thou Art the Man raise the crisis. The Sealed Packet and Hagar's Visit come in the middle. Mr Wetter is Interviewed precedes the chapter called Recompense. The Envoi closes the novel at the last. Yates ends a tale of a false marriage and its reckoning.
61308-history-of-english-literature-volu:
Volume 1 of a History of English Literature, by Hippolyte Taine, appears here in the World's Great Classics set. The set was printed in New York in 1899, with near two hundred plates and portraits of great authors. Clarence Cook served as art editor. A front plate shows Shakespeare before Thomas Lucy, charged with poaching a deer.

The plate note says little is firmly known of Shakespeare's youth, when his energy ran to lawless pleasures. Taine's famed history, by contrast, builds a firm method, reading English letters through race, place, and time. Volume one starts with the old roots of English writing and moves toward the age of Shakespeare, in a grand, system-driven survey that shaped how literature was taught.
61443-a-house-divided-against-itself-vol:
Mrs Oliphant wrote a novel in three volumes, here the second. William Blackwood and Sons issued it at Edinburgh and London in MDCCCLXXXVI. Chapter Seventeen opens the hosted form on a loggia at night. Frances has just left, and her sister Constance stays behind with their father.

Constance weeps in secret, sure no one hears her on the loggia. Waring, unseen, marks how much more distinct she is than Frances in all things. A young soldier's unwanted heart and watchful strangers vex her new solitude. Readers gain the grave middle of a tale of family strain in Italy.
61444-a-house-divided-against-itself-vol:
Mrs Oliphant wrote A House Divided Against Itself, here in volume three. Blackwood put it out at Edinburgh and London in 1886. Chapter thirty-three opens in a drawing-room at Eaton Square. Lady Markham receives young Gaunt with gracious kindness. Frances hovers about him, full of questions, and her mother insists he stay to luncheon. Markham's hansom draws up at the door as they talk.

Gaunt had been unwilling to come, in a crisis of his life, yet the welcome soothes him. All about him is familiar to Constance: her mother, her sister, and the rooms where she spent her life. Questions about Constance are hard for him to answer, since he longs for her. Frances is bright, and Gaunt's suppressed passion shows through his calm. Oliphant closes her tale of a split house with love and held-back fire.
61632-letters-from-england-volume-3-of-3:
Letters from England purport to come from a Spanish nobleman traveller. Longman printed volume three in London in 1814, third edition. The letters are cast as Don Manuel Alvarez Espriella work in Spain. A head note owns the Spaniard is imagined, the work Southey's.

Letter fifty four weighs the Bible in English homes for good. Curiosity and credulity, a learned pig, and show freaks follow. Newspapers, puffs, and reviews get a sharp letter of their own. Quakers, Christmas customs, whist, and commerce fill later letters here. Despard conspiracy and the growth of trade power fill two more of the letters.
6176-pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-:
Shon McGann's Tobogan Ride opens Parker's third volume. Shon lies on buffalo robes in a mountain hut, singing of Farcalladen Rise with knees pressed to saddle, sparks from hoofs, and hearts beating hard toward the glen. He vows never to go back to Farcalladen more.

Pretty Pierre, Jo Gordineer, the Honourable Just Trafford, and Prince Levis share the hut, pipe smoke, and song. Pere Champagne, The Scarlet Hunter, and The Stone complete the volume. Attention here rests only on the third set of tales, not on any tale belonging to another set. Song and snow carry the volume's tales along.
6188-northern-lights-volume-3:
When the Swallows Homeward Fly opens Parker's third Northern Lights volume, as an arrogant sun stalks into evening trailing gold and crimson banners, and swift twilight streams over land. Two men on a high hill watch it pass, one with a look like light in a window to a lost traveler.

That man made a journey few attempted and fewer finished, traveling on foot and alone, save dogs and Indian guides, to snowy Arctic regions where a continent's shoulder juts into northwestern seas. Ice hummocks housed him, pemmican and raw fish fed him. George's Wife and Marcile complete the volume.
61949-the-impending-sword-a-novel-vol-1-:
Impending Sword is a novel by Edmund Yates, issued in London in 1874 in three volumes. This is volume one of the three, printed for Tinsley Brothers in the Strand. Yates is named as author of Black Sheep, The Rock Ahead, and The Yellow Flag. A verse from Shakespeare on vengeance from heaven stands as its motto.

The volume is affectionately inscribed to friends of the author in New York City. Its contents are headed Book the First, The Empire City, in the list. Chapters run from The Curtain Rises and The Letter of Instructions to The Shadow of Parting and Helen Diary. A mysterious figure enters the list soon after those domestic titles. The catalogue sample shows talk of a returned traveller from Europe. He talks of being made a prince or a duke abroad. That talk gives a note of the ambition that drives the plot.
6208-the-trail-of-the-sword-volume-3:
The third part of The Trail of the Sword begins with a chapter whose title turns water into wine. Three months on, George Gering looks ahead with delight to a pair of sea journeys. His appetite for one journey sharpens his appetite for the other, although treasure hunting pleases most men no more than a wedding does.

Gering already carries Jessica's promise to marry him, and he soon departs beside William Phips toward Spanish territory. When he reaches New York again, word that Hudson's Bay posts have fallen spreads alarm through the town. Colonel Richard Nicholls grows furious at the news, while Jessica, staying at Government House, feels deeply shaken.
62084-the-deceased-wife-s-sister-and-my-:
Volume three of The Deceased Wife’s Sister and My Beautiful Neighbour closes the tale. Richard Bentley and Son issued the book in London in eighteen hundred seventy four. Its last part bears the name My Beautiful Neighbour alone. A young scholar tells the tale in his own first person.

Martelli, his new tutor, proves sound, brisk, and cold of fancy. Greek and Latin lie at the man’s finger ends. Yet not five lines of verse could his wide lore yield, the youth notes. His rule recalls a stern French master of the boy’s school days. His stiff bow shows he knows his place in the house. But the youth’s mind strays from its tasks. A strange fair shape, met on a midnight walk, haunts his thoughts. No path to her door can his wit yet find or force.
6213-the-translation-of-a-savage-volume-:
The Faith of Comrades opens the third volume of The Translation of a Savage. Francis Armour steps out of his wife's room, goes downstairs without noise to the library, and takes a seat there. Nothing feels lonelier, he reflects, than facing his own conscience alone.

An enemy can hand a man a harsh hour, a friend can hand him a grieving hour, and time by himself can hand him a quiet hour. Yet when conscience settles upon each small rise of memory and gestures slowly, a labourer driven around a treadmill suffers no greater pain. The butler comes in to learn what is wanted, and Armour dismisses him with a silent wave.
6221-the-trespasser-volume-3:
Gaston Belward spends his mornings in the family solicitor's office, turning over old papers with a strange sense that something waits to be found. A clerk brings him a small box found inside another box of the Belward-Staplings, a distant branch of the family, and the key still sits in its lock. The find opens the last part of his story, where past deeds press hard on present choices.

These closing chapters carry Belward afar, set him between two worlds, and bring the old Adam of his nature face to face with love. A woman and a man confront what they cannot bear, and an old biblical call sounds over the end. Parker closes his romance of claim and heritage with passion, guilt, and a plea for return.
6226-the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-3:
Moray has been shut from the outer world for months, with a new jailer in place of Gabord and sentinels who refuse all news. He hears nothing of Alixe, little of Doltaire or Bigot, and no sign at all of Voban. The chapters here take him through a chamber of torture and past the bars of his cage. Then comes a steep path of conquest, with a dancer and the Bastille waiting in his tale.

This middle volume is the prison book of Parker's memoir, tense with waiting, watching, and small acts of will. Moray studies his jailer as closely as his jailer studies him, and every scrap of news becomes precious. It shows a captive officer keeping his mind sharp while his fate is argued by powers far beyond his cell walls.
6232-the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-:
The night and morning after Guida's marriage pass slowly, and the day wears on toward the sailing of the Narcissus. Guida works at home with feverish unrest, settles her grandfather in his great armchair for his afternoon sleep, and spins and sings as he drowses. From her kitchen door she can see blue water, a perfect sky, and Noirmont Point, round which her husband's ship will soon vanish.

This middle volume follows a new wife left behind while a ship puts to sea, with neighbours watching and tongues ready to judge. Maitresse Aimable fingers her rosary for Guida, and the island's small world presses close. Parker writes the parting in domestic detail, so that a single afternoon of spinning, waiting, and watching carries the weight of a marriage just made.
62344-my-shipmate-louise-the-romance-of-:
My Shipmate Louise: The Romance of a Wreck, volume two, is a sea novel by Clark Russell. Chatto and Windus of London published the three-volume work in 1890. It carries chapters fifteen to twenty-eight.

Chapters promise a singular plot, a wreck sighted, a night adrift, and a search of the wreck. The volume opens on a rumour running through the cuddy. A sailor, buried by old Keeling, is said to be alive aboard. He lies in handcuffs or leg-irons somewhere, the whisper runs. Soon the crew gather that a plot is afoot, and Hemmeridge is under arrest. A ruffian has lain hidden in the ship's hold for weeks, fed by confederates.
62375-my-shipmate-louise-the-romance-of-:
My Shipmate Louise, Volume Three, is the closing volume of a sea novel by Clark Russell, printed in London by Chatto and Windus in 1890. Its subtitle calls it the romance of a wreck. The publisher's list at the front shows the three-volume world it lived in, with Bret Harte, Ouida, and James Payn in the same season. The contents here begin at Chapter Twenty-Nine.

The captain begins a story, then makes a proposal, and a form of agreement is drawn. A tragedy follows, and the carpenter calls a council. The narrator assents, takes a captaincy of his own, and converses with Wetherly. Cape Horn, land, and the island build the long climax. An escape and a sailing away lead to the conclusion. Russell was the sea novel's master, and this wreck is among his set pieces.
6239-the-lane-that-had-no-turning-volume:
Annette has kept her dot ready for many months, chest, bed, linen, and yarn inventoried each day, first with pride and then more shyly, as Benoit does not come. He promised to return with the first drive of logs in summer, when the little church of St. Saviour's would bless their marriage. Benoit has the brightest scarf, the merriest laugh, and the quickest eyes in Pontiac, and almost anyone would have believed him.

This volume gathers eight Pontiac tales around Annette's wait and a miller's marriage. Mathurin, a lime-burner, a woodsman's story of a great white chief, Uncle Jim, a house with a tall porch, and Parpon the dwarf complete the set. Parker writes village courtship and work with affection and irony, letting a delayed lover stand for all the hopes a parish pins on one summer. The comedy is gentle, the ache beneath it real.
6252-michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-sword:
Leicester, a man of high place whose hand has tied and untied knots of court intrigue for years, stoops in this volume to a small game that earns him scorn. He has turned the Queen's mind and foiled Spanish, German, and French diplomacy. He checkmated the Medici by hidden means, yet he stands hated by most and loved by none save a royal mistress who now keeps him more from custom than affection. His rise, built on labour and rashness alike, begins to cost him.

This third volume sets a young woman against the Earl, as she refuses to measure swords with him and yet will not yield. She tells him plainly that she has friends, and that in her greatest need she will go seeking them, thinking of the Queen. Parker writes court power as a trap, where the grandest player can look smallest when he bullies the unfriended.
6258-donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-eg:
Wyndham Bimbashi's career in Egypt has been a run of mistakes, Parker begins, for he is opinionated, unlucky, and fond of grave acts on his own light responsibility. He scorns the native mind and the native official, and lacks the gift his fellow countrymen often show of working through local custom toward sound rule. High-handed acts of his cause riots in native villages, and the man at the wheel must answer for the course he steers.

This third volume pairs that tale with a tyrant and a lady. A woman by the Nile writes steadily for an hour, then looks up at muddy water, laden boats, and Muslims at prayer with faces toward Mecca. Parker sets British bluster beside Egyptian patience, and lets both meet on the river. The two stories show power misused and power endured, where one officer's temper can shake a district.
6270-embers-volume-3:
Camden Town opens this volume in verse, asking how many years of sun and snow have passed since the poet wandered its streets and shade. Days turn out to be years, and years forever, while joys and ills press on heart and brain as the only true measures of age. The poet, young in years, feels old in all these, and wonders if he knows the man his younger self begot.

This third volume of poems runs from Camden Town through Juniper Cove and its twenty years after, listening, nevertheless, Ishmael, and over the hills. A deliverer, a desert road, a son of the Nile, a farewell from the harem, and an Arab love song follow, with a camel driver, a tall Daboon, and Nell Latore. Parker writes travel and memory in short lines, where a place name alone can open a whole past.
6277-the-money-master-volume-3:
A young singer at the Manor Cartier asks who will walk the wood with her, for she fears to walk alone and has known no dangers. Applause breaks out at the last note, with cries of encore, and she looks round with frank pleasure on the little group about her. A particular person answers, the Man from Outside, sitting near a bright wood fire on a cool night near June, delicate and fluent in French with a slight English accent.

This third epoch holds only three chapters: the man from outside, a refusal to go, and a good market. The singer is asked for a perfect song, a clear fountain tune ringing in her head all day, while toasts rise to Jean Jacques Barbille. Parker writes a brief, bright interval, where music and company soften a life that has known harder dealing, before misfortune gathers again.
6283-the-world-for-sale-volume-3:
It is a fine day, Fleda says, and Ingolby, blind, agrees, though she wonders from delicacy how he knows. He explains with a dreamy smile, hands smoothing a coverlet like a wrinkled map, that the blind gain new senses. A light breath of wind, fresh crisp air, the smell of sun, a light frost showing dry ground, and wild fowl crying south all tell him. One sense less gives more power to the rest.

This final book runs from two life pieces and a fowler's snare through a secret man. The return of Belisarius, at long last, man proposes, a sleeper, and the world for sale follow. Fleda watches a primeval scene and dreams of sight restored, with a hovering sense of invasion at its edge. Parker closes his western tale with patience, as love learns to see without eyes.
6294-no-defense-volume-3:
A planter sighs at his writing table on Christmas Day and looks out over lands he made his own on the Thomas River, hours from Spanish Town. Plateau, mountains, and ravines frame the estate. He has done his duty to slaves and folk, with presents, a morning breakfast, and festivities. A feast in Creole style follows for attorneys, overseers, and officers. He turns with cynicism from an overladen table centred on stewed wild boar.

This third book brings a letter, strangers, Salem, and Lord Mallow intervening, with a clash of race and Sheila having her say. The coming of Noreen and a visit with the governor follow, and the question of what happened next hangs over all. Parker moves his Irish tale to Jamaica, where a planter's Christmas plenty cannot hide old wounds, and Dyck Calhoun, seen at Spanish Town, carries prison's mark into a new world.
62966-the-little-review-may-1914-vol-1-n:
The Little Review for May 1914 is the third number of a new Chicago literary magazine. Margaret Anderson edited it from the Fine Arts Building in that city. Literature, drama, music, and art stand on its masthead as its fields.

The table of contents shows the magazine's range and temper. An opening essay argues the cause of literature in America. Anderson herself takes up the challenge of Emma Goldman in these pages. A short play, fiction, and an impression piece fill the creative pages. The opening essay attacks a plea for state honours for writers. Its author holds that no great writer begs official prizes and subsidies.
6298-carnac-s-folly-volume-3:
Months pass, and destiny makes new drawings, Parker says, as Carnac goes with his mother to paint at Charlemont. Tarboe works the mills with success. Junia hears from Carnac in a letter that reads like a friend's yet carries sadness. Then she leaves west again at an hour's notice to nurse her aunt. Quebec politics boil as the Dominion government nears the polls, and even secluded cottages on the St. Lawrence argue the administration's virtues and faults.

This third book moves from a great decision to Carnac as candidate, news heard by Junia and Tarboe, a secret meeting, and point to point contests. A man who would not, a blue paper, a challenge, and an exit follow, with a woman's letter and a dream by Tarboe. Parker closes the tale with politics, painting, and a way home found at last.
63142-harry-joscelyn-vol-1-of-3:
Mrs Oliphant wrote Harry Joscelyn, shown here in Volume One of a three volume novel issued at London in 1881. Oliphant had writ The Chronicles of Carlingford. Chapter One is named The White House. A mother walks a long, low room and wrings her hands as the tale opens.

Her daughter sits calm and knits by the fire. Harry is in a loud row with his father in the next room. The daughter says such rows come as sure as night after day. The mother says she can never get used to them. Wind roars down the valley outside. The scene sets a house split by strife between father and son. Love and pride drive the long tale that follows.
63241-medical-jurisprudence-volume-1-of-:
Volume 1 of Medical Jurisprudence is a work in three volumes by J. A. Paris and J. S. M. Fonblanque. Paris was a doctor of medicine and a fellow of the Royal Society and of the Royal College of Physicians. Fonblanque was a barrister at law. A Latin motto from Hebenstreit stands on the title page, on the bond that joins medicine and law.

A note by the transcriber states the rules of the text. Words in italics in the first print are marked by underscores here. Some slips of the press have been set right, and the changes are listed in a note at the end of the book. The work treats the ground where the art of healing meets the law: proof, poisons, and the duties of the medical man in court, as its title and plan set out.
63385-alone-on-a-wide-wide-sea-vol-1-of-:
Alone on a Wide Wide Sea, volume one, is a novel by W Clark Russell, author of My Shipmate Louise and The Romance of Jenny Harlowe. Chatto and Windus of London published the three-volume novel in 1892. Russell was the sea novelist of his day, and the title promises his element.

The first volume opens inland, in Piertown, a western city of wide streets and terraces under hills, crowned by its Abbey Church. Orchards, a red-glittering river, and the salt breath of a near ocean set the scene. The chapters move from a boating trip to the riddle of Who Am I, and on to Alphonse's conjectures. Then the sea takes the book: on board the Notre Dame, a terrible night, and Captain Frederick Ladmore. A kind little woman closes the volume, with two more volumes of the wide sea still to come.
63386-alone-on-a-wide-wide-sea-vol-2-of-:
W Clark Russell opens the middle volume of a sea tale with a publisher's page of new novels, then the title. Chatto and Windus issued volume two at London in 1892. The tale runs to three volumes in all.

Chapter nine, The Cry of a Child, opens at sea near one in the morning. The narrator has been shut in his cabin all day. He climbs to the poop deck under a bull's-eye lamp. The ship looks so lonely he could think himself the only living soul aboard. Later chapters bring Alice Lee and fresh clothes for the castaway. One asks, Am I a Calthorpe? A gipsy, a fortune, and a dying friend close the volume. Russell wrote the sea as few landsmen could.
63562-harry-joscelyn-vol-3-of-3:
Mrs Oliphant wrote this novel Harry Joscelyn, volume three of three. Hurst and Blackett printed the final volume in London in 1881. Chapter one, After Ten Years, opens in the Fell country quiet. Harry vanished from the White House ten years before this.

Joan has married Philip Selby and rules Heatonshaw as mistress now. She can scarce recall her old Joscelyn habits and customs there. No child measures her years, a misfortune borne with submission. Philip himself would gladly risk children for the blessing denied. Chronicles of Carlingford stands as her best known past work on the title page.
63903-the-duke-s-daughter-and-the-fugiti:
The Duke's Daughter and The Fugitives, volume three of three, is a novel by Mrs Oliphant, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1890. This volume continues The Fugitives. Chapter six opens on a morning when Latour is more cheerful than usual. Men have come to inspect the woods, and though they are not picturesque figures, they make the village street lively.

That liveliness delights Janey and cheers Helen in spite of herself. The sun shines down the street, catching a little window in a thatched roof, the weather-cock on the tower of the chateau, and the church spire. A ruddy glow touched with frost lies over all the country. Groups of men take their way in a broken stream toward the woods. Some are burly French farmers; some are the poachers of the commune, who know every tree.
64080-morley-ashton-a-story-of-the-sea-v:
Morley Ashton is a story of the sea by James Grant in three volumes. The hosted text holds the first volume of the three. Grant had past fame with a romance of war and a fairy tale. The book came out in London in the year eighteen seventy six.

Parts open with a blind fate, a lodge, and a sly man named Hawkshaw. Feuds, doubts, and a last parting fill the shore side of the tale. The hero then ships on a London craft and meets an old mate at sea. Moon light, tropic seas, and a shark scene mark the wide sea road. Poor Ethel at home gives the tale its soft shore heart.
64081-morley-ashton-a-story-of-the-sea-v:
James Grant wrote this tale of the sea, in three books of which this is the second. It was printed at London in 1876. He had made a fame with tales of war in past years. The list of parts of this book shows the run of the tale at sea. Mariquita Escudero stands at its head. Then the crew of the Hermione grows cross, and Rose and the ship's medic come to the fore.

A man goes over the side, a white face is seen, and the medic hears dark talk in the bunks of the crew. Plans for the guard of the ship are laid, and the ship sails to the wind. A storm, four men cast on a shore, and the finds of Captain Hawkshaw crowd the mid parts.
64082-morley-ashton-a-story-of-the-sea-v:
Morley Ashton, a story of the sea, closes in this third of three volumes. James Grant wrote the tale, fresh from The Romance of War's success. Tinsley Brothers of London brought the set out in the year 1876. Twenty-five chapters run from Sail Ho to the anchor let go at last. Ethel stands at the heart of this last volume's sea peril.

The fortitude of Ethel and a door in the bulkhead open the list. Ethel among the mutineers and a snare laid fill the early chapters. Pedro's wound, remorse, and a modern Spanish rogue's tale follow on. Ignez de Moreno and her dressing closet stand in the mid list. The great crime of Pedro Barradas darkens the late chapters here. Eight against eighty and a mangrove creek fight precede the close. The crew had seized the ship to run her for themselves.
64321-the-convict-ship-volume-3-of-3:
Clark Russell wrote a sea novel in three volumes, with volume three printed in London in 1895. Russell was known for The Wreck of the Grosvenor. Adverts at the front list new library novels by Grant Allen, Walter Besant, and others. Chapter heads in this volume are told from a woman's view aboard the ship.

She witnesses the departure of officers and soldiers, and listens to convicts debating below. In the cuddy a crowd of convicts roar out a vulgar popular song of the time. She sups with her sweetheart amid the risk and noise. Hunger, plots, and the rough order of a convict transport drive the last volume to its close at sea.
6441-uncle-robert-s-geography-uncle-robe:
Francis W. Parker and Nellie Lathrop Helm, in the Home Reading Series, send Uncle Robert to visit a farm family, where children's knowledge of farm life is warmly recognised. Children feel his sympathy for their work and are led to closer study, for everything they see and do matters, exalting daily life. Descriptions of farms should cover plant and animal life and the means and processes of farm work.

Frank draws a map of the farm, and drawing, modelling, and painting enter early, for children draw boldly unless criticism outruns skill. A new thermometer, animals, flower garden, sunlight and shadow, and a barometer follow, with a walk in the woods, birds and flowers, and a thundershower. Susie plants mignonette seeds in soft, warm soil and asks if they will grow. Parker writes geography as farm life, learned by doing.
64556-lodore-vol-2-of-3:
The author of Frankenstein wrote a novel in three volumes, here the second. Richard Bentley issued Lodore in London in 1835. A verse from Ford on life's storms fronts the title page. Eighteen chapters fill this middle volume of the set. The contents list runs from Chapter I through Chapter XVIII, with no titles given for any of them.

Mr Villiers becomes the steady guest of Mrs Elizabeth and her niece. His bright, ready spirit lifts the gloom of their dingy London house. Silence and neglect had walled the two women off from the sun. Readers gain a grave tale of love, duty, and a father's hard design.
64557-lodore-vol-3-of-3:
Lodore, in its third volume, is a novel by the author of Frankenstein. Richard Bentley published it in London in 1835, in three volumes. The contents of this last volume run to eighteen chapters and a conclusion. Verses of Ford and Shakespeare stand as mottoes at its head.

The volume opens on a morning after a night of fear for Ethel, its heroine. She has slept peacefully, and wakes late to a knock at her door. Saunders has returned, bearing a letter she has awaited in dread. The letter, from Villiers, breathes caution in every line of it. He will not come to Duke Street, he writes, for safety's sake. She must send a few lines back by the messenger instead. If what he apprehended has happened, they must bear a day's separation. The closing movement of the novel turns on that threatened parting.
6457-the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-a:
Frances Burney's diary and letters, volume three, covers 1792 to 1840, with notes by W. C. Ward and Lord Macaulay's essay as preface. The volume opens with French political emigrants at Juniper Hall and Miss Burney's marriage to M. d'Arblay. Arrivals, the Doctor's five daughters, a visit to Arthur Young, and the Duke de Liancourt's abortive efforts at Rouen and escape to England fill the early pages.

Madame de Genlis's hasty retreat, a nobleman of the ancien regime, ducal vivacity and sadness, and graceful offers of hospitality follow, with severe decrees against emigrants and revolutionary societies in the background. A mid letter turns indignant at a man whose first prepossession the writers conquered by pains, only to see him act as coadjutor with Barras and other villains. Burney writes revolution as lived experience, in letters and diary entries close to events.
65328-mrs-arthur-vol-1-of-3:
Mrs Oliphant, who wrote The Chronicles of Carlingford, stands behind this novel in three volumes. Hurst and Blackett printed the first volume of Mrs Arthur in London in 1877. Lines from The Taming of the Shrew and from Dibdin head the tale.

Is Mr Curtis here, a voice asks at the door in chapter one. The Bates family, packed in their little parlour, bursts out laughing. I should think he was — rather, says Charley Bates. Ask Nancy, says Matilda, the eldest daughter. Curtis's courtship of Nancy is plainly the house joke, and Mr Bates sits in his big chair at the heart of it. Oliphant's warm, shrewd eye for family life drives the three volumes.
65329-mrs-arthur-vol-2-of-3:
Mrs Arthur, volume two, is the middle volume of a three volume novel by Mrs Oliphant, issued at London in 1877. Oliphant had written the chronicles of Carlingford, named on the title page. Lines from Shakespeare and from a Dibdin song stand at the front. The second volume opens on its hero, Arthur Curtis, and a letter he has forgotten.

Old Davies had given him the letter days before, and he had not thought of it since. It lay crushed in the pocket of his coat. The sight of his sister, and all the clashing feelings of the time, had put it out of his head. What could there be pleasant in such a letter at such a time, he asks himself. A final sermon on his folly, he fears, on his very wedding day.
65413-the-lives-of-celebrated-travellers:
The Lives of Celebrated Travellers, volume two of three, is a set of travel biographies by James Augustus St John. Harper of New York issued this stereotype edition in 1832. Its motto, from Pope's Homer, praises men who wandered from clime to clime, noting manners and surveying states. The volume opens with Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, the botanist who lived from 1656 to 1708.

Tournefort's life runs from Aix through France, Spain, and the Pyrenees, where he was taken for a robber. Commanded to travel in the East, he visited Candia, Mount Ida, Constantinople, the Black Sea, and Georgia. The life of Dr Thomas Shaw follows. A table preserved in the copy traces Shaw's road through Egypt and down the Nile to Syria, where he was taken prisoner and ransomed. It lists extraordinary lights, prodigious flights of storks, and waterspouts.
65615-the-master-of-aberfeldie-volume-1-:
James Grant wrote a Scots novel of a house, a will, and crossed love. Volume one came out in London in 1884. Grant wrote The Romance of War and The Cameronians. Deer stalk on the hills starts the tale in the wild. Hawke Holcroft steps in as a key new man at once.

Uncle Raymond's will and the Grahams of Dundargue set the knot. Olive and Allan, love's grief in two tongues, and a ride fill it. A picnic at Dunsinane and a gold bangle mark bright turns. Eveline's suitor and a truth told to Holcroft stir strife. Allan turns strange, and Olive shifts her heart. House tale fans get Grant's full store.
65616-the-master-of-aberfeldie-volume-2-:
The Master of Aberfeldie, volume two of three, is a novel by James Grant, author of The Romance of War. It was printed at London in 1884. The volume opens with a chapter called Mystery. All the guests have left Dundargue but Hawke Holcroft, who departs in two days for his chambers in town.

Allan, the Master of Aberfeldie, must keep polite and easy terms with Holcroft as a guest. Yet he feels an undefined change in the man's manner toward him. The Master, a man of the keenest sense of honour, writhes when he hears Holcroft address Olive or Eveline. The chapters run through suspense, an oubliette, lovers, a wedding, and mistrust. Later chapters march with the Black Watch and cross to the land of the Pharaohs. Grant blends Scottish house drama with military adventure. The volume ends mid-tale, to be finished in the third.
65617-the-master-of-aberfeldie-volume-3-:
The Master of Aberfeldie, volume three, by James Grant, was published at London in 1884. Hurst and Blackett issued the third volume of the three volume novel. Grant wrote The Romance of War and The Cameronians, the title page notes. Suspicion opens the contents of this final volume as chapter one.

At Tel-el-Kebir and at Grand Cairo carry the tale to Egypt in the next heads. The telegram and dead and buried in the sand fill the war chapters. A skirmish in the desert, then Hurdell Hall, bring the scene home to England. Sir Harry, the cub hunting, and Allan adventure fill the middle contents list. Among the dwellers in tents and Kismet close the Egyptian thread of the tale. Scotland and the Egyptian war of 1882 meet in this Grant romance.
66083-the-little-review-may-1915-vol-2-n:
Little Review for May 1915 is a monthly magazine of the arts. Anderson edited it from the Fine Arts Building in Chicago. Volume two, number three, it sold at fifteen cents a copy. A year cost a dollar fifty by post to subscribers then. Contents list literature, drama, music, and art across the number.

Poems by Dawson, Bodenheim, and Fletcher fill the verse pages first. Anderson writes What We Are Fighting For as the issue's argument. Comfort, Soule, Aldington, and Lowell treat ignition, solitude, and poets. Hecht's Sermon in the Depths and Sandburg on Spoon River follow. Mother Jones and Elizabeth Gurley Flynn get a notice by the editor.
66120-the-scottish-cavalier-an-historica:
The Scottish Cavalier is a historical romance in three volumes by James Grant, published in eighteen fifty. Grant had written The Romance of War and memoirs of Kirkaldy of Grange. Volume one opens with a preface that explains the tale's sources in detail. Grant meant to add notes, then chose to fold them into the preface.

The hero is Walter Fenton, set among famous names of the late Stuart age. Many minor figures, the author insists, truly lived and breathed in those days. Douglas of Finland courted Annie Laurie, whose song still bears her name. An old halberdier who fired guns at Sedgemoor got forty pounds for the service. Hugh Blair's Edinburgh tavern and Lord Mersington's disgrace are both vouched for. The tale looks back to the days of Dundee and the Jacobite cause.
66122-the-scottish-cavalier-an-historica:
Volume three of The Scottish Cavalier is a historical romance by James Grant. Henry Colburn published the three volume novel in London in 1850. Grant had written The Romance of War and a memoir of Kirkaldy of Grange. This final volume opens with the chapter Lilian. She is being carried off in a coach over frozen snow. Her cries for aid are lost inside the closed vehicle.

The contents run through the revolution in Scotland. Chapters treat the sack of Holyrood and the night of the revolution in Edinburgh. Claverhouse rides to the rescue in one chapter. The pass of Killycrankie and the last hour of Dundee come near the middle. Later chapters move to Saint Germains and the battle of Steinkirke. A veiled picture, a secret stair, and an iron room supply the gothic touches. Love and principle close the tale.
66413-second-to-none-a-military-romance-:
Second to None: A Military Romance, Volume Two, continues James Grant's three volume novel, printed at London by Routledge in 1864. Grant also wrote The Romance of War, The Captain of the Guard and The Yellow Frigate. The second volume's twenty-five chapters follow a British expedition against the French coast. It opens with the march to Dol and a skirmish.

The chapter heads sketch the campaign and the love plot together. Hussars again, my nurse, news of the army and Bourgneuf follow. Love and illusion, I become a soubrette, Hautois and the boudoir turn to intrigue. A story of Ninon de l'Enclos is told inside the tale. Discovered, suspense, the bloodhound and the forest of Saint Aubin du Cormier raise the danger. Grant writes the romance of the old wars with a soldier's library behind him.
66581-colville-of-the-guards-volume-2-of:
James Grant wrote a military novel in three volumes, of which this is the second, published at London in 1885. Grant had written The Romance of War and The Cameronians. Contents open with The Queen's Shilling. Chapters move in London, at number 60 Park Lane, and through a chapter called So Near and Yet So Far.

Going to the Front takes the hero east. At Jellalabad, a fight with the Mohmunds, and the Lughman Valley follow. A fancy ball and the Tenth Hussars lighten the middle. Lost and its sequel close the list before At Cabul. Grant's novels of Scottish soldiers were Victorian staples.
66582-colville-of-the-guards-volume-3-of:
Colville of the Guards, Volume Three, is a military novel by James Grant, printed in London in 1885. Grant also wrote The Romance of War and The Scottish Cavalier. The set ran to three volumes, and this one closes the tale. Its chapters open at sea with the Flying Foam.

Ellinor, left in peril, wakes in a ship's cabin among strange faces. The action moves to the Bala Hissar and the fort of Mahmoud Shah. A fugitive, a new snare, and a house by the Fleethen thicken the plot. Later chapters ride with Roberts' column and fight the battle of Charasiah. The fate of Ellinor resolves before a close among the birks of Invermay. Grant, an old soldier's son, fills the book with the Afghan war's dust and drums.
66680-the-flowering-plants-of-south-afri:
The Flowering Plants of South Africa, here volume three, is a magazine of hand coloured figures with descriptions of the flowering plants native to South Africa. I B Pole Evans edited the work from Pretoria, where he led the Division of Botany and Plant Pathology and directed the Botanical Survey of the Union. L Reeve and Company in London and the Speciality Press in South Africa issued the volume in nineteen twenty three.

Pole Evans gave the volume to Sir Frank Umhlali Reynolds of Lynton Hall, Natal, whose love of gardening is surpassed only by his public spirit, he says. Plate eighty one opens the set with Clematopsis stanleyi of the Transvaal and tropical Africa. A note traces the plant through the Kew Bulletin of nineteen twenty and the Botanical Magazine of eighteen ninety one. Botanists and gardeners get fine plates with learned notes, plate by plate.
66873-the-cameronians-a-novel-volume-1-o:
The Cameronians, volume one of three, is a military novel by James Grant, printed at London in 1881. Grant inscribes the story to George Routledge, his old friend and publisher. In the preface he tells of the old Scottish regiment from which the tale takes its title. Its hero is described as a member of that regiment.

The regiment, Grant warns, is on the point of losing its identity. After July of that year it would be joined with the 90th Perthshire Light Infantry as the Scottish Cameronian Rifles. It would lose its scarlet uniform, its colours, and its royal yellow facings. Grant doubts the merits of the new regimental system and fears endless confusion. The chapters follow Hew through love-making, first impressions, cover-shooting, and a vow. A revelation, a crisis, and Cecil's departure carry the volume on. The novel opens a three-volume tale of love and soldiering.
66874-the-cameronians-a-novel-volume-2-o:
The Cameronians, volume two of three, is a novel by James Grant, printed in London by Richard Bentley and Son in 1881. Grant wrote The Romance of War and Old and New Edinburgh. Bentley were publishers in ordinary to Queen Victoria. Readers should start at volume one.

Chapters open with a weak invention of the enemy and Cecil receives his conge. In the Prince Street Gardens, a fruitless task, and the regimental ball follow. Hew triumph, I have come for your sword, and the court martial pace the mid part. Gone, the initials, and turning the tables raise the strain. By the Morava, a mystery, on duty, and the Castle of Palenka carry the war east. Margarita, Captain Guebhard, the Black Mountaineers, and Cecil comes to grief close the volume. Army tale fans get Scots regiment romance.
66875-the-cameronians-a-novel-volume-3-o:
James Grant wrote The Cameronians, a novel in three books put out in London in 1881. Grant had won a name with The Romance of War. Book three is the last of the set. Its parts pick up threads left loose in the first two books.

The book opens in the rose rich grounds of Eaglescraig, a Scots home in French style. News at last, a chance meet, and a pair split by fate lead the first parts. A strange charge, a grim proof, and a wire from afar raise the heat. The tale then sails to war, with a scout ride and the fight at Zaitchar. A ride for life or death, a note from Mary, and the heights of Djunis fill the crest. Wounds, a rescue, and a last part that crowns all close the long tale.
67135-the-lives-of-celebrated-travellers:
The Lives of Celebrated Travellers, volume three, is a biographical collection by James Augustus St John. Harper printed this stereotype edition in New York in 1832. A Pope couplet on wandering from clime to clime fronts the title. The contents of this volume open with Mungo Park. Park was born in 1771 and died in 1806, the heads state. He was born at Fowlshiels near Selkirk and apprenticed to a surgeon. He finished his education at Edinburgh and removed to London. Sir Joseph Banks became known to him there in the account.

He sailed as surgeon on an East Indiaman before Africa called. The African Association engaged him to trace the course of the Niger. Fever, delirium, and the horrors of the rainy season follow. He studied the Mandingo language and visited native kings. St John retells explorers' lives for the general reader.
67226-the-king-s-own-borderers-a-militar:
The Kings Own Borderers is a military romance by James Grant in three volumes. The hosted text holds the first volume of the three. Grant had past fame with tales of war and a yellow frigate. The book came out in London in the year eighteen sixty five.

Verse at its front calls up grand old fields of Spain and lost chiefs. The front note says its hero is a gent who serves as a plain rank man. That was a real old way for young gents to learn war in the field. The march of Sir John Moore in Spain frames the heroes first wars. Some scenes, the author owns, are not pure made up tale at all.
67228-the-king-s-own-borderers-a-militar:
The King Own Borderers is a military romance in three volumes by James Grant, printed in London in 1865, and the hosted text is volume three. Grant had written Second to None and The Romance of War. A verse on the grand old fields of Spain heads the book.

Chapters in this last volume open with Playing with Fire and The Poisoned Wine. The army marches, halts at Azumar, and advances into Spain. Later heads name a message from the enemy, a prisoner, and a court martial. The retreat, fresh disasters, and a smile of fortune pace the mid part. The combat of Lugo and the battle of Corunna stand near the close, then a burial and a night of revelations. Readers should start at volume one for the full Peninsular War tale.
67337-the-two-dianas-volume-1-of-3:
Alexandre Dumas wrote a romance in three volumes, with volume one printed at London and Boston in 1894. The claim of Dumas to stand first among historical romancers, past or present, can hardly be disputed, the introductory note says. His magic pen finds rich material in the period of the tale. The action covers the later years of Henri the Second and the brief sad reign of his eldest son Francois the Second.

Francois was the ill fated husband of Mary Stuart, whose later history has hidden her brief time on the French throne. These years saw the spirit of the Reformation in France grow toward open war. The name of John Calvin won its lasting fame then, and his followers, Coligny among them, began the crusade for freedom of worship. Two Dianas, court love, and coming massacre fill the volume.
67338-the-two-dianas-volume-2-of-3:
Two Dianas, volume two, is a historical novel by Alexandre Dumas in English. Dent of London and Little, Brown of Boston issued it in 1894. Portraits front it, with Diane de Poitiers as the chief plate. Van Muyden drew and etched the original illustrations for the set. Contents open as divers occurrences artfully fall out together in France.

How Arnauld du Thill caused Arnauld du Thill to be hanged follows. His bucolic dreams and the Peuquoy family's arms, hopes, and tears ensue. The misfortunes of Martin Guerre fill the next two chapter heads. Mary Stuart's loveliness flits across the course of the story there. The other Diane and a grand scheme for a great man follow.
67462-the-elizabethan-stage-vol-3:
The Elizabethan Stage, volume 3, by Chambers, was printed at Oxford at the Clarendon Press in 1923. A frontispiece shows a theatre from the Venice Terence of 1499. This volume holds chapters nineteen to twenty-three. They treat staging at court, and staging in the theatres of the sixteenth century. Staging in the seventeenth century, the printing of plays, and playwrights follow.

A note on symbols explains the editor's marks for uncertain dates, earlier or later than the year named. Italic dates mark production rather than publication. The court chapter opens with a survey of earlier dissertations, naming Graves on the court and the London theatres as the most valuable for its subject. Chambers's four volumes remain the great quarry of fact on the early English stage: documents first, theory second.
68293-dulcie-carlyon-a-novel-volume-1-of:
James Grant wrote Dulcie Carlyon, a novel in three volumes, from Ward and Downey at London in 1886. Grant gives the book to the memory of his eldest son, a captain in the Cheshire Regiment. He calls the work a military story in that dedication. Volume one opens in the Howe of the Mearns, with a peer and his wife in hot debate. Lord Fettercairn, his lady, and their youngest son Lennard, a captain, trade sharp words.

Chapters bring a wedding, a spurned offer, and Dulcie herself at Revelstoke Cottage. A secret packet, a farewell, and a silver locket drive the plot. Dulcie is left alone in the world, and the tale moves to the Buffalo River and Elandsbergen. Grant mixes Scots home scenes with war abroad.
68754-glenarvon-volume-1-of-3:
Glenarvon is a tale in three parts, of which this is the first. It came out at London in eighteen sixteen. One part is lost in its count of heads, a note warns. The tale opens in a town of the west isle past a learn doc named St Clare. His kin, a man of wild muse, had spent his small store and long roamed the world.

That kin bore the name Camioli and read the days to come to those who would hear. One night past years he came back to his home town with his small girl child in his arms. The docs wife barred the mean clad guest at the door, not told his name. He went off to seek his kin, the head wife of a nuns house, past a long drear road. He slept that night in a cleft of a high hill.
68773-glenarvon-volume-2-of-3:
Volume two of the novel Glenarvon, in three volumes, was printed at London for Henry Colburn in 1816, with an Italian motto of desperate grief pressing the heart. The story follows Lady Calantha Delaval among the great houses and troubled tenants of Ireland.

The volume opens in the morning at her father's castle, where crowds of discontented Catholics throng the outer courts with petitions for redress, thrown in at the windows. Sir Everard bursts in at breakfast with a huge paper, his case written out clear as the Duke commanded, and demands it be delivered instantly. Seeing Calantha, he weeps aloud over his own ruin, crying that the devil and all is broke loose since she went away, while the company turns aside to hide its laughter. Gondimar answers his despair with a smile at his unimpaired rotundity.
68776-glenarvon-volume-3-of-3:
Glenarvon, Volume Three, is the final volume of the three volume novel printed for Henry Colburn at London in 1816. The title page carries no author's name. An Italian motto of desperate grief heads the volume. Its chapters are numbered in the seventies and beyond, for the tale is nearly done. Chapter seventy-two opens with a meditation on love and guilt rather than with an event.

Love, though when guilty the parent of every crime, the chapter begins, springs forth in the noblest hearts. The flame kindled by Heaven burns brightly and steadily to the last. But the flame unsupported by pure feelings rages and consumes us. Then that which was a paradise becomes a hell, and its victim a maniac and a fiend. The volume carries the novel's guilty lovers toward their catastrophe in this high moralising style.
68916-modern-literature-a-novel-volume-2:
Robert Bisset wrote Modern Literature, a novel in three volumes, of which this file holds the second, printed at London in 1804. The volume opens not with plot but with a long account of Brighton in the last years of the eighteenth century. Its contents list reads like a tour: the prospect from the church, ships sailing for the Thames, bathing rules, the Steyne, and the round of a visitor's day from beach to library.

Bisset mixes scene painting with talk of news, politics, and the parade. Dinner gets its due, with soles, turbot, and down mutton praised and the wine found wanting. The novel pauses its story to hold up a famed watering place whole, as readers of the day liked their fiction served.
69428-the-wellfields-a-novel-vol-1-of-3:
Jessie Fothergill wrote The Wellfields, a novel in three volumes. Richard Bentley and Son issued Volume One in 1880. Fothergill had written The First Violin before. Probation bears her name as well. The book goes to her friends at Loweswater. Pleasant days there called it forth, she says. A Prelude opens the tale at page one.

A Saxon lord built a church at Wellfield long ago. He called it the White Church in its day. Under the Hill marked its place by a wooded rise. Stage One brings Ems and a German society scene. Of the Wellfields itself comes at chapter four. Father and son arrange accounts in the fifth. Avice reads a new book's chapter later. Monk's Gate opens Stage Two of the tale. Old church, German years, and a north country house weave Fothergill's quiet drama of inheritance and love.
69489-the-wellfields-a-novel-vol-3-of-3:
The Wellfields, volume three of three, is a novel by Jessie Fothergill, published in London in eighteen eighty. Fothergill had won notice with The First Violin and Probation before this book. The last volume is built in two parts, called Stage Four and Stage Five. Stage titles include a reed shaken in the wind and a consummation.

The opening chapter finds Wellfield near the end of his money and his hopes. His father's affairs are wound up, and almost nothing remains to him at all. A few hundred pounds at most stand to his name in the bank. Then his employer offers him a post as foreign correspondent at a fixed wage. That offer lands just as he thought of cutting his tie and leaving. Torn between need, thanks, and pride, he covers his face in feeling. Later chapters move to Wellfield itself, to Jerome, and to a mystery solved.
69495-the-professor-s-experiment-a-novel: The Professor's Experiment is a novel in three volumes by Margaret Wolfe Hungerford, who wrote as Mrs Hungerford and was famous as the author of Molly Bawn. This file holds volume two of the three. The surviving opening pages carry the publisher's list of her novels rather than the tale itself. Reviews from the Academy and the Spectator praise her light, bright manner, her wit and gaiety, and her charming Irish girls. The middle volume carries a love story through complications the final volume resolves.
69498-the-wellfields-a-novel-vol-2-of-3:
The Wellfields, a novel by Jessie Fothergill, is shown here in its second volume of three. Bentley published it at London in 1880. Fothergill had already won readers with The First Violin and Probation. The volume's contents run through stages of the story, with chapters of danger, spells, and Indian summer.

Nita and Jerome return to the Abbey to find Mr Bolton back from Burnham. Later stages bring living pictures, a second meeting, and the friendship of Herr Falkenberg. The lion and the mouse, an enemy's work, and a farewell and return fill the closing chapters. Father Somerville gathers the threads together near the end. Fothergill writes a full Victorian novel of family, love, and fault, spread across three volumes. This middle book carries its people through meetings in England and Germany toward the last volume's reckoning.
69640-woodburn-grange-a-story-of-english:
William Howitt wrote this story of English country life, volume one. Wood printed Woodburn Grange in London in 1867, three volumes. Contents open with the last of a long line, Sir Roger. The first of a new line and old time ways follow.

The Woodburns and neighbours, Betty Trapps, and Thorsby fill mid chapters. A hay field fete, farmer samples, and a friends party come. A pic nic on the island closes volume one contents here. Sir Roger line ran from the Norman Conquest to this century. Rich marsh land and deer filled moorlands framed the first Sir Roger domains there.
69642-woodburn-grange-a-story-of-english:
Woodburn Grange, volume two, was written by William Howitt. Wood published the story at London in 1867. Three volumes make the novel of English country life. Ten chapters fill this volume. The Claverings and Heritages opens it. Letty's Wedding and a Quaker yearly meeting follow. Millicent Heritage attends that meeting, and much comes of her visit. Thorsby falls and is converted, then sinks worse. Woodburn and Rockville end the volume at war. Chapter one begins the morning after an island frolic. Henry Clavering has come back, to George's joy. Mrs Woodburn asks her daughter Ann a careful question: has he altered his opinions at all?

Ann shakes her head, tears starting. A long attachment stands between Clavering and Ann, the narrator explains. Every one at the Grange loves his sense and kindness. Only his opinions divide them.
70062-coloured-engravings-of-heaths-vol-:
Volume three of Coloured Engravings of Heaths shows the heath family in painted plates. H C Andrews, botanical painter and engraver, made and issued the work in London in eighteen hundred nine. His shop stood at Five Knightsbridge. Each drawing was taken from a living plant only.

Latin and English text stands with each figure in the book. Fine cuts show the parts that mark one kind from the next. The whole follows the plan of Linnaeus for plant kinds. Andrews had first drawn heaths in seventeen hundred ninety four. Two volumes had not held the genus, to his surprise. Near three hundred kinds and forms now bound the tribe, he finds. Seeds once thought shy in England now ripen free if caught in time.
70082-the-heathery-or-a-monograph-of-the:
Andrews devoted six volumes to The Heathery, a monograph of the genus Erica. It carries coloured engravings, Latin and English descriptions, and dissections of all the known species. Henry Bohn published this third volume at London in 1845, in a second edition corrected and enlarged.

A concluding dissertation reckons the family at about three hundred species and distinct varieties, so that the genus stands half delineated at this volume's end. The Cape of Good Hope remains the great source of heaths, Andrews writes, and he gives practical counsel on growing them. Fogs on low ground are their great enemies. Watering wants more care than is commonly given, and a plant once drooped for thirst rarely survives. The species accounts then begin with Erica acuminata, each giving the Latin description, an English rendering, the plant's native country and flowering months, and a key to the plate.
70367-accounting-theory-and-practice-vol:
