Accounting Theory and Practice is a text book for schools of trade rule by Roy Kester. He held a chair of the art at a great school of New York. The host text is the first of three parts. It is the first year book of the set. A new form of it came out in nineteen twenty two.

The book is sworn to the sire and dame of the hand. Its first words tell of the way of teach the book holds. That way had been put forth and used in a few schools. It has since won wide use in the class room. Men with no past drill in the art grasp its core with ease by that way. The new form shifts some parts to a new place. It adds new stuff as well.
70532-the-seven-books-of-paulus-gineta-v:
The Seven Books of Paulus Aegineta, volume two of three, is a medical classic Englished from the Greek by Francis Adams. It was printed at London in 1846 for a society of medical publishing founded three years before. Adams' commentary claims a wide scope on its title page. It embraces a complete view of the knowledge held by the Greeks, Romans, and Arabians on all subjects tied to medicine and surgery.

A Latin motto from Seneca stands at the front: those before us did much, but did not finish. They are to be honoured like gods all the same. The second volume opens with the fourth book. Its sections treat skin diseases in order: the thick skinned sickness, leprosy, lichen, itching, and white patches. Stains of the skin, outbreaks, night sores, blisters, and burns follow in the same careful run.
70556-accounting-theory-and-practice-vol:
Accounting Theory and Practice, by Roy Kester, is a text-book for colleges and schools of business training. Kester taught accounting at the School of Business at Columbia University. The Ronald Press first held the copyright in 1918, and this second volume had reached a twelfth printing by 1922.

The volume is the second-year book of a set of three. Its first chapter treats the corporation: kinds of stock, from common and preferred to watered and treasury stock. The accounts for stock sales, premiums, and forfeits get close care. A second chapter builds the voucher system for a factory's buying. Voucher checks, registers, and the index of creditors are all shown in form. The book teaches by worked forms, not by rules alone.
70686-the-tallants-of-barton-vol-1-of-3:
Joseph Hatton wrote a tale of fortune and finance in three volumes, with volume one printed at London in 1867. Hatton had written Bitter Sweets and Against the Stream. The wheel of fortune turns without cease, a saying of Confucius warns at the front, and who can say within himself, I shall today be uppermost. In the shadow of Berne Hills opens the tale.

The merchant's son and daughter are brought in, then Hall Farm with the Somertons and a landscape painter. The Meter Iron Works Company raises the money plot. The Dibbles and their new lodger, the two friends and the two vignettes, and a sentimental chapter follow. Paul Somerton takes up a delicate and dangerous task. Barton Hall stands white and Italian in the Vale of Avonworth below the hills.
70827-the-tallants-of-barton-vol-3-of-3:
Joseph Hatton wrote this tale of fortune and finance, volume three. Tinsley Brothers printed the final volume in London in 1867. A Confucius line on the wheel of fortune fronts the book. Contents open with wedding bells and a coming home scene.

Lord and Lady Verner and Dame Fortune grim joke follow next. A deed of vengeance, explanations too late, and an inquest appear. A police chief bold stroke and detective philosophy fill mid chapters. Beginning of the end and closing scenes end the three volumes. In the firelight stands one more chapter before several persons quit the stage for ever.
71074-the-legend-of-perseus-volume-1-of-:
The Legend of Perseus, volume one, is a study of tradition in story, custom, and belief by Edwin Sidney Hartland, published in London by David Nutt in 1894. The work runs to three volumes. This first volume treats the supernatural birth. Hartland was a leading folklorist, and his Perseus is the Greek hero whose story he tracks across the world.

The first chapter sets out the legend as the classical writers preserved it, with its three trains of incident. The Danae type of the story is then traced in modern folklore: in Italy and Greece, in the Irish saga of Balor, and in German, Swedish, and Russian tales. The Assyrian hero Gilgamesh is brought into the comparison. The second chapter takes up the King of the Fishes type, from Brittany to Scandinavia. Hartland's method is the comparative one: one tale, many lands.
71112-far-above-rubies-vol-1-of-3:
Far Above Rubies is a tale in three parts by Mrs Riddell, of which this is the first. It came out at London in eighteen sixty-seven. Riddell was known for tales of town and wealth. Parts of this book treat a squire, a house past, a girl in her room, and life at a hollow. A man named Black wins his point in one part.

The tale opens on the lane to a hollow, told in long praise of its charms. It is no plain lane of cut hedge and bare bank, but one of old elms and beech, with turf fit for a glad ride. Brambles, ivy, rose, and sweet suckle twine at its sides. Moss, fern, and a score of wild blooms in their terms fill the banks. That lush lane sets the scene of the house tale to come.
71114-far-above-rubies-vol-3-of-3:
Mrs J H Riddell wrote Far above Rubies, a novel in three volumes issued in London by Tinsley Brothers in eighteen sixty seven. The hosted text is volume three. Riddell had earlier written George Geith and The Race for Wealth. Thirteen chapters fill the volume. Chapter one is A Glimpse of the Canvas. Arthur Dudley feels cheated as the close opens.

Whether the moneys had ever come into his hands or not, Arthur still felt a sense of having been cheated, the tale says. He had been made the catspaw wherewith Mr Black chestnuts were drawn out of the fire, he feels. To the letter Mr Black statements might be correct, but in spirit he had deceived him grossly, he holds. Great Successes and Like a Man Hand follow. At Kemms Park and The Paper War fill the middle. The Bubble Bursts and Sunset at Berrie Down close the tale.
7135-the-great-conspiracy-volume-3:
Logan's third part of The Great Conspiracy opens at chapter eleven, The Causes of Secession. It recalls that from the Republic's birth some citizens hated it, and when they could not rule, worked by conspiracy, sedition, mutiny, nullification, secession, or otherwise to weaken and destroy it. Edward McPherson's documentary History of the Rebellion states the process well, Logan says, noting a considerable body in slaveholding states always disaffected to the Union.

They resisted the Constitution's adoption, then sought to refine away the general government's rights and powers. By artful expedients over years, using excitements from passing questions, they finally perverted public sentiment. Only this third part's argument is traced here, as Logan builds the case that secession was no sudden passion but a long conspiracy.
71375-niebuhr-s-lectures-on-roman-histor:
Niebuhr's Lectures on Roman History is a set of talks on the past of Rome, in three parts. The host text is the first part of the set. Two hands made the English form from a text set by a man of lore of the north land. It was put out at London in eighteen seventy five. The first words of the two hands set out their aim.

That aim was a true form of the work in English, with no adds of their own. In that they walk in the steps of the man who set the north text. He kept him self to the mere task of a true text. Niebuhr gave the talks twice at Bonn, the first words go on. The first set ran in the cold term of eighteen twenty six.
71385-niebuhr-s-lectures-on-roman-histor:
Niebuhr's talks on Roman history fill three books, this being the mid one. Chepmell and Demmler turned Isler's form into English. The book came out in London in 1875. The First Punic War leads this book's long list. Carthage's first days and its realm's reach start the war tale.

Sicily's land is drawn, and the siege of Agrigentum comes next. Rome builds a fleet and wins at sea with board bridges. Duilius wins near Mylae, and Ecnomus sees a great sea fight. Regulus lands in Africa, wins, then falls to Xanthippus. His death tales are weighed with a keen, cold eye. Past men get Niebuhr's famed voice in brief.
7152-cecilia-or-memoirs-of-an-heiress-vo:
Burney's Cecilia reaches its third volume at book eight, continued, with a chapter titled An Event. Cecilia, scarce less unhappy in her decision than in her uncertainty, sits dissatisfied with her situation, her views, and herself, still distressed and uncomfortable when Delvile calls the next morning. He cannot discover what her determination has been, and fearfully asks his doom with hardly any hope of favor.

Cecilia, above affectation and a stranger to art, refuses to keep him an instant in suspense, since she herself is no longer in suspense. She owns she may have seemed trifling, but insists she has been nothing less, and that Delvile would excuse her of caprice if he knew half the distress of her irresolution. Only this third volume's course is followed here, toward the heiress's hard won resolution.
71542-john-g-paton-missionary-to-the-new:
John Paton's autobiography, Missionary to the New Hebrides, appears here in its first part, a new and cheaper illustrated edition from Fleming Revell. The front matter gathers commendations. Theodore Cuyler calls it the most robust and fascinating life story he has met in many a day, and says Paton was made of the same stuff as Livingstone. Arthur Pierson, who wrote the introduction, calls it unsurpassed in missionary biography.

Letters from missionaries in Mexico, Japan, China, and India echo the praise. The Christian Advocate ranks the book beside Livingstone's own writings, a hero of the cross for the present age. Paton's brother edited the autobiography. This first part covers his early life and the road to the New Hebrides, the cannibal islands where he made his name. The two-volume boxed set sold at two dollars net.
7156-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-3:
Part three of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter eight, The Question of the Seal, with Henry the Eighth waking about five o'clock from an unrefreshing nap. Troublous dreams, he mutters, and his end now at hand, as warnings and failing pulses confirm it. Yet a wicked light flames in his eye as he vows he will not die till he go before, meaning the man whose doom waits.

Attendants find him awake and ask his pleasure on the Lord Chancellor waiting without, and the king cries admit him eagerly. The chancellor kneels by the couch reporting that peers in robes stand at the bar, having confirmed the Duke of Norfolk's doom, and humbly await further pleasure. The king's face lights with fierce joy, crying lift me up, for in his own person he will go before his parliament.
71856-the-boy-mechanic-book-3:
Boy Mechanic, book three, promises eight hundred things for boys to do in its pages. Popular Mechanics Company of Chicago copyrighted the book in 1919 under Windsor. Eight hundred and two illustrations back the building plans through the volume. An electric locomotive model and track system leads the title page list of projects.

A boys motor car, parcel delivery bicycle, and aerial cableway follow in the list. Miniature tank, sailing canoe, houseboat, submarine camera, and diving tower continue the bill. Hammocks, a kitchen for hikers, and an ice yacht round out the named builds. Workshop boys of 1919 gained a year of projects in one fat manual.
7195-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-3:
Part Three of Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer finds Tom dodging through lanes to shake off returning scholars, then falling into a moody jog toward Cardiff Hill. He crosses a small branch two or three times, trusting a juvenile superstition that crossing water baffles pursuit, and at last he slips behind the Douglas mansion into a dense wood.

Under a spreading oak, in dead noonday heat that has stilled even the birds, Tom sits on a mossy spot to brood alone. The scene shows the boy at his most romantic and solitary, turning a walk into a small epic of escape. This part holds the woodland mood and Tom's lonely wanderings, before the tale turns back to village trouble.
72103-travels-into-north-america-volume-:
Travels into North America is an account of the colonies by Peter Kalm, a Swedish naturalist. John Reinhold Forster translated it into English for this London edition of 1771. Kalm was a professor at the university of Abo and a member of Sweden's Royal Academy. The work runs to three volumes, of which this is the second.

Its title page promises natural history above all else. It also promises a full account of plantations and farming in the colonies. The civil, church, and trade state of the country comes into the plan. The manners of the people and remarks on many subjects fill out the rest. This volume opens in New Jersey in December 1748. Kalm asks there why people multiply faster than in Europe. Land lies free for the taking, taxes are low, and liberty is great.
7244-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Three opens in slow torture on a lovely autumn morning. The Yankee and his company ride through sylvan solitudes in the first freshness of the day. Fair green valleys spread below hilltops, streams wind through them, island groves and huge lonely oaks cast black blots of shade, and distant castles fleck the hazy hills.

Broad lawns sparkling with dew carry the riders onward, and Twain lets the beauty of the land sit oddly beside the chapter's grim title. The Yankee's modern eye notes both the landscape and the hard customs waiting beyond it. This part holds the country ride and its mix of charm and menace, before the plot tightens again.
72519-proper-pride-a-novel-volume-2-of-3:
An anonymous novel in three volumes reaches its second volume in a London edition of 1882. Verse lines head the title page: life may change but not fly, and love repulsed still returns. Chapter one is titled The Neilgherries. The hero goes to the Nilgiri Hills for the rest of his two months' leave.

The narrator calls those Blue Hills the most wholesome, delightful, and beautiful range in the world. Sir Reginald rides up the old road, nine miles to Coonoor, after a night of heat and mosquitoes below. He whistles for two miles, then stops his horse in admiration. Later chapters are set in Afghanistan and at Monkswood. A chapter cries that Mary has found her husband.
72680-rose-blanche-and-violet-volume-1-o:
Rose, Blanche and Violet is a novel in three volumes by Lewes, printed at London by Smith, Elder and Company in 1848. Lewes also wrote Ranthorpe and the Biographical History of Philosophy. This hosted text is the first volume. A French motto from De Maistre stands on the title page: there is no true virtue without victory over ourselves. Lewes dedicated the book, in French, to Benjamin Morel of Dunkirk, as an affectionate souvenir.

The preface is a small essay on the moral in fiction. He became so conscious of this in the progress of his story that he abandoned his original intention. Talent dazzles us, but will carries us victoriously through the struggle. The novel of the three sisters is built to test that creed.
72682-rose-blanche-and-violet-volume-3-o:
Volume Three of Rose, Blanche, and Violet is the last of a three volume novel by Lewes, printed at London by Smith, Elder and Company in 1848. Lewes also wrote Ranthorpe and a biographical history of philosophy. A saying of de Maistre fronts the volume: there is no true virtue without victory over ourselves. This volume holds Books Six, Seven and Eight of the novel, and an epilogue.

Book Six opens in the spring of 1841. Cecil and Blanche are enduring the wretched, comfortless state of a cheap boarding house. Cheapness has grown ever more important to them. Book Seven turns to Rose, Violet, Frank and the honeymoon. Book Eight brings Captain Heath back, and then The Forgery, Ruin and The Gambler's End. A chapter called The Sinner that Repenteth and one called Those Left to Weep close the tale.
72743-miss-cheyne-of-essilmont-volume-1-:
Miss Cheyne of Essilmont, volume one, is a novel by James Grant. Hurst and Blackett issued it in London in 1883. Grant also wrote The Romance of War and The Cameronians. The contents run to twenty chapters in this volume. The tale opens out with the royal buckhounds. Alison Cheyne rides beside Captain Goring after the hunt. He has learned her name from Debrett, he owns. She colours at this simple avowal of interest.

Alison is also called Lisette by her friends. The name is an old Scoto-French one in her family. Later chapters bring a ring, a luncheon party, and a widow. A written proposal and evil tidings stir the plot. A Captain Dalton and a Cadbury plot enter the list. The Firefly, a yacht or ship, closes the volume's chapters. Grant wrote military and society tales in great number.
72744-miss-cheyne-of-essilmont-volume-2-:
James Grant wrote this novel of Alison Cheyne in three volumes. Hurst and Blackett printed volume two in London in 1883. Contents open with Tom Llanyard and a disastrous night at home. A ball, a visit, doubting, and Aldershot camp scenes follow.

Jerry last appeal, a secret life, and old versus new love appear. A journey, a snare, and a Paris hotel fill the middle. Papers in the Rue des Beguines and a monster rout come next. Alison thinks of Bevil Goring only, the first chapter says plain. A challenge, a frontier post, and a march to Prah end the contents of volume two.
72745-miss-cheyne-of-essilmont-volume-3-:
Miss Cheyne of Essilmont is a novel by James Grant. Hurst and Blackett published it in London in 1883. This is the third of three volumes.

The final volume opens during the Ashanti war in West Africa. Troops halt at Prahsu and hear strange tales from Coomassie. A falling star and a speaking child unsettle the city. Later chapters return to Hampshire, Bayswater, and a foreclosure. Grant wrote many military and Scottish novels. His war scenes draw on the campaign reporting of his day. The volume carries the family story to its close.
72822-famous-composers-and-their-works-v:
Famous Composers and Their Works, Volume Three, is a musical biography set edited by John Knowles Paine, Theodore Thomas, and Karl Klauser. Millet of Boston published it in 1891, illustrated with photographs. The volume opens with Joseph Joachim Raff, shown in a photograph from life taken at Wiesbaden in 1878.

Raff was the son of an organist and teacher who left a Würtemberg town in 1822 to settle at Lachen on the lake of Zurich. There the boy was born on May 27 of that year. He showed early the ability that does not always fulfil its promise. He could translate Homer at seven, and preferred books to rude outdoor sports. The volume gives life after life in that full, admiring manner: composers for the parlour.
733-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Edward Gibbon carried his history through the reign of Theodosius in this third volume, with notes by H. H. Milman. It covers the death of Gratian, the ruin of Arianism, the civil wars against Maximus and Eugenius, and the penance and death of Theodosius himself. St. Ambrose and the court at Milan play large parts.

The volume then turns to the final destruction of pagan worship and the rise of saints and relics among Christians, and to the division of the empire between the sons of Theodosius. Gibbon's narrative stays stately and sharp, weighing emperors, bishops, and generals alike. It is a key stretch of the story, where one empire becomes two.
73972-a-bankrupt-heart-vol-1-of-3:
A Bankrupt Heart, a novel in three volumes by Florence Marryat, author of Love's Conflict and Parson Jones, opens its first volume in a London printing of 1894. Ten chapters make this volume. A title note warns that the story, being already dramatized, has all rights reserved.

Chapter one sets Llewellyn at the window of her room in Lord Ilfracombe's house in Grosvenor Square. She gazes at the dust-laden, burnt-up leaves of the square gardens at the close of July. All the fashionable world is already out of town. She was reared in the country, and her thoughts run to Wales, where the same sun ripens corn and decks the hedges with flowers. She sighs for Usk, her birthplace, then draws a letter from her pocket. Llewellyn is nominally the earl's housekeeper, holding an inferior place in his house.
73973-a-bankrupt-heart-vol-2-of-3:
Volume two of A Bankrupt Heart is a novel by Florence Marryat, published in London in 1894. White and Company issued the three volume set. Marryat had written Love's Conflict and Parson Jones before it. The story was already dramatised when this edition appeared. Ten chapters fill the middle volume. It opens with Nell Llewellyn between life and death.

For seven weeks Nell has lain ill before waking to herself. A sunny October afternoon brings her first clear moment. She watches the tassel of the blind bob in the breeze. Betsy Hobbs, a farmhouse helper, dozes by the window with her knitting. Nell feels too weak to question why she lies there. Her gaze roves the room with a child's apathy. The volume resumes the tale from that sickbed.
74071-short-story-masterpieces-vol-3:
Short Story Masterpieces, volume three, holds Russian tales Englished by John Cournos. The Home Correspondence School of Springfield issued it in nineteen thirteen. Berg Esenwein, editor of Lippincott Magazine, wrote the author studies within. A portrait of Nikolai Gogol fronts this Russian volume of the set.

A general first study treats the Russian short story as a form of art. Pushkin and the new era follows, with his tale The Snow Storm printed. Gogol, the first Russian realist, is paired with his tale The Cloak. Turgenev the emancipator gives The District Doctor as his sample story here. Tolstoi, artist and preacher, closes the set with A Long Exile tale.
74361-shipbuilding-from-its-beginnings-v:
Shipbuilding from Its Beginnings, volume two of three, is a picture history of ships and boat craft. The author is Van Konijnenburg, a Dutch engineer of the state water service. The work was issued at Brussels between 1895 and 1905. Its publisher was an international body for navigation congresses. Captions appear in Dutch, German, English, and French. The second volume treats the Mediterranean sea as its ground.

The plates begin with Egyptian boats of remote times. Figures show men paddling and rowing in early craft. One plate shows the making of papyrus boats. Museum pieces at Leiden supply some of the images. The set traces hull forms from the first rafts onward. It was made for engineers and students of navigation. Few books of its day matched its sweep of images. The middle volume holds the ancient Mediterranean craft.
74460-suspense-volume-1-of-3:
Henry Seton Merriman wrote a novel in three volumes, with volume one printed at London in 1890. Merriman had written Young Mistley and The Phantom Future. The book is given to the truest gentleman he had met, his father. On board the Hermione opens the contents, then the exception and a problem. A storm, the compact, and a shadow follow.

A sportsman's death, a joint command, and a divided responsibility fill the middle. Fjaerholm, a commercial transaction, bad news, and off close the list. Brenda, what are you thinking about, Mrs Wylie asks aboard the yacht. It was hardly a question, and she returned placidly to her novel without awaiting a reply. The younger lady's book lay unheeded on her knee, its pages fluttering in the breeze. A yachting party sails toward trouble.
74462-suspense-volume-3-of-3:
Suspense, volume three, closes a novel by Henry Seton Merriman, printed at London in 1890. Merriman also wrote Young Mistley and The Phantom Future. The last volume holds fifteen chapters, from The Sport of Fate to The End of It All, with a place called Plevna named along the way.

The volume opens on Theodore Trist, a silent man of immense self sacrifice and stern discipline. He weighs a strange undertaking and its dangers without flinching, resolved to find a certain man sober and manage the rest. As he walks down a broad staircase past gay guests, he catches himself nursing a groundless dislike of Hicks, and owns the fault. Merriman builds his close on such quiet tests of character.
74548-great-short-stories-volume-1-of-3:
Great Short Stories, volume one, edited by William Patten, gathers detective stories of fame. Collier published the set at New York with copyright in 1906 for the set. A frontispiece of Robert Louis Stevenson stands in the front of the volume. The collection draws famous examples from the literatures of France, England, and America.

The Murders in the Rue Morgue by Poe opens the contents of volume one. The Mystery of Marie Roget and The Purloined Letter give Poe three tales here. The Sign of the Four by Doyle follows as a full Sherlock Holmes novel. A Scandal in Bohemia stands next in the contents list of the volume. Dupin and Holmes share one cover in this starter shelf of detection.
74640-the-italian-volume-2-of-3:
The Italian, or the Confessional of the Black Penitents, is a romance by Ann Radcliffe. The hosted text holds the second of its three volumes. Radcliffe had won fame with a past tale of castle dread in the hills. This book came out in London in the year seventeen ninety seven.

Ellena hides in nun dress in a music room as the volume opens. She scans the monks and guests for the face of her love Vivaldi. Her veil guards her from the abbess eye and from his eye alike. Plots of kin, church courts, and hid cells drive the Gothic chain. Dread and soft love in turn rule the famed Radcliffe mode.
74643-the-italian-volume-1-of-3:
Ann Radcliffe's The Italian, or The Confessional of the Black Penitents, volume one of three, was printed for Cadell and Davies at London in 1797. Radcliffe signs herself author of The Mysteries of Udolpho. The story opens about 1764, when English travellers near Naples stop at the portico of Santa Maria del Pianto, a church of the Black Penitents. A tall, thin man paces behind the pillars, muffled in a cloak, his one visible eye expressive of uncommon ferocity.

He glides away into the church and vanishes from their search. Inside, the building shows a simplicity and grandeur more solemn than the usual splendour of Italian churches. The stranger is seen again, passing toward a confessional. Radcliffe's last romance sets its machinery at once: the mysterious monk, the confessional, and the Italian landscape of devotion and dread.
74655-lady-bell-volume-1-of-3:
Lady Bell is a story of the last century, in three volumes, by the author of Citoyenne Jacqueline. The hosted text is volume one, printed at London in eighteen seventy three. Its contents run to nineteen chapters. Chapter heads move from an old queen's drawing room to a squire's wooing, a marriage in a day, and an election.

The first chapter opens in that drawing room scene. Old Lady Lucie Penruddock speaks to her grand niece, young Lady Bell Etheredge. She says she will go no farther till the duchess's chair comes. In the meantime she will tell the girl who the tops are in the room. The girl may then use her eyes for an honest purpose, the elder says. Later heads promise an imprisoned princess, betrayal, flight, and life with the players.
74770-the-greatest-story-in-the-world-pe:
Horace G Hutchinson wrote a history of mankind around the Mediterranean, published in 1923 as the first of three periods. He states his claim at once: the greatest story in the world is our own story. A front picture shows the Great Pyramid from the air. Plates include a Babylonian clay tablet telling of the deluge.

Chapters begin before history was written and move through Egypt and Babylonia. The Minoans in Crete, the Jews, and the Persians follow. Greece in its glorious days, Macedon, and Rome and Carthage take up the middle. Rome as mistress of the world and the dispersal of the Jews close this period.
74806-queenie-s-whim-volume-2-of-3:
Rosa Nouchette Carey wrote a novel in three volumes, here the second. Richard Bentley and Son issued Queenie's Whim in London in 1881. Carey had written Nellie's Memories and Wooed and Married before. Fourteen chapters run from a new school-mistress to a firm yea or nay.

Queenie learns she will take charge of the Hepshaw girls' school in a month. Joy and color flood her face as she thanks Garth Clayton warmly. Dora, a king of Karldale, a golden harvest, and little Nan crowd the volume. Readers gain a wholesome middle tale of work, love, and duty.
74807-queenie-s-whim-volume-3-of-3:
Queenie Whim, volume three of three, is a novel by Rosa Nouchette Carey. Richard Bentley and Son issued it at London in 1881 in full. Chapters carry quoted titles, from In the Gloaming to Garth Wife at end. Dora and Garth open this last volume after a restless night apart.

Dora wakes fresh in her travelling dress; Garth has tossed half the night. Her thoughts run to her sister Flo, ill at a foreign school abroad. German doctors and a sister letter have scared their father at home. Beatrix, Flo, and Dora trade places in a web of family care. Secrets, conspirators, and cross purposes crowd the closing chapters.
74994-john-g-paton-missionary-to-the-new:
Volume three of John Paton's autobiography continues the story of the Scottish missionary to the New Hebrides. His brother edited the book, published by the Fleming Revell Company in 1898. The first two parts had appeared in 1889 and became, in the editor's words, a missionary classic.

At his brother's urging, Paton carried the account through the twelve years since the earlier volumes. A historical note and a report on the progress of the gospel in the New Hebrides accompany the life. The editor says he spared no pains, using corrections from friends abroad and from the missionary himself. Paton's tales of the islands of Vanuatu, of danger, conversion, and stubborn hope, were read in churches across the English-speaking world.
75276-a-crown-of-shame-volume-3-of-3:
Volume three of A Crown of Shame is a tale by Florence Marryat, out in eighteen eighty eight. A White house of London brought out the three book set that year. Marryat wrote Love Conflict and My Sister the Actress in past years. Seven parts run through this last book of the set in its scheme. Rosa walks the tulip tree road at Beauregard in its first part.

She bears Maraquita babe in her arms in her best rose gown and silk wrap. Her mood is sour and cross as she paces that long drive. White hose, soft shoes, and long black curls mark her proud dress. Front leaves list the house new tales in cloth gilt and board forms. Gilt cloth at six and board at two are its set trade marks.
7533-a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-3:
The third volume of Beverley Nichols's old ballads opens with Clerk Colvill and his lusty dame walking in the garden. It runs through some of the darkest and finest of the old songs. Sir Aldingar, Edom o' Gordon, and Chevy Chace follow, with Sir Lancelot du Lake, Gil Morrice, and the Child of Elle. Child Waters and King Edward IV and the Tanner of Tamworth add love and disguise.

Sir Patrick Spens, the shipwreck ballad, closes the main sequence before the Earl of Mar's Daughter, and color plates picture Clerk Colvill, Gil Morrice, Child Waters, and the Earl's daughter. Nichols's selection favors narrative force over prettiness: betrayal, murder, and loyalty told in stark verse. The volume is a strong draught of the ballad tradition at its most dramatic.
75726-driven-to-bay-vol-1-of-3:
Florence Marryat wrote this novel in three volumes, and this is volume one. White and Company printed it in London in 1887. Marryat was known for Love Conflict and My Own Child. Contents name Jack the sailor and Vernon the lover at first.

Iris Harland enters next, then the new rich and breakers ahead. A wolf in sheep clothing and two women hearts raise tension. The ship Pandora, a find, and a farewell to England follow. Courtship and a stern remonstrance close this first third of the long sea tale. White and Company issued the London edition in 1887.
75727-driven-to-bay-vol-2-of-3:
Driven to Bay, volume two, is the middle part of a three-volume novel by Florence Marryat. It was published in London in 1887 by White and Company. Marryat wrote many novels of society and sensation, among them Love's Conflict and Spiders of Society, as the title page records.

Fifteen chapters fill this volume. They open with a chapter called Maggie, then move into the doldrums and a chapter on a widow. The setting turns to the sea: chapters stand on the poop deck, watch the glass fall, and ship heavy seas. A rescue, a whaler, and a game of dominoes follow, with confidences and a scene in the smoke room. The letter closes the volume. A voyage, a widow, and danger at sea carry the tale toward its third volume.
76146-fossil-plants-vol-3:
A C Seward wrote Fossil Plants, a text book for students of botany and geology, here volume three, issued by Cambridge University Press in nineteen seventeen. Seward taught botany at Cambridge and was master of Downing College. The volume holds two hundred fifty three illustrations. He gave the book to the memory of Charles René Zeiller, a French scholar of fossil plants who died in nineteen fifteen.

Volume three treats pteridosperms, cycadofilices, cordaitales, and cycadophyta. Chapter twenty eight treats recent cycadales first, as a key to fossils. Chapter twenty nine continues pteridosperms with Lyginopteris, Telangium, and Lagenostoma. Chapter thirty treats Medulloseae at length. Students get stems, seeds, and fronds of coal age plants described and figured in close detail. The book is a standard, learned guide to plant fossils.
76371-the-silver-dial-volume-2-of-3:
The Silver Dial, volume two of three, is a novel by Mary C Rowsell, printed in London by Swan Sonnenschein in 1886. Rowsell wrote St Nicolas Eve, Love Loyal, and Traitor or Patriot. A line from Henry the Fifth stands at the front, on many lines closing in the dial centre.

Chapters here run from eighteen to forty three. Dagger and Poison Cup opens the set, then a noisy committee and a chilly greeting. Unjust suspicions, a moonlight meeting, and worse than silence pace the mid part. A cause celebre, give up the plans, and the old love or the new raise the stakes. Time changes, a visit to the dial, Gretchen, and a clean confession close the volume. The text names Sabina and her father bidding adieu to Radegund in grey twilight. Readers should start at volume one.
76372-the-silver-dial-volume-3-of-3:
Silver Dial, volume three of three, is the closing part of a novel by Mary Rowsell. Swan Sonnenschein of London issued the volume in 1886 in three decker form. A line from Henry the Fifth about lines closing in a dial centre heads the book. Contents here run from chapter forty eight to the end of the tale.

The horologe, shoemaker holiday, and love alchemy mark the chapter heads in this part. A visit to Doctor Wolkenberg and playing with fire raise the middle stakes. Saint Stephen Tower, a dilemma, and the three ravens fill the later list. Readers of the first two volumes reach the purpose all lines converge on.
76714-the-little-review-july-1917-vol-4-:
The Little Review for July 1917 is one monthly issue of Margaret Anderson's magazine of the arts, volume four, number three, priced at fifteen cents. Anderson edited the magazine in New York, with Ezra Pound as foreign editor. The masthead declares that the magazine makes no compromise with the public taste.

The issue's contents join Wyndham Lewis's Imaginary Letters and his Code of a Herdsman with poems by Eliot and Pound, nightpieces by John Rodker, and verse by Louis Gilmore and Maxwell Bodenheim. Lewis's herdsman code, printed first here, instructs the artist to mock the herd with its own grimace, exploit stupidity, and cherish a personal vocabulary. The Eliot poems listed include The Hippopotamus and Lune de Miel. The number is a small landmark of literary modernism in its combative, little-magazine form.
76780-a-broken-blossom-vol-2-of-3:
Florence Marryat wrote A Broken Blossom, a novel in three volumes. Samuel Tinsley and Company of London published this second volume in 1879. Marryat had earlier written Love's Conflict. Nine chapters carry the story through this middle volume.

Titles promise a secret, serpents, and a revelation. One chapter is named for Arthur Thrale, another for Charlie. All for Tessie stands between them. The volume opens at a meal in an old banqueting hall. Stained glass, black oak chairs, and faded cushions fill the room. Ancestors look down from the panelled walls, nearly rubbed away. Sunlight throws ruby and violet lights across the cloth. Still the narrator shudders at the chamber's weird air. To her the whole place spells ruin, though the host plays his part like a king.
76781-a-broken-blossom-vol-3-of-3:
A Broken Blossom is a novel in three volumes by Florence Marryat, and the hosted text is the third and last volume. It was printed in London by Samuel Tinsley and Company in 1879. Marryat had also written Loves Conflict.

Ten chapters carry this last part from A Little Quarrel through Mr. Charteris, The Wolf, and The Barons Story. The tale is told in the first person by a young woman at St. Pucelle, near her guardians house. Later heads name The Black Cloud, The Death Blow, and Broken as the close draws near. One chapter is called Salle du Sabbat, which hints at dark turns. Readers who start at volume one will find the end of a tale of love, risk, and loss here.
76808-a-sailor-s-life-under-four-soverei:
A Sailor's Life Under Four Sovereigns, volume one of three, is a naval memoir by Admiral of the Fleet the Honourable Sir Henry Keppel, printed at London in 1899. The contents begin with the years 1809 to 1822. Keppel then goes to sea in the Tweed in 1824, and four chapters follow that ship.

The Galatea and the Magicienne carry the young officer on. The Childers brig takes him to the Carlist question and the Carlist War, and then to the west coast of Africa and Cape Coast Castle. A rendezvous of cruisers and shore time follow. The Dido corvette closes the volume, with chapters on China, the Straits of Malacca, and Borneo. Portraits and scenes illustrate the book, from Sir Francis Burdett to a successful operation. Keppel served from boyhood in the sailing navy to high command in the age of steam.
76810-a-sailor-s-life-under-four-soverei:
Volume three of Henry Keppel's Sailor's Life Under Four Sovereigns was published by Macmillan in 1899. Keppel, Admiral of the Fleet, carries his memoir from chapter sixty-six to chapter one hundred and six. The volume opens at Fatshan Creek and a visit to Sarawak, then moves through India to England. Shore chapters follow: groom in waiting, country house visits, a shore journal, and home life. The Cape command fills the middle early chapters, with his flag in Brisk and Forte.

Zanzibar sport, shooting hippopotami, precedes the long China command that dominates the volume. North China ports, a Yangtse trip, memories of Gordon, Peking, and Chefoo to Japan mark the route. The book closes with a last visit to the Straits and farewell notes. An index ends the third volume of the sailor's life.
76885-dead-sea-fruit-vol-1-of-3:
Dead Sea Fruit, volume one of three, is a novel by the author of Lady Audley Secret. Ward, Lock, and Tyler printed it in London in 1868. The tale opens in a sleepy Belgian canal city named Villebrumeuse, under a July sun.

Chapters open with Quite Alone and a retrospective survey. Take back these letters, meant for happiness, and un menage a deux follow. The editor of the Areopagus, at Bayham, and Mr Jerningham quest pace the mid part. Greenlands, how they parted, and there is always the skeleton come next. The green eyed monster, Miss St Albans, and in the green room close the volume. The text opens on the marble image of Hubert Van Eyck against a warm blue sky. Readers should start here, at volume one.
77028-uncle-tweazy-and-his-quizzical-nei:
Volume two of Uncle Tweazy and His Quizzical Neighbours is a comi-satiric novel printed at London in 1816. Simpkin and Marshall published the three volume set. Its author hides behind an earlier work, The Observant Pedestrian. A motto from Thomson's Winter promises a picture of the world held up to itself. The first chapter opens after breakfast. The narrator's uncle proposes a visit to the Rectory.

A new paragon there has won lavish praise from Doctor Tonic. The walk passes through a shrubbery of lime trees. The low white house is ringed with honeysuckles and roses. A young lady, Miss Fitzclarence, leans on the old pastor's arm. The uncle steals only a sidelong glance at her. His expressive countenance, once she sits opposite, stays with the narrator. Neighbourhood folly is the book's sport.
77097-the-magic-ring-vol-1-of-3:
The Magic Ring, a romance from the German of Baron de la Motte Fouque, opens its first volume of three in an Edinburgh printing of 1825. A long letter to a Berlin friend serves as preface. The translator recalls praising the Baron's works over dinner at Charlottenburg, and calls him a chevalier without fear and without reproach. The friend's talk, he says, led him to make the translation.

The letter sketches the Baron's early devotion to letters and his friendship with the Schlegels. It notes that the Magic Ring was the one work of his the translator had tried as a learner of German. Fouque, author of Undine, built his fame on tales of knights, enchantment, and old German legend. The romance that follows belongs to that chivalric line.
7752-godolphin-volume-3:
Constance, Countess of Erpingham, sits alone as a young bride in the third volume of Lytton's Godolphin, in a splendid room full of flowers and scent. Below, the old Mall in June crowds with riders and walkers, yet her brow has lost its glad pride, as if the gift she wanted also pierced her heart.

Her husband asks if she will ride today, while talk turns to diplomacy, assemblies, and her conquest over Lady Delville. Through a bride's lonely hours, the volume shows how rank and wealth can leave a woman alone in a city that worships both.
7759-falkland-book-3:
Lady Emily Mandeville's journal fills Book Three of Lytton's Falkland, in dated entries of joy and guilt. Julia arrives kind and silent, and Emily weeps in her arms without words, a confession and repentance both. No letter comes for days, then a note: he has returned, and she is wild with fear.

Sunday brings the meeting she cannot resist, though she knows his reasons are sophistry and his spell blocks escape. A dinner and ball follow, with Falkland among the guests. The journal form lays bare a woman's heart day by day, between longing, shame, and a love she cannot master.
77812-master-tales-of-mystery-volume-2-o:
Master Tales of Mystery is an anthology of detective stories, gathered by Reynolds, and the hosted text is the second of three volumes. It was published in New York by Collier in 1915. The title promises tales by the most famous authors of the day.

Jacques Futrelle leads the volume with six tales of the Thinking Machine. The first is The Problem of Cell 13, the best known of them all. Its hero bears a name loaded with nearly all the letters of the alphabet, and a string of degrees behind it. Oswald Crawfurd and Henry Rowland follow with single tales. Baroness Orczy gives The Fenchurch Street Mystery. Louis Joseph Vance closes the set with The Mystery of Seven Minutes.
77931-the-moors-and-the-fens-volume-1-of:
F G Trafford wrote a novel in three volumes, of which this first was published at London in 1858. A happy home opens the contents. The wilfulness of youth and an introduction to Mr Alfred Westwood follow. Mina gets a chapter by name. A chapter renders a change of abode necessary. Fancy and fact, then brother and sister, continue.

Dead men's shoes and the baronet's first born build the middle. A bone of contention and the spider and the fly come next. Ernest begins to see the value of life by chapter fourteen. Trafford was the pen name of Charlotte Riddell, later famed for ghost stories. Smith, Elder published the novel.
77990-violet-osborne-volume-1-of-3:
Lady Emily Ponsonby wrote Violet Osborne, a novel in three volumes issued in London by Hurst and Blackett in eighteen sixty five. The hosted text is volume one. Ponsonby had earlier written The Discipline of Life and Mary Lyndsay. A line from George Herbert heads the book, on the one joy of doing kindnesses. Violet Osborne is the young heroine.

Chapter one opens at a small party in Mrs Osborne house. A gentleman asks which of the charming girls is her daughter, then asks her not to tell him. He likes to make folk out for himself, guessing character from looks. Mrs Osborne, a little deaf, hears just the word charming and takes it for her party. It is Violet birthday, and her mother says Violet begins her life today. God grant it may be a happy one, she adds. A tale of a girl growth follows.
77992-violet-osborne-volume-3-of-3:
Violet Osborne, volume three of three, closes the novel by Lady Emily Ponsonby, author of The Discipline of Life. Hurst and Blackett published it in London in 1865. Its title page motto, from George Herbert, praises the one joy of doing kindnesses.

The final volume opens after Lionel's return. He has taken up his abode at home on tolerably friendly terms with his father. He appears duly struck with the change in Ida, and speaks warmly of her appearance, but shows no hurry to bring matters to a crisis. A fresh acquaintance has to be made after so long an absence, and Ida is still three months short of seventeen. Most people, the narrator notes, would consider a delay desirable. The old governess, with fewer teeth and a stronger taste for slumber, still ostensibly chaperons. Ponsonby's novel is a study of patience and family duty.
78111-how-they-loved-him-vol-2-of-3:
How They Loved Him, volume two, was printed in 1882. White published Marryat's novel in London that year. Three volumes make the whole work. A page of new novels at all libraries fronts this copy. Eight chapters fill the second volume. For Ever, In a Strait, and Deserted open it. Over and Sir Gilbert Conroy follow. Smooth waters and a revelation come late. The Indissoluble Link closes the list at page 288. Chapter one carries a motto from Byron. Two lives entwined from the first endure to the last, the lines say. Fenella Barrington's feelings at this period fill the opening. To paint them in black and white is near hopeless, Marryat writes.

Fenella was very young when love overtook her, and very lonely. No watchful parent shielded her innocence.
78143-nourmahal-an-oriental-romance-vol-:
Nourmahal, volume three of three, is the final volume of an oriental romance by Michael Quin. Henry Colburn published it in London in 1838. Quin had written A Steam Voyage Down the Danube and A Visit to Spain. The volume runs to nineteen chapters and closes with notes to all three volumes. Its first chapter opens not in prose but in song.

The song sends a message to an absent lover: tell him the balmy breath of spring has waked the hills and vales from winter sleep. The blithesome birds sweep in airy circles, and the brooks murmur soft as the turtle-dove. But tell not that I love. A passage preserved in the copy shows the heroine's household. The ladies of the harem, her companions as much as her attendants, had all been out with her on this occasion.
78239-nourmahal-an-oriental-romance-vol-:
Michael J Quin wrote Nourmahal, an oriental romance, in three volumes, of which this is the second. Henry Colburn published it at London in 1838. Quin was the author of A Steam Voyage Down the Danube. The volume carries twenty chapters. It opens with a passage from Hindoo drama: white umbrellas float like trembling lotuses, and elephants advance with golden bells. Maidens ride them, blazing with jewels like rays of light.

About the hour when Jehangire ascended the throne at Agra, the conspirators entered Muttra. Twenty thousand Rajaputs under Man-Singh attended them on the road. Hussein Bey, late governor of Cabul, met the prince in the market-place. His Tartar cavalry and Afghan footmen had escorted him home to prove his standing. Quin builds his romance on the Mogul court, its successions, marches, and intrigues.
78315-oliver-constable-miller-and-baker-:
Sarah Tytler wrote a Scots tale of a miller whose name brands the book. Volume two came out in London in 1880. Tytler wrote Citoyenne Jacqueline and Scotch Firs. Oliver takes up Jack Dadd's friend rite in this book's start. Harry Stanhope's thought of a yeoman's life comes next.

Oliver's call to the women of his class takes a full part. His first try, the year's trip, and the feast fill the mid parts. Agneta Stanhope and a talk on Wordsworth stand in the list. A split in the chapel comes from his stiff stand. Mill and bake house men rise at the close.
78319-oliver-constable-miller-and-baker-:
Oliver Constable, Miller and Baker, is a novel by Sarah Tytler, shown here in its third volume of three. Smith, Elder published it at London in 1880. The volume's contents begin with Harry Stanhope's want, then Fan's triumph. The devil shall not have Harry, one chapter vows, and the next names the price at which Harry Stanhope was rescued.

The last penny paid, Oliver's return, fresh service, and life and death fill the closing chapters. Do they believe in me now, the final chapter asks. Harry had entered on the part of a yeoman farmer on a fine summer afternoon, with hay making and hop picking in view. By midwinter the part had worn thin, with only threshing before him. Tytler, a Scottish novelist, wrote of country folk and their betters with a steady moral eye. This last volume brings her miller, her baker, and their circle to their reckoning.
78326-lady-bell-volume-2-of-3:
Volume 2 of Lady Bell is the mid part of a story of the last century, by the author of Citoyenne Jacqueline. It came out in London in 1873 from Strahan and Company, in three volumes. The contents of this volume list a run of chapters that move from the past into the present of the tale. The first is A Message Out of the Past.

Freed by the Visitation of God stands second, then Keeping House Together and Friends in Need. Bow Bells and the Family in Cleveland Court stands fifth in the list. A Gay Young Madam, Making an Acquaintance at the Pantheon, and Opinions Differ stand there too. Boulton's Coins and Wedgwood's Dishes and A Party on the Water carry the list on. The novel is a tale of the age before its own, in the London of bells and courts.
78458-donovan-volume-3-of-3:
Donovan, Volume Three, is the closing volume of a novel by Edna Lyall, printed in London by Hurst and Blackett in 1882. Lyall also wrote Won by Waiting. A verse from Elizabeth Barrett Browning stands on the title page: God's greatness flowing round our incompleteness, and His rest round our restlessness. The set ran to three volumes.

The contents map the end of Donovan's testing. Cobwebs and Questions opens the volume, then A Crown of Fire and a plain Good-bye. Via Crucis, temptation, and a chapter asking what forgiveness is carry the moral weight. Contrasted lovers, duty's call, and Via Lucis turn toward the light. Trevethan speaks, and the last chapter joins the lovers' hopes in one. On a cliff verge, in the early pages, Donovan and his dog Waif settle for an evening while service goes on below. Lyall's religious novel was a Victorian best-seller of conscience.
78503-a-fatal-silence-vol-1-of-3:
Florence Marryat wrote A Fatal Silence, a novel in three volumes published in London by Griffith, Farran, Okeden and Welsh. This file holds volume one. The story opens on market day at Haltham, a little town in an uproar. Oxen flounder along the road, sheep and lambs follow, and ducks and geese add their noise.

Above the crowd stands Miss Stafford on a raised pathway. She watches Lottie and Carrie Gribble, the children in her charge, who have run into the midst of the excitement. The chapter list promises an unwelcome meeting, a discovery at a farm, a cross-examination, and a confession. Paula leaves Deepdale, a solemn promise is made, and Hal breaks the news. Marryat builds a sensation novel of secrets kept and hints dropped: a silence at the centre of the story that the plot slowly works to break.
78549-joshua-haggard-s-daughter-vol-2-of:
Volume two of a three volume novel came out in London in 1876. Its writer is named only as the author of Lady Audley's Secret. Chapter heads are verses, such as O let my joys have some abiding, and We are in love's land today. The book opens on a quiet Sabbath after the first volume's turns.

Joshua Haggard's life was rarely moved from its scene, the tale notes. Visits between Combhaven and Penmoyle show small shifts of dress and custom that feel like a strange land. Cynthia tries to be useful, Helena draws all eyes, and false love is unmasked. Sorrow, tide turns, and night talk fill a mid Victorian tale of love, faith, and family rule.
78596-a-fatal-silence-vol-2-of-3:
A Fatal Silence, Volume Two, is the middle volume of a three volume novel by Florence Marryat. It was printed at London by Griffith, Farran, Okeden and Welsh, who also had a Sydney house. Marryat was the author of Love's Conflict and Véronique. The rights of translation and reproduction are reserved on the title page.

The volume's chapters follow Paula. The first is Paula Is Married, and the second A Triumphant Return. Paula's Visitors comes next, then a chapter named for Lady Bristowe. A Mysterious Loss deepens the plot, and The Widow's Stratagem follows. As the middle volume of a sensation novel in the three volume form, this part carries the marriage plot forward while losses and stratagems gather around the heroine. The hosted text is the second volume only, opening in the middle of the story.
78598-a-fatal-silence-vol-3-of-3:
A Fatal Silence, volume three, closes a novel by Florence Marryat, author of Love's Conflict and Veronique. The set ran to three volumes, and this last one was printed at London and Sydney. Its eight chapters move from The Doctor and the Widow to the final unmasking, by way of a terrible discovery and an unsigned letter.

The volume opens at Deepdale, where Hal Rushton hurries home to a wife who has just given birth. The young parish doctor, Charles Addison, fresh from hospital work, meets him at the door with the news: a little daughter waits upstairs. Hal frets over the missing nurse, engaged unseen in the country, while the tale turns toward the fate of Paulie and the wife's deception.
78689-the-contrast-volume-2-of-3:
The Contrast, volume two of three, is a novel by the author of Matilda and Yes and No, published in London by Colburn and Bentley in 1832. Its motto, from Shakespeare, warns what discord follows when degree is taken away. The volume opens with verses in Byron's manner. They promise to sing of knights and dames such as the times may furnish, and to colour artificial manners with nature.

Some years have passed over Sir North Saunders's head since the first volume left him. He is neither richer nor poorer, wiser nor better, and can still eat as much and walk as little. One great epoch has occurred in the life of a politician of his calibre: he has turned sixty. He has also lately acted as a justice of the peace, suing out his dedimus and becoming one of the quorum.
78772-dead-men-s-shoes-vol-1-of-3:
The first volume of a three-volume novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret. John Maxwell and Company published it at London in 1876. The author dedicates it to Sir J Cordy Burrows of Brighton. A friendship of nearly twenty years stands behind the gift. Eighteen chapters fill this opening volume.

The story starts on Battersea Bridge at December sunset. A girl-woman reads a letter there, alone. Her black silk dress was once handsome, and her sealskin jacket is worn bald at the edges. Passers-by wonder at beauty so poorly clad. Chapter titles name Sibyl Faunthorpe and her diary. Uncle Trenchard, a prodigal's return, and a mysterious visitor follow. The writer was Mary Elizabeth Braddon, queen of the sensation novel.
78773-dead-men-s-shoes-vol-2-of-3:
Volume two of Dead Men's Shoes, a novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret, was printed at London in 1876 in three volumes. A dangerous triumph opens the contents, then half confidence, received by the county, and Jenny's visitor. Will fortune never come with both hands full asks a later chapter. Startling information, town talk, and between love and gold follow.

Sir Wilford has his own way, Marion is raised to distinction, and at the How lead to Tilberry steeplechase. Joel Pilgrim, Alexis comes to grief, and fallen by the wayside fill the close of the list, with bitter almonds and village slander last. Sir Wilford Cardonnel pays a second morning call at Lancaster Lodge, supported by his strong minded sister Phoebe. Sensation fiction spins its web of money and marriage.
78774-dead-men-s-shoes-vol-3-of-3:
Dead Men's Shoes, Volume Three, is the closing volume of a sensation novel by the author of Lady Audley's Secret. John Maxwell of London printed the set in 1876. The author's name stays off the title page, as was her habit in that house. Chapter verse mottoes from the poets head the divisions.

The contents open with Trot's history, then Gaining Time and At Bay. A father's claim and a wedding eve quicken the plot. Dark surmises, a scene in the surgery, and Stephen Trenchard surprising his friends fill the middle. Alexis investigates, Levison cross-examines, and the Podmores think of emigration. A committal for trial and a dark tale darkly finished lead to the epilogue. Alexis wakes on the first morning with a throbbing head and a vague sense of trouble. The book is full-strength sensation fiction from its queen's own publisher.
78878-jack-brag-vol-3-of-3:
Jack Brag, volume three of three, was printed in London by Richard Bentley in 1837. The author, who also wrote Sayings and Doings and Maxwell, is not named on the title page. Jack is a bold, self pleased fellow whose boasts drive the fun.

The last volume opens with Jack in bed at a sea side hotel, cured of sleep by the mumbo jum of Sir Stumpy Dubs. A strong dose from the night before has left his head and limbs aching for days. Sun, sea, boats, and garden flowers fill the view from his window, yet Jack sees and hears none of it. His mind stays on the past night and what lies just ahead. Readers who read the first volumes find the close of a brash comic tale here.
79372-saint-mungo-s-city-vol-2-of-3:
Saint Mungo's City, by Sarah Tytler, is a novel in three volumes, and this is the second. Chatto and Windus printed the set in London in 1884. Tytler had written The Bride's Pass and Beauty and the Beast before this tale of a Scottish city.

The volume opens in a winter of typhoid fever, the worst outbreak in memory. Rory of the Shelties lies stricken, and the sickness spreads to suburbs and country along the Aytoun Water. The first signs, the tale notes, came after the excesses and exposure of Fair week. Chapters bring Athole Murray to the rescue and a partnership for young Tam. A dinner-party, a stand by Peter and Murray, and the death of Fenton of Strathdivie follow. The reading of the will closes the volume, with Jean Mackinnon's portion at stake.
79373-saint-mungo-s-city-vol-3-of-3:
Sarah Tytler wrote Saint Mungo City, a novel in three books put out in London in 1884. Book three is the part held here. Tytler had told tales of a bride pass and of beauty and the beast. The city of the title is Glasgow.

The Miss Mackinnons open the book with a neat plan. A fraud had stripped two of the sisters to make the third, Bethia, rich. The pair will not take from a sister what was willed away from them, says Miss Janet with pride. Law men come to Saint Mungo Square, and Claribel Drysdale stands by her flag. Auld Tam grows sure of a grim thought, and Sir Hugo lays his suit at the feet of Eppie. A gift of self, a new sum, and a sketch of a poor court close the book.
79461-nora-vol-1-of-3:
Lady Emily Ponsonby wrote a novel in three volumes, of which this is the first, published at London in 1870 with a motto from Cowper on fierce passions. Ponsonby had written The Discipline of Life. Chapter one opens on an old gentleman at breakfast. A little girl, he exclaims to himself. He is only fifty eight, hale and healthy, though called old.

One muffin and four thin bits of toast compose his breakfast, this day and every day. Hurst and Blackett published the novel at Great Marlborough Street. The right of translation was reserved. Three volume novels like this one filled the circulating libraries that ruled Victorian fiction reading.
79591-lady-wedderburn-s-wish-vol-2-of-3:
Lady Wedderburn's Wish, volume two of three, is a tale of the Crimean War by James Grant, author of The Romance of War. Tinsley Brothers published it in London in 1870. The second volume's twenty-four chapters open in barracks again and pass the last night at mess. Confidences and the girl I left behind me follow, and the major's story concludes.

The route for Varna then sets the regiment moving east: dark days, a surprise, and Mary beginning her pilgrimage. London chapters intervene, with Piccadilly, a lonely street, and an alderman. The troopship and the voyage follow, then under arrest, the bridge of sighs, and the vale of Aladyn, ending at Varna. The first chapter gives Wedderburn his orders by telegraph. Sir Edward Elton tells him they depart the fifth, leaving a fortnight to get his outfit for the East.
8168-gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrate:
Book three of Rabelais's Gargantua and Pantagruel turns from war to a question: should Panurge marry? Panurge seeks counsel everywhere, from theologians, lawyers, doctors, and philosophers, and each answer deepens his doubt. Urquhart's translation of this book appeared posthumously in 1693, with a new edition of books one and two under Motteux's editorship. And the text here draws on those editions, with passages restored from the 1738 edition edited by Ozell.

The third book is Rabelais's most discursive, a comic symposium on marriage, fate, and free will that ends with a decision to consult the Oracle of the Holy Bottle. Its learned jokes and lists remain famous. For readers following Pantagruel's company, this is the philosophical heart of the sequence, and its funniest debate.
8463-memoirs-of-henry-hunt-esq-volume-3:
Volume 3 of Henry Hunt's memoirs continues the radical orator's story, written by himself in His Majesty's jail at Ilchester, in Somerset. Hunt, jailed in the Peterloo era, uses the volume to defend his career, attack his enemies, and argue for parliamentary reform, with Pope's lines on faultless pieces again as epigraph.

Readers meet early nineteenth-century radical politics from inside, as Hunt tells it: crowds, trials, and the press wars that made him famous and hated. The memoirs are vivid and one-sided, which is their value as history. Together with volumes 1 and 2, they form a prison-written account of a movement.
8473-life-on-the-mississippi-part-3:
Part 3 of Life on the Mississippi drops readers into chapter 11, The River Rises, where a big rise turns small craft into a nuisance. Twain's boat runs chute after chute, a new world to the young pilot. Broad-horns, flatboats, appear in the worst places: cramped bends, and the head of a chute, where a collision seems certain.

This section shows Twain learning the river's dangers in high water, with humor and close observation of boats, crews, and currents. Readers get the pilot's education in mid-course, after the geography of part 1 and the cub-pilot chapters. It is river life at its most crowded and comic, with the Mississippi itself as the chief character.
8513-the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-vo:
Volume 3 of Émile Zola's Lourdes, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, covers the third day of the pilgrimage. At seven on a fine August Sunday morning, Guersaint is already up and dressed. He secured one of two little rooms on the third floor of the Hotel of the Apparitions, and now he goes to begin the day's devotions.

Zola follows the pilgrims through the third day's processions, hopes, and disappointments, with Pierre and Marie at the center. The volume shows Lourdes as a small city of faith and commerce, where miracles are sought and counted. Readers following the trilogy get the pilgrimage at its height, in Zola's detailed, naturalist manner.
8528-eve-s-diary-part-3:
Adam's voice takes over in Part 3 of Mark Twain's Eve's Diary, and his gruff tone softens into fond observation. He reminds himself to allow for Eve's youth, since she is still only a girl. Everything strikes her as wonderful, and a fresh flower stops her with delight, prompting her to pet and caress it.

This section gives Adam's gruff, fond view of Eve, after her own diary entries in earlier parts. Readers get Twain's comic marriage, told from both sides, with Adam learning to love wonder itself. The part suits readers who know the whole diary, and those who want Adam's voice alone.
8553-the-seaboard-parish-volume-3:
George MacDonald closes The Seaboard Parish in volume 3. Its contents include A Walk with My Wife, Our Last Shore-Dinner, A Pastoral Visit, and The Art of Nature. The Sore Spot, The Gathering Storm, The Gathered Storm, The Shipwreck, The Funeral, The Sermon, Changed Plans, and The Studio follow.

The final volume brings the parish story to storm and loss, with a shipwreck and a funeral testing the minister's faith and his people. MacDonald's seaside parish, with its sermons and family life, ends in reflection on nature, art, and grief. Readers following the trilogy get its resolution, gentle and earnest, by the sea that shaped it.
8584-roughing-it-part-3:
This third part of Mark Twain's Roughing It picks up at chapter twenty-one, as the stagecoach nears Carson City, capital of Nevada Territory, on the twentieth day of the journey. Twain and his companions are sorry to stop: they have grown fond of stage life, fed on wonders daily, and now face a humdrum village walled in by barren, snow-clad mountains. Sagebrush, greasewood, and alkali dust replace the road's variety.

From Carson City the narrative turns to Nevada settlement, mining hopes, and the daily grind of a raw frontier town. The comedy sharpens as Twain's grand plans meet dust, disappointment, and small-time scheming. Readers who enjoyed the overland journey will find the same voice now applied to staying put, and the same mix of tall tale and sharp observation that made the book endure.
8595-normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its:
Mont St Michel opens this third part of Gordon Home's illustrated tour of Normandy, first seen from the coast road out of Avranches. Home describes the long approach across sands and causeway, the walled rock rising from the bay, and the small villages, wells, and farmyards passed on the way. Sunset light, grey seas, and the tide flooding the road all shape how the mount first appears.

After the mount, the tour moves on to Coutances and the Cotentin coast, then St Lo, Bayeux, Caen, and the shore toward Trouville, ending with notes on Norman history. The chapters blend road notes, building detail, and old stories, so a reader can follow the same ground Home walked. It works best as a companion for anyone planning to visit, or simply picturing, these towns.
8703-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-3:
This third volume of Gustave Dore's Bible gallery moves from judges to kings, opening with Deborah's song of triumph after Israel's victory. Deborah and Barak sing praise for a people who offered themselves willingly, recalling the Lord marching out of Seir and Edom while earth trembled and mountains melted. Jephthah met by his daughter, and Jephthah's daughter with her companions, follow, with Samson slaying the lion, Samson and Delilah, and the death of Samson.

Naomi and her daughters-in-law, Ruth and Boaz, the return of the ark, and Saul and David, with David sparing Saul, complete the volume's arc from tribal judges to the monarchy's beginnings. The passages, chosen to match Dore's engravings, favour dramatic turning points. Readers meet some of the Old Testament's most retold stories in compact form, and can trace how Israel's leaders rose, fell, and passed power onward.
8723-the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volum:
This third volume of Emile Zola's Rome, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, is Part III of the novel, opening with Pierre, after a long ramble, once more before the Vatican. A harassing attraction ever leads him there. On a Wednesday evening he meets Monsignor Nani, assessor of the Holy Office, fresh from his weekly audience with the Pope, where he reported the Congregation's morning proceedings. Nani, smiling with pleasant civility, offers Pierre a chance to see the Pope in public while waiting for a private audience.

From that meeting, the volume follows Pierre deeper into Vatican circles, where politeness masks surveillance and delay. Zola contrasts Pierre's earnest hope for a hearing with a system skilled at wearing petitioners down. The middle volume tightens the novel's suspense: will Pierre ever reach the Pope, and what will Rome do with a priest who wants the Church to change?
8792-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
This third part of Cary's Purgatory covers cantos eleven through eighteen, the terraces of pride, envy, and wrath. Canto eleven opens with a paraphrase of the Lord's Prayer, addressed to the Almighty Father who makes the heavens his dwelling, not confined by bounds. Viewing his primal effluence with intenser love there. The proud, bent under stones, join their voices to the prayer for daily manna, for peace, and for forgiveness.

Envious souls with sewn eyes, wrathful souls in blinding smoke. Virgil's great discourse on love and free will follow, as Dante learns why disordered love is the root of sin. The part is Purgatory's teaching heart, moving from punishment to philosophy without losing poetry. Readers who want Dante's moral theory in its clearest form will find it here, carried by prayer, example, and Virgil's patient argument on the mountain road.
8798-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Cary's Paradise concludes in this third part, cantos twenty-two through thirty-three, the highest heavens. Canto twenty-two turns, astounded, to Beatrice as guardian of his steps, like a child running to where he trusts most. She soothes him like a mother calming a pale, breathless son. She reminds him that he is in Heaven, where all is holy and all is done zealously and well. Asks what change her song and smile have wrought in him.

From the contemplatives' heaven, Dante rises through the fixed stars, the primum mobile, and the Empyrean, to the rose of the blessed and the final vision of God. The part's last cantos, with Bernard as guide, are among the most famous in literature. Readers finishing the Comedy here meet Dante's attempt to say the unsayable.
884-memoirs-of-extraordinary-popular-del:
Charles Mackay devoted this third volume to three more delusions: alchemy, fortune telling, and animal magnetism. The alchemists, searchers for the philosopher's stone and the water of life, run from Geber and Avicenna through Albertus Magnus, Roger Bacon, Nicholas Flamel, and Paracelsus to Cagliostro and St. Germain.

Fortune tellers and magnetisers follow, with their dupes and their arts, and Mackay notes that dissatisfaction with one's lot drives much human folly, yet also much progress. His moral is clear: reason must guard against wonder. The volume completes his classic survey of crowd madness, and it still reads as a warning.
892-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
This third volume follows Rome through civil war and the reign of Theodosius, the emperor who tried to hold a splitting empire together. Gratian dies, Arianism falls, and Theodosius fights Maximus and Eugenius, wins, does penance under St. Ambrose, and dies, leaving the empire to his sons.

Gibbon then traces the end of pagan worship, the rise of saints and relics, and the final division of East and West. Milman's notes accompany the text. The volume marks the hinge of the whole history, where one Roman world becomes two, and where faith begins to shape the state as much as armies do.
8943-adela-cathcart-volume-3:
George MacDonald wrote Adela Cathcart as a frame tale: a sick young woman is cheered by stories told aloud by family and friends. This third volume carries on the frame with Uncle Peter, and adds tales such as The Giant's Heart, The Cruel Painter, and The Castle. Each story is meant to lift Adela's spirits and stir her mind.

MacDonald's tales blend fairy wonder with moral depth, and the talks between stories let his characters weigh what each tale means. The book shows his gift for using fantasy to heal and teach. Readers who love Victorian fairy tales will find this volume warm, strange, and full of heart.
8956-the-literary-remains-of-samuel-tayl:
Henry Nelson Coleridge collects and edits the third volume of Samuel Taylor Coleridge's literary remains, published in 1838 and inscribed to John Hookham Frere. Contents open with a letter to a godchild from Lincoln's Inn, March 26, 1838, followed by a Formula Fidei on the Holy Trinity from 1830. One piece presents the absolute as pure subjectivity, good by its very nature, and as the ground and will behind all possible being.

Later remains range through theology, philosophy, and literary criticism, in fragments, notes, and letters that show Coleridge's mind working after his poetic prime. Henry Nelson Coleridge, the poet's nephew and son-in-law, preserves material that might otherwise have vanished. Scholars of Romanticism value the volume for Coleridge's late thought. General readers will find demanding but rewarding glimpses of a mind that never stopped theologizing, even in private notes.
9166-the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volu:
Émile Zola wrote Paris as the third book of his Three Cities trilogy, translated by Ernest Vizetelly. This volume holds Book Three, called The Rivals. On the Wednesday before mid-Lent Thursday, a great charity bazaar fills the Duvillard mansion for the Asylum of the Invalids of Labour. Five thousand cards admit all Paris society.

The opening of the bombarded mansion to crowds is an event, watched by police in nearby streets. Duvillard planned the bazaar, and his wife obeyed his bidding. Zola uses the glitter to expose wealth, power, and charity as show. The volume drives the trilogy toward crisis.
9317-a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-3:
Ian Maclaren's Book Three, A Fight with Death, centers on Saunders, Drumsheugh's grieve, brought to death's gates by fever caught in Glasgow. A London doctor at Lord Kilspindie's lodge looks in from the moor and gives him six hours, more or less. He buttons his gloves, climbs into his brake, and leaves the verdict behind.

Bell hears it from behind the door and gives way utterly, but Drumsheugh will not accept it while Saunders still lives. Dr. MacLure's fight for the man follows, quiet and stubborn. The volume is Maclaren at his most moving, a parable of hope against medical pride.
9445-samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-:
Part three of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren picks up Samantha's church and home battles in mid-stream. Told in Holley's broad farm dialect, it follows Samantha and her husband Josiah through meeting-house strife and neighborly trials. This part opens as Josiah's temper shifts, and a silver wedding invite stirs the house. The tone stays comic, but the stakes feel real.

Lodema's sharp tongue, fair work, and church funds tangle through the chapters, with Samantha striving to keep peace and win a hearing for women. Josiah, slow to change, gives ground in small, telling ways. A reader gets more of Holley's beloved farm wife: jokes, grit, and a steady push for justice inside the church walls.
948-ethics-part-3:
Baruch Spinoza's Ethics continues in Part Three, on the origin and nature of the emotions, translated by R. H. M. Elwes. Spinoza notes that most writers on the emotions treat them as matters outside nature, rather than as natural phenomena following nature's general laws. He sets out to correct that error.

He defines joy, sorrow, desire, love, and hate as states of mind and body, following from causes as surely as any motion. His geometric order stays strict, and his aim is practical: to know the emotions is the first step to mastering them. Part Three is the heart of Spinoza's psychology, and it still rewards close reading.
9752-night-and-morning-volume-3:
Volume three of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning opens in a Paris quarter, before a curious temple-like building. Pilasters painted green and gilt, a semicircular front, and an entresol mark the odd house, which local virtuosi took for a Roman temple copy. The novel's plot thickens around this Paris scene, as fortunes and schemes cross. Lytton's eye for streets and rooms stays sharp.

Book three carries the tale through Paris society, art, and intrigue, with the temple house as its emblem. The prose favors polished scene painting. A reader gets the middle book of a Victorian novel of ambition, set in a Paris both fashionable and strange.
9881-clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-:
Samuel Richardson's great epistolary novel tells its story entirely through letters, and this third volume carries Clarissa Harlowe's ordeal forward. Her friend Miss Howe urges her to marry Lovelace, while Clarissa recounts, in alarm, how Lovelace tricked her away from her family.

Letter by letter, readers watch Clarissa weigh duty, love, and fear, blaming her first secret letters to Lovelace for all that followed. Richardson's slow, inward method makes her mind the scene of the drama. This volume is essential for anyone following one of the longest and most famous novels in English.
a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-3:
Volume 3 of Beverley Nichols's A Book of Old Ballads draws again on Percy's Reliques and the English and Scottish ballads gathered by Child and Kittredge. It opens with 'Clerk Colvill,' warned by his wife never to ride by the wells of Slane, and riding there anyway to meet the mermaid who is his death.

Border and battle pieces dominate the middle of the volume: 'Edom o' Gordon,' the great hunting fight of 'Chevy Chace,' and 'Sir Patrick Spens' sailing to his drowning. 'Sir Lancelot du Lake,' 'Gil Morrice,' 'Child Waters,' and 'King Edward IV and the Tanner of Tamworth' mix romance, murder, and comedy, and 'The Earl of Mar's Daughter' closes the set. Four ballads carry colour plates.
a-collection-of-old-english-plays-volume: In the third volume of his old English plays, Arthur Henry Bullen prints one play for the first time. The other plays in the volume had likewise not been reprinted before. Bullen notes that a promised Heywood play defeated him, its handwriting being too hard to read. He hoped an expert in old handwriting might yet secure it for a later volume.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Part 3 sends Hank riding with Sandy through lovely country that turns to slow torture behind her endless tale-telling and armour he cannot scratch himself in. Their road passes freemen ground down by lords and Church, and Sandy narrates her own story of a castle, ogres, and swineherds in the approved romance style, at approved romance length.

The journey ends at the castle of Morgan le Fay, Arthur's sister, a queen beautiful, musical, and casually murderous with her prisoners and servants. Hank must manage her whims, her dungeons, and her terror of her guest's reputation as a magician.
