The part mixes travel writing, dialect comedy, and a hard account of what common people owed their betters in Twain's sixth century.
a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-3: The third volume of Ian Maclaren's Doctor of the Old School follows Saunders to the gates of death by fever. A London doctor at a shooting lodge gives him six hours and leaves in his carriage. Bell hears the verdict from behind the door and gives way to grief. The volume tests the parish doctor against a famous oracle from the city.
a-far-country-volume-3:
Winston Churchill opens book three of his novel with the fame of Hugh Paret's city. It is a byword for sudden, fabulous wealth. It turns out a full-fledged millionaire, so it was said, nearly every week. Distinguished Englishmen, Frenchmen, Germans, and Italians on the grand tour made a point of visiting, and exhausted their adjectives on the place.

This final volume brings Paret's climb to its reckoning. The corporation lawyer who mastered the city's machinery faces the emptiness of the life he built, the marriage it starved, and the claims of a conscience he outran for years. Churchill closes his panoramic novel of American business with judgment and a hard-won turn toward honesty.
a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-3:
William Dean Howells opens the third part of his New York novel with a banquet swelling in the promoter Fulkerson's fancy. The magazine Every Other Week has succeeded, and Fulkerson dreams of a dinner at Delmonico's with the literary and artistic people of the whole country, fully reported in the papers. His genius is for turning literature into an event.

Around the scheme the novel's strands tighten: old Dryfoos's pride in his money's new respectability, his son Conrad's feeling for the poor, and the artists' and writers' jostling for place. Howells keeps his large cast in motion with talk as the main action. The volume carries the magazine from experiment to institution, with the costs showing.
a-history-of-science-volume-3:
Henry Smith Williams devotes the third volume of his history to the modern development of the physical sciences. The contents begin with Newton's successors in astronomy, Halley, Bradley, Herschel, and Laplace among them, and the slow solution of the shape of the earth. New fields then open one after another.

Chapters cover the birth of paleontology, modern geology, and meteorology, then heat, light, electricity, and magnetism. The conservation of energy and the ether get chapters of their own. Williams, helped by Edward H. Williams, writes plainly for lay readers and keeps the human story of each discoverer in view. The volume carries science from the telescope age into the laboratory age.
a-life-for-a-life-volume-1-of-3:
Volume one of A Life for a Life, an 1859 novel by Dinah Maria Mulock Craik, opens a story issued in the three-volume form Victorian readers expected. Craik was a popular novelist of domestic life, best known for John Halifax, Gentleman. This first volume begins the tale that the following two volumes carry to its close.

As the opening installment, it sets out the characters and the stakes implied by the title, in which a life answers for a life. Craik's fiction is known for its earnest moral feeling and its close attention to home and work. Readers who finish this volume hold the first act of the full novel, in the same divided form in which its first audience read it.
a-popular-history-of-france-from-the-ear: François Guizot continues his history of France through the later Hundred Years' War. It runs from Charles the Sixth and the dukes of Burgundy to Charles the Seventh and Joan of Arc. The volume then follows Louis the Eleventh and the wars in Italy under Charles the Eighth and Louis the Twelfth. Illustrations of Joan entering Orleans, Chinon Castle, and the States General at Tours mark the passage from civil strife to a kingdom taking firmer shape.
a-romance-of-youth-volume-3:
Francois Coppee carries his hero into later boyhood in A Romance of Youth, Volume 3 of the English edition. Amedee now studies and dreams beyond the Gerard family's rooms. The engraver's daughters are growing into young women beside him. Childhood's pretend marriage starts to cast a real shadow over all three hearts.

Paris widens for Amedee in this volume: schools, streets, and first ambitions enter the tale. Money stays scarce, and pride becomes a young man's defense. Coppee follows the shift from games to glances with a poet's patience for detail. Family sorrows and neighbors' kindnesses still steer the plot more than grand events do. The romance of the title gathers force quietly, in visits and small services. Readers midway through the set will feel the design: a whole youth built from humble rooms, preparing the joys and regrets that the final volume must settle.
a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-volume-3:
André Theuriet closes his pastoral novel in this third volume. It contains the seventh, eighth, and ninth chapters of the whole. They are The Strange, Dark Secret, Love's Sad Ending, and Love Heals the Broken Heart. Those titles state the book's movement plainly. The secret that has shadowed the heir of Vivey and the woodland queen comes out at last.

Theuriet resolves his tale among the forests where it began, with grief given its full weight before any healing. His strength throughout is place: paths, clearings, and seasons rendered by a writer who knew the Lorraine woods from boyhood. Readers of the earlier volumes will find the loose threads of the unfinished will and the forest loves tied off here.
adela-cathcart-volume-3: George MacDonald continues Adela Cathcart in this third volume, where the contents run from My Uncle Peter continued through The Giant's Heart and A Child's Holiday. Interruption, Percy, The Cruel Painter, The Castle, What Next, Generalship, and An Unforeseen Foresight complete the volume. The first chapter resolves that Chrissy shall tell her uncle her story that evening. A walk together shows her startling at every voice behind her, turning pale, then smiling at herself as a goose.
amelia-volume-3: Henry Fielding's Amelia, volume three, carries Booth and Amelia into the later books of the novel, where Dr. Harrison counsels, strangers appear and town wit is sampled. A masquerade and its consequences, Colonel Bath in great glory and a visit from Captain Trent test the couple's fortunes. The volume closes the Saintsbury edition's Amelia with the history looking backwards before it goes forward.
an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-volume-3:
Neighbors fill An Attic Philosopher in Paris, Volume 3, the third English portion of Emile Souvestre's journal of a poor Paris scholar. The attic floor is a small village: workpeople sharing walls, sounds, and sorrows. Peter the bookbinder's death gives the volume its gravest entry, the philosopher standing by a fellow lodger whose books outlast him. Souvestre writes the funeral of a nobody as an event of state in the republic of the poor.

Inside, the diary keeps its method of meditation tied to errands: a visit, a loan, a small feast, each weighed for what it teaches. The philosopher argues with his own envy when richer men's carriages pass below. Kindness in these pages is work, done on schedule like binding or sewing. Readers in the third volume get the journal's deepest register, grief and gratitude sharing one small room above a Paris most novels never climbed to see.
ancient-records-egypt-breasted-1906-vol-:
Breasted's third volume of Ancient Records, published in 1906, covers the nineteenth dynasty. Seti I and Ramesses II dominate its pages: campaigns in Asia, the great battle of Kadesh, and the peace treaty with the Hittites that followed. Temple inscriptions at Karnak and Abu Simbel supply many of the texts in Breasted's translation.

The Kadesh poems and the treaty text rank among the most studied documents of the ancient world. Later records in the volume trace the dynasty's slow strain under invasion and internal dispute. Breasted arranges all of it with dates, sources, and sober notes. Volume three gives the Ramesside age its full documentary weight. Egypt's voice here is proud, detailed, and increasingly defensive.
andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-military-:
Inside the stockade is where Volume 3 of John McElroy's Andersonville begins, at chapter forty-three. He reflects that no community ever had so little ebb and flow. A city's tides purify it, like the ocean's. The prison's stagnant mass has none. The morning walk, the Rialto where prisoners gather and trade, and the cursing of the Confederacy fill his chapter heads. Between set pieces, an exchanged prisoner tells the story of the battle of Spotsylvania Court House, news from the world of the living.

McElroy writes the middle months: monotony as torture, rumor as currency. Readers deep in the memoir get its hardest truth here. Andersonville killed by inches and by sameness, and this volume's genius is to make the reader feel the sameness without ever being dull.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-3:
Tertullian fills volume three of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, the 1885 set edited by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson. Tertullian of Carthage, writing around 200 AD, was the founder of Latin Christianity's voice. No early writer is fiercer, funnier, or more quotable.

His apologetic works answer pagan slanders and demand fair treatment for Christians before the law. Other treatises rule on prayer, dress, idolatry, and the games, with a rigor that spares no one. Tertullian coined much of the Latin vocabulary of theology, including the word for Trinity. The volume gives the whole of his surviving early work in English dress.
arabian-nights-lane-1877-vol-3:
Volume III of Lane's Thousand and One Nights, in the 1877 printing, completes his pioneering scholarly version. Edward William Lane first issued the work from 1838 to 1840, with drawings and notes drawn from his years in Egypt. The final volume carries Shahrazad's tales to their close in his measured English.

Lane's set taught Victorian Britain to take the Nights seriously as literature and as evidence of Arab life. His omissions are famous, but so is his fidelity where he does translate. Volume III rounds out a version that stands beside Payne's and Burton's as one of the three great English Nights.
arabian-nights-payne-1882-vol-3:
Volume III of Payne's Thousand Nights and One Night, dated 1882, carries the Calcutta text forward in English. The tales turn and turn again: voyages, transformations, and lovers parted by fate and reunited by wit. John Payne's rendering stays complete and unexpurgated, the quality that made his the first full English Nights.

Between Burton's ornate version and Lane's trimmed one, Payne's stands as the full record for its age. Readers who follow the sequence feel the great story-cycle breathing at its own slow, hypnotic pace. Volume III holds the middle of the early nights, with six volumes still to come.
aristophanes-plays-rogers-loeb-1924-vol-:
The third Rogers volume of Aristophanes, published in 1924, completes the Loeb set with Lysistrata, the Thesmophoriazusae, the Ecclesiazusae, and Plutus. In Lysistrata the women of Greece end a war by refusing their husbands until peace is made. Its fame has only grown with the centuries.

The Thesmophoriazusae traps a spy inside a women's festival, mocked in Euripides' own style. The Ecclesiazusae hands Athens to its women, who decree shared property and shared spouses. Plutus, the last play, restores the god of wealth's sight and upends rich and poor. Rogers's rhymes carry the bawdy, topical energy across twenty-four centuries. With this volume the eleven surviving comedies stand complete.
arnold-history-rome-vol-3:
Crisis grips Rome in the third volume of Arnold's History of Rome, from 1838. The Gracchi seek reform, Marius and Sulla march armies on the city, and the free state totters. Arnold, a liberal Englishman, watched ancient liberty die with a keen, wary eye.

He treats the late Republic as a warning for any free people. Wealth, faction, and armed ambition rot the laws from within. Each reform missed makes the next blow worse. His account gains urgency from that parallel, and the volume closes his history with a somber lesson on how republics fall when citizens cease to guard them.
athenaeus-deipnosophists-yonge-vol-3:
Volume three completes Yonge's translation of Athenaeus's Deipnosophists. The banquet of the learned reaches its last courses in this volume. Each dish still sets off cascades of quotation from vanished books.

Slaves, drinking customs, and famous courtesans occupy the later talk. Athenaeus's guests display learning as a competitive sport to the end. The whole work preserves fragments of hundreds of lost Greek writers. Historians of food, music, and daily life mine it constantly. Yonge's three volumes gave English readers the complete ancient feast. Chatty and enormous, the Deipnosophists remains a quarry no classicist can ignore for long.
b09-zwingli-latin-works-3:
The third volume of the Latin Works and Correspondence of Huldreich Zwingli covers 1528 to 1531. Clarence Nevin Heller edited the volume, with introductions by George Warren Richards, in the 1929 Philadelphia issue. The translators of the earlier Jackson edition rendered the Latin texts into English.

Zwingli's last years were his hardest: dispute with Luther over the Lord's Supper, and war clouds over the Swiss cantons. He died in battle at Kappel in 1531, and the correspondence runs to that end. These pages show a reformer holding a city, a pulpit, and a cause at once. The volume completes the standard English record of his Latin works.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-3:
Volume three of Michael L. Rodkinson's English Babylonian Talmud holds Tract Erubin, the laws of Sabbath boundaries. Erubin rules seem narrow, but they shape how a whole town keeps the Sabbath together. The 1918 edition continues Rodkinson's twenty-volume translation, the first full English Talmud.

An erub is a shared boundary that lets people carry in public space as if it were one yard. The tractate works out how such boundaries are made: walls, wires, shared food, and joined courtyards. Disputes run over every detail, from a ditch to a leaky wall. The volume shows the rabbis' genius for building community by law.
badauni-muntakhab-vol-3:
Scholars, saints, and poets crowd the third volume of Badauni's Muntakhab, in T. W. Haig's 1899 English version. Rather than battles and decrees, this book offers lives. It forms a kind of who's who of the mind in Akbar's India.

Brief lives trace teachers, mystics, calligraphers, and verse makers of the age. Badauni judges each man by his faith, learning, and character. Praise and blame fall in his usual tart measure. For readers of Mughal culture, the volume is gold: a portrait gallery of a golden age, drawn by a man who knew many of its sitters.
bancroft-history-us-vol-3:
Wars with France shake the colonies in the third volume of Bancroft's History, from 1856. Colonial rights are asserted more boldly as the stakes grow higher each year. The road bends, year by year, toward revolt against Britain.

Bancroft builds his case that liberty was America's birthright from the start. Frontier fights and imperial policy grind against each other in his pages. Assemblies learn to say no, and to mean it. He writes with rising drama here. The stage is set for the crisis volumes that follow in his vast narrative of a people becoming a nation.
beauchamp-s-career-volume-3:
Volume three of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career covers chapters nineteen to twenty-five, the heart of the election. Candidates raise knockers, ring bells, and beg for votes in Bevisham. Nevil's partner Cougham walks where the young hound wants to run. Lord Palmet and certain electors show the borough's price.

A day at Itchincope gives rural relief from the canvass. The examination of the Whigs and a fine blow struck enliven the contest. A drive into Bevisham, a holiday, and an adventure of the boat vary the political grind. Meredith watches democracy at the doorstep, where principles meet beer, bribery, and local pride. Nevil learns his countrymen faster than they learn him. The volume is election reporting raised into comedy and moral study.
bill-s-paper-chase-lady-of-the-barge-and:
W. W. Jacobs places this tale third in The Lady of the Barge and Others, again in the night watchman's voice. Sailormen have their faults, he grants, but closeness with money is seldom among them. He knew one miser in all his years at sea. Thomas Geary shipped aboard the barque Grenada, homeward from Sydney. At sixty he had saved hard for forty years, toward some six hundred pounds.

Geary's hoard, in paper money, becomes the paper chase. Bill and Jimmy quarrel over its hiding place in the fo'c'sle. Bill will take care of it; Jimmy can't trust him. If the place isn't named in a minute, Bill is off to tell the skipper. Jimmy stamps his foot: he hasn't got it, and it's Bill's silly fault. Jacobs builds farce on greed at close quarters.
blundell-s-improvement-odd-craft-part-3:
Blundell's Improvement is a comic short story by W W Jacobs, printed as part three of his Odd Craft set. Jacobs sets the scene at Turnbull's farm, where Venia Turnbull has two suitors calling on a hot Sunday. Sergeant Dick Daly, quick with a compliment, holds the lead.

John Blundell, slow and stubborn, will not leave the room, though Venia's father hints hard at a walk. A trip down to the water gives Blundell his chance to scheme. His odd conduct after that shocks the farm, and he proposes to Miss Sippet on the very day Venia weds him. Jacobs tells it dry and deadpan. Farm courtship, male pride, and a happy muddle make a short, neat tale of manners.
byron-letters-vol-3:
Volume Three of Byron's Letters and Journals, in Prothero's 1898 edition, covers his final years. Byron settled in Italy, wrote his greatest poems, and grew restless for action. The Greek war for independence gave him a cause at last.

The letters trace his life with the Shelleys, the feuds of the Italian years, and the writing of Don Juan. Then comes his sailing for Greece in 1823 to aid the rebels. He died at Missolonghi in 1824, aged thirty-six. This closing volume completes the standard record of Byron's life in his own brilliant words. Prothero closes the set with a full index to all three volumes.
carlyle-cromwell-letters-vol-3:
The Protectorate closes Carlyle's Cromwell in this third volume of the 1904 Lomas edition. Cromwell rules England without a king, facing parliaments, plots, and his own failing health. His death in 1658 ends both the book and an era.

Letters and speeches show triumph turning to loneliness and strain. The great Puritan governs, exhorts, and mourns in his own stark words. Carlyle's devotion to his hero never wavers to the last page. The full set stands as a founding act of Cromwell scholarship. It lets a maligned ruler argue his own case before posterity at last, in full.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-3:
Frederick faces a ring of foes in the third volume of Carlyle's history, in the 1884 printing. The Seven Years' War begins, and Prussia stands against Austria, France, and Russia at once. Defeat stalks the king through his darkest campaigns.

Carlyle tells of endurance raised to the level of tragedy. The great king's genius and grit hold a small state together. Battles turn on hours, and hope on rumor and weather. His devoted English champion spares no detail of the strain. The volume shows hero-worship at its most intense, wedded to research of staggering depth and labor.
carnac-s-folly-volume-3:
Carnac's Folly, Volume 3, by Gilbert Parker, is Book III of the Montreal novel. Parker opens months later, with destiny redrawing the board. Carnac has gone painting at Charlemont with his mother. Tarboe runs the mills successfully. Junia has heard nothing but one letter. It might have been written to a friend, she thinks. A sadness under it troubles her all the same.

A great decision follows, and Carnac becomes a candidate. Junia and Tarboe hear the news. A secret meeting, a challenge, and a blue paper raise the stakes. Denzil takes a hand in the game. A woman writes a letter, and Tarboe has a dream. Halves, Pardner, Halves closes the contents in lumber camp speech. Parker's hero must settle his hidden marriage, his business, and his election together. Canadian politics, in this telling, is another kind of log drive.
cecilia-or-memoirs-of-an-heiress-volume-:
The third volume of Frances Burney's Cecilia, or Memoirs of an Heiress, brings its heroine's trials toward their close. Book Eight opens with Cecilia scarcely less troubled by her decision than by her doubt, distressed and unhappy with where she stood, what she thought, and herself.

Delvile calls the next morning, fearfully asking his doom with hardly any hope of favour, and Cecilia answers him without affectation or art. Her resolution, and the distress of her long irresolution, drive the volume's emotional centre. Readers who have followed Cecilia through London's routs and snares will find this final volume the most moving of the three.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130005-3:
Memorandum of 1 April 1980 to the Director of Medical Services, from the Psychological Services Staff, revises a table on test reliability. It answers points in the staff's own response to the Inspector General's report on the Professional Applicant Test Battery. A copy of the original Table 1 is attached beside the new version.

Two changes matter, the memo states. An eighth test, Numerical Operations, joins the list examined. Sample sizes also grow almost across the board, taking the total from 426 applicants to 500. Black male numbers rise from 119 to 168, and black females from 79 to 103. White females fall slightly, to 107, because five had not taken the new test. With bigger samples the estimates grow more precise, it notes. For the full group, all eight reliabilities pass the level reported in the text, and half pass a higher one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130014-3:
Memorandum of 31 March 1980 to the Deputy Director for Administration encloses an outside expert's letter on the Inspector General's PATB reports. The writer's name is sanitized throughout. The cover note stresses the letter was not solicited in any way. The Psychological Services chief had offered to write it after reading the reports, it explains.

The sender calls the letter an important companion to the office's fuller rebuttal. He asks that it go to the Inspector General, the Director, and his deputy, as part of the formal response. The letter itself, dated March 24, 1980, is organised in four parts. Its author finds the consultants off the mark on the Strong-Campbell Interest Inventory, and calls their wider concerns those of isolated academics. The whole report was superficial and sloppy, also hostile, he writes. A final part suggests next steps for agency selection policy. Names remain masked under STATINTL marks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100030024-3:
Dated 6 July 1981, a short memorandum to the Chief of the East Asia Division passes on a report of American prisoners of war sighted in Laos. The writer forwards a private letter and asks that the sighting be checked in the field if that has not already been done. Names in the routing account are blacked out in the released copy.

The attached letter, dated 25 May 1981, came from a program manager at a Hmong refugee camp in Thailand. It describes the start of the rainy season after six dry months and the writer's camp work. One passage in it refers to American prisoners seen in Laos, which is why the letter reached the Agency at all.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100070011-3:
A thank-you letter from a former senior officer opens a long file released under a sanitized title. Writing on 13 June 1983, R. Jack Smith tells the editor of Studies in Intelligence that he cannot attend an awards ceremony on 20 June. He thanks the journal board for honoring his essay on Colonel Lawrence K. White.

Smith recalls a retirement party for Sherman Kent and the jokes that carried his farewell speech. The rest of the file is a draft historical essay on the Agency and its overseers. It weighs the wide freedom the CIA was given, the risks that freedom carried, and the slow end of easy congressional trust.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100200002-3:
Draft law to fund aid for Afghanistan is ordered in National Security Directive 5, dated 18 March 1989. Agency routing slips dated 21 March 1989 show the paper moving to the Director, his deputy, and the heads of analysis, operations, and the National Intelligence Council. The directive itself is short and marked confidential.

With Soviet forces leaving Afghanistan, the text expects the Soviet-backed regime to fall and aid to be vital for rebuilding. It directs that draft legislation go to Congress to allow funds and other resources to pass from any department to the Agency for International Development. That agency would lead in drafting and running the program, with other departments in support.
cia-crest-cia-rdp02-06298r000900060006-3:
Level sensors built around displacers are described in a Fisher instruction manual dated May 1980, Form 1802. It covers the caged 249 Series and the Type 259B sensor. The manual gives maintenance steps and parts lists for the sensor alone. Fitting, calibration, and care of the attached controller or transmitter sit in a separate manual.

Type entries distinguish cast iron cages rated at lower pressure classes from steel cages rated higher, with screwed or flanged connections of one and a half or two inches. Cage heads can be turned to eight positions. Maintenance opens with safety steps: drop the vessel level, drain the cage, release pressure, and cut electrical and pneumatic inputs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100090001-3:
Political actors in El Salvador and how they interact are mapped in a secret reference aid dated April 1984, ALA 84-10039. The aid came from the Latin American analysis office with the Office of Global Issues. It rests on information available as of 9 April 1984 and runs to a long, detailed listing.

A summary notes that the military has dominated the country's politics through most of the century, even as it helps move the country in new directions. Party entries follow, with leaders named and origins explained. One entry covers PAISA, a rightist party formed in October 1982 by nine deputies elected that March. Guerrilla plans for urban unrest also appear in the entries.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100360001-3:
Communist and radical leftist influence in Bolivia is the subject of a secret memorandum dated 30 July 1984. The summary dates the rise from the October 1982 start of civilian President Hernan Siles Zuazo's term. Closer ties with Cuba, the Soviet Union, and Nicaragua mark the foreign policy shift it describes.

The paper reports that the pro-Moscow Bolivian Communist Party holds the labor and mining posts in the cabinet. Radical advisers close to Siles are said to be building their own armed forces. Those forces, the paper judges, could not stop a rightist military coup but could carry out disruptive attacks after one. It expects leftist influence to keep growing while Siles stays in office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100450001-3:
Grenada's first national election in eight years is previewed in a secret memorandum dated 21 November 1984. A deputy assistant secretary of state for Caribbean affairs requested the paper. It rests on information available as of 20 November 1984, ahead of the 3 December vote.

Two opinion polls put the three-party New National Party coalition, led by 66-year-old Herbert Blaize, ahead. The rival Grenada United Labor Party of former prime minister Eric Gairy keeps loyal followers enough for some seats, the paper says. A left party tied to Maurice Bishop's name has little support. The paper also warns that the next government must revive the economy and hold its coalition together.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000201250001-3:
China's improving economic performance is reported in a Directorate of Intelligence memorandum dated 24 February 1984. Gains are clearest in personal consumption and agriculture, the paper says, and economic policy making shows more order and direction. Groundwork for closer economic ties with the West is also noted.

Five years of reform are changing basic ties between the state, the firm, and the individual, the paper argues. It gives a first estimate of 7 percent national income growth for 1983. Yet rapid growth exposes a further need: restructuring the price system. Irrational prices are blamed for shortages, wasted energy, poor quality goods, and swollen costs. Capital equipment imports, up sharply, also figure in the account.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000302130002-3:
Thailand's Communist Party after defeat is the subject of a memorandum dated 16 October 1984. The Southeast Asia Division prepared the paper. July arrests of more than 20 party members and several alleged sympathizers open the account, showing that Bangkok still watches the party closely as the rural insurgency fades.

Military fears of urban terrorism or a turn toward the Soviet-aligned Indochinese parties are judged exaggerated. The paper holds that the party is still reeling from four years of government operations and mass defections. A rigid leadership is expected to limit compromise with internal critics or warmer ties abroad. Short-term capacity to build a serious urban network is doubted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000302220002-3:
Taiwan's shift away from quiet diplomacy is analyzed in a memorandum dated 14 November 1984. The summary reports that, after three years of a low-key approach, Taipei is moving back to a tougher and more public defense of its international standing. The change has not yet touched ties with the United States.

Hardliners among President Chiang's senior advisers have gained influence, the paper says. They could use American military ties with China to push a loud campaign in Washington on arms and other issues, aimed in part at disrupting ties between Washington and Beijing. Advisers who favor quiet lobbying, such as Fred Chien, would likely oppose that course as dangerous. A sharp reaction from Beijing is expected if hardliners win.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000302230001-3:
United States-China economic relations are the subject of a confidential paper dated 20 November 1984, written as a contribution to an interagency study. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, with a contribution from a Department of Agriculture writer. A release note ties the paper to the Agriculture Department file.

Since a December 1978 party plenum, the paper reports, China has been reshaping and reforming its economy, turning from isolated self-reliance toward wider world involvement. An October 1984 plenum gave the reform program a sweeping endorsement. Many goods would be produced and priced by supply and demand. Joint ventures and co-production with foreign firms are picked out as a prime area of trade growth.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100640001-3:
China's economic reforms are judged in a confidential intelligence assessment dated April 1985, EA 85-10058. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, using information available as of 11 March 1985. Its subtitle pairs performance so far with prospects ahead.

Key judgments say the reform experiment shifted direction and grew sharply in 1984. Where farming had led before, new steps widened the scope. Farmers gained more room for commerce and commodity production. Factories and shops could test new wage programs from April. Rules published soon after let state industrial firms produce goods in short supply once state plans were met. The paper tracks what these openings mean for output and control.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201350001-3:
China's progress in making integrated circuits is measured in a memorandum dated 12 March 1985. The Office of East Asian Analysis produced the paper at the request of a Commerce Department trade official. Building a modern microelectronics industry is named as one of Beijing's primary technology tasks.

Many Chinese circuits are unreliable and wasteful, so Beijing imports most devices needed for key computers and military projects, the summary reports. Chinese output lags the West by about ten years: devices are bigger, use more power, and run more slowly. Weak links include poor coordination between research and production units and scarce test gear. A broad reform of research and a large import program form the reply.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201440001-3:
Japan after the sidelining of Kakuei Tanaka is weighed in a memorandum resting on information available as of 22 March 1985. The Northeast Asia Division prepared the paper. Tanaka, the ruling Liberal Democratic Party's long-time kingpin, suffered a stroke this month.

His fall could shorten Prime Minister Nakasone's tenure and, at worst, crack the party that has governed Japan for thirty years, the paper warns. At best, months of doubt will pull the party's focus from all but the most pressing issues. If Tanaka is lost for good, the roster of Nakasone's backers and rivals will change. The ten-year power struggle around Tanaka would end, bringing a new cast of senior leaders around the prime minister.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302150001-3:
China on the eve of the Vice President's visit is sketched in a memorandum dated 2 October 1985. China Division staff prepared the paper. Deng Xiaoping and other senior leaders should be in a hopeful mood for the visit, the summary reports.

Party meetings in mid-September gave Deng most of his aims. The leadership is younger, better schooled, and more set on economic reform, the paper says. Deng also cut the political weight of the military and of the party's conservative wing. The meetings backed guidelines for the 1986-90 plan that keep market policies in place. A mixed year forms the backdrop: fast industrial growth, inflation, loose credit, and a serious rise in corruption.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302240001-3:
China's September party conference is previewed in a memorandum dated 28 October 1985, EA M 85-10195. The paper sums up the main findings of a study to come, titled China's Party Conference: The Waning of the Ancien Regime. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared both pieces.

From 12 to 24 September the party held a run of meetings without precedent. In two Central Committee sessions and a special conference of delegates, Deng weakened the conservative old guard, the summary reports. He promoted allies to top party bodies and cut the weight of senior military officers. He also won a fresh endorsement of economic reform. A quarter of the 210-member Central Committee is among the figures touched by the changes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100030001-3:
Stanley Sporkin comments on an American Bar Association report in a long letter to Frederick Hitz. The report, by a working group of the Bar's task force on intelligence, is titled Oversight and Accountability of the U.S. Intelligence Agencies: An Evaluation. Sporkin calls it a commendable effort on a complex and timely topic.

The report finds that oversight mechanisms, internal and external, work well and need little change. Sporkin backs that finding wholeheartedly. Still, he offers four general observations and then points to passages needing revision or clearer wording. One concern leads the list: the drafters, he argues, assume too great a role for in-house counsel in the oversight process. Critics of the intelligence community frame his worry.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100030010-3:
Stanley Sporkin sends his finished answers to an American Bar Association questionnaire in a letter to Frederick Hitz. The letter carries no date in the released text. It stresses that the responses are his personal views and not those of the Director, the Agency, or its officials.

The questionnaire opens with criteria for evaluation. Sporkin agrees that intelligence agency activity should face congressional oversight, and that the intelligence budget should stay under the controls of the authorization process. On covert action, he rejects any added approval mechanism. A prior approval rule, he answers, would paralyze decision making. Current arrangements go as far as is wise, he holds, and may already strain the balance.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000200360013-3:
Exemptions from territorial jurisdiction is the heading of a legal text excerpt on state immunity. The passage quotes a Supreme Court ruling on state immunity. The ruling deals with what happens when the Secretary of State certifies a ship's immunity. The courts must accept that certificate, the ruling says. It counts as a final finding by the political arm of government.

Once such a certificate reaches the district court, the court must free the ship. The court may go no further in the case. The excerpt then turns to a 1945 Supreme Court decision. In that case, the Mexican government claimed immunity for a ship it owned. The ship was used in trade. The claim was denied, after a libel had been filed against the ship. The suit was filed in a California district court.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000701420010-3:
The Deputy Director of Central Intelligence names Agency representatives to an export control group in a letter marked OGC 82-00150. B. R. Inman writes to D. Lowell Jensen, Assistant Attorney General for the Criminal Division. The letter answers one from Jensen dated 18 December 1981.

Two officers are designated, one as representative and one as alternate, to the Interagency Working Group on Export Control Enforcement. Their posts are Associate General Counsel for Intelligence Community Affairs and chairman of the Technology Transfer Intelligence Committee. Inman notes that the intelligence community holds no enforcement role under export control laws. Its task is to pass on information about foreign availability of controlled goods, while guarding sources and methods.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000100030131-3:
Graves of American sailors in Tripoli, North Africa, are the subject of a rough-scanned file of reports and clippings. The dead were officers and men of the ketch Intrepid, killed in an explosion a century and a half earlier. Thirteen officers and men died on a mission that blew much of the Tripolitan fleet apart.

A search for the graves began with State Department help in the 1930s, working through hundreds of records. Five bodies washed ashore after the explosion, and their graves were at last plainly marked. An account of research on the burial place, translated from Arabic by Shafic Ibrahim, tells of hearing of the five graves in May 1938. A naval officer's signed report also appears in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200480014-3:
Vincent Davis lists reasons why he does not wish to work directly for any government department or agency in a memorandum dated 2 May 1977. The memo, marked number 3 in a series to Admiral Turner, names the CIA in particular. It runs on Patterson School letterhead from the University of Kentucky.

Labels lead his case. Davis has spent his career avoiding tags such as liberal or conservative, hawk or dove, and the mark of any single agency. In past consulting he spread small jobs across Defense, State, aid and information agencies, and others, so no one owned him. He admires a man who refused to be anybody's puppet, and draws a parallel with Turner's wish to stay Admiral rather than Mister.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200480023-3:
Stansfield Turner replies to Vincent Davis from his southern Europe command in a letter dated 28 February 1977. He thanks Davis for three recent letters full of information and leads on people. The congratulations, he says, were a gentle lead-in to an overwhelming job description.

Turner admits to some nerves but says he is excited by the challenge of the Director's post. He is starting to weigh his personnel choices and keeps a bank of talented names to call on, so nominations should keep coming. A dissertation mailed back to Davis's office on 16 February, insured but not registered, is flagged for the staff to watch for. Press clippings fill much of the rest of the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200500020-3:
Vincent Davis writes to Stansfield Turner with condolences and campus news in a letter dated 11 September 1978. He was sorry to hear of the death of Turner's father some weeks before. Davis and his wife lost three of their four parents within three years of moving to Kentucky, he writes, and so can share the burden.

The second topic is a lawsuit by the University of Kentucky against Iranian students arrested over disturbances at Turner's visit on 12 April. Davis first guessed the students would turn it into a showcase trial with national media and a lawyer such as William Kunstler. Some of them have instead hired inexperienced counsel, he reports, though his general point may still hold.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401030001-3:
DCI Schedules, October 1979 is a set of scheduling worksheets filed under that month. The topic index kept here, though, covers July 1979. The index groups the Director's actions by subject. The subjects are academic relations, analysis, openness, and SALT. Security, tactical versus national intelligence, and training appear too. Under each subject, the index lists what was produced. It may be a memo, letter, study, or chart. Each entry gives its addressee and date.

The entries include a study of United States capabilities. The study asks how well the SALT II Treaty can be monitored. A summary chart was prepared for Senator Bayh. A Gambino paper deals with uniform handling of personnel security cases. Other entries give comments on intelligence support to Navy operating forces. One asks about publishing unclassified material. Daily appointment pages follow the index.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501230017-3:
DCI Invitation (Social), 11-14 October 79 is a form for one invitation. The invitation was received 11 September 1979. It covers the annual fall Board of Advisors meetings of one school. The school is the Patterson School of Diplomacy and International Commerce. It sits at the University of Kentucky. The meetings ran from Thursday 11 to Sunday 14 October 1979. They were split between Lexington and Lake Cumberland. A reservation form was attached. The suspense was 17 September.

The papers behind the form include a memo dated 7 September 1979. It came from the Patterson School. Its director, Vincent Davis, figures in other letters in this series too. The form carries its standard parts. They are the advice line, and the Director's accept-or-regret decision. Mrs. Turner's invitation is noted. Routing to the Deputy Director, or to the national intelligence staff, is shown.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501230044-3:
Calendar September 1979 preserves pages from a desk calendar for that month. It may have been an appointment book. Each day is ruled into quarter-hour columns. The columns run from 8:45 in the morning to 5:00 in the afternoon. The surviving pages pair September days with small monthly calendars. The small calendars cover August, September, and October 1979. They are printed alongside the days.

The entries themselves are almost entirely absent from the released copy. The grids stand blank, or carry only faint, illegible marks. So the file shows the form of the Director's scheduling, not its substance. Page numbers and day counts appear in the margins. One margin notes Monday, September 17, the 260th day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601420088-3:
Turner wrote on 24 January 1978 to defend staff cuts. His letter goes to a past operations officer. The man's name is withheld in the release. Turner says he shares the worry in the man's letter. He holds that he must make the agency stronger. Demands on it grow each year, he notes.

Excess staff was plain before he came, he argues. Over-watch and thin work at headquarters were plain too. No one well placed has faulted the choice, he says. His letter cites the age of senior grades. The average sits near fifty years. He asks how the branch would replace them all at once.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601430041-3:
Town Hall Journal, volume 40 number 1, comes from Los Angeles and is dated January 3, 1978. The journal serves the Town Hall forum of California. Its front pages carry a forecast talk on business and finance for 1978. The speaker is a bank economist, and the notice asks if real growth can hit the hoped pace.

No meeting was set for the Tuesday of January 10, the journal notes. Inside, the forum's mix of talks and guests fills out the issue. Leaders from business, labor and public life use the hall as a stage. The record shows the kind of civic forum material that sat in the Director of Central Intelligence's files that winter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601450058-3:
Joining instructions for the Oxford conference of September 7 to 10 fill this file. The International Institute for Strategic Studies sent them to members. A routing slip from the agency sits at the front. The note from the institute director goes with the pack.

Practical points fill the pages that follow. Rooms, meals and the shape of the days at Christ Church all get cover. The 20th annual conference drew members from many lands. Papers like these show the ground work behind a big meet: who stays where, and how the host keeps track. The file pairs the slip with the full set of instructions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480019-3:
Vincent Davis wrote on 14 March 1978 from the University of Kentucky in Lexington. He held the Patterson Chair in international studies there. His letter sends on copies of the WORLDVIEW '78 program. The program featured Scott Breckinridge speaking later that week. A poster for the event goes with it, playing on the Director of Central Intelligence's name.

Davis calls the enclosures mere file matter, fit for archives or wastebasket alike. The wider file holds program papers for the Patterson school: social hour notes, a shift of format for 1978-79, and a fall meeting planned at Lake Cumberland Resort. A newsletter in the file reports summer internship work by students. The pack shows a campus world-affairs program in full swing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601550002-3:
FBI National Academy gets a plain history in this Central Intelligence Agency file. The text stresses how much training matters to good law work. J Edgar Hoover is quoted to that effect. Hoover founded the academy and led the FBI for decades. The bureau's push for professional standards goes back many years, the history says.

Roots lie in the early 1930s. Alarm at a rise in lawlessness moved President Franklin D Roosevelt to call a national conference on crime. That conference urged a national center to train police officers. The academy grew from that call. The file gives the school's own account of its birth and growth.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601560074-3:
Houston Clubber opens this Central Intelligence Agency file with a feature on a famed golf architect. Robert Trent Jones is the subject. The sun never sets on his world, the piece says. His courses host national and world title events across many lands. The writer traces the mark he left on the game.

Club house news fills later pages. The Texas Room stayed busy and fine, its head waiter reports. A long list of guests with pleasant memories follows. New members from real estate, building and steel get their names in print. The file is a club magazine kept whole: sport, food and the social roll of a Houston institution.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601580018-3:
Middle East peace terms drive this journal debate on a plan by Gidon Gottlieb. Gottlieb proposed an accord patterned on the Evian agreements. Those accords ended the Algerian war for France. The file prints an exchange among Gottlieb, Jacques Soustelle and a former Jerusalem bureau chief of the New York Times.

Soustelle opens amazed at the parallel drawn. The Middle East case differs from Algeria, he argues. The Evian accords proved a dismal failure in his telling. No paragraph of them was ever carried out, he says. Jewish refugees who fled Algeria fill his account. The file, kept by the Central Intelligence Agency, is a sharp print debate on whether old accords can guide a new peace.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00280r000100220001-3:
Survey of foreign activity in non-nuclear energy technologies fills this report. The Scientific and Technical Intelligence Committee issued it in June 1978. Its mark is STIC-78-004, graded confidential. Copy number 264 is printed on the cover. The survey looks abroad at work on energy beyond the atom.

Coal, solar and other non-nuclear paths form the field, as the title frames it. The report sorts which lands were active and how far they had got. Such a survey served energy planning at home in a decade of oil shocks. It shows the Central Intelligence Agency and its partner services turned, for a time, to a plain question of fuel and power.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100040007-3:
Admiral Stansfield Turner interviewed is the subject of this program file. A public affairs staff sheet heads the transcript. The show is 60 Minutes on the CBS network. Dan Rather is the reporter. The sheet gives a broadcast date of February 8, 1981, in the evening.

Rather opens by noting how rare such access is. A reporter is seldom let into the world of spies, he says. Turner had run the Central Intelligence Agency for four years, the piece notes. A fellow Annapolis classmate, Jimmy Carter, had picked him for the post. The transcript prints the talk that followed, as Turner looked back on the job.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100090002-3:
Summary of advisory groups' recommendations to the Director of Central Intelligence fills this list. The groups were staff panels set up to air views from the ranks. Their first ask is stark: lie detector tests every five years for all cleared staff. The ask reaches to Congress staff, the FBI, State, Justice and the White House.

A national intelligence operations center comes next on the list. Other asks treat fitness reports and the training of supervisors who write them. Job grading and appeals get a place too. Collection duties close the sampled heads. The list shows what staff panels thought most needed fixing in the house in that era.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200470027-3:
Robert B Leachman wrote on November 1, 1978 from the Philosophical Society of Washington. The society sits on K Street in the capital. His letter praises the CIA as a center of scholarly attainment. The agency adds to the intellectual life of the area, he writes.

The society is a century old and still vigorous, he notes. It bridges all specialties among learned bodies. Persons in Turner's position can strengthen such links by membership, he argues. The letter is an invitation dressed as praise. It shows how Washington's learned world courted the spy chief as one of its own kind that year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200650009-3:
Status reports on advisory group suggestions get a memo dated 5 April 1978. A deputy executive secretary writes to the Director. The memo answers Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence,'s request of 24 February. Summaries of progress are attached to it. Two groups' recommendations are covered.

Handicapped employees sent their suggestions on 2 November. The Federal Women's Program Board sent theirs on 9 November. Both groups have been told the status of their asks, the memo notes. The file shows the advisory system at work: staff panels speak, the house acts or explains, and a report goes back to the top and to the groups.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660026-3:
Recommendations to the Director of Central Intelligence from the Federal Women's Program Board get a tasking memo dated 15 November 1977. The memo goes to the acting administration chief, by way of the acting deputy director. The board made its asks at its 9 November meeting with the Director. They all treat personnel management.

The asks are to be reviewed for the Director. Word is due by 19 December on if and how each could be carried out. One ask would publicize the criteria for the Executive Development Roster. The file shows the follow-up machine at work: a staff board speaks, and the house must answer by a date.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680015-3:
Agenda items for a talk with the Director of Central Intelligence lead this issues file. Use of the polygraph as a clearance requirement comes first. Creation of a national intelligence operations center comes second. Personnel evaluation and resource allocation for security follow. Personnel management and position classification authority close the list.

The body opens on the polygraph issue. All federal bodies use two base rules for access to classified facts, it notes. Executive Order 10450 is one. A community directive is the other. The file is a briefing pack of standing issues, each set out for a decision at the top of the house.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680024-3:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) conference with a selected group of Black employees is arranged in this memo. The Director of Equal Employment Opportunity writes to the Director. The meeting answers the Director's own request. Named employees are invited to the DCI conference room. The deputy director would sit in as well.

The date set is Thursday 6 July 1978, at 0900 hours. An attachment lists the invited staff. The memo routes by way of the Director's special assistant. The file is short and formal. It records a set meeting between the top of the house and Black employees, arranged as part of the equal opportunity work of that year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300850033-3:
Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, wrote to A Vernon Weaver Jr on 6 December 1978 about Harvard. He had met Larry Fouraker the past week, he writes. Fouraker was dean of the Harvard Business School. In passing, Fouraker mentioned a letter he had sent the President. It urged the President to come talk at the school.

The talk would serve a program for leaders of small businesses. Turner volunteered a small service. If Fouraker sent a copy of the letter, Turner would forward it to Weaver. A long shot, Turner grants. But a President might be looking for just such a chance to speak on small business issues, he adds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301090018-3:
Pace University commencement awards for 1980 fill this campus file. The Pleasantville and Briarcliff campus issued it for the class of 1980. Two top awards lead the page. The Trustees' Award goes to the students who did most for the welfare of the university. Richard J Kneeley and Lauren F Cardillo take it here.

A scholastic achievement award follows. It honors skill in scholarship, class discussion, research and general performance. Robert C Bernabeo is named for it. More awards fill the pages after. The file came with the papers of the commencement at which Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, spoke that spring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301100016-3:
Press Club of San Francisco publishes this newsletter, volume 29 number 29. The file was kept for word of a luncheon at which the Central Intelligence Agency chief would speak. A front item treats a new retired member category. Only 40 members had applied for it, the treasurer told the board. The category is dubbed the Gray Cats in club slang.

A committee would soon judge the applications on hand. More applications would be welcome, the board said. Directors also voted to raise prices on some food items. The newsletter is club housekeeping in print, with the director's luncheon billed among its draws that summer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401130003-3:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation form 79-337 logs a Gridiron Club dinner in this file. The form was received on 26 December 1979. A letter from Grant Dillman brought the invitation. The event was a reception and dinner. It was the Gridiron Club 1980 spring dinner, set for Saturday 15 March 1980.

Reception would start at 1800, dinner at 1900. The Capital Hilton Hotel is the place named. A formal invitation was to follow, the form notes. A recommendation mark sits in the form's action space. The file is the staff sheet for a press club rite: the yearly dinner where Washington journalists roast the powerful.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401150056-3:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation form 80-77 logs a Virginia Oxonian dinner for Friday 25 April 1980. A form letter from Daniel Carrell and J Kennerly Davis Jr brought it, received on 24 March. The dinner was the third annual of its name. R James Woolsey Jr was the featured speaker. Cocktails would start at 1845, with dinner at 2000.

A suspense date of 27 March is marked on the form. The dinner gathered Oxford men in Virginia for a yearly night. Woolsey, a lawyer with a defense past, would address them. The file is the staff record of the invitation, one of a run of spring dinners weighed by the director's office in 1980.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501410001-3:
Press clippings gathered by the Agency for August 1980 fill a large file of newspaper and journal pages. Early pages carry Washington Post reports from late August on a House bill to bar naming covert agents abroad. Debate in a House panel over who could be charged under the bill takes up much of that opening coverage.

Later pages range far more widely across the month's news. One long piece from Strategic Review, dated summer 1980, weighs past United States forecasts of Soviet arms spending. Other clippings track Soviet defence outlays, gross output shares, and claims about a long arms build-up. Read as a whole, the file shows what Agency staff clipped and kept on public debate that month.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601570003-3:
National Intelligence Estimate NIE 11-4-78 sets out Soviet goals and hopes in the contest for world power. The estimate carries a preface noting broad backing across United States intelligence bodies. Its contents run from Soviet arms policy to foreign policy and the outlook ahead.

Arms chapters cover nuclear forces, forces for Europe, forces facing China, and tools for distant action. Foreign policy chapters treat detente with the United States and West Europe, hold on East Europe, and moves in the Third World. Later pages weigh the home outlook, the next leaders, and breaks that could alter the course. All findings are stated as the estimate's own judgments.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601720015-3:
Career guidance services across the Agency are surveyed in a memo from F. W. M. Janney. Janney, Director of Personnel, replied in July 1978 to a request from the Director. He states that no action is required and the memo reports what exists.

Formal career counseling dates from 1973, the memo states, when study group advice entered the rules. Each career service must run its own program and name its counselors in its handbook. Later pages report how each directorate lists help, from job advice to career planning. Named officers, their grades, and phone contacts are given so staff can find the service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601730014-3:
Senior staff losses and promotion needs are weighed in a paper on executive promotion policy. The paper opens by noting a second straight year of heavy losses at the top. Losses run above 20 percent a year, with a third such year feared.

Pay caps and squeezed pay gaps are blamed for weak drive to stay in top posts. Charts compare Agency leaders with the rest of the federal service by age and years served. Agency leaders average age 51, against 52 across government, the paper states. The feeder group of GS-15 staff averages age 48 and shows long time in grade.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t02051r000200350026-3:
Moves toward Korean reunification are reported in a Wall Street Journal article held in Agency files. South Korean President Roh Tae Woo voices hope for results within a few years. His remarks came in an interview the day before a North Korean speech at the United Nations.

Deputy Foreign Minister Kang Sok Ju called there for a joint Korea with shared armed forces and assembly. The article notes his calm tone, a shift from past harsh words by both sides. Roh had offered that summer to meet Kim Il Sung and sought a six-power summit. Trade steps and the United States troop presence also figure in the report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t02051r000200370006-3:
Landsat sales to private hands are weighed in a note dated 27 March 1989 with two tabs attached. Tab A holds a law review article on the Land Remote Sensing Act of 1984. Tab B holds press reports on the system's money troubles.

The note argues that market weakness was a core worry when the act was passed. It quotes the act's policy that the state should not rival private operators. Press pages report an urgent House hearing on a threat to shut the system that month. Speakers plead for funds to keep Landsats 4 and 5 flying through fiscal 1989.
cia-crest-cia-rdp06-02395r000401800003-3:
Names and phone contacts for a defence disclosure body fill a directory dated 11 January 1984. The body is the National Military Information Disclosure Policy Committee, known as NDPC. It sits in the Department of Defense in Washington.

Mr. L. Britt Snider heads the list as member for the Secretary's office and chairman. Entries then run office by office through the Pentagon and the services. Each entry gives a name, rank or grade, room, and phone number. Staff roles cover foreign disclosure, arms control, and technology transfer desks. The directory served staff who had to route disclosure queries to the right desk.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100170001-3:
Produced solely by the Agency, the 1970 handbook was prepared by the Office of Economic Research. Arms outlay and ship data came from the Office of Strategic Research, the title page states. Front notes explain rounding, marks, and how secret versus open data are flagged.

A star marks open data, while N.A. means not available and Negl. means negligible. Profile pages put Canada at 21.1 million people and 69 billion dollars gross product. One table tracks caustic soda output from 1960 to 1969 by country. United States output in that table rises from 4,511 to 8,726 thousand metric tons.
cia-crest-cia-rdp09t00207r001000020055-3:
Talk about the Agency fills a television panel transcript dated 21 September 1974. The program was Agronsky and Company, aired on WTOP TV in Washington at 7:00 PM. Hugh Sidey hosts, with Carl Rowan, Peter Lisagor, and George Will among the voices.

Rowan is pressed on his past seat on the Committee of Forty and its secret acts. Talk turns to Chile and to claims that the Agency sought to sway foreign rule. Will doubts that any agency can topple governments at will as often as critics claim. Rowan holds that some secret work should go on and some should not.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-01569r000100010007-3:
Clearance rules for staff joining the Central Intelligence Group are set in C.I.G. Directive No. 8. The directive is dated 9 May 1946 and is copy number 52. It carries the backing of the whole Intelligence Advisory Board.

Staff must be native-born citizens of excellent character, the directive states. No close kin may be subject to a foreign power under the terms set. Loyalty, honesty, care with secrets, and sound money habits must all be beyond doubt. Past checks by War, Navy, or State may ground a clearance in set cases. Ten years of honourable government service can also serve, with a fresh check still required.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m00666r000300780001-3:
Chemical weapons are the target of a ban drive set out in National Security Decision Directive 136. A White House memo dated 2 April 1984 sends the directive to top officials. It is marked System II 90421 and lists the Vice President, State, and Defense among those sent copies.

The memo states the President chose to table a draft treaty at the Geneva disarmament talks. The draft seeks a full, worldwide ban on chemical weapons, the memo states. The Arms Control and Disarmament Agency chief is on the send list as well. Front pages carry the standard council warning on handling secret council material.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m02313r000100940004-3:
Revised page 2 for a directive on world debt is sent under a White House memo dated 21 June 1983. The memo goes to the Vice President, State, Treasury, Defense, and other top officials. It carries a confidential attachment and council handling marks.

Page text backs United States support for a growth in IMF resources, as agreed. It urges steps to shun trade barriers and lay ground for freer trade ahead. An interagency group must watch the world debt scene and brief top levels on shifts. The group will also test how weaker or stronger world growth would change the debt picture. Bridge loans and the use of named funds are listed for study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp11s00229r000202110001-3:
China's foreign trade in 1985 and the outlook for 1986 fill a paper dated 28 March 1986. The Directorate issued it as EA M 86-20029. Beijing had tightened grip on trade in reply to falling reserves and a fast rising trade gap.

Reserves fell by 25 percent from September 1984 to September 1985, the paper states. Oil and oil goods brought in close to 6.4 billion dollars in 1985, about a fifth of export earnings. A held oil volume could cost at least 1.6 billion dollars in 1986, it warns. Trade chiefs had also taken back control of new trading firms. Findings are stated as the paper's assessed view.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100370001-3:
Praise from the British Security Coordination fills a file catalogued with commendations and awards for 1944. A letter in the file hails work by the office's man in Switzerland. It calls the Wood traffic one of the great secret intelligence feats of the war.

The writer states he saw the history and yield of that traffic while in London. He adds warm praise for how fast the whole secret service side was built up. Such growth in so short a span struck all who knew the work, he writes. He hopes the body built in war will live on into the days of peace. Handling sheets bound in the file set strict rules for who may see such papers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100070027-3:
Keeping AQUATONE past 1957 is urged as a swift choice in a memo dated 19 April 1957. The memo goes to the Director and the Deputy Director. It asks if the capacity stays in civilian hands past the photo season now starting.

Delay is already hurting morale and effect in the unit, the memo warns. The unit was built for a short, hard burst of work, not long idle waits. Two paths are set out: reshape it for standby use or phase it out. RAINBOW work may stretch the U-2 life through 1958, it argues. Staff, gear, budget, and Air Force and Navy support all hinge on the call.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100220002-3:
Flight logs list hundreds of missions in a table with no title page in the copy held here. Columns give date, mission number, type, area, base, pilot, and a result grade. Type marks split photo flights from ELINT flights in the key.

First rows run from 20 June 1956 over European satellite areas and the USSR. Middle East flights fill most rows through the autumn of 1956, graded fair or poor in many cases. Later rows shift to China, Korea, and Cambodia in 1965 and 1966. The last rows shown reach into April 1967 with Taiwan Strait flights listed. The log serves as a bare index of who flew where and when.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100260008-3:
Pilot pay and supply gripes fill a trip report on Los Angeles and Edwards Air Force Base. Page 2, marked SAPC-2460, treats talks held on Monday and Tuesday of the visit. Each pilot was briefed on state and federal tax duties for the work.

Pilots living in California owe that state's income tax, they were told. Lockheed would be named as employer on their state returns by arrangement. Single pilots judged the 250 dollar monthly living grant too low for base life. Meals meant a 60 mile round trip to Lancaster on many days, they argued. Missing kit such as plotters, computers, and spare pressure suits also drew sharp words.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100260134-3:
Pilot hiring from Tactical Air Command is treated in a memo dated February 1956. The memo goes to the Project Director after a 24 February visit to TAC headquarters. About 15 pilots were sought for AQUATONE overseas work, the memo states.

General Wayland was briefed on the mission and proved keen to help. TAC is very short of pilots with the needed flying skill, he warned. His deputy counted only a handful of such men in the whole command. The offer of five or six pilots was then pulled back in favour of a wider search. A fallback pledge stands: five fighter pilots may be drawn if the need turns dire.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100380014-3:
Situation Estimate for Project CHALICE covers fiscal years 1961 and 1962 in a March 1960 paper. The estimate, marked OITAL-0914, sets doctrine for planning and running project flights. Upon approval it may also ground the budget case, the text states.

Contents span target choice, concept of operations, sortie rate, and support needs. Ties to other forces are treated for quiet times and for open war. Route photos are expected to yield bonus data on Soviet airfields, industry, and missile sites. Data on Soviet air defence sites is named as a further key gain. Enclosures treat U-2 life expectancy for overflights and base use plans.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100390095-3:
Staffing strain in OSA fills a memo dated 13 September 1963 to the Assistant Director. The writer spent two weeks as an outside watcher while a new man, Walt, broke into the Programs Staff. The 1965 budget round forced Walt to take charge fast, the memo states.

Change to program staff methods came slowly by design, and some pushback was met. One deep flaw is named: when a key man leaves, detail and continuity walk out with him. An admin officer is urged at once for legwork and paper work. Wendell's people are swamped, with load still growing and no relief in sight. Praise for how EAD was set up closes the memo on a warm note.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200010013-3:
Soviet or Cuban moves to end Cuba overflights are weighed in a 1963 draft memo. The draft gives comments on a State paper dated 27 May on the same theme. For now, both regimes swallow the flights while they firm up Cuba's place, it judges.

Six courses open to the other side are taken in turn. A UN push and a World Court case are each judged weak ground for Cuba. Soviet pressure points such as Berlin might be traded against the flights, the State paper holds. The draft replies that such pressure would aim at the United States itself. No move of the kind is looked for soon, it concludes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200020003-3:
Daily go and no-go sheets for Cuba flights fill a file dated from 28 September 1962. Copy marks read 2315-63 on the sheets held here. Three missions stood approved, two from 10 September and one from 27 September.

Mission 3094 was called off as weather worsened over the target area. Mission 3095 flew on 29 September and found an SA-2 site, the sheet records. A cruise missile site at Ciguanea on the Isle of Pines was also found. Aircraft 343, 352, and 342 were all in commission at Del Rio, Texas. Later sheets show 352 back with Lockheed and 342 at Edwards Air Force Base.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300150017-3:
June 1962 is called the most productive month yet in a commander's report dated 3 July 1962, IDEA-0824. The report goes to the Chief, DPD from the detachment. Mission GRC-112 did much to calm partner nerves, the commander writes.

Aircraft 358 and 378 flew 68 hours 30 minutes in the month. One LOW NOTE mission and five NESTEGG missions were flown, the report states. Two new hostel rooms were finished just as a fresh crew arrived on 26 June. Weather forecast skill rose sharply through the month, it adds. Repeat faults on air speed and cabin altimeter gauges are logged in the maintenance pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300150107-3:
Standing up a new U-2 detachment is scheduled in a memo dated 3 October 1960, CHAL 1206. Branch chiefs met under the Chief, Operations Branch to fix the deployment plan. The detachment will hold two aircraft with special equipment fitted.

In place date is set as 15 September 1960 in the basic plan. Headquarters control of spying flights stays put, the memo states. Other CHALICE sites must accept cuts to man and equip the new unit. A week by week schedule runs from 1 October to 1 December 1960. It ends with transition training done on at least two pilots and full readiness.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400250051-3:
Memorandum dated 21 October 1966, numbered 2569-66 and sent to the Director of Central Intelligence through the Executive Director-Comptroller, seeks approval of a new delegation of contracting officer authority for OSA. A named officer, redacted in this release, has been appointed Chief of the Contracts Management Division and contracting officer in place of a reassigned predecessor. Both he and his deputy are described as lawyers with past contracting service in the Office of Logistics.

The authority sought is broad: sign all contracting papers that commit Agency funds, in any amount, once a deal sits inside an approved activity program or budget. Any paper raising a real policy question must instead go up, with a short written brief, for decision. The only change from the 1962 delegation is the office title, updated from OSA/DD/R to OSA/DDS&T throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400380156-3:
Transcript of a telephone call at 1600 hours on 28 August 1958 records Mr Bissell talking with Colonel Burke. Their subject is a message to be sent to their man at a place left redacted. Bissell presses for speed and candour. The man is to be told the whole story. He is urged to push for the first choice of starting point, and told a second choice would serve well. Settling early for a third choice, in ignorance, would waste time.

Burke notes the working strain of dealing with two sets of people and two sets of approvals, yet agrees it can be done. The matter is rated of the highest priority, and the man is to seek out the decision maker in person, even out of town. General Cabell has advised giving the specifics of where and why, and a share of the results is named as the price expected.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500190011-3:
Richard Helms, Deputy Director for Plans, sent the Acting Director of Central Intelligence a CIA memorandum in 1962 enclosing a translated Soviet article. Lieutenant-General N. Korenevskiy wrote the piece for a top secret special collection of Military Thought, the Soviet defense ministry journal, under the title on the role of space weapons in a future war.

Korenevskiy weighs satellite bombers, space-to-surface missiles in low orbit, and manned ships as tools for gaining control of space. He cites American projects by code names given in the text and a 1960 statement by General Thomas White on manned flight. The article ends by urging close study of American plans, doctrine, and technical work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500390055-3:
Second version of a 25 May 1959 memorandum for the record, marked GUS-0087/B, lays out operating factors for a follow-on reconnaissance aircraft. Survival is again the main test, judged through detection, altitude, speed over the target, and tactics. A larger radar return, the memo states, must be offset by greater height above known defensive weapons.

Longer passages consider how Soviet defenses would react over the USSR. Radar detection and tracking for most of a route are expected, yet the memo rates a fighter intercept as unlikely, given height, speed, and short reaction time. It ends by backing airborne electronics collection, citing a United States Air Force Security Service test as the most effective method.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500390136-3:
Memorandum dated 16 April 1958, from J. A. Gibbs, Deputy Project Director, reports a visit made the day before to the Materials Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. Gibbs went to learn what the lab knew about high modulus fiberglass and plastic materials for aircraft, and what development contracts it held, including work with Owens-Corning.

Lab staff gave contract figures for plastic and ceramic adhesives and for high temperature fibers, and forecast strength values for flake glass material. They also held, unanimously, that aircraft firms design poorly in fiberglass because their habits come from sheet metal work. Attached reports on fiberglass properties close the memo, with added notes on static testing each Gusto airplane.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040043-3:
Fire response during duty hours, in and around the hangar, is laid out in Detachment H SOP H-10-18, dated 21 October 1966. Action falls into five steps, in set order: alert all staff, move aircraft out to the run-up pads, call the base fire department, fight the fire, and save gear. Safety of people is named as the first concern at every stage of the plan.

Anyone who finds a fire reports it at once to the Administration Office. That office then announces the fire and its place over the loudspeaker system. One set of steps covers a fire on the hangar floor. A second set, for offices and shops, adds securing classified material before staff leave.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040133-3:
Work of the Intelligence Section at a reconnaissance detachment is defined in SOP H-50-19, dated 27 January 1970. The Director of Operations enforces it. Tasks named at the start are intelligence reports, mission overlays, tracker film viewing, and related duties that support each operational flight the detachment flies.

Route material arrives from Operations in a sealed envelope and is stored in a named safe in the intelligence vault. Once a route is approved, the section draws a penciled overlay of the pilot's chart, with turn points, coordinates, camera on and off points, and flight lines in red. Staff also attend the pre-mission briefing, move the overlay to the Command Post, issue escape packets, and run post-flight critiques.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600050033-3:
Asking Unit Supply for property is the subject of ATTG Reg 67-3, dated 20 March 1972, for the 1130th group at Edwards Air Force Base. The Chief of Supply runs the system, and all group staff must follow it. Property is split into two kinds, supplies and equipment, and each kind follows its own request path through Unit Supply.

Supply items are requested on DD Form 1150, in two copies, with the item name, stock or part number, and unit of issue filled in. A need within fifteen days needs a written reason. Other items use local forms: office and cleaning supplies at the service counter, hand tools on their own form, and vehicles on a SLOE request approved by Support.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600050042-3:
Care and use of official vehicles for the 1130th group is governed by ATTG Reg 77-1, dated 12 April 1972. It covers all group vehicles, Air Force marked cars and trucks and those registered with the State of California on tax exempt plates. The Director of Support enforces the rules and keeps contact with the main base on vehicle matters.

The vehicle maintenance chief schedules periodic, safety, and lubrication checks with user sections. Drivers must check lights, gauges, brakes, horn, and other safety gear, and log any fault found on AFTO Form 374. Drivers also change flat tires and wash their vehicles. A car pool form at the end records shared use at sixty cents per day.
