cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050005-3:
OXCART directive 50-3055-5, dated 15 July 1965, governs A-12 test and training flights inside the continental United States. It replaces a November 1962 version. The stated aim is to back the flight test and training programs with the most safety and security that can be managed. Flights outside the continental United States fall under a separate annex named in the text.

The area commander and flight test center must see that each flight is planned, briefed, and flown to that standard. Suitable emergency fields are picked along the route in a set order, from other project bases down to dry lake beds. Flights must reach the terminal fix with at least 5,000 pounds of fuel in reserve.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800020007-3:
Quarterly IDEALIST report for 1 January to 31 March 1974 is forwarded 19 April 1974 by Wendell L. Bevan Jr. Flight testing of the B-3 camera, serial 230, resumed on 19 March after a study period. It ended on 27 March. NPIC review of the film was still under way at quarter's end. Testing of serial 229 stayed on hold from 5 February, with a restart planned for the fourth quarter.

A maintenance section reports an autopilot study. NPIC study of B-3 film showed the camera had missed its required sharpness. Review pointed to the autopilot not holding the aircraft steady enough. That finding was confirmed by later checks described in the text. A life support conference in Washington on 19 and 20 March is also listed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800210006-3:
Draft memorandum for the Deputy Director for Science and Technology gathers, in one place, the policy choices on closing the Office of Special Activities. Its attachment is meant to serve both as a decision paper for the deputy director and as a working guide for other staffs. Planning uses the OSA position control roster of 30 April 1974 as its base.

Numbered decisions follow, one per OSA staff or asset group. Each gives a discussion, a recommendation, a phaseout timing, and space for approval or remarks. One staff, covering medical support, pressure suit work, and pilot selection, is marked for dissolution, with staff returned to their parent service within thirty days after TACKLE ends. The Budget and Finance Staff, by contrast, would move intact into OD&E.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250002-3:
Memorandum 9297-68, dated 8 October 1968, sends the research and development quarterly report for July, August, and September 1968 to the Director of Operations, OSA. OXCART life support opens the attached report. A meeting on 11 and 12 July sorted life support assets into three groups: storage in the 5/90 kit, loans from that kit, and permanent transfer to named holders.

Suit work fills much of the quarter. Cockpit and in-flight checks of the S-1010 pressure suit in late August left all project pilots with safe assemblies, and most comfort problems settled. The David Clark Company was adding changes for comfort and safety, among them a full-size sunshade and a new anti-suffocation valve. A methane fuel briefing for the NRO closes the report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000100140014-3:
Memorandum to the Acting Deputy Director for Administration argues that forms control should not have moved from the Organization and Methods Staff to General Services. Forms work is one of the staff's best tools for simplifying work and developing procedures. Losing it cut the staff's reach, the memo states. The whole management control program of the agency was weakened as a result.

Facts bearing on the problem follow. A 5 January 1953 statement by the Chief, General Services, is checked against the record. The Hoover Commission itself made no recommendation on forms control. A task force report on records did discuss the subject, however. The memo ends with a proposal. Forms control, with the Machine Records Branch, should move to the Office of the Comptroller, where it would better support that office's duties.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030006-3:
Procedure for accidents involving government owned vehicles sets out what the Coordinator of Information's staff must do when a crash occurs. Any accident, however minor, must be reported under the procedure. A copy of the procedure, with Standard Forms 26, 27, and 28, is to ride in each vehicle under the Coordinator's control and leave it only when a report is made.

Sections cover claims for loss of or damage to private property, employee responsibility, and accidents where a private driver damages government property. Report assembly and filing rules follow. Where an animal is hurt but not killed, three statements on its value before and after injury must be included. The closing section covers hit and run cases: get a description of the car and occupants, then alert police in nearby communities.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030042-3:
Procedure dated 9 August 1950, from the Chief, Supply Branch, fixes how stock levels are set and stock replenished. For expendable standard and CIA forms, the minimum or reorder level is monthly use times six months supply; the maximum adds a twelve month supply. On reaching the minimum, a twelve month supply of forms is ordered, rounded to the nearest thousand.

Order routing depends on size. Runs above 25,000 copies of a form go on Form No. 36-7 to the Management Officer, then to the Government Printing Office. Smaller or urgent runs go on a reproduction requisition instead. Non-expendable stock uses a lead time rule: items needing three months for delivery are reordered at four months supply. Levels are rechecked each quarter against actual monthly use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030123-3:
Procedure governing the functions of the Transportation Division lists what that division may approve under delegated authority. Its chief and assistant chief review, authorize, and issue travel orders. They approve transfers of staff between official stations, with payment of travel, household goods, automobiles overseas, personal effects, and dependents. Temporary duty travel and travel to and from overseas posts also fall under their authority.

Allowances above the lowest first class rate can be approved where that class is unavailable, where a compartment is needed for security, or where extra fare trains and planes are used. Household goods shipment limits are stated, with a 3,000 pound allowance under the cited restriction and storage of the balance in the United States. Closing sections cover privately owned automobiles and CIA driver's permits for Washington staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030141-3:
Memorandum dated 29 June 1950, from the Chief, Services Division, gives allotment account charges for fiscal year 1951. It is a revised copy of the same guidance held elsewhere in this slice, issued to end confusion over charges in the past fiscal year. Travel is charged to the traveler's branch. Freight on purchases follows the account that paid for the goods, and freight to field stations falls to the station concerned.

Postage stamps stocked by the Supply Branch are a Stock Account charge. So are standard office furniture and equipment held in stock, including safes, adding machines, and dictating machines. Reproduction supplies held for the Reproduction Branch also go to stock. Printing and photographic equipment, from Multilith presses to ditto machines, is charged to the office requiring it. National Security Council purchases stay charged to the council, as before.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050059-3:
Order dated 1 December 1950, issued over the authority of the Director of Central Intelligence, delegates powers to the Deputy Director for Administration and his assistant. Its list matches the delegation the National Security Council issued the same day for council staff matters, and the two orders were plainly prepared together. Personnel appointment and termination, allowances abroad, and transfers between stations head this version as well.

Travel advances on vouchered funds are named here in plain terms, along with first class fare allowances where lower class space is not available or a compartment is needed. Sub-delegation rules fill the second half: the Personnel Director and his branch chiefs may exercise the personnel powers, and the Chief of Administrative Services may exercise several travel powers. All earlier inconsistent delegations are rescinded.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050095-3:
Memorandum dated 17 January 1950, from Jess Larson, Administrator of General Services, sends agency heads a working agreement between two offices. The parties are the General Accounting Office and the General Services Administration. Comptroller General Lindsay Warren and Larson signed the agreement the same day. It states how the two offices will share their linked duties under the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949.

The attached text stresses property accounting. Agencies must build property accounting into their own accounting systems. The administration's overall property management rests on sound agency records, the text argues. Underlying property records form the supporting layer, and their quality decides the quality of the whole system. Copies of the agreement could be had by phone from the administration. Its provisions were to be reviewed from time to time in light of experience.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200060030-3:
Copy of the 27 November 1946 agreement moving the State Department printing plant at 2430 E Street, Northwest, to the Government Printing Office. A policy committee of three governs the plant: one member each from the Department of State, the Central Intelligence Group, and the Government Printing Office. The committee sets regulations on priority of work, physical and personnel security of the plant, and any other matter of substance among the parties.

The plant stays at its present address, subject to space changes the committee agrees. Unclassified work may be produced at the plant or elsewhere at the printing office's choice. Printing office equipment may serve other federal work, provided that work never blocks priority production of classified or special map material for State and the intelligence group. A fiscal note on reimbursement vouchers is bound at the end.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00216a000100040002-3: A declassified CIA evaluation of summer area programs. This CREST record grades the Agency's warm-weather training efforts. Summer school for spies, reviewed. Grading the summer courses of the secret school. Preserved in the CREST archive. Summer school, scored and filed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00252a000100020031-3:
Second reorganization paper in this run proposes a Training Staff built around three deputies, each with clearly defined duties, in place of one deputy and two division chiefs. Under the Deputy for Staff Intelligence Training would sit the training of OSO staff staff concerned with directing operations and with collecting, reporting, and processing intelligence. Covert training and other branches take their own deputies, shown on the charts that follow the text.

Instructor numbers may still fall short, the paper admits. The hope is that staff training load will fall as covert load rises, letting instructors shift across. The Deputy for Special Projects carries instructional work, in administration, language, and technique courses, plus services duties. Recommendations close the paper: approve the structure soon, and have the posts and grades in the attached table authorized.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00252a000100040002-3:
Memorandum for the record, dated 20 November 1951, covers a Training Advisory Committee meeting of 14 November 1951, held from 1400 to 1600. A maritime training problem was presented first, approved in principle, and sent on to the Joint Training Committee. Next came a proposal to extend the operations course from four weeks to five. Rising student numbers were said to be forcing instructional standards down unless more time was given.

The extension was agreed, with a further check of other courses for items to cut or shorten, so the overall course stays level. Personnel complaints follow: operating offices have not sent experienced staff to TRC, a heavy administrative load on the center. Course enrollment churn, with students arriving and leaving without stated reason, was also raised. Both problems were expected to ease once amalgamation took place.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00252a000200090006-3:
Outline dated 17 July 1950 for a talk at FSI walks through the agency's structure in note form. Early points cover intelligence operating procedures issued by the Director, with briefing of attaches going abroad as an example. Advice to the National Security Council must carry the concurrence or dissent of the member agencies, the notes observe, which sometimes waters results down. The legal staff's role follows, with a note on one hundred aliens under Public Law 110.

Security investigation by I&S is sketched next: full checks on all personnel, averaging three months, with waivers for long service military staff. The NIS program is outlined: chapters allocated through an interdepartmental committee, rough shares of forty percent Army, thirty percent State, and five percent each for Navy, Air Force, and CIA. The Graphics Division closes the notes, holding about 6,000 films and over 2,000 ground photos supplied last month for 123 requests.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100050035-3:
National Manpower Mobilization Policy states the aims and rules for using the nation's people in a defense effort. The primary aim is to guard national security through the fullest development and use of human resources. Manpower must be found for the armed forces, for producing the goods and services the forces and aid commitments need, and for the civilian economy. Training programs should steadily grow the supply of highly skilled people, and civilian health and welfare must be protected.

Where demand for critical skills outruns supply, the paper directs review of the competing needs. Distribution is then set by the relative urgency of the need, as between the armed forces and the civilian economy. Contracts and plants should sit near labor supply rather than move the labor, where cost and security allow. Each department carries out the policy itself and supervises it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100140008-3:
Course listings for offices under the Deputy Director for Administration open with Inspection and Security. Its indoctrination covers the functions and organization of CIA and the techniques of investigation as practiced by I&S investigators. The course runs three weeks, given at five week intervals. About thirty people from I&S and other offices serve as lecturers, and the average class holds seventeen students. A medical technician course follows, tied to field need, with a present class of four and two instructors.

General Counsel offers a short course every two weeks for OPC and OSO staff, on the office's functions and the legal problems met in the field. Clerical training entries close the file. Typing classes run three weeks, from elementary to steno-typing, with dictaphone and electric typewriter practice. Shorthand is taught at intermediate and advanced levels, and English usage is given as an integrated course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100140026-3:
Office memorandum from the Assistant Director for Communications answers a survey of non-O/TR training activities with a report on his office's courses. The Communications Training Branch teaches staff of Communications, Operations, Policy Coordination, and Special Operations. Its aim is to qualify each student for the communications duties of his posting. Courses run in staff and clandestine radio operating and theory, teletype and power equipment upkeep, teletype procedures, covert surveillance, and cryptographic systems.

Detail follows for the cryptographic course. Office of Communications students take 160 hours; OSO and OPC students take 120 hours, the extra forty hours being practice on clandestine systems. A briefing course caps at forty hours. Classes enter weekly or every two weeks as instructors allow, with four instructors now and ten planned. Closing items cover informal courses in frequency propagation study and crystal grinding, taught one student at a time as need arises.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100070005-3:
Memorandum dated 10 December 1953 from the Chief, Management Training Division, to the Chief, Logistics Office, summarizing the Human Resources Program run in that office. Eight groups of supervisors took part, 101 people in all, starting in July and ending with the last group meeting on 25 November. Follow-up meetings with each group were planned about every eight weeks.

Findings cover an office made of four very unlike parts, uneven leadership and morale, and weak coordination at the top. Attached material lists problems raised in group talks and in half-hour talks with each member. Eleven common management problems, drawn from a year of the program across the Agency, were also laid before General Cabell and senior staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100070023-3:
Report dated 28 February 1953 from the Chief, Management Training Division, to the Assistant Director for the office named in the text as OCD, on the Human Resources Program run there. Eight groups of supervisors, from division chief down to unit chief, took part between 10 November 1952 and 18 February 1953. An interim report had gone forward on 12 December.

Praise is given for keen, hard-driving staff and for units working short-handed so members could attend training. Problems set out include weak coordination of existing staff, no settled Agency-wide idea of management yet, and too few senior staff who grasp human relations as the key to the work. Supervisors also sought a hand in picking staff they would direct, fuller briefing of new staff, and more space for some work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000200030008-3:
Statement of functions and activities for the Office of Training. It sets out what the Director of Training must do. It also gives the duties of each part of the office. The office runs all Agency training. It arranges places at outside schools, at home and overseas. It also helps shape the CIA Career Service Program. That program picks, grows, and places staff.

Parts of the office cover general training and covert training. A support staff serves both sides. An assessment and evaluation staff serves both as well. Course detail follows for language work and area study. Reading improvement gets its own section. That course ran thirty-five hours. In fiscal 1953, 517 people were trained. The next year, 875 were expected. A junior officer program closes the survey.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100020030-3:
Proposed changes to the Confidential Funds Regulations. The set went forward for review and approval. The scan is partly garbled. Its heads and lists still read in places. Items cover how covert staff are classed. They also cover how policy on such staff is stated. Rules on travel funds appear as well. Pay for staff under cover is covered too.

Legible sections sort Agency covert people into kinds. Staff employees and staff agents are named. Covert consultants and covert associates appear too. Contract staff form another kind. Other passages cover deals with outside agents. A special contracting officer may sign for the United States. The worth of a service is also weighed. That worth rests on the work and its place in the whole. Its weight and hardness count as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100030075-3:
Dispatch CDS No. 55, dated 18 September 1950, sent by air pouch to all field stations, setting procedures for pay and allowances for staff heading abroad for permanent duty. The aim was faster payment by the Central Payroll Office into United States bank accounts, and fewer underpayments, overpayments, and later fixes on pay accounts.

For each person, a Foreign Duty Data Sheet, Form 33-2, was to be filled in at headquarters. Net salary and post and dependency allowances were figured on a four-week basis, then split as the person directed between the overseas station and a bank at home. Stations were to cable headquarters on a person's arrival, and on dependents arriving later. Quarters payments waited on a claim form, though a chief of mission could advance funds meanwhile.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100050028-3:
Hazardous Pay Plan Committee papers, with names partly redacted. One paper defines the hazard at stake. Hazard means constant jeopardy to life and limb. The danger may come through violence or by accident. It arises while an Agency staff member does his duties. Some jobs are hazardous by their nature. Fire guards and explosives handlers are named. Parachute training counts as well. So does handling certain secret material.

Work abroad adds its own hazards. Case officers abroad can become targets. Foreign intelligence services may watch or seize them. Being named in public can wreck a career. That risk exists through no fault of the person. Later pages turn to strain on character. Long secret work can narrow a person's social life. One case in an Army hospital ward is cited. The papers argue that harm can grow over years.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020013-3:
Daily schedule for an intermediate intelligence course. The course served Agency scientific analysts. It ran from 1 June to 26 June 1953. The Intelligence Training Division ran it. Week one opened with reporting and orientation. Aims of intermediate training were set out. Case work projects filled many hours. Source materials were explored on the first day.

Later weeks mixed lectures with case work. Set talks covered the intelligence cycle. Logic and method in scientific intelligence featured too. One talk covered Soviet government and party structure. A seminar treated Communist ideas and practices. A closing account calls the course an experiment. The Office of Scientific Intelligence had asked for it. A picked group of its analysts attended. Broadening their view of intelligence was one aim. Current work of other agencies was another.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020095-3:
Mission and functions statement for the Agency Support Staff. The staff serves all Office of Training work. Headquarters and field work both fall in scope. Overt and covert work are both served. Two branches carry out the staff mission. One is the Administrative Services Branch. The other is the Training Aids Branch.

The staff chief advises the Director of Training. Support matters are the chief's field. The chief also speaks for the Director. High level liaison work falls to the chief. Field support elements answer to the chief too. The Administrative Services Branch has four sections. A security officer is attached to it. Its work covers personnel and finance matters. Registration, transport, and records are covered too. General office services round out the list. Field commanders get help with procedures.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100060019-3:
Agenda for group meeting number one, held 15 June 1953. Agency plans directorate training officers attended the meeting. Communications staff attended alongside them. It sat at 10:30 in the morning. The place was 1500 L Building. Procedures for group and joint meetings came first. Scheduling, agendas, and minutes all needed agreement.

Copy counts for training notices came next. Each training officer needed a set number. A training regulation on missions followed. Policies on training at outside facilities were listed. Follow-up on training requirements came after that. New business closed the agenda. Training bulletins were part of that business. The record praises the training committee highly. Liaison with the training office worked well through it. Chiefs of planning staffs might attend such meetings. Briefing of attaches gets a caution in the record. One capital's briefing should not go to the center.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000200020051-3:
Task force report dated 31 March on the Near East program. It concerns language and area training. Henry Lee Smith Jr. signed the report. It went to the Foreign Service Institute leadership. Government language specialists needed stronger programs. That need had long concerned the Institute staff. Foreign Service officers were the first concern. Staff from many agencies were also involved.

CIA and military staff both appear in the report. Not all officers need the same length of training. Past teaching was split two ways. The Institute taught some officers itself. Universities taught many others at their sites. Results over five years were examined closely. University programs were judged not satisfactory overall. They missed the special needs of government specialists. A pilot program in Washington is proposed instead. Intensive, better joined teaching would run there. Further teaching would follow at overseas posts. Arabic language filled the mornings in the plan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000010066-3:
Negotiated Agency contract, number FS-99, in a long scanned file. Much of the scan reads poorly. The contract form and its structure stay legible. A table of contents lists the parts in order. Eleven parts make up the contract body. Signature and corporate seal pages appear early. The contractor bound itself by due authority.

Later pages carry the standard contract clauses in full. Payment, changes, and records duties appear among them. Inspection and correction of defects are covered. Assignment of claims gets its own clause. Termination and disputes provisions follow in the set. Because the OCR is rough, names and sums cannot be read with confidence here. The file still shows the full shape of a government deal. Schedule terms sit above general provisions in force. That order of control is stated in the text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000050107-3:
Memo dated 17 February 1956 on Project AQUATONE. A revised signal table of organization is the subject. Papers were enclosed with the memo. They were redrawn for easier identification. Signal duties are defined more precisely there. New staff and a better grasp of the work drove the change. Operational needs set the shape of the table.

A brief explanation follows for each part. The headquarters part directs all Agency project signal work. It coordinates work from the center. Administrative support has set duties there. A signal center part sits in Washington. It was to open in early February. A subordinate site gets its own section. That site needs cryptographic staff on hand. Numbers are given as an addition to another service's staff. The detachment signal center handles message traffic. It also maintains the teletype gear there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000110038-3:
Agency contract approvals list for contract number A-101. The list is dated 27 April 1956. Its number is SAPC-5726, copy one of five. Procurements listed are approved as proper charges. Each row gives a date and a CNCC number. Vendor names and purchase order numbers follow. Caps on spending are set for most rows.

Several rows cap work at an hourly straight-time rate. Materials at cost are added on top of labor. One Hewlett Packard row appears in the list. Stone and manufacturing firms appear as vendors too. One row raises a charge to 26,197 dollars and fifty cents. Another raises a cap to 8,106 dollars even. Later rows run into March 1956 dates. Caps there reach thirty-five thousand dollars. One cap reaches ninety-six thousand dollars. Required markings sit beside many of the rows.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000130126-3:
Negotiated Agency contract number CM-2391, a short contract file. The contractor sat at 1048 Potomac Street, Northwest. That address is in Washington, District of Columbia. The contract amount reads as 3,498 dollars. The parties executed it on 4 May 1956. Inspection was set at a site named in the schedule. The contractor must furnish facilities under the deal.

Supplies must be delivered as the schedule sets out. Services must be performed as set out too. Duties are governed by the schedule and provisions. In any clash, the schedule controls the outcome. Corporate certification pages follow the contract face. Schedule text deep in the file is partly garbled. One legible passage treats an operator's sitting position. A temporary arrangement for that position is described. Comfort of the operator is the point at issue.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000190067-3:
Trip report dated 27 July 1956 to the Agency Director of Operations. A visit to Watertown Strip during USCM is the subject. A plant visit to Hycon forms part of the report. The visitors introduced a photographic specialist there. A tour of the plant followed the introductions. Malfunctions at the strip are reported in detail. Bearing failures had been corrected before the visit.

Thirteen items of one kind are noted in passing. Addition to a printer is discussed as well. A roll of film was judged good by comparison. Normal program standards supplied that comparison. Camera use in operations was discussed at length. Configurations needed thorough investigation, it was determined. Immediate work on them was also urged. The drift sight gets close treatment later. A slot in its gearing caused tracking loss. The sight tracked for about four seconds, then slipped. Blunt corners on a part were an old problem.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100100005-3:
Final report dated 16 April 1952 on Top Secret control. An Organization and Methods examiner wrote it. It went to the collection and dissemination chief. A uniform control system across CIA is the problem. Problems unique to certain areas form a second part. General control problems form a third part. The survey ran from 23 January to 16 April.

Areas visited are listed in the report. The central control office heads that list. Research and reports, operations, and estimates offices follow. Procurement, comptroller, and security offices were visited. Communications, personnel, and training offices appear too. Administrative services close the long list of areas. A new record method is proposed in the text. It would replace the central posting record. It would replace the source card file as well. Weekly logs from areas would end under it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100110004-3:
Office memo dated 6 November 1950 on management studies. Studies of administrative staffs in Operations are summed up. The deputy director for Operations sent the memo. It went to the Management Officer of the Agency. Three staff studies from October 1950 are named. Foreign Documents, Operations itself, and Contact Division are covered. Comments from the divisions are forwarded as papers.

Constructive suggestions in the studies are welcomed. Detailed replies went to points raised earlier. Findings are answered one by one in the papers. Field administrative staff briefing gets an early answer. All such staff were briefed in the home office. That happened before field duty or on home leave. Exchanges between field and home offices were limited. That limit is admitted in the findings reply. Routing slips from the deputy chief are sent with it too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100110031-3:
Memorandum dated 28 April 1950 on personnel and space. It went to each assistant director and staff chief. The Director of Central Intelligence signed it. Its number is ER-1-190 in the text. No added Washington space can be expected soon. That bar runs prior to 1 January 1951. Building up staff must be restricted meanwhile. Planned facilities must fit current space allocations.

Most efficient use of space is the stated test. COAPS will push special efforts under the memo. Essential substantive functions will be redefined by it. Work of doubtful value should be dropped or deferred. Solutions for indexing and liaison problems are sought. Reproduction and dissemination needs should shrink where possible. The Management Staff will direct its own special effort. Cooperation of all chiefs is demanded in the memo. Their current plans must fit the space facts. Conferences and discussion between all parties are offered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100140010-3:
Memorandum dated 10 February 1950 on translations. The Acting Chief of the Foreign Documents Division sent it. It went to the Agency Assistant Director for Operations. Detailed tables cover work for OSO and OPC. The period runs from January 1948 to January 1950. Verbal request prompted the submission of the tables. A summary for OSO work opens the detail.

Completed OSO work covered twenty-nine languages. Chinese led the list at 582 pages. German followed at 434 pages in the table. Arabic, Dutch, and Serbian follow in size. Czech and Russian appear further down. OPC work covered seventeen languages instead. Italian led that list at 330 pages. French and Chinese follow in the OPC table. Monthly project figures fill the later tables. January 1949 saw ten projects completed by FDD. Ninety working days were spent that month. Nine days per project was the average.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100190024-3:
Sanitized organization chart and table of organization file. Opening pages are marked exempt in the release. A summary of outgoing communications follows in the file. EE Division traffic for June through August 1953 is tabulated. Cables, dispatches, and memorandums are the columns. Finance matters and salary contracts head the subjects. Home leave and marriage actions are listed.

Reassignment problems and transfer actions appear as subjects. Theatre clearance approvals and security clearances follow. Personal effects shipment and routine information are listed. Efficiency reports show twelve dispatches and twelve memos. Pseudonym information shows six dispatches in the table. Disciplinary action shows a single dispatch entry. Duties of the Agency personnel officer fill later pages. Military personnel requirements are determined by that officer. Use of military staff follows set criteria. Needed military skills form the first criterion.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150009-3:
Part four of the Agency indexing study covers an automatic classifying system. The Kybernetes Corporation built that system. A video approach to searching is its basis. The firm was a branch of Self Winding Clock Company. Its office sat at 9 East 40th Street, New York. A working model was shown in March 1953. Magazine subscription records were its special purpose.

Producing and controlling those records was the aim. Using the sign-up records was included. Gear searches recorded information by set rules. Several separate functions follow from its findings. Copying among them is done by machine where chosen. A closed-circuit workplace television system is used. Fit for general information searching was studied. First study results are outlined in the part. Early findings from that study are summed up. A flat-bed design would be adopted. Search pattern sets could expand as needed. Six-place patterns could hold letter material.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150018-3:
Appendix XIII of the Agency indexing study covers limits of IBM accounting machines. Pattern searching by scanning machines contrasts with sorting. Conventional punched card machines perform that sorting. They were designed for accounting purposes originally. A sorter needs the entry position known. Meaning rests on geometrical coordinates in that scheme. Column number gives the longitudinal dimension there. Position within the column gives the other.

Decisions must be made in advance for sorters. Which column records a given data type is fixed. Units sold of an item form one example. Price and date shipped form two more. Discount and total amount owed follow them. Salesman code and shipping point close the list. Broader coverage breaks that fixed scheme apart. Entry counts grow as fields widen steadily. Standard cards run out of locations entirely. The whole range of possible entries cannot fit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200220001-3:
Handbook No. 1 on travel, dated 3 March 1953. Agency personnel in travel status are its audience. Processing of individuals in that status is assisted. Employees handling travel details get a guide. General information for the traveler is included. The handbook supplements existing CIA regulations and notices. It does not supersede or revise any regulation. Walter Reid Wolf signed it as Deputy Director, Administration.

Seven sections structure the travel processing guide. Travel orders form the first section covered. The Central Processing Branch forms the second. Information for the traveler forms the third. Travel advances and travel vouchers follow next. Regulations authorizing travel form the sixth section. Transportation and storage of effects are covered there. Furniture, household, and personal effects are named. Public law extracts close the handbook volume. Payment must rest on legal authorization always. Public Laws 110, 600, 830, and 92 are cited. Standardized Government Travel Regulations are referenced too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00259a000100030003-3:
Agenda and minutes for an OTR staff meeting, 28 September 1954. Four items stood on the agenda that Tuesday. The Incentive Awards Program came first among them. A forthcoming Agency Orientation Course was reported on. The Community Chest Campaign formed the third item. A conference report of 18-19 September closed it.

Minutes record the awards program in some detail. Suggestions had grown from a trickle in 1952. Accepted suggestions in 1953 saved over $82,000 yearly. Submissions in the current first half rose slightly. Either 1953 half-year period was surpassed by it. New legislation takes effect 30 November 1954. Monetary awards to government employees are liberalized there. Much greater increase in suggestions is presumed from it. Conferees from two directorates appear later. Principal officials of DD/I and DD/P attended. A recognized need was the group consensus recorded. What need it was sits in redacted lines.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100070003-3:
Senate report number 90 copy on science promotion. The Labor and Public Welfare Committee submitted this report. Mr. Thomas of Utah presented it in March 1949. Senate bill 247 is the measure accompanied here. The bill promotes the progress of science. National health, prosperity, and welfare are its aims. National defense is secured among its purposes. The committee reports favorably without amendments.

Adoption of the bill is recommended by the committee. A general statement opens the report body. Nationwide demand for a foundation ran for years. Presidents recognized the need in official statements. Several Congresses debated the need in hearings. Scientists, educators, and students voiced it too. Early and prompt enactment is urged onward. Analysis by sections of the bill follows. Section one provides the act's short title. A 1949 act is named in that title. Section two establishes the Foundation itself. Independence within the executive branch is specified.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100090001-3:
National Security Council directive on covert operations. International Communism is named as the foe as one. The USSR and Communist China lead that naming. Governments, parties, and groups ruled by them follow. Their covert acts aim to discredit the United States. Free world powers share that targeting with it. Open foreign work must be added to accordingly. World peace and national security ground the decision.

The Central Intelligence Agency already holds espionage charges. Counterespionage work abroad is also its charge. Creating a new agency seemed unwanted here. Charge for covert operations rests with CIA. Linking with espionage and counterespionage is required. The Director of Central Intelligence holds overall control. Set purposes of covert operations follow next. The Director bears further duties in the text. Planning must fit United States foreign policy. Military policy fit is required alongside it. Advice comes from the Operations Coordinating Board.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100150068-3:
Memorandum on the status of the Strategic Services Unit. It serves the Executive to an Assistant Secretary. A memorandum of 18 January 1946 is referenced. Information given supports a reply being prepared. The Chairman of the House Military Affairs Committee asked. The Office of Strategic Services was terminated first. Its personnel, records, property, and funds moved.

Some functions went to the State Department instead. The rest transferred to the Department of War. Executive Order 9621 effected those transfers. Its date is 20 September 1945 in the text. The order took effect 1 October 1945. The Secretary of War may discontinue transferred activities. Compatibility with the national interest is his test. Affairs relating to them would then wind up. Secretary Patterson wrote on 27 September 1945. Liquidation by the unit continued from the OSS. Functions tied directly to combat were eliminated. Field army operations support ended with them. Figures answer the chairman's questions later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000200080128-3:
Notes on appropriation hearings, sent by the General Counsel to the Director on 29 May 1946, set out how a House subcommittee hearing was expected to run. The committee would first put its broad approach and the proposed bill in brief form. The Director would then be asked for, or could offer, a general statement. Much of the material, the notes say, could be given off the record where security was at stake.

The suggested statement covers the end of the wartime intelligence office, the transfer of its work to the Secretary of War, and the role of the new unit. The notes stress a dual goal left by the war's end. Though the scan is rough in places, the memorandum reads as practical coaching for a first funding hearing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000200130005-3:
Budget estimates for the Legal Staff for fiscal year 1952 make up a short set of forms sent to the Budget Officer. A summary sheet gives the unit's figures under vouchered and unvouchered funds, with a total line for the office. The stated total runs to a six-figure sum for the year. A second part lists what the Legal Staff does inside the Central Intelligence Agency.

That list casts the staff as legal adviser to the Director and to all parts of the Agency. It also speaks for the Agency in legal matters beyond its own walls. As a record, the forms are thin but pointed: they tie a small law office's cost to a brief claim about its role. The date line rests on a form first sent in April 1950.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000200130113-3:
Personnel estimates from the Office of General Counsel, dated 7 December 1948, open with the office's mission before turning to staff numbers. The office answers for all legal matters touching the Agency's affairs. It advises the Director, assistant directors, and other officials on legal problems. Its work covers contracts, claims, property, finance, and fiscal steps, plus how new laws bear on Agency business.

The estimates also cover review of regulations and special orders, and contact with the Judge Advocates and other legal offices. Dissolving companies and other corporate legal work fall inside the remit where operations need them. Read with the mission text, the figures show a law office sizing the staff it needed to serve a new agency across a wide legal field.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400050002-3:
Pages from the Congressional Record for the Senate, dating to February in the Eisenhower years, record floor debate over Formosa and its straits. One senator urges that the time is wrong for a full debate on the question. He speaks of President Eisenhower's wish to work with Congress and to settle such problems on a shared, two-party basis. Another senator's claims about consultation are left for a fuller answer later.

The speaker insists there is no intent to rewrite the history of the United States or to rest policy on half-truths. Members of the Foreign Relations Committee, he says, will answer at the proper time. Kept in an Agency file, the extract shows the Senate handling of a live Asia question that intelligence staff were then following closely.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050173-3:
A sanitised copy of a 17 July 1951 memorandum asks whether retired officers may serve the Agency as intermittent consultants. The Office of National Estimates wanted named retired men to advise on national estimates. Pay was set at fifty dollars for each day of such service. Expected use ran to an average of ten to twelve days a month. They would do no staff or clerical work, serving only at the call of the estimates office.

Two legal worries drive the paper: a possible bar on the service itself, and harm to the men's retired standing or retired pay. Names and the office's exact needs are blacked out in this copy. The reasoning that follows tests the plan against the laws on retired officers holding paid work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500080008-3:
Added financial security for staff hurt on hazardous work is urged in a memorandum of 23 October 1953 to the Acting Deputy Director for Administration. A July paper from an administration chief had asked for an Agency policy on one hard case. Staff or their dependents would be repaid for a loss where injury or death came on duty. Yet the facts of the work could void the person's own insurance cover.

The problem, the writer notes, was not new: it had surfaced in career service planning and in past opinions from the same office. One past view weighed the government's liability where normal compensation did not reach. Express limits in the Federal Employees' Compensation Act bound what managers could do on their own. The memorandum seeks a policy within those limits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090007-3:
An Efficiency Rating Manual opens with a contents list that maps the whole system in two parts. Part I covers who is rated, which forms are used, and the kinds of ratings given. Regular ratings, trial-period ratings, and special ratings each get a section with their timing. Duties of the rating official, the reviewing official, and the rating committee follow in order.

Part II gives aids for running the system: a check list, a timetable for the yearly round, and a plan for meeting with rating officials. A plan for talking over ratings with staff is also included. The manual turns a government-wide duty into desk steps. Supervisors used it each rating season to grade staff in a form headquarters would accept.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090016-3:
Personnel Director Memorandum Number 17-52, dated 8 April 1952, sets uniform steps for periodic step-increases in pay. It covers staff paid by the year in permanent posts under the Classification Act of 1949 schedules. The Director's policy, the memorandum states, is to follow that act as closely as the Agency can. Extra and longevity increases are left for later instructions.

Eligibility turns on pay basis, post type, and the service and rating terms the following paragraphs spell out. Cited regulations are worked into each step so offices apply the same test. Step-increases were the steady raises staff earned inside a grade, so a single Agency method mattered for fairness. The memorandum gives personnel clerks one procedure to follow for every case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140001-3:
House Committee Print Number 173, dated 4 October 1950, analyses what a veteran or a dependent must show to win compensation or a pension. It was printed for the Committee on Veterans' Affairs of the 81st Congress. John E. Rankin of Mississippi chaired that committee, and its full membership is listed. Elements of entitlement are broken down one by one, with the rates payable under each head.

Service connection, degree of disability, and the standing of widows and children each get close treatment. Tables and summaries turn a thick body of veterans' law into a working reference. Agency lawyers kept the print because staff with service pasts raised these questions often. It is a committee staff work, built for daily use rather than debate.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140047-3:
Disability benefits for military and civilian personnel are set side by side in an analysis prepared for Agency use. A warning opens the text: the mass of differing benefits makes any full comparison unwieldy. Length of service, rank, reserve or regular standing, and age all change the military result. So the analysis gives examples from set cases that show the general picture.

Civilian staff of CIA draw death and disability benefits under the Federal Employees' Compensation Act. That act is called the most generous system yet devised, and its reach is broad. Injuries at work and diseases caused by the work are covered, and medical costs, including hospital care, are paid by the government without charge to the worker. Wage loss pay follows in the list of salient benefits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700120010-3:
An agreement made on 9 August 1949, effective 5 July 1949, sets the terms for a career agent sent abroad, with the name removed. The recitals state the bargain plainly. The government wants the employee's services for CIA in conditions that call for a cover for operations. The employee agrees to serve overseas under the Office of Policy Coordination and to supply his own suitable cover.

Article I turns to the cover job itself. It must fit the man's professional past and skills in a believable way. He must act outwardly in line with that cover at all times. Later articles cover pay, secrecy, family matters, and what happens at the end of service. The typed form turns a double life into contract language.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000800140008-3:
An untitled memorandum of agreement, marked secret, sets a contractor to studies and experimental investigations for the United States. The officer signing for the government is left unnamed in this copy. Work is to run on the cost basis the articles prescribe. The contractor must carry out the studies with the utmost secrecy and dispatch, under the instructions of authorised government personnel.

A specification is folded into the contract by reference, as if written out in full. Reports on progress are owed as the work moves. A large part of the materials bought will be consumed or built into equipment in the course of the job. Cost, property, and inspection clauses fill the later articles. The subject of the research is never named in the legible text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040006-3:
Senate Report Number 475, ordered printed on 8 June 1949, is the committee case for S. 2020, the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. Mr. McClellan's committee had studied government property management and the reshaping of the agencies that handled it. It reports the bill and urges that it pass. A historical section opens the argument.

Need for a sound, businesslike property system, the report says, had long been plain. In 1943 the House passed a bill to that end, and the Senate committee backed it. War pressures pushed that effort aside before it finished. The report then works through the new bill title by title. Where the bill text in this file states the law, this report explains the reasoning and the waste it meant to cure.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100020043-3:
An annex to F.O.O. Number 7713 of 29 June 1951 sets Italy's part in housing United States Armed Forces. The Italian Government will provide, free of cost and for sole American use, the areas, buildings, and facilities listed in Schedule A. Where further government areas or buildings are needed, Italy will grant them if other demands allow. For private ground listed in Schedule B, Italy will use its good offices with owners to secure fair rentals.

American forces must maintain and repair the buildings and installations handed over free. Later clauses handle costs, claims, and the standing of the forces on Italian soil. The annex is the facilities half of a status arrangement, the sort of paper that decides who fixes a roof on a foreign base.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100040005-3:
Appendix A gathers the times Congress has tried to compel the executive to hand over confidential documents. The first case reaches back to March 1792, when the House set up a committee to probe the failure of Major General St. Clair's expedition. The committee was empowered to call for persons, papers, and records. Its right to inquire rested on the House's hold over public spending, the summary notes.

The Secretaries of War and Treasury appeared in person. When President Washington was asked for the campaign papers, a cabinet meeting settled the answer: he would send only such papers as the public good allowed. Case after case in the same pattern follows. The appendix is the ancestry of every later fight over executive privilege.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200020079-3:
A Veterans Administration press release of 1 August 1946 announces wider insurance benefits for veterans, effective that day. President Truman had signed the congressional act amending the National Service Life Insurance Act of 1940. As first written, that insurance met the needs of men and women at war. The amendments loosen it to draw holders in peacetime as well.

Endowment policies, not in the original law, are now offered. Holders may name beneficiaries outside the narrow classes the first act allowed. Lump sum payments and total disability benefits are added as fresh features. About six million NSLI policies in force could gain from the changes, the Administration states. The release came from its Public Relations Office in Washington, marked for immediate use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030005-3:
A report by the shipping editor of Lloyd's, tied to a reference paragraph A-3(c), survives in a scan that is only partly legible. Readable passages describe the shipping intelligence organisation Lloyd's built up and the services it supplied. That work, the report notes, became known not only in Washington and London but more widely. The United States Navy figures in the account of who used the service and how it reached them.

Lloyd's shipping intelligence rested on a worldwide web of agents reporting vessel movements. Wartime and post-war demand from governments made that web a valued source. Because whole lines are garbled in the scan, the report's finer points cannot be recovered with confidence. Its subject, authorship, and the praise it records for the Lloyd's organisation are nonetheless clear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030014-3:
Stanley Ross and his report on communism in Bolivia are dissected in a memorandum dated 1 December 1953 for the Deputy Director for Plans. Many copies of the Ross report had reached the United States Government. It asserted that Bolivia was the gateway for communist penetration of the Western Hemisphere. Each copy came with pressure to cut American economic support to the present Bolivian government.

Ross, the memorandum reports, had close ties to tin mining interests hurt by the nationalisation of the mines: Patiño, Hochschild, and Aramayo are named. Since 1 November, eight copies had come to CIA's notice, some direct and some through State, the FOA, and Ambassador Lodge. Both State and the FOA reported the same pressure. The memorandum weighs the report as advocacy, not bare fact.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200110114-3:
The Statute Laws of Cyprus Number 25 of 1947 prints the Diplomatic Privileges (International Organisations) Law of that colony. It was enacted by the Officer Administering the Government and Commander-in-Chief of Cyprus, and is dated 24 November 1947, in the name of H. Turnbull as printed. The law deals with immunities, privileges, and capacities of international organisations. His Majesty's Government in the United Kingdom and foreign governments are members of the bodies in view.

Part I applies where the Governor in Council declares an organisation to be one of the covered kind. The Governor may then by order grant the organisation legal standing and set privileges for it and its staff. Later parts sort the detail for named bodies. A copy sat in Agency files beside plans for work on the island.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00039a000100050059-3:
Weekly Activities Report number 10, covering 2 to 6 March 1954, was sent on 10 March 1954 by the Chief of the Language and External Training School to the Director of Training. Its main figures concern language training. A large group of people were in classes, and others were in self study programs across sixteen languages. The language laboratory logged its highest weekly use yet.

Other entries track support for students and new course offers. Written reports on each student's progress were sent to training liaison officers, with weekly written reports to follow. The school notes National Security Agency courses in Russian and Hungarian with no applicants so far, and a request for a course in Tibetan. It also notes a Foreign Service Institute series on how foreign policy is made. Notice of advanced management courses for senior staff on university campuses is recorded.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100300018-3:
Senate report number 1482, dated 2 June 1954, from the Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs, supports S. 3318, a bill to provide for a continuance of civil government for the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. The committee reports the bill without change and urges that it pass, in Calendar number 1504 of the 83rd Congress, second session.

The purpose is to allow funds needed to keep the government of the trust territory going. The cap is not more than seven million five hundred thousand dollars a year, counting islands run by the Department of the Interior and those moved to naval charge. The report explains why a law was needed. The House Appropriations Committee had struck a budget request of five million eight hundred twenty five thousand dollars for the territory, on the ground that no basic law yet allowed such spending.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200160004-3:
Senate report number 1794, dated 12 July 1954, from the Committee on Finance, supports H.R. 9709, a bill to extend and improve the unemployment compensation program. The committee reports the bill without change and urges that it pass, in Calendar number 1808 of the 83rd Congress, second session, with the House bill taken up in the Senate.

The bill would extend protection under the unemployment insurance system to around four million workers who lacked it, the first major extension of cover since the system was set up in 1935. The report stresses that the system has always been mainly a state program, and the bill keeps that method, since job problems vary by place. It also notes the President's economic report of 28 January 1954, which found benefit levels too low and benefit periods too short in some states.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200170003-3:
Report number 407, dated 5 June 1953, is titled Outstanding Magazine Articles Relating to International Affairs. It is a weekly digest from the Division of Public Studies, Office of Public Affairs, Department of State, reproduced for Agency use only. Short digests cover current magazine editorials and articles of special bearing on United States foreign relations, without claiming to mirror overall opinion.

Magazines digested include America, Nation's Business, American Mercury, The Commonweal, farm papers, The New Leader, Business Week, U.S. News and World Report, Christian Century, The Nation, Newsweek, Time, Barron's, Life, and New Republic. A subject index covers Asia, a big power conference, the Bricker amendment, China and Korea, President Eisenhower, and foreign affairs topics. One digest recounts the case of a reporter held abroad and the refusal to trade a steel mill for his release.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130196-3:
Draft regulation dated 30 January 1956, proposed as S 20-550, titled Details of Agency Employees, states Agency policy and procedures for the detail of Agency employees. A detail is set apart from temporary duty: temporary duty involves duties tied to the employee's regular position, in a different location, while a detail does not.

Definitions follow. A detail is assignment to duties not tied to the employee's own position, and may be internal or external. Internal details may be formal or informal, and external details are always formal. Either may be reimbursable or not. Internal means within the Agency, external means to another department or agency, formal means documentation is required, and reimbursable means costs are borne by the gaining agency. Later rules set approvals: a detail bringing a total of six months or more in twelve months needs Office of Personnel approval.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100010027-3:
Memorandum dated 4 February 1952, from the Assistant Director for Collection and Dissemination to the Deputy Director for Intelligence, is titled OCD Personnel and Space. Tables show the office's current personnel position as of 1 February 1952, with staff on duty, pending, vacancies, and ceiling, and the increases said to be needed for its assigned jobs.

Units listed include the Assistant Director's office, administrative and operations staffs, the CIA Library, the Biographic, Industrial, Graphics, and Special Registers, and the Liaison and Machine Divisions. The memo argues that the increases are large chiefly because the office serves other offices and staffs, so its workload rises as they grow. The writer compares it to a restaurant that doubles its tables and must add cooks and waiters. Later sections support single needs, such as added hands to order the still photo collection.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070120-3:
House Document number 156, 83rd Congress, first session, prints a message from the President relative to the conduct of foreign affairs. The message is dated 1 June 1953 and was sent to the Committee on Government Operations. The message opens with the change in the nation's world role over recent decades and its position of leadership among free nations.

National security, the message argues, entails mutual security with other free nations, whose freedom depends heavily on United States strength and the wisdom of its use. To meet the test, the nation must achieve the most efficient and cohesive organization for the conduct of its foreign affairs. Later passages discuss the transfer of the Technical Cooperation Administration. The transfer is not meant to change the character of the technical cooperation program as a long range effort. The program aims to help other peoples develop their economies and raise living standards.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100160003-3:
Untitled questionnaire in an Agency file lists numbered questions put to the agency about its classification practice under Executive Order 10501. The first questions ask what distinction the agency makes between defense information, as described in section 1 of the order, and security information as generally used. They also ask whether the two classes could be merged without harm to security.

Further questions ask what share of documents originating in the agency are classified under the order or other authority. They ask the shares at top secret, secret, and confidential, plus any share marked official use only or a like term not authorised by the order. The same figures are asked for documents received. Later questions ask whether the agency upgrades the classification of documents received whose contents remain unchanged, why, and with examples, and what share of documents received from other agencies are so upgraded.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100230050-3:
Untitled bill text in a garbled scan is the Special Migration Assistance Act of 1952, as its citation clause states. A declaration of objectives says the purposes are to let the United States take a fuller part in the defense of democratic ideals against communism. It also aims to reinforce its own resources and assure world peace and stability, in the act's own words.

Means listed are admission to the United States of properly selected refugees from communism. They also include relief of dangerous tensions in Europe by admission of skilled people from designated overpopulated countries. Provision of facilities, services, and payments for refugees, and their education and training for resettlement, are also named. Later sections treat visa limits. A proviso covers a person to whom a visa would be refused solely for past membership in a party or organization, other than the Communist Party, on proof to an official's satisfaction.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020025-3:
Pages from the Congressional Record, House, shown here in a mixed order, open with the closing articles of an interstate compact. The articles give Congress consent for a state to join it on its terms and reserve the right to alter or amend it. A state could withdraw by action of its legislature or governor, effective six months after notice to the other states.

Floor debate follows on a bill for financing banks for cooperatives, which Mr. Hope describes as a bill of some importance with no opposition, put on the Consent Calendar to pass it as fast as possible in the closing days of the session. Mr. Johnson of Wisconsin questions the chairman in the exchange. A further portion prints commission text requiring a report of findings and recommendations to Congress by 31 December 1954, with the commission to expire ninety days after that report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200040005-3:
Copy of the 16 December 1953 congressional lunches memorandum, in a scan with heavier letter garbling than its companion copies, sets out the same weekly program and schedule for the Director's approval. The opening three dates are 21 December 1953, 11 January 1954, and 18 January 1954, for Vorys, the House Appropriations Republicans, and Saltonstall.

In the portion shown at the middle of this copy, the Kansas entry is the fullest: Congressman Edward H. Rees, chairman of the House Civil Service Committee, is said to have always offered to be of any assistance possible and to be extremely helpful in the career service program. Including Senator Frank Carlson, chairman of the Senate civil service committee, at that lunch is floated as advisable. The memo adds that Rees would not desire detailed treatment, a point on which this copy breaks off in the passage shown.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200060021-3:
Memorandum for the files dated 12 March 1956, marked secret, records congressional calls made by the Director on Friday 9 March. He telephoned Chairman Vinson of the House Armed Services Committee and confirmed his intention to move forward with the Langley site for the Agency building. Vinson had the correspondence sent the day before and had no objection.

Chairman Cannon of the House Appropriations Committee was out of town, so the Director spoke with George Mahon. He described his effort to reach the Chairman, and said he wanted another meeting with the Agency subcommittee soon. He also reported to Mahon on an Agency office head who had been the subject of a second hand report that an employee was painting his house on government time. He explained the man's strained finances. A later call covers a congressman's private intelligence briefing and the Joint Committee problem.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200060030-3:
Memorandum for the Director dated 20 March 1956 concerns Chairman Dawson of the House Committee on Government Operations. Congressman McCormack had suggested the Director call Dawson and offer to appear before his committee. The writer recommends against that, and instead an invitation to Dawson to come down and discuss problems of mutual interest.

Dawson had come for lunch during the last session and was briefed thoroughly by Colonel White, Mr. Kirkpatrick, and others on the conduct of Agency business, detail given to Appropriations Committees, and the internal audit system. Asked then whether his committee should organize a subcommittee on the Agency, his reaction was negative, though he was impressed and appreciative. His great interest in the African problem might be stated as a reason for a new invitation. Later pages note Agency comment of 10 March 1956 on surplus property bills.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200100099-3:
Joint State and ICA message CA-585, dated July 1956, announces CODEL Hickenlooper, travel of Senator Bourke B. Hickenlooper of Iowa and Mr. Pat Holt, consultant to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Posts addressed include Barranquilla, Berlin, Bogota, Buenos Aires, La Paz, Lima, Panama, Rio de Janeiro, and Santiago.

The Senator was a member of the Foreign Relations Committee and ranking minority member of its subcommittees on American Republic affairs and on technical assistance programs. He expected to depart the United States on 28 July for Latin America. The trip was to study the technical assistance program. Holt would depart 24 July, visit Colombia, then join the Senator in Panama for the major part of the trip. Posts are asked to prepare an outline for post summary in advance and arrange field trips to technical assistance projects; in Bolivia a trip to Santa Cruz was scheduled. Mission directors are asked to report reactions afterward.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100080004-3:
Printed bill S. 2368 was introduced in the Senate on 29 June 1955 by Mr. Smathers for Mr. Kennedy and sent to the Committee on Government Operations, in the 84th Congress, first session. Its title is to add a new title relating to real property management to the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949.

The new Title IIA, Real Property Management, begins with a declaration of policy in section 220. The provisions are stated to be necessary to provide for the more effective and efficient management of real property owned or leased by the United States. Section 221 gives the Administrator, sixty days after the title takes effect, complete authority and responsibility for management of all real property, with stated exceptions. Later aims include improvement of office space quality, for morale and efficiency, and relocation of offices to cheaper areas.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100130026-3:
Printed bill introduced in the House on 5 January 1955 by Mr. Forrester and sent to the Committee on the Judiciary, in the 84th Congress, first session, without a bill number in the portion shown. Its title is to authorize the admission into evidence in certain criminal proceedings of information intercepted in national security investigations, and for other purposes.

Covered information is that obtained by the heads of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Army G-2, Air Force intelligence, and Naval intelligence. It was obtained through interception of wire or radio communications on the Attorney General's written approval. Crimes listed in the middle include treason, sabotage, espionage, sedition, and seditious conspiracy. They also include violations of chapter 115 of Title 18, the Internal Security Act of 1950, and the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, plus conspiracies. Such information is deemed admissible despite section 605 of the Communications Act of 1934.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670018-3:
Chronology of Executive Pay, 84th Congress, is an Agency working paper, partly garbled in the scan, that traces the executive pay bill from its first steps. Word was received in the late spring of 1955 that the Administration was considering a broad revision of the Executive Pay Act of 1949. Staff talks followed between the Agency and the White House personnel office on provisions touching the Agency.

One entry records a letter of 13 July 1955 from the Director to the Director of the Bureau of the Budget. The letter set out the pressed salary status of the Director and Deputy Director. It backed the Hoover Commission view that the Director's pay rise to that of the Deputy Secretary of Defense, and the Deputy Director's to that of under secretaries. Later entries follow the Senate committee's report in late July 1955.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670036-3:
Second copy of the committee print Analysis of S. 2628 and H.R. 7619, printed for the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service in 1956, read here for its agency tables. Table A lists positions by department or agency, and its contents run past the executive departments and the Executive Office to legislative, judicial, and independent agencies.

The independent list includes the Administrative Office of the United States Courts, the Court of Claims, the Export-Import Bank, and the Farm Credit Administration. It also includes the Federal Civil Defense Administration, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, the Federal Reserve System, the General Accounting Office, and the General Services Administration. A middle passage urges that the Assistant Director of the Administrative Office be included, as in the Executive Pay Act of 15 October 1949.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100680026-3:
Draft bill to amend the Foreign Service Act of 1946, as amended, and for other purposes opens by rewriting section 1 of the Act of 26 May 1949. The Department of State is to have, beside the Secretary, an Under Secretary of State, three Deputy Under Secretaries of State, and ten Assistant Secretaries of State. All are appointed by the President with Senate advice and consent.

The Counselor and the Legal Adviser, also presidential appointees confirmed by the Senate, are to rank equally with an Assistant Secretary of State and receive the same salary. Officers already in post need not be reappointed when the act takes effect. Later sections amend the Foreign Service retirement fund: section 9 rewrites parts of section 811 and repeals section 811(b), and section 10 rewrites section 821(a).
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100720003-3:
Notice of Pending Legislation is an Agency form from the Legislative Counsel, Office of General Counsel, circulated 20 January 1955 for Legislative Bill number H.R. 2616. Check boxes mark the attached bill as sent for comment on whether it is of interest to Agency activities and whether further action by the office is needed. Comments are due through channels by a stated date.

The bill, by Mr. Lesinski of Michigan, would grant longevity pay step increases to federal employees on an equal basis on completion of ten, thirteen, and sixteen years of service. The attached print, 84th Congress, first session, amends subsections (a) and (b) of section 703 of the Classification Act of 1949, at 5 U.S.C. 1123: each department shall grant an added step increase, to be known as a longevity step increase, as a reward for long and faithful service. A distribution list closes the form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200190001-3:
Notice of Pending Legislation on S. 709 is sent by the Legislative Counsel to the Director of Security, and a second copy, dated 2 February 1955, goes to the Deputy Director for Administration. The comment from the Deputy Director of Security states the point of Agency interest in one sentence. The proposed bill requires the release of personnel and confidential files to the Congress or its committees, on the request of an Agency employee.

The bill print, 84th Congress, first session, shows S. 709 introduced on 26 January 1955 by Mr. Dirksen and sent to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. Its title is to authorize the release of the personnel files of federal officers and employees to congressional committees at the request of the officer or employee concerned. The forms mark the bill as sent for comment on its interest to Agency activities.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200280001-3:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, marked for internal use and reviewed by the Office of General Counsel, comments on H.R. 5843 and S. 1874, identical bills to provide leave of absence for officers and employees stationed outside the United States, for use in the United States, its Territories, or possessions.

The bills are substantially the same as the home leave provisions of H.R. 3820, on which the office had commented before. One change is noted with approval: section 2062(f) as proposed would require that home leave taken in Territories or possessions be used outside the area of employment, a limitation absent from H.R. 3820 and called a necessary feature. Continued Agency efforts to gain home leave benefits for its employees, through support of these bills, are recommended. The bill print amends subsections (d), (e), and (f) of section 203 of the Annual and Sick Leave Act of 1951.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200370001-3:
Memorandum on proposed legislation to establish a United States Academy of Foreign Service, H.R. 233 of the 84th Congress, first session, gives the Agency's personnel comments on the bill. The Director of Training's comments are called useful, and the memorandum weighs what such an academy would mean for the Agency.

An academy might improve the cover of some Agency personnel who are integrated with the State Department, the memorandum says. It could give access to a pool of carefully selected, well educated candidates. If quotas were set, the Agency would want them drawn so it need not take more graduates than it needs. Redrafting should also make the one year of special study abroad apply only to Foreign Service officers, and make clear that a graduate assigned to another department leaves the act's purview. The bill, by Mr. Zablocki, was introduced on 5 January 1955.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200460001-3:
A CIA legislative file on H.R. 5560, opened with a notice of pending legislation dated 23 June 1955, concerns duty-free entry of personal effects and household goods. The bill would make permanent the provisions of Public Law 633 of the 77th Congress, which covered personnel returning from extended overseas duty. The Director of Logistics supplied the Agency's comments.

Logistics calls the bill of distinct interest to CIA, because the exemption was set to expire at midnight on 30 June 1955. Without it, civilian and military personnel alike would have to declare and pay duty on goods brought home. The comments urge every possible action to pass the bill and to make it retroactive to 1 July 1955. The file also carries long tariff-law excerpts on customs offences and penalties.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200510023-3:
A CIA memorandum to the Legislative Counsel reviews two 83rd Congress bills, S. 2762 and H.R. 9909, on cutting off pay and retirement rights. Both target federal employees who refuse to testify before congressional committees on grounds of self-incrimination. H.R. 9909 also covers employees convicted of certain listed offences, and reaches civil service annuities and military retired pay.

The memo notes that affected employees would keep their own contributions to the Retirement Fund, so the loss falls on the annuity that Congress granted and may withdraw. It questions, without deciding, whether retirees could lose rights already acquired. Given the President's position and support in Congress, it concludes the Agency should accept the proposals as proper public policy. The file also holds related correspondence on the bills' penalties.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100030002-3:
A CIA memorandum of 24 February 1956, addressed to the Deputy Director (Intelligence), answers a question about how a naturalised person can lose United States nationality. It quotes Title 8 of the United States Code, sections 1484 and 1485.
