Under section 1484, a naturalised national loses nationality by keeping a continuous residence of three years in a foreign state where he was formerly a national or was born.

Section 1485 then lists the people that rule does not reach. They include those living abroad in United States government employment, those abroad because of disability from government service, and those representing bona fide American educational, scientific, charitable, commercial, financial, or religious bodies. The quoted text also covers age and residence exceptions, registration duties, and rules for children who lost nationality through a parent's foreign naturalisation before 1948.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100170007-3:
Two CIA letters to the Attorney General answer a Court of Claims case. They are dated 13 June and 15 July 1952. The claimant's name and the case number are redacted. The petition was filed on 21 May 1952. The claim grew out of a deal with the Office of Strategic Services. The office writing holds the records the case needs.

The July letter traces where those records went. The Office of Strategic Services was abolished on 1 October 1945. Its staff, funds, and records passed mainly to the War Department. There the Strategic Services Unit kept them. The petition concerns a set of photographic negatives. Twenty-six enclosures go with the reply. They are copies of letters from those files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100210039-3:
A CIA memorandum of 27 September 1955 records a meeting held that morning on the crypto security law, section 798 of Title 18. Officers from the General Counsel's office, Security, and several technical and staff components attended; their names are redacted. The meeting took up the office's memorandum of 25 August and how the law should be used in practice.

Discussion exposed practical worries. One officer doubted that secret writing supplies and equipment could be brought under a law written for cryptography and communication intelligence. Others raised the problem of telling people who counts as an unauthorised person, and whether a stamp could mark protected material. Staff officers warned against stretching the law beyond its purpose, and suggested the law chiefly concerns NSA, which the Agency might consult early. A June 1955 memorandum on applying section 798 is attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100300020-3:
A CIA paper argues that armed service spying must be fully coordinated. It covers service participation in the federal espionage and counterespionage system. Service intelligence units in overseas command areas had run such operations for years. They acted under a strict reading of NSCID 5, with no formal agreement. More regions were growing critical in the contest with the Soviet Union. So the need for secret collection kept rising.

The paper urges a formal agreement. The Director of Central Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense would sign it. It would state when service units may run operations as agreed activities. It would provide joint procedures fitted to each overseas commander's area. And it would keep all United States espionage and counterespionage coordinated. That way every capability is used to best effect.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030092-3:
A CIA memorandum of 16 September, from the Assistant General Counsel to the Acting Director, reports on a proposed omnibus bill revising the United States espionage laws. The bill grew out of a spring 1946 interdepartmental committee of G-2, naval intelligence, and the FBI, whose recommendations went to the Attorney General from Secretary of War Robert P. Patterson on 27 June 1946. Since then the State and Treasury Departments and others had commented.

The Bureau of the Budget had long tried to clear the bill, and the President was personally interested in it. But the Departments of Justice and Treasury still differed materially over several provisions, and the President wanted those differences settled before the bill reached Congress. CIA had never been asked formally for comment, though it held an informal copy. The memo argues that, given the objections set out below, the Agency should state its interest and its objections.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030119-3:
A bill draft would establish a National Intelligence Authority and a Central Intelligence Agency. Its policy statement gives the foreign intelligence mission in full. The service would supply the President with foreign intelligence of the highest calibre. It would also supply the Secretaries of State, War, and the Navy. Such intelligence would help form policy and avert armed conflict. It would assure the common defence.

The findings condemn the old, scattered system. Collection, evaluation, and dissemination were spread across many departments. That proved unsatisfactory before, during, and after two world wars. The text then turns to staffing rules. The Director may appoint retired officers of the armed services to civilian posts. He may do so despite the dual-pay bars in the Acts of 1894 and 1916. The Director's own pay mixes service pay with a top-up to the salary fixed in the Act.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300030028-3:
A CIA legal memorandum of 16 November 1951 answers a question on recreational facilities. Lawrence R. Houston signed it. It went to the Assistant Deputy Director for Administration. The question was whether appropriated funds could pay for such facilities. Research showed a restrictive line of rulings.

The Comptroller General reads 31 U.S.C. 628 as barring the spending. Funds may not buy or rent recreational property. They may not pay for recreation supervision either. This holds even where a base lacks facilities. It holds even where public facilities are far away. It holds even where morale suffers. So any CIA spending needs a ground in unique operations. Security needs are the strongest such ground. A need for physical fitness for set duties could also help. The choice, the memo says, is a factual call for the addressee.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300240115-3:
An executive order sets the system for safeguarding official information in the interests of the defence of the United States. Its preamble balances two needs. Citizens must be informed about their government. At the same time, national defence requires protection against hostile action, covert or overt, including espionage. Certain official information must be guarded uniformly against unauthorised disclosure.

Section 1 fixes three classification categories, and no others. They are Top Secret, Secret, and Confidential, in descending order of importance. Top Secret is for defence information needing the highest degree of protection. Its unauthorised disclosure could cause exceptionally grave damage to the nation. A break in diplomatic relations is one example given. Later sections set handling and storage rules. Top Secret material needs the strongest storage, such as a vault or an alarmed area. Secret and Confidential material may rest in metal cabinets with an approved lock.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100040002-3:
A CIA directive sets out a program for the production of training publications. It comes from the Director of Training and cites OTR Regulations 1-1 and 1-2. The Director is responsible for manuals on training, intelligence methods, and doctrine. Duties are split three ways. The Plans and Policy Staff runs the program. The Schools decide what is needed and produce manuscripts. The Support Staff edits and prepares them for publication.

The Staff will survey what the Schools need and what they have under way. It will help find authors and set up working committees. It will advise on revisions and route finished manuscripts for printing and dissemination. Each School must now list the manuals it has produced. It must also list those in process, with completion dates. The aim is to keep authorship with the experts while holding central control.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030009-3:
An opening statement to House subcommittee hearings on manpower utilization is dated 3 November 1955. The speaker is Thornton W. Luckart, Director of Administration. He represents Secretary Marion B. Folsom of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare. The statement reads Folsom's letter of 26 October 1955 into the record. The letter answers the subcommittee's questions on manpower control steps.

Folsom subscribes fully to the subcommittee's objective. Government programs should run at the lowest cost that meets their aims. He took office on 1 August 1955. Since then he has pressed for economical administration across the department. The letter lists personnel utilization audits on a selected basis. It closes with assurance of wholehearted agreement. Payroll numbers, Folsom writes, should be carefully scrutinized on a continuing basis.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040008-3:
A committee guide explains the functional surveys departments and agencies are to make. A memo attached analyses how to set up such a program. Survey findings face no limits from existing legal or rule-based limits. Where limits bind, the advice should let Congress weigh remedies. Full records must back every finding. Agencies should plan a full review at once. The aim is to bring structure, programs, and housekeeping into line with modern business practice.

Signs help choose which function to survey. Recent management reports, low output, and backlogs point the way. Heavy overtime, low morale, and high turnover also signal problems. A function employing many people deserves a look. So does one lately expanded or moved. The analysis then covers the work itself: tasks done, steps followed, manpower needed, and records kept.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040017-3:
A CIA memo of 25 November 1955 reports manpower use in the Office of Basic Intelligence. It went from the Assistant Director for Basic Intelligence to the Deputy Director (Intelligence). OBI's major functions serve the National Intelligence Survey program. They rest on NSCID No. 3 of 13 January 1948. The office coordinates the NIS program overall. It also reviews, edits, publishes, and disseminates the surveys.

More than 40 producing components feed the program. All OBI functions rank equal in priority. A ten percent cut would remove seven positions. No single function could be eliminated; that would stop all NIS output. The cut would have to fall across the board. Delay would follow in supplying finished surveys to agencies that need them urgently. Slower NIS production would also defy long Agency policy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000200050015-3:
An Office of Communications order, No. 23-53, is dated 30 November 1953. It sets up the Communications Career Service. It rescinds Order 24-52 of 21 July 1952. The service is open to all staff employees and staff agents of the Office. Its members devote themselves permanently to communications work. They accept the duties of running the Agency's classified electronic communications facilities.

A Career Service Board administers the program. The Assistant Director and Deputy Assistant Director sit ex officio. A chairman and two members come from the staff and division chiefs. Non-voting members include an executive secretary and the Communications Training Officer. The Board advises the Assistant Director on career matters. It handles rotation and promotion reviews. Supporting data include a table of organization and lists of staff by grade and anniversary date.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000200070031-3:
An extract from Sherman Kent's Strategic Intelligence poses a problem. Should there be a separate administrative unit for collection and dissemination? Kent first defines his terms. Collection means the exclusive right to procure all raw material the professional staff needs. Dissemination means the exclusive right to distribute raw material and finished product to consumers.

Kent's answer is blunt. Such a unit, he writes, is little short of preposterous. A library can well acquire basic material of general utility. But vesting a librarian with exclusive rights over a specialist's research needs is another matter. His example is a study of the Iranian Tudeh Party's views on the Arab League. The specialist would have to tell a collector in advance what he needs. On dissemination, Kent sees no reason to distribute raw material outside the parent organization. Inside, it must circulate promptly and effectively.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100010043-3:
A progress report covers the Geographic Area of ORR for February 1957. It comes from the Office of the Chief, Geographic Research. Production hit high levels. Twice as many reports went out as in January, and 36 percent more maps. A new February record was set for servicing map requests. Major attention went to unconventional warfare and photo intelligence studies. Soviet operations in Antarctica were also evaluated.

The Cartography Division completed 90 maps and charts. Ninety-two went to CIA, four to the Air Force, and two to State. One map was made for Vice President Nixon's trip to Africa. The Map Library Division received 4,770 maps from foreign sources. It sent out 27,019 map sheets in answer to 1,138 requests. That was more requests filled than in any month of 1956 except August.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100010052-3:
A CIA briefing contribution weighs the denial of geographic material to the Soviets. Practical difficulties come first. The government is closely tied to a free economy. It has ethical and statutory duties to share information with the electorate. International commitments, including the International Geophysical Year, also require open data. Denial is therefore feasible only case by case, and before publication.

Technical journals cannot be denied at all. Little of significance in geography could be kept from the Soviets, given their advanced instrumentation. Commercial secrecy sometimes works, as with the Warden gravimeter. No blanket denial of aerial photography is feasible. Photography of certain strategic cities and industrial complexes might be denied through commercial cooperation. Oceanic gravity data draw Soviet interest. Geodetic survey results, from Africa to the Inter-American survey, are also listed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410012-3:
A status table lists Geography Division projects as of 2 January 1958. MR-53's text and maps are in reproduction. MR-54 has maps and charts initiated, numbered in the 26300s. Far East entries lead with the Ningsia, Suiyuan, Chahar, and Shensi geography, still delayed. Sinkiang is in progress for the first quarter of 1958. Tibet remains delayed and open.

A Northeast Thailand regional analysis should be ready for editing in January. Several escape-and-evasion entries rest on ADTIC research. Some are delayed, others in abeyance. New December entries carry February to April 1958 dates. A Norilsk urban study has its first draft of text in hand. Another study, coordinated with OSI, will be ready for reproduction in January. Analyst names are mostly redacted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410021-3:
A Cartography Division project status list is dated 1 October 1957. The USSR-Satellites Branch leads. USSR railroad construction from 1946 to 1950 heads the list. Bulgaria sheets cover smelters, mines, ferroalloy deposits, and coal and petroleum. New items include a selected Soviet order of battle for the Black Sea area. Sino-Soviet Bloc airline routes to the Free World also appear.

Population sheets are prominent. They show USSR population by administrative division for 1950-55, total distribution, and urban population by regions. Cities over 100,000 are listed. Czech industry sheets multiply: textiles, chemicals, manufacturing centers, electrical machinery, and locomotive plants. Plotting charts for Athens and Tripoli serve the DD/S. France and Italy forest types serve the NIS program.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490005-3:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 239 of 5 March 1957. The committee reviewed Chapter I on NIS 39A, Communist China. The draft was approved with certain changes. State's later comments on Sections 11 and 12 were still to come. The Task Group was asked to review agency comments. Any fundamental changes to Section 19 would go to all members for final approval.

The chapter was placed under control. Five sections carried contributor controls on their source comments, and Section 19 was controlled in full. On outline guides, an inter-agency meeting of 28 February 1957 took up Section 56. A contributor's draft guide is under study by the interested agencies. State added its own Section 56 proposal on 4 March 1957. Supplement VI changes move source comments to the end of each section.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100006-3:
A progress report covers the Geography Division for August 1957. Production was exceptionally good. Five reports on unconventional warfare areas were completed. Three followed the coordinated feasibility study format set on 2 April 1957. That format came from a working group of the Army, Navy, Air Force, and DD/P. The studies were all on Europe. A list of area-selection considerations accompanied them.

Completed work lists report numbers and titles. They include transborder routes from the Indian subcontinent to Sinkiang and Tibet. Oil and partition in Algeria appears. A Nationalist China Chapter I section and a North Korea study are listed. Soviet post-IGY intentions in Antarctica drew additional indications. Geographical highlights of the Gulf of Po Hai, China, and railroad construction in Communist China also appear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100033-3:
A set of branch comments, headed Recommendations and Problems, comes from monthly reports for December 1957. The Cartography Division opens on its Chart and Graph Section. Work assigned there has grown for months. People have been temporarily transferred to keep current. If the trend continues, the unit's duties and organization must be re-evaluated.

The Europe-Africa Compilation Branch suggests a critical review of NIS Chapter I maps. It calls the series a best seller worth refining. It proposes one international boundary symbol on classified maps. It also proposes dropping the terrain disclaimer from D/GC maps. The disclaimer, it argues, discourages the second look the rendering deserves. The USSR-Satellites Branch notes an index it built to OCI materials. Map release questions follow, covering scales the Army Map Service may receive.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100020027-3:
A CIA legal paper works out the status of a class of personnel facing injury or death. The scan is garbled in places, but the argument can be read. The writer assumes first aid will be given at once. Where injury is severe, an escort must take the person to a doctor and arrange transport. The legal problems arise over payment. Private medical care may need reimbursement. Government care may go to someone not automatically entitled to it.

Collateral questions follow: hospitalization, dental services, lost pay, and death payments. Members of the U.S. Armed Forces are set aside; acting in their duties, they are covered by statute. The paper then weighs benefit scales for non-citizen employees. The Director has discretion to pay on the citizen scale in some cases. Percentages payable to widows, children, and dependent parents are spelled out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100030080-3:
A CIA schedule lists a summertime movie program running July through September. Films show at 1230 hours on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays. Foreign language and English films are mixed. The program serves entertainment, language practice, and area knowledge. The first entry is a silent English film, Ten Days That Shook the World. It is billed as a classic of Bolshevik revolutionary action.

Russian films dominate the list. They include Admiral Ushakov, The Russian Question, and travelogues of Soviet Georgia, Tadzhikistan, and Armenia. Japanese entries include a Nikkatsu world newsreel and a war bond film. German films and Russian newsreels also appear. An English entry, Communist Blueprint for Conquest, comes from the Strategic Intelligence School. Another, titled USSR, serves general area study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100050006-3:
Extracts from an Official Secrets Act set out penalties for spying. The text is Part 3 of the act. A person acting for a purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the state commits an offence. The acts listed include approaching or entering a prohibited place. They include making sketches, plans, models, or notes useful to an enemy. They include collecting or passing secret codes, documents, or information.

Punishment reaches fourteen years where defence works or secret codes are involved. Other cases carry up to three years. Proof rules follow. The prosecution need not show a particular prejudicial act. Conviction may rest on the circumstances, the accused's conduct, or his known character. Later clauses cover forged passports and official documents. Personating a person holding government employment is also an offence. The text speaks of the Government of India.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100150005-3:
An internal memorandum presses for faster issuance of revisions to overseas per diem allowances, the daily rates paid to Agency staff travelling abroad. It cites a Bureau of the Budget circular tied to the Standardized Government Travel Regulations, with an attached schedule of maximum per diem rates. The complaint is that field stations learn the current authorized rates too late.

The writer asks that the revised rates reach the heads of field stations at an earlier date, so personnel abroad are not left working from stale figures. Fifty additional copies of the reference circular are requested for wider distribution. Parts of the scan are garbled, but the request itself, and its aim of keeping overseas staff current on the rates they may claim, are clear enough.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100160022-3:
A summary of a proposed revision of the Civil Service Retirement Act sets out new annuity terms for federal employees. The scan is garbled in places. It describes a yearly annuity built from an employee's average salary over the highest five years. Set percentages apply for each year of service. A higher rate applies once service passes twenty years.

Other provisions continue an annuity after thirty years of service. They allow an involuntary separation annuity at age fifty with twenty years of service. The existing option after twenty-five years of service, at any age, is also kept. The reduction for retiring under age sixty is cut sharply. It falls from three percent for each year under sixty to one percent. A separate two percent figure is stated for part of the range. The summary survives in the Agency's declassified files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100210062-3:
A policy memorandum asks how long a second overseas tour should run when it follows straight after a first one. Its stated purpose is to fix Agency policy on the length of a subsequent tour. The employee in view has just completed a tour of duty abroad. He is staying on rather than coming home.

The answer given has two parts. The Agency may require the employee to serve the full set period for the later tour. Only then would he receive travel to and from the post at government expense. Back-to-back tours, the memo adds, would often suit both the Agency and the individual. The discussion weighs home leave eligibility rules. It cites Public Laws 600 and 830, along with a Comptroller General decision. It admits that parts of the law are not clear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100100002-3:
A revision of the Office of Training's report to the Killian Committee opens with the office's structure. It lists four schools, a Plans and Policy Staff, and a Support Staff. It also lists an Assessment and Evaluation Staff. The office trains every category of Agency personnel. It trains some personnel of other intelligence services as well. Its curriculum lists 128 formal courses, though not all are offered at the same time.

During the reporting period an average of 55 courses were in operation. Average student attendance stood at about 800. Over five percent of total working hours went to formal or on-the-job training. The revision notes one strain. It is covert training, where instructors must be well rounded in all phases of clandestine work. They must be able to teach staff, contract agents, and foreign service members one to one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100110001-3:
Expansion of the Junior Officer Training Program is the subject of a reply. The reply answers a Management Staff memorandum of October 19, 1955. The writer clarifies a request first made to a Management Staff representative. That request dates to September 26, 1955. Whether to continue the program, he notes, had already been settled. A deputies' meeting in the DDCI's office settled it on August 31, 1955. The decision was not only to continue the program, but to expand it.

The method proposed would recruit as many junior officer trainees as the Agency can take within a set figure. Trainees would be assigned against Agency-wide position vacancies until trained. They would then move to operating components with professional vacancies. Controls would keep total on-duty strength within the authorized personnel ceiling.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200050025-3:
A performance report dated December 29, 1955, is sent to the Agency's Director of Training. It follows one junior officer trainee through his first assignments. His name and his offices were removed in review. He was assigned in October 1954. He worked on an estimates staff through December. From January to July 1955 he held familiarization and training assignments in two other offices. He then returned in August 1955 for reassignment.

The report stresses one point. Although the postings were meant for training, he performed at the level of an experienced intelligence officer. In one office he spent about four months on a special project. He wrote a study of the new role of aviation in Soviet military doctrine. The study compared captured Soviet field manuals with older ones. The piece was published. It was coordinated with an Air Force and Navy team at the Pentagon.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200100001-3:
The November report of the Committee for Language Development reaches the Agency's Director of Training on December 12, 1957. The committee had met on November 21. It discussed achievement award policy and award applications. It also took up the Language Data Records on Form 444c submitted through October 31. The state of proficiency test development was a fourth topic. A restrictive reading of the Schedule of Awards, agreed in October, had governed the first thirteen applications.

Test planning fills much of the report. The R&S Building auditorium was reserved for two stretches. The first ran from March 31 to April 11. The second ran from May 12 to 16. The tests would cover roughly 425 people in French, 309 in German, and 308 in Spanish. They would cover 143 in Russian and 127 in Italian. Smaller groups would be tested in Polish, Chinese, and Portuguese.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300020009-3:
Weekly Activities Report number 48 comes from the Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School. It opens, as these reports often do, with significant items: none to report. The activities that follow are heavily cut by redactions. One item records a meeting arranged for a purpose. A specialist could pass on counsel about modern Chinese intelligence descriptions. The school expected to carry that work forward with another office, toward official descriptions.

A second report in the file gives a concrete case from the Qualifications Review Panel. An application for intermediate Chinese at Yale was deferred. It was filed for a Far East division man. His aptitude rating was low. The panel also lacked firm information on his present proficiency. He had not yet returned to headquarters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030008-3:
Weekly Activities Report number 36, dated September 11, 1958, from the Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School, leads with the fall term. The Fall Trimester of the Voluntary Language Training Program launched on Monday, September 8, with fifty-three courses in sixteen languages and a student enrollment of 340. Classes were being given for the first time in Turkish, at the beginners level. Continuing classes ran in Arabic, Chinese, Czech, Finnish, French, German, Greek, Italian, and Japanese.

The report also weighs outside training options with start dates in September and November, and an Office of Training course scheduled to begin on October 6. On Chinese, the picture is tight: three candidates are in hand, and one of them, the school judges, should probably be discouraged from taking its intensive course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030026-3:
Weekly Activities Report number 18, dated May 8, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School. It opens with a hunt for expertise. The chief was asked about a specialist on the ethnic groups of the USSR. He replies that his own school has general familiarity with the subject. The sort of specialist wanted, though, is more likely found elsewhere. He points to places like the Russian Research Center at Harvard or the Russian Institute at Columbia. He has no names to offer.

The report also answers Far East division queries. It describes a planned full-time course, a year long. The target start was September or October 1958. Three students were lined up. Help was promised in collecting and reproducing text materials. The course aim was clear: skill in reading many types of print and handwriting. Skill in writing clear, concise summaries was the second aim.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300040007-3:
For November 12 to 18, 1958, the Registrar's Weekly Activity Report number 46 covers a week of division business. It is dated November 20. Much of it concerns the NEA division. It reports meetings on its training problems and a headquarters returnee to be briefed on his role. It also reports plans for officer orientation and training assistance. Language ratings were taken up with the school chiefs.

Testing logistics fill another item. Requests in the awardable languages would be handled by the training officers. Admission would be on a request-registered basis. The Registrar also looked ahead to the large numbers expected for testing in March and April. He planned to set aside a third day each week to absorb them. He had checked the plan inside the Agency's Language and Area School.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050006-3:
Weekly Activity Report number 37 of the Registrar's office covers September 10 to 16, 1958. Its main item reports early returns from an IBM tabulation of the Office of Training's internal training through 1957. One pattern stands out in the figures: employees who attended internal courses took about three courses each. Required courses account for a large share of the enrollments counted.

A second item concerns outside release. Selected Cable Analyst training material was reviewed for whether it was proper and desirable to release it to the State Department. The part dealing with the training program itself was in proper order, and State was told there was no objection. A part touching the Agency's career development arrangements was treated more carefully.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050015-3:
Weekly Activity Report number 28 of the Registrar's office covers July 9 to 15, 1958. Arrangements were completed for a DD/I and DD/P briefing for candidates to the senior defense schools. At least four DD/P speakers and Mr. Amory would take part in the briefing, set for July 23 and expected to fill most of the day. A lunch on July 21 would cover the Harvard program.

University ties appear again in a meeting on July 11 with Glenn Ferguson, assistant dean of the new Graduate School of Public and International Affairs being established at the University of Pittsburgh. They discussed the school's aims and the likely extent of Agency participation. Ferguson allowed that the degree curriculum on offer would benefit the Agency less than other parts of the government.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300070004-3:
Weekly Activities Report number 40 comes from the Agency's School of International Communism and the USSR. It covers October 3 to 9, 1958. A planned lecture arrangement was cancelled, as proposed in the school's previous report. Readings were arranged instead, to supplement the lectures that remained. Teaching help flowed the other way as well. The Language and Area School called on a member of this school. He assisted in two days of tutorial work and discussion in the Czech language.

Staff members also sat in on previews of a publication. Another staff was preparing it, a 170-page work on developments during 1958. Parts of the report are garbled in the scan. Some names and the titles of individual lectures cannot be read with confidence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400030077-3:
Intelligence School Weekly Report number 5 covers January 31 to February 6, 1958. Outside lecturing leads the items. Twenty Agency speakers had been scheduled for the next Strategic Intelligence School course. Invitations were out for talks at the school. One invitation was for a talk on the intelligence community. On February 4 and 5 the Dependents Briefing was conducted. It served twelve wives on their way overseas.

A further item concerns exhibits being gathered from various DD/I offices. Course completions crowd the rest of the report. Students finished Instructional Techniques number 30 on January 31. Twenty-three students completed Writing Workshop number 17 on January 30. Intelligence Orientation number 38 started on February 3. It had ninety students enrolled, the largest class since September 1957.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400040058-3:
Weekly Report number 35 comes from the Agency's Operations Support Faculty. It covers August 26 to September 2, 1958. Its first item takes up a sales problem. The operating divisions showed little interest in the Budget and Finance Procedures Course. After talks with the Comptroller's Office, Mr. Saunders called a meeting. Budget and finance chiefs attended. At the meeting, the necessity and importance of this kind of training were reaffirmed. A count of Class B stations was ordered. It would show what enrollment could be expected.

The rest of the report is logistics for visiting groups. It covers reserved parking for six National War College buses. It covers smooth entry to the R&S Auditorium and coffee at the break. The whole program was recorded. Planning is also reported for two days of mid-career briefings. They were set for September 8 and 9.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400060029-3:
Weekly Activity Report number 3 comes from the Agency's Instructional Services Branch. It covers January 15 to 21, 1958. Four 16mm prints had been delivered to the branch. One was sent on at once. The others were to be distributed to the Operations School and another unit. A paperwork debt came with them. The original agreement called for a copy of the film's script with the print. So many changes were made during production, though, that a new script had to be transcribed. It was taken from the sound tape.

The Visual Aids Section reports finished work. It produced a large color chart, thirty by eighty inches, titled Psychological Assessment. It produced a second color chart on the A&E testing program. Auditorium equipment questions awaited the architect's advice. The advice would say what could be fitted into the design.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400090008-3:
A weekly activity report of the Junior Officer Training Program covers October 29 to November 4, 1958. It gives its significant item to one man's unpaid labor. His interest in the program is called beyond the call of duty. His cooperation is praised the same way. Since the new program opened, he had given up all his Saturdays. He had persuaded colleagues to join him. Together they assessed trainees who arrived late. The trainees themselves, the report adds, had formed a favorable attitude toward him.

The report also quotes a supervisor's assessment of a woman trainee. She is called a superior employee. Her test results and training record were no better than average. Her first trials handling agents, though, showed no weakness. She promised to be one of the few women the Agency could trust in that role.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000100100008-3: A weekly summary report of the Office of Training tallies students in tabular form. The tables sort enrollment by course. They cover the full-time intelligence and operations courses. They cover specialized and tutorial training, and clerical instruction. A separate count serves a field training entry. The scan is heavily garbled. The individual figures are largely illegible. The report can therefore be described only in outline. It is a weekly census of how many students sat in which courses. It was kept for the Agency Director of Training.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000100100017-3: A weekly summary report dated August 17, 1953, lists the students in Office of Training courses. Full-time courses come first and part-time courses after. The full-time side is headed by the Basic Intelligence courses then running. The part-time side reaches outside the Agency. Students sat at the Air War College, the Armed Forces Staff College, the Industrial College of the Armed Forces, and the Naval War College. Three sat at the National War College, and three at the Strategic Intelligence School. Many figures are garbled.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000200030014-3:
A tentative master schedule lays out the thirty-first course of the Strategic Intelligence School, run by the Department of the Army's intelligence staff in the Main Navy Building in Washington. The course runs from November 8 to December 20, 1954, and the schedule is printed as a week-by-week grid of lectures and hours.

The first week mixes an introduction to armed forces intelligence with the significance of strategic intelligence, intelligence organization, research methods and techniques, and the components of strategic intelligence. Later weeks turn to the world area by area: the sociological and political factors of Africa, the Arab states and Israel, economic factors in Latin America, and the military geography of Africa. It is the Army's own training calendar, kept in the Agency's files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000200040004-3:
A memorandum dated July 19, 1955, for the Director of Training sets down observations on the Clark Committee report on the Agency. The writer had already made the points orally. He made them to the top staff of the DD/P area, at the Director's request. He had asked that they be briefed downward through the chain of command. The purpose was to put to rest exaggerated notions. Rather alarmist rumors were gaining currency from the press handling of the report.

The gist is reassuring. The committee's findings, conclusions, and recommendations are not so damaging. Taken together and in the whole, they fall short of the rumors. Twice within a short space of time, the writer notes, the clandestine services had been thoroughly investigated. In each case they had come off clean and whole.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000200050003-3:
A survey of the Agency's Language and Area Training School counts the school's people and students. It finds thin staffing. The instructor table of organization carries a block of vacancies. All of them are linguists. Against them stand consultants and a handful of full-time and part-time instructors. The vacancy rate, the table shows, runs at half the instructor strength. Courses being conducted are all in the language field. The survey totals enrollment course by course.

Laboratory load is measured too. It sets student hours demanded of the language laboratory against the hours available. The recommendations are practical. Staff should be shifted to the chief's office. The laboratory technicians should be put on rotating shifts across the day. Saturday duty should be rotated between them as paid overtime.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000200060020-3:
A memorandum dated October 19, 1954, reports an interview about the Army Psychological Warfare Officers Course. The writer had questioned, on October 14, an officer then on duty with the Agency who had taken the course from April to June 1954. That class held sixteen students: eleven Army officers, two naval officers, one Marine Corps officer, and two USIA civilians, though an average class runs to twenty-five or thirty. The course is given three or four times a year, with no entrance examination.

The work, as described, mixed short essays and set questions each week with a one-hour oral critique. Once during the course every student had to write a paper of about twenty pages, choosing from a list of some fifty topics or proposing one of his own.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400080010-3:
An eyes-only memorandum dated July 13, 1953, gives the Inspector General an objective evaluation of the services furnished by the Personnel Office. To avoid loose generalization, the writer takes each major personnel function in turn, then the office as a whole. On recruitment, he splits the judgment in two: numbers and quality. Applicants for professional-level positions, he finds, are generally available in numbers adequate to fill many vacancies with reasonable dispatch.

He also names services the office is not rendering but should. Chief among them: minimum qualification standards for each significant category and level of position, set as soon as possible. Publishing such standards, he argues, would let the Agency build a clear, equitable, and constructive promotion policy on top of them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400110007-3:
Annex 4 of the Director's Report to the National Security Council is dated December 4, 1951. It is the Office of Training's account of itself. It is organized under basic concepts, the training problem, accomplishments, and conclusions. The background section recalls the Agency's first five years. In those years it could recruit substantial numbers of people with useful backgrounds. Their backgrounds already included intelligence training and experience gained elsewhere. That easy supply was ending. The annex argues the training task that replaced it.

One accomplishment stands out. It is a course in strategic intelligence. The course was built on a method acceptable both to the producers and to the users of national estimates. It was open not only to Agency staff. Selected personnel from the other departments that share in producing national strategic intelligence could attend. It was taught through lectures, seminars, and research projects.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400140013-3:
A memorandum dated November 21, 1955, comes from Matthew Baird, Director of Training. It asks the Director of Central Intelligence to approve a survey. The survey would cover major overseas training activities. The Office of Training, it explains, carries responsibility for the conduct of training overseas. It gives varying degrees of support to training at Agency installations. Those installations sit in Europe, the Middle East, and the Far East. It is also responsible for one more field. That is the analysis, approval, and coordination of cold and hot war training plans.

The Director's wish is practical. On his visits to stations he does not expect special assignments laid on. He wants to gather informal word on the highlights of training at each place. He wants the same on training support. He wants it gathered in the most expeditious way. The memorandum carries the approval line for the Director's signature.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100080015-3:
An interim report on the Management Staff's survey of the Security Office goes to the Director of Security. It tells him the work has two phases. This report covers only the first. That phase is an analysis of the office's overall organizational pattern. The mission it works from is the Agency's security program. The team was to cover its preparation and execution. In major parts it covers security policy and counter-intelligence work. It covers physical security, and security determinations on personnel.

The analysis draws two activities together. Counter-intelligence and technical research, it argues, share one objective. That objective is preventing penetration of the Agency by foreign intelligence organizations. The office receives information from its own elements. It analyzes anything that might point to a penetration, or an attempt at one. The report tests the office's shape against that duty.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100160007-3:
A regulation statement defines the Office of the Comptroller. The Comptroller's mission is stated in one sentence. He is in charge of all budget and finance work in the Agency. He is responsible for program and financial analysis. He will provide machine records service. Everything else in the statement hangs on that charge. The functions follow the money.

The Comptroller recommends the Agency's fiscal and budget policies. He sets the procedures that carry them out. He develops, prepares, and executes the Agency's budget and finance programs. He advises Agency officials on finance and budget policy. He supervises the running of all budget and financial programs. He maintains effective reporting on the Agency's activities, in budget and financial terms. He assists the Director in presenting the Agency's case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200080005-3:
An exhibit on page production and dissemination works through one publication's journey step by step. The sample is Soviet Press Extracts, marked SECRET, dated January 24, 1949. It was handled by two employees of the Agency's Library Branch. One was a standard distribution clerk graded CAF-4. The other was a messenger graded CAF-3. The clerk's part comes first.

He checks the dissemination order. He opens two sealed and tied bundles from the reproduction branch. He pulls the pre-printed labels. He sorts the piles for dissemination from the order. He prepares the document receipt in an original and two copies. The messenger then takes the sorted piles. He affixes the receipt copies, inner-wraps and seals the package. He stamps it Secret four times on each side, and fixes the label. One receipt copy is held until the signed original comes back, then destroyed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200110029-3:
Appendix B to the first report of an ad hoc production review group surveys what the Office of Reports and Estimates actually produced from February 1946 to 23 May 1949. Output is sorted into broad types. They include evaluations, reports and estimates in several series, and periodical issues such as dailies and weeklies. Supporting services of common concern for other Agency parts and outside agencies complete the list. Staff and current work are used in the sense set by a Council directive.

Each series is then traced to its start. Situation Reports grew from a Navy request for a basic handbook on chosen countries, joined with a felt need for basic country studies. Branch periodicals began in a narrower way and spread as working-level staff elsewhere asked to join the distribution list. The appendix gives a full census of early Agency publishing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300170005-3:
A second copy, near in wording to a companion memo, records the CIA briefing of Edwin Weisl, Sr., Cyrus Vance, and Edwin Weisl, Jr. on 16 January 1959. The briefing began at 4:45 p.m. at the Agency, under an arrangement the Director had made with Weisl senior. The Director attended with Messrs. Scoville, Sheldon, Stoertz, and Warner. Vance had telephoned in advance to add Weisl junior to the party.

Weisl senior said hearings would soon be held by the Preparedness Investigating Subcommittee, in part with the Space Committee, both under Senator Johnson. The memo judges that the men were in effect assisting the senator, a point backed by their room in the Capitol and by a call from the Space Committee staff director. Discussion covered Soviet missile emphasis and the Bison, with detail in an attached memo.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300200047-3: A roster of the House Foreign Affairs Committee lists members by party, with new members marked by a star. Thomas E. Morgan of Pennsylvania chairs the committee, and the Democratic side includes A. S. J. Carnahan, Clement J. Zablocki, Omar Burleson, Edna F. Kelly, and Wayne L. Hays, among others. Republican members include Robert B. Chiperfield, Frances P. Bolton, Chester E. Merrow, and Walter H. Judd. The sheet is a reference list only, giving names, states, and party marks, with no debate or report text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020096-3:
A monthly report for the Map Library Division for July 1958 survives mainly as statistics tables, and much of its narrative page is garbled in the scan. The tables sort receipts of map sheets by source: material made inside the Agency, sheets on automatic receipt and bought for stock, and sheets from other domestic and foreign sources. Specialty sheets and series sheets are counted apart, and atlases and other reference material get their own lines.

Processing tables follow, counting titles indexed and cataloged for special maps and series, and reference work is tallied by type, including place name questions and other inquiries. Sheet and title counts run through the tables in columns that are hard to read in places. The record is most useful as a snapshot of the library's intake scale and of how its work was measured month by month.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200220002-3:
A draft memorandum dated 3 September 1958, sent to the Deputy Director for Intelligence, weighs a possible site for launching a satellite from Communist China. Reports cited include word from Tokyo on 13 August that final arrangements were made at the Khrushchev-Mao meeting for a launch on 1 October. A July report added that a Soviet embassy officer in Mexico spoke of Soviet help for a Chinese launch. The Geography Division, while studying missile test ranges in China, matched stated needs for Soviet launching sites against geographic factors and found a probable location.

Soviet help would likely mean Soviet staff, missiles, and equipment. The steppes of Inner Mongolia north of Peiping fit the ground needs: level to rolling short-grass plains. Rail spurs and ground support gear would still have to be built, and danger to people near the site is treated as high.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00423a000100130004-3:
Executive Order 10501, on safeguarding official information in the interests of the defense of the United States, is reproduced in full. Its preamble holds two ideas together. Citizens must be informed about their government's work. National defense, though, requires that the country be able to protect itself against hostile action, open or covert, including espionage. Some official information tied to defense must therefore be guarded in a uniform way against unauthorized disclosure.

The order then sets classification categories for official information and rules for marking and handling it. A custody section limits possession and use of classified defense material to places where secure storage exists and unauthorized persons are kept out. When material is not under personal watch, the same standard applies. The text is the standing federal rule of its period for classifying and protecting defense information.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200050006-3:
A budget analysis on overt intelligence collection, dated 1 November 1954 and made as a tab to a cost table, asks a pointed question. What joint arrangements beyond the standing Council directives would make overt collection work well in 1956? Publications procurement comes first. A Council directive had set up an advisory committee on foreign language publications. Its subcommittees on procurement, use, and reference were building shared approaches to handling foreign language material across the member agencies.

Map procurement follows, a program for getting foreign maps and related material for the whole community, with needs coordinated centrally. Later passages cover shared indexes and liaison among Agency offices, Army intelligence, State, and the Air Technical Intelligence Center to cut duplication. Radio monitoring is also treated: a central service under a Council directive monitors foreign propaganda and press broadcasts, watched by a named monitoring element.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200050033-3: A tabulation from May 1954 sorts organizational units and their activities as shown in a government-wide estimate of effect in strategic intelligence for fiscal 1954. Columns divide work into categories such as collection, requirements coordination, and production, and rows name units across the defense, CIA, and State structures. Marks show where a unit is only partly counted in a category or in the survey itself. The sheet is a reference table only, with no narrative text beyond its headings and notes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300050005-3:
Paper IAC-D-103/3, dated 4 October 1956, carries the First Semi-Annual Report of the Standing Committee on Exchanges, the report itself dated 1 October 1956. The committee was set up by Intelligence Advisory Committee action on 28 February 1956. Its aim was to gain the most intelligence value from East-West delegation exchanges, with paper IAC-D-103 as guide and terms of reference.

Plans look forward: the committee would assess the intelligence results of exchanges held so far and bring that knowledge to bear on future suggestions to the State Department. It judges that gains from three named exchanges had generally confirmed the judgment behind the program. They were the United States Automation Delegation, the Polio Exchange, and the Housing Exchange. The report is the committee's first half-yearly exchange report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300070012-3:
A draft post-merger version of National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 1, dated 26 May 1958, is laid out as an annotated working text. A head note says the most significant new language has been underlined, while minor rearrangements and editorial improvements are generally not marked. Margin notes tie each passage to its source, whether the standing directive, a Council action paper of March 1957, or a presidential memorandum. The directive's frame comes from Section 102 of the National Security Act of 1947.

Overall coordination is assigned first. The Director of Central Intelligence shall coordinate the foreign intelligence activities of the United States under existing law and Council directives. That duty covers all aspects that together make up the national foreign intelligence effort. Later duties include setting policy for a continuing interchange of intelligence and related information among community parts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300090029-3:
Minutes numbered IAC-M-346 record a committee meeting at a quarter to eleven on 10 June 1958, with Director Allen W. Dulles presiding. The member list again covers State, Army, Navy, Air Force, the Joint Staff, the Atomic Energy Commission, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Much of the visible discussion turns on the Lebanon situation, read in the light of comments by General Schow.

A staff member drew attention to a recent report bearing on appreciation of that situation, and another cited relevant parts of the most recent estimate on Lebanon, SNIE 36.4-58. Admiral Frost and Mr. Cumming both commented on the seriousness of the situation in Indonesia. The minutes record these exchanges in brief, sanitized form, with names and judgments kept but some passages removed before release.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300130033-3:
Paper IAC-D-5/1, dated 26 February 1953, submits terms of reference for an interagency source control mechanism. A working group drawn from the member agencies had prepared the terms under an earlier committee directive of May 1952, and Secretary James Q. Reber sends them in for approval. Each agency is asked to send its agreement in writing, and to name a principal and an alternate member for a source group, by 5 March.

An appendix lists the working group members by agency, from the CIA and State through Army and Navy names. The mechanism itself would give the community a shared way to control sources that more than one agency touched, though the detailed terms sit in the enclosed pages. The paper is an early piece of community machinery, from the period when the advisory committee was building standing procedures.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000100080085-3:
A letter dated 7 April 1959, sent to all suppliers, puts into effect an engineering study or change proposal procedure. Its aim is more uniform practice among suppliers when spending engineering effort and building modification kits under time and materials and open type contracts. The procedures in an attachment are to be followed as closely as practical, and approvals will be issued by the groups named there. The work covered is generated for two named efforts, rendered in the scan as FOG and the Project, with approvals from the respective group for each.

Most of the procedure, the letter notes, was already being followed in varying degrees, and suppliers are asked simply to adopt it. Attachment rules add that approval may be given in person but will always be confirmed in writing. Approval is the contractor's authority to draw spares from the depot and to procure or build against the requirement.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000200090119-3:
An agreement of employment is made between the Lockheed Aircraft Corporation, a California corporation with its main place of business in Burbank, and an individual employee. The employee's name is removed in this copy. Recitals explain the setting. The United States and the company enter contracts from time to time under which the company supplies the government with competent technicians. The technicians maintain and service aircraft and give related services.

The company therefore employs the employee for work on assembly, disassembly, repair, maintenance, and flight line servicing of aircraft. The work is done at locations the government designates, in connection with the company's performance under any such contract. A leave section in the middle provides vacation with pay at the rate of one week for each thirteen weeks of continuous service. The leave is taken at the end of the agreement or on its termination under the article named.

Column heads cover expenditure issue, unliquidated and total obligations, allotment authority, and unobligated balance. Seven-figure totals appear for the lead accounts. The file is a raw ledger print with no narrative text and partly garbled digits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00900a000100130004-3:
Numbered advice from an Agency study takes up ledger posting first. The study would end the posting of single debts one by one. In their place, staff would post monthly sums built from expense run papers and adding machine tapes. The number record would gain two new columns, one for sums owed and one for free balances. Those columns would keep legal control of the books.

The reviewers find the costs of the change greater than the gains. Extra columns mean extra work for the staff who keep the books. Book balances would drift away from true expense figures. Pay forms dropped in fiscal year 1960 would have to start up once more. Later items cover reply times for dispatches, and the set advises against a fixed limit there. One section would file only Agency papers for its own work, a step already in force.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100020078-3:
Report to the Killian Committee covers work by the Agency's Business Machines Service Staff. The period runs from 1 September 1957 through 31 March 1958. Outside computer services head the list of items. One job for the Office of Communications went on contract computers run by outside firms. Later work of that kind was to run on the Bureau of Standards 650 computer. That change would cost about one fifth as much. The saving in that area is put at 11,000 dollars a year.

Flexowriter machines form the other main item in the report. In the Office of Personnel, the machines filled in Forms 50 and 52 on their own. As a by-product, they also punched cards for accounts and statistics. The saving there is put at about 6,000 clerical hours, or 11,000 dollars, a year. The scan is partly garbled at those figures.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100050002-3:
Meeting record dated 11 October 1956 covers a briefing for the Assistant Director for Current Intelligence and his assistants on Management Staff recommendations for the CIA Watch Office. The Watch Office sat inside the OCI Secretariat. Management Staff staff had audited its functions in detail and had also looked at other Agency watch and night duty units and at the NSA Watch Office.

One question put at an earlier meeting frames the paper: whether OCI was asking too much of its Watch Officers. The answer given was yes under current conditions, though steps could ease the load. Proposals included four ten-hour shifts per man each week, continued use of temporary assignees in peak periods, and a Personnel review of Watch Office position grades.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100010148-3:
Notice No. 5 of the Agency's ORR, dated 17 January 1955, issues the first part of the 1955 revision schedule on the USSR. The full schedule weighs United States and other priorities. It also weighs the time since each topic was last revised. Contributions were due in Room 1217, M Building, by set dates in February and March 1955. They were grouped by journey and by town brief.

Early items pair road and rail journeys with town briefs. One item is a Moscow to Tula road journey, with town briefs for Tula, Voronezh, Orel, Kursk, and Ryazan. Rail journeys run toward Penza, Kuybyshev, Chkalov, Tashkent, Alma-Ata, and Novosibirsk. Later pages urge staff not to ask travellers questions whose answers were already to hand in Washington. They also list embassy travel reports from late 1954.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020066-3:
Memo dated 30 October 1956 revises an Agency questionnaire for Rumania and Bulgaria. It cites St/I Office Notice No. 82 of 4 September 1956. For Rumania, the listed items in Parts I and II are to be kept as they stand. Other items are kept with more detail added. One such item seeks facts on a reinforced concrete factory built to supply dam work. It asks the size of the labour force at the plant. It also asks the daily output of the concrete plant.

New Rumania items call for regular reports on volunteer youth brigades at building sites. Their strength and their work sites are both to be reported. A second section then does the same work for Bulgaria. It lists Part I and Part II items to retain. It also lists items to expand with added detail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020084-3:
Submission dated 2 October 1956 gives economic needs for the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List. The list runs from 1 November 1956 to 28 February 1957. It covers the Near East and Africa, and it is filed as ORR 10150. Each question bears a class mark: S for Secret, C for Confidential, or U for Unclassified. For Cyprus, topics one through four and part of one more are marked retain.

A new item for British East Africa asks for any facts on diamond smuggling. It covers smuggling, or tries at smuggling, of diamonds to the Soviet Bloc. The routes run through European or Middle Eastern channels. Type and number of stones are asked for. So are the persons or firms involved, the money side, and the ways the stones move. Other sections treat Tangier finance and Portuguese African lands. Several topics there are kept as they stand.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100030092-3:
Agency needs submitted in July, the year partly garbled, are framed for one source. The source has access to Hungarian money affairs. First questions ask how large Hungary's foreign debt was. The debt is to be split two ways. One part is debt owed outside the Bloc. The other is debt owed inside it. More items ask how that debt was shared out. They ask whether it was refinanced from time to time, on what terms, and with whom. They ask whether long term joint refinancing was in prospect.

Other questions cover Hungary's trade balance inside the Bloc, in credit or in debit, and its rough size. They ask whether Bloc pressure to take set goods blocked sales for Western exchange. Later items probe Hungarian trade methods and strengths in open markets. Weak points are named as well, such as shortages and poor workmanship.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100050009-3:
Memo dated 7 July 1957, from the Chief, S/CST, revises needs for the Agency's Construction Branch reading panels. The branch made all-source economic reports on the building of fixed sites in the Sino-Soviet Bloc. It also reported on the making of building supplies in the Bloc. Its scope covers building groups, costs, methods, and design standards. It covers the making and the spread of building supplies of many types.

Areas of interest are mainly Bloc countries and lands near them. Strong interest is shown in any trade deal between any country and a Bloc member. The deal counts when it involves building work or the supply of building supplies. Site classes listed include power plants and power lines. They include water supply and sewers, pipelines, bridges and tunnels. They include sites below ground, housing, hospitals, schools, and government buildings.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100050027-3:
Reading panel requirements dated 1 July 1957 cover transportation, with geographic area and subject coverage set out for the Agency's Transportation Branch, S/TR. The branch fed estimates of Bloc intentions, capabilities, and weaknesses through study of Sino-Soviet Bloc transportation. Transport is flagged in the paper, citing DCID 15-1, as a field of common or overlapping interest needing continuing interagency liaison.

Port and shipping detail shows the depth expected. Items call for port description and location, depths, channels, rules, cargo handling facilities, warehouses, docks, cranes, and trucks, plus cargo handling capacity by cargo type and its limiting factors. Building, repair, and upkeep work under way or planned, clearance capacity, vulnerability, and capital investment in ports are also listed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100170051-3:
Briefing paper on the Services Division, Communications Branch, gives its charts, budget, and table of posts. The figures in it are redacted. The mission is quoted in full. The branch makes all-source economic reports on the systems of the Soviet Bloc. It covers the sites and work of the Bloc's set-up communications systems. It works with the rest of the United States government on that task. In its own field, it adds to national estimates.

A list of major reports and of man-hour use follows the charts. Named items include Project 40.295, Foreign Radiobroadcasting Reception Potential, dated 21 October 1954. They include Project EIC-R-12, on Soviet Orbit powers and aims for electromagnetic warfare. The file also holds a warm thank-you letter from Wilbur Schramm. He thanks branch staff for help and advice on a study, and for easy use of Agency materials and sites.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180005-3:
Excerpts in the Agency's files from Working Group I minutes M-139 of 24 September 1957 deal with COCOM listing criteria. The State member reported that a proposed Criterion (c) in the chairman's draft matched, in substance, State's reading of the present Criterion (e). If that reading was to be set down in precise words as an interpretation of Criterion (c), State wanted the phrasing discussed, since small points of wording could be improved.

The chairman planned to tell the Executive Committee that State, ICA, and MDAC agreed in substance with his proposed reading, while Defense and Commerce did not. He saw little gain in a long fight over each word when the split was already clear. Later talk turns to China trade and why goods bought by the Sino-Soviet Bloc were treated as bought for strategic ends.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180131-3:
Untitled copy in the Agency's files of the paragraph 9 work program text sets two tasks. Working Group I would keep the joint control system under steady review. It would propose changes as conditions changed. The Executive Committee would promptly take up a full review of the whole Sino-Soviet strategic situation. Two reasons are stated for the review. Controls toward China had changed in fact. The Bloc was to be judged as a single unit, despite wide gaps between its parts.

The aims and study list are spelled out in full here. Sector studies should be as current as possible. They are addressed to the Sino-Soviet Bloc as one body. Where feasible, they are broken down by part: the USSR, Poland, the Eastern European satellites, and Communist China. Listed sectors include minerals and metals. They include electronics and communications gear, and petroleum and petroleum products.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180159-3:
Draft marked ES-DRAFT, dated 23 January 1957, in the Agency's files, sets out a general policy for economic defense. Its first point holds that the lasting threat to free world security from the Sino-Soviet Bloc calls for measures by the United States and the free world. The measures would slow growth of the Bloc's war potential and reduce its unity. The second point frames the program as part of a wider system of military and political alliances, resting on joint work and shared sacrifice by free nations.

United States support for free world joint trade control arrangements follows from that framing. Measures the United States takes, and those it urges on others, should be weighed for their effect on the whole economic defense system and on the alliances. Later points cover keeping a working joint control structure, and extending two-way arrangements that win support for agreed controls.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200010066-3:
Monitoring text in the Agency's files, dated 15 September 1954, carries a Chinese Statistical Bureau communique in full. The communique covers growth of the national economy in 1953. NCNA broadcast it from Peking on 13 September 1954, in English Morse. It opens by calling 1953 the first year of China's first Five-Year Plan. It credits party guidance for the year's results. It credits a drive across the country to raise output and practise economy from September. It credits planned purchase and supply of food from November as well.

Trade figures in the text give the year's totals. Imports and exports in 1953 ran 36 percent above 1952. Imports rose 38 percent and exports rose 33 percent. Trade with the USSR and the People's Democracies made up 75 percent of China's total foreign trade that year. The evidence title says 1952. The document itself reports on 1953.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200080014-3:
Untitled paper in the Agency's files argues that civil aviation is a strong Cold War weapon in less developed lands. Such nations, the paper says, are eager for the prestige of showing their flag. They want it shown on international airlines. Modern aircraft stand in their eyes for progress. Many small nations were backing international airlines bound to lose money for good. The Soviets had no reluctance to encourage that course in non-Bloc countries. Deeper economic trouble there raised the chances of Communist entry.

Afghanistan, Yemen, and the United Arab Republic are named as places where the Soviets backed leaders' air ambitions. Civil air aid, unlike military aid, looked peaceful and helpful to the economy that received it. Other Soviet edges are named as well. One is a ready supply of technicians for posts no one wants. One is skill at using local feeling against empire.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120037-3:
Agency Current Support Memorandum No. 561, dated 10 March 1958, traces Czechoslovakian airline fluctuations under ten years of Communist control. Scheduled operations of Czechoslovakia Airlines, CSA, on external routes from February 1948 to February 1958 largely reflect changes in Soviet civil air policy, the paper argues. The route pattern rose and fell as Moscow's line changed, rather than on commercial grounds alone.

After the USSR concluded reciprocal air agreements with Bloc members, the satellites exchanged rights with each other as well. Any Bloc country sharing a route with Aeroflot was allotted the same type of Soviet-built aircraft the USSR used on that joint route. Czechoslovakia, called the most sophisticated of the satellites in air operations, was treated accordingly in aircraft and route assignments.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130045-3:
Agency ORR contribution to SNIE 20-56 covers the impact of recent developments upon Western Europe. It includes a shipping section on the canal stoppage. Its main point is plain. The stoppage will tighten an already tight charter market for dry cargo. Indicators are listed in detail. Between 27 October and 17 November, the weekly coal freight rate index rose from 166 to 176. The wheat index rose from 183 to 192 in the same span. Both indexes stand against a 1951 base of 100.

Second-hand ship prices tell the same story. Dry cargo ship prices rose as much as 15 percent from mid-November to early December. They reached the highest levels of modern times. Liberty ships that sold for as little as 500,000 dollars a year earlier were fetching over 1,000,000 dollars. A petroleum passage adds a point. Soviet oil output in the Sixth Five Year Plan would rise by an average 12.8 million tons a year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130054-3:
Paper in the Agency's files takes up pay incentives for workers and managers in the USSR. It explains a planned wage overhaul. The Sixth Five Year Plan calls for a complete overhaul of the wage and salary structure. The aim is a better system and a greater material incentive. The incentive would raise output and lower production costs. The fresh look at employee pay is the first since 1935. In that year a basic revision of the wage structure took effect.

Four lines of change are listed in the paper. The tariff, or base, rate would form a larger share of a worker's total earnings. Proper wage levels would be set between industries and occupations. Faults and disorder in pay and bonuses would be cleared away. Those faults touch administrative and technical staff. Output norms and the system of payment for above-norm output would be revised as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130063-3:
Agency paper dated 1956 totals USSR loans and credits from 1946 to July 1956. Since 1946 the USSR had extended approximately 5 billion dollars in loans and credits to other countries of the Sino-Soviet Bloc. Communist China, at 1.5 billion, and East Germany, at 1.4 billion, had received about 58 percent of total Soviet aid to the Bloc. Most of that Bloc aid, about 65 percent, went to buy Soviet-owned properties or for military assistance.

The contrast with the Free World is drawn sharply. Since 1954 Soviet credits there came to about 450 million dollars, some 95 percent of it to Yugoslavia, India, and Afghanistan, the rest to Finland and Argentina.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130090-3:
Agency report dated 20 February 1956, ORR Project S-48, covers atomic civil defence in the European Satellites. A note warns that it is an uncoordinated report prepared at the request of OCI, not to be quoted or used as reference, giving the immediate views of its authors. In the past, the paper says, civil defence in the Satellites had stressed training and protective construction aimed mainly at aerial attack of the Second World War type.

Information describing larger nuclear weapons or the possible area of heavy radioactive fallout had not been spread to the general public. Even so, the Satellites had built a significant civil defence potential, with staff organisation, auxiliary paramilitary bodies, and training under way. Later pages note public lectures on atomic weapons and defence, including mention of the Bikini tests, and atomic lectures and self-help group instruction in enterprises in one Satellite country.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200140008-3:
Paper in the Agency's files on transport in the Baltic States warns at the start that its figures are rough. Much information on transport sites had been collected in recent years. No firm current estimates of railroad or highway capacity existed. Capacity turns on many factors and seldom allows an exact answer without careful study of masses of detailed data. The estimates give only the general level of working capability, which might shift under changing conditions.

For railroads, the limiting factors listed run to track and yards: single against double track, signalling, and train control methods. Yard and terminal trackage, frequency and length of sidings, types of motive power in service, and locomotive repair sites are named. For roads, bridges in the area are reported able to carry at least 25 metric tons. Grades run not over 5 percent. Minimum horizontal radii run to about 150 feet.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200200083-3:
Agency memo dated 1 February 1958, from the Chief, S/OM, reports branch work for January 1958. During January the branch submitted two branch projects. It submitted one contribution to an area-wide project. It submitted current support papers as well. Eight current support papers were published in the month. One of them appeared as a CSM. After the December report went in, word came that three more projects had been published in December itself.

Those December publications are named: Industrial Planning in Communist China, issued 31 December; Non-Military Civil Defense Construction in the USSR, issued 6 December; and Reorganization of Soviet Economic Management, issued 31 December. January's own list includes a Soviet Shelter Program paper, Sino-Satellite Scientific Technical Cooperation, and an evaluation of reporting for July to September 1957. It includes a blackout exercise reported in the USSR, and increased building of air raid shelters in Bucharest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100060037-3:
Memo dated 9 November 1951 concerns production of a political-economic summary for SHAPE. By a memo of 31 October 1951, the Army had forwarded a report to the IAC chairman. The Army acted as executive agent for the Joint Intelligence Committee. The report came from the Director of Intelligence, SHAPE. It asked for a brief weekly summary of key political and economic developments in the Soviet orbit. State's intelligence office considered itself well fitted to produce the summary. Its continuous review work was the ground given.

A first weekly summary was due on 8 November. The Agency was to forward it to SHAPE. The memo questions whether the Agency should take on the duty. SHAPE's Director of Intelligence had advised that intelligence then being furnished missed SHAPE's needs. The need in view was for political-economic material. That failure is why a separate weekly message was requested.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100090016-3:
Memorandum dated 19 December 1952 from James Q. Reber, Assistant Director for Intelligence Coordination, asks two offices in turn about external research projects. Last spring each office had shown interest in projects listed in an attached Tab A.
