The Agency had explored having a named contractor undertake three of the projects and found it not possible, a name redacted in the scan. Each office is now asked to state its present interest in each project, and whether it wants the Agency to seek other contractors for projects it still wants.

A second ask looks forward: a list of the external research projects each office plans to undertake for the rest of fiscal year 1953 and for fiscal year 1954. Replies were wanted by 3 January 1953, as a basis for preliminary discussion of the program.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200060090-3:
Memo dated 24 October 1957 in the Agency's files goes to the Project Director. Its subject is a review of requirements. The Ad Hoc Requirements Committee reaffirmed that every effort should be made to obtain political permission for broad authority to pursue the requirements in its recommendations of 9 October 1957. Urgency drives the paper: time is the controlling factor on several targets.

The committee calls attention to one target in particular. Vital intelligence might be secured by recoverage of Tyura Tam close to 7 November. That date was expected to bring important Russian events and announcements on space satellite and missile advances. Among the highest priority requirements, the long range bomber question stands out as the most critical problem. Navy recommendations for coverage of Molotovsk, linked in the paper to Severomorsk, are also taken up. A light angle of 10 degrees or more lasts only into early November there, so coverage must be prompt.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000300150143-3:
List in the Agency's files names positions to be cleared for access to TALENT materials, in Headquarters, United States Air Force, and in Air Force commands. The Office of the Chief of Staff heads the list. It names the Chief of Staff, the Vice Chief, and the Assistant Vice Chief. It names the Deputy Chief of Staff for Operations with his assistant, and the Secretary of the Air Staff. It names the Deputy Chief of Staff for Development, and the Assistant for Special Projects.

An Aquatone Liaison Officer section follows, naming its chief, staff officers, and secretary, and the chief of the Western Field Office. Later pages run into the 180s and 190s of positions, reaching AFOIN-3 intelligence staff officers. They name the Chief Deputy Director for Targets, the Chief of the Policy and Management Group, and the Chief of the Requirements Office. Air intelligence specialists close the set.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400030136-3:
Untitled Top Secret report in the Agency's files, dated 1 March 1958, is in message form, marked no copy to be made. The report covers Khabarovsk Krai in the USSR. At Sovetskaya Gavan, naval facilities come first. Preliminary identifications list 3 submarines confirmed, 2 possible submarines, 3 destroyers, 1 possible hospital ship, 1 cruiser, and about 47 torpedo boats with miscellaneous craft. New construction southwest of Shipyard No. 263 has a new torpedo boat pier for 24 boats, support facilities, a major warehouse, and POL storage.

Alekseyevskoye Airfield has a concrete runway running southwest, 8,000 by 250 feet, cleared of snow. An apparent special weapons storage and handling installation sits on its north side. Aircraft there: 25 Badger, 14 Beagle, 2 Bull, 2 unidentified. Vanino Airfield has a surfaced runway of 6,000 by 200 feet, showed 71 probable Fresco aircraft, and appears an active training field. A secured installation southwest of Svobodnyy holds at least 2 buried bunkers with drive-through buildings, and 2 underground structures under construction.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000500030009-3:
An index to photographic coverage held under the heading Operation Softtouch forms the whole file. Organised in numbered books with control numbers for each item, the lists name Soviet sites caught on film. Early entries cover Balaklava airfield, the Tyura Tam launching complex and launch pad, and areas of the Kapustin Yar missile test range. Other entries name the Omsk oil refinery, Tashkent, and a direction finder site at Lugovoye.

Later books add recent coverage around Murmansk, including Severomorsk airfield, Rosta, and submarine bases at Sayda Guba and Polyarnyy. A third book treats an unidentified construction project at Mozhaysk. For that site the index lists range and location maps, aerial photography dated 5 July 1956, location sketches, and perspective views. Read as a finding aid, the file shows which installations had been photographed and how each piece of coverage was filed and controlled.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600080003-3:
A tentative list of conferees fills the file, set out as a table with name, serial number, rank, service, and organisation for each person. Most entries are Army officers of field grade rank. Early names come from the Continental Army Command and from headquarters of the First through Sixth Armies. Others serve at the Infantry School, the Army War College, and staff sections marked G-2 and G-3. One Marine Corps major appears among the Army names.

Later pages add officers from the Psychological Warfare Center, with several lieutenant colonels and colonels listed there. Special Forces staff follow, including men from the 10th Special Forces Group. A few entries reach beyond the Army: officers tied to the Pacific command, a Navy captain, and Air Force officers. The scan is rough and some names read poorly. Even so, the table preserves who was expected at the meeting and where each officer served.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600090048-3:
A report of an Intelligence Advisory Committee working group on emergency plans, dated 3 April 1956, fills the file. The Director of Central Intelligence had proposed that the committee study how it would work in war. Its group was charged with weighing the effect of war on committee work. It also had to spot problems likely at Operation Alert 1956 and propose fixes. Earlier papers from February 1956 set the task.

Background reaches back to June 1955. The National Security Council heard the President say that future relocation tests should include council meetings. That way, plans could be proven able to keep the Council meeting often and working well in war. The Council's own relocation plan, NSC 5521, won approval days later. Among its recommendations, the report urges that committee meetings sit at or near the Alternate Joint Communications Center during the first phase of an emergency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700020008-3:
A long secret paper introduces the idea of services of common concern. It starts with Pearl Harbor. That shock taught the government that its intelligence setup was badly flawed. Drafters of the National Security Act of 1947 could have built one single agency for all needs. They chose not to.

Special units had to stay close to military and political planning, the paper argues. So the Act instead gave leadership that could link the separate bodies and answer to one higher authority. Inside that frame, shared services could grow by slow steps. Later sections sort which shared tasks CIA found easiest to run. Those touching core department work the least caused the fewest frictions with other departments. Closing pages contrast the calm setting in which early directives were drafted with harder conditions that came later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700020017-3:
A draft directive, numbered 1/2, sets rules for CIA support to departments. It rests on paragraph three of NSCID No. 1. First come policies. Member agencies should work as one joined system, linked and leaning on each other. Their work should grow stronger and more skilled. A weakness in any one agency is thus a worry for its own chief at once.

If that weakness touches national security, it also becomes the Director's worry. Some flaws a chief can fix alone. Others lie past his reach, and then Director and committee support may rightly be sought. A budget cut by Congress or a department cannot stay a private matter when security work is hit. Under the procedures, the Director, after talks with the agency head and the committee, will comment on department budgets for foreign positive intelligence work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070058-3:
A first yearly report of the Scientific Estimates Committee, dated 24 September 1953, covers September 1952 to August 1953. The committee was born on 14 August 1952 under DCID 3/4. It rests on NSCID No. 3 and on advice from a survey of how scientific and technical intelligence was then produced. Standing members come from CIA, the Joint Staff, State, the three services, and the Atomic Energy Commission.

The atomic member in fact took little part, the report notes. Its role would stay limited to matters of direct concern. Atomic energy intelligence sat with a separate joint committee in any case. The group keeps no standing subcommittees. Ten ad hoc working groups formed during the year instead. Its chief charge is to join up scientific views for national intelligence, not to run production. Later pages score work under each duty. One watch kept is the state of biological warfare intelligence, tracked through an existing service working group.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100110001-3:
A Navy memorandum dated 1 March 1957 forwards fleet tables for a study coded EDIC/IR-27. Martin McMahon, the Navy member of an ad hoc working group, sent it to the group's chairman. The study covers Sino-Soviet bloc merchant shipping needs and strength for 1956 to 1960. Two copies of the fleet tables came with the memo.

Figures are current to 1 January 1957 for the bloc fleet, and 30 November 1956 for free world fleets. A comparison table sets the two side by side by ship type. Bloc cargo ships number 784, against 11,030 in the free world. Tonnage gaps run wider still. Country notes follow on naval auxiliaries fit to carry cargo or passengers. East Germany, Rumania, Bulgaria, and North Korea have none of 500 tons or more. Poland has one, and Communist China lists cargo ships, oilers, and transports.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100170005-3:
A Commerce paper dated 3 April 1958 urges a softer line on phthalic anhydride exports to the European Soviet bloc. It supplements an earlier paper, OC 1392. That paper had urged refusal of three export bids, and the Operating Committee agreed. Commerce warned then that a technical review was under way. That review is now done, and it drives the new stance.

The chemical does not merit control, Commerce now holds, by many lands or by the United States alone. Refusal at home adds nothing to safety. It merely hands the trade to European makers. Future bids should thus be viewed with favour. The paper also backs a formal appeal by Monsanto in one case, and a plea to reopen another. Tables put free world capacity near 393 million pounds a year in 1956. Bloc output in 1954 sat far lower, at 40 to 46 million pounds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100450004-3:
A study of the petrochemical industry in the Soviet bloc opens with its roots. Early Soviet interest grew from a search for alcohol not drawn from food. That alcohol fed the synthetic rubber trade. Stalin flagged the need as urgent in 1946. Still, seven years passed before synthetic alcohol was made for sale by a petrochemical route. The study judges the Soviet trade more than fifteen years behind the United States.

Present aims run to fast growth in textiles, plastics, and like goods drawn from oil. Those goods serve the Seven Year Plan of 1959 to 1965, for both defence and home use. A large share of 100 billion rubles for the chemical trade will go to petrochemicals. One deputy minister put planned use of liquid gases at over 2.5 million tons by 1965. Later pages note a West German plant sale talked out in Moscow in 1957, with no word since of building work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470011-3:
Minutes of the sixteenth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee record a session held on 12 June 1956. April minutes were approved at the start. Next came a paper on diamond supply in the USSR. CIA would keep weighing fresh facts on the topic. The paper was approved as a summary of what was known so far.

Sharper debate met a request to review radio and television technology and its possible military uses. One member objected that such work sat with a working group, not this body. The vice chairman replied that the intelligence side made it a fair task here. Staff noted that Item 1517 was already defined in fine detail. Commerce said it would welcome studies, and urged that the request widen to more items than that one. A working group would be named to own the project. Priority goals for economic defence intelligence closed the talks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470020-3:
Minutes of the seventh meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee are dated 6 April 1955. The group met on 17 March. First item: winding up old subgroups. A paper proposed dissolving two leftover working group arms, and no member objected. Their unfinished tasks were then weighed one by one. An East-West trade collection group had won terms in July 1953 yet produced no solid advice.

The services had also lately sent their own attaché guides on gathering economic defence facts. So that subgroup should fold, the secretary argued, till the Executive Committee asks for more. A Far Eastern group faced the same fate. The acting chairman added a steer: if the real need is enforcement facts, the committee should aim there. CIA was asked for an interim report on whether secret collection needs in this field were moving ahead well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490082-3:
A draft copy of the minutes of the fifth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee fills the file. The meeting ran on 18 January 1955. This draft is dated 20 January, two days on. Its core matches the final record: the Executive Committee's handling of a paper on Soviet external financial operations leads. Members must study that paper and grade its problems.

Working groups must also test their own tasks against those operations. Two listed functions would be cut as overlaps. CIA's view is stated in this copy with care: no new single unit should be built for the field. The real task is to share the work among units already standing. A second paper sets this draft apart. It reviews trade controls against Communist China, paragraph by paragraph. Its tabling here was meant to draw member views. A State member's query on one point opens that debate in the record.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100500008-3:
Minutes of the sixty-sixth meeting of the Intelligence Working Group are dated 11 October 1954. The group met on 30 September. A name change heads the record. A paper of 25 August had proposed calling the group the Economic Defense Intelligence Coordinating Committee. Members found that name too long. The meeting settled on Economic Defense Intelligence Committee instead.

The secretary was told to seek top committee approval for the new name. Next came planning. Past support for the parent body had run on a catch-as-catch-can basis. Requests had to squeeze into research programs already set, and service suffered. CIA had urged the parent body's executive arm to state its coming needs early. That way agencies could serve the economic defence program faster and better. Talk then returned to goods intelligence: should a lasting record of facts used in list reviews be kept? The point was left for deeper thought.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510089-3:
A summary of intelligence conclusions, dated 27 December 1955, weighs the cost of differing trade controls on Communist China. It comes from CIA's Office of Research and Reports. Tighter lists for China than for the Soviet bloc form the backdrop. First finding: goods not barred to the bloc cannot in fact be barred to China. They can simply move through bloc hands.

Costs are then counted. Extra overland freight and premium payments fall on China and the bloc alike. The bill for China is put at 37 to 43 million dollars. Added freight for the bloc runs higher still. Yet the verdict is cool: neither bill will slow the growth of China's economy in any real way. An annex counts foreign exchange losses from American controls held alone. Parts of the scan are rough, but the core sums and the verdict read clearly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050016-3:
A distribution list sends out the edited record of a propellants seminar held on 13 and 14 June 1956. The list is dated 30 April 1957. Each entry gives a name, an office, an address, and the count of copies sent. First names sit in the research world: a Battelle Memorial Institute engineering chief in Columbus, Ohio, and a propellant information agency man at a Johns Hopkins laboratory in Silver Spring, Maryland.

State Department and Air Force names follow. A guided missile intelligence officer at the Pentagon and a Bureau of Standards doctor appear. Commerce names crowd the middle: export control staff and their security officers, each with room numbers in the Main Commerce building. Defence names close the list. Parts of the scan garble some names and titles. The shape of the list, though, is plain: one copy each to the working world that made and used the seminar record.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200080004-3:
A charter pack for the defence secretary's international security staff fills the file, dated 24 June 1952. It sets out, office by office, who answers for what. A note on top gives the deputy for psychological policy a direct line to the defence voice on the Psychological Strategy Board. The first enclosure covers the Office of Military Assistance.

That office owns the building and running of aid programs under the Mutual Security Act of 1951. It is the hub for military goods and training aid inside the staff office. It also links the Pentagon to the American military voice in Europe, the Joint Chiefs, the Munitions Board, the services, and aid teams abroad. Programs it shapes go up for approval and budget action. Later enclosures treat other arms of the staff, among them work on NATO policy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200160050-3:
A status memo dated 9 December 1953 runs through open diversion cases one by one. First is a Salzburg case running back to November 1952. A report due on 20 October has never come. Vienna says it will be sent soonest. Paris has now cabled to ask when it might land. The Villach copper case follows: a full summary is on its way to Washington under separate cover.

Rome cables that Italian authorities weigh freeing the copper to its legal owner. The embassy there is moving to block that step. A Bonn to Antwerp case comes next. Diversion can safely be presumed, the memo states, yet no fresh word has come on the ship Jura. A second order of 625 tons from a Belgian works is traced through a Brussels note. Later items chase a storage site and a name that may link two cases.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200100016-3:
A letter dated 25 May 1956 from C Cabell to Percival Brundage at the Bureau of the Budget presses two atomic clearance points. A day earlier, Agency legislative counsel had sent the Bureau views on Defense plans to amend the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. One change earns strong backing here: letting Q-cleared staff swap restricted data with others cleared under section 143. That fix, Cabell writes, is urgently needed.

The letter then raises a home problem. CIA staff whose work needs restricted data must first be cleared under section 145. CIA probes its own staff before hiring, through its own arms. Its standards are as high as any, Cabell argues. Yet the law's path does not fit that fact. A second snag follows: even Q-cleared guests from another agency may not swap restricted data with section 143 holders, on one reading of the act.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300030031-3:
A personnel form describes a new post: special assistant to the Legislative Counsel. It sits in the Office of General Counsel, under job code 0975.01. The job summary opens the form. The Legislative Counsel plans, directs, and joins up the Agency's dealings with Congress and other government arms. His assistant gives skilled and admin help across all his fields of concern.

Duties are then spelled out. The holder reads the Congressional Record each day, hunting items that touch the Agency. Problems found are solved, or set on the path to solution. A joined comment is drafted for higher levels, sent up through the counsel. The post also serves as a liaison point with congressional committees. It wins data on committee work that Agency arms ask after, and fields committee queries in return. The form is a classification review paper, built to fix the post's grade.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300090017-3:
A memo dated 8 July 1958 from Lawrence Houston, General Counsel, sends guidance on home leave. Attached is counsel's reply to a staff query: how long must a home leave traveller spend inside the United States, its territories, or its possessions, as law demands? Some travellers wish to take leave on the way, at a stop outside the country. That wish can cut the home stay short.

The attached paper, dated 23 June 1956, works a live case. Rules demand at least twenty-three days of saved leave for paid home leave travel. One staffer wished to spend three weeks, fifteen working days, in the States, and about two weeks in Europe on the same trip. Counsel reads section 5a(3)(A) of the governing public law against that plan. Draft wording for the Agency rule is also offered, tying the right to two years of steady service abroad.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300150001-3:
A draft Agency rule on firing staff sits under a plain routing sheet title. Its text rests the whole scheme on two shields. Section 6 of the CIA Act of 1949 frees the Agency from laws that force it to print its staff's names, titles, pay, or numbers. Firings will thus run under the Director's grant in section 102(c) of the National Security Act of 1947.

Despite the Act of 24 August 1912 and any other law, the Director may end any worker's post when he deems it needed or wise in the nation's interest. The rule then walls off all outside tests. Its own standards alone will govern such firings. No worker may claim care under any other law or rule. No appeal lies to the Civil Service Commission.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300150010-3:
A memo dated 15 April 1959 reports one office's part in a drive for greater efficiency. It goes from the General Counsel's office to the acting deputy director for support. The office, it states, now sits at its set ceiling of twenty posts. 

Bills work will swell, the office warns, from now through the end of this Congress. Legal staff have been reading and marking bills farmed out one by one. To meet the load, one lawyer will step off pure legal work. The shift is not a full post, so his spare hours go to the office's legal history. A second shift frees the deputy counsel. Since he took the bill work on, he has less time to steer the whole office. The next senior lawyer now runs the East Building shop day to day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300200005-3:
A clearance file clears one speech on Soviet research for the open press. Counsel's note of 21 April 1959 raises no bar. The talk, on running research in the Soviet Union, was given at a national conference on research management. It may now run in the printed proceedings. No copyright claim and no pay turn on the act, counsel notes.

The security side signs off a week later. The speaker had filed the set form in March, with the text. The Denver Research Institute will print the piece. From a security view there is no bar, the personnel security chief writes, once two more clearances land: the deputy director for intelligence, and counsel. The talk's own text opens the back pages. It sketches how the USSR runs its labs. Most applied work sits in one great bloc of institutes, it says.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300210013-3:
A staff paper lays out a plan for a legal reference book of the Agency's own. Its charge is plain. Build, and keep current, a sound and trusted study of the base legal points that are CIA's alone. 

The need, the paper argues, is plain from the past. Since the Agency's birth, counsel have met each legal snag as it came up, case by case. Years of that work have piled up craft and rulings. In sum they form a body of law that bears straight on Agency work and on its ties to other shops and to Congress. None of it sits in one book. Worse, much of it lives in the heads of a few old hands. A past try shows the shape. In 1953 the office printed a study of secret funds, though its title hid how much law the text held.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400050029-3:
A file builds a rule to guard the wells of the Agency's work: its sources and methods. Houston's memo to the support chief sends a draft round. The aim, in his words, is to put the Agency in a stronger place when it must refuse to bare its stock. Court suits and Hill hearings are the ground it is built for. 

The security chief's slip, clipped to the file, adds no fresh points. The title as drawn tells the tale well, he holds. Two marks are agreed. The rule should be open in itself, not stamped secret. Yet it should bear the state-use tag, to keep its spread in hand. A Warner note rides with the draft. The text is a fresh pass on one talked through the day past. Warner owns he is not wholly pleased with the title. He asks for thoughts, and for speed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100050008-3:
A pack of house rules and lists runs the 1959 War Planners Conference from the desk side. The list runs in two parts. Part one gives the grid: hours, rooms, themes, and the man at the front for each meet from 16 to 26 March.

Part two names who sits where. Each shop's men are listed by the group they join, with seats set by count. They are no more than a guide, the pack grants. A group may swap in points of its own. A man not on a list who wants a seat must ring the desk. House notes sort the rest of life: beds, trips, cash, badges, health, and guards. A watch man keeps each room's stock safe. One stern note shuts the pack: notes a guest takes home to the field may ride the pouch in plain form only.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100080005-3:
A memo dated 31 July 1959 asks if a first-days course should live or die. The CIA Introduction is a three-hour first look at spy work and its frame. All new hands must sit it. The writer, the school's own brief man, sets out the past of the course for the school chief's call.

In its first form it bore a plainer name: the Agency Indoctrination Course. Back then it was the sole such brief most staff could get. Men from peer shops could sit in from 1955, the year a twin course for state guests split off. Three talks made the frame: the tongue of the trade; the ring of shops; and the Agency's charge, tasks, and shape. In 1957 a film on how spy work flows took one talk's place. In all, some sixteen thousand men and women have sat the course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200070010-3:
Background and proposed positions on China Committee matters, prepared for the May 1953 Consultative Group meeting, make up this briefing paper. An opening section sums up the China Committee's activity over its first six months. A fuller record from the committee secretariat was expected before the meeting, so this summary aims at broad understanding rather than fine detail.

A separate work program paper is described, setting out a plan for a major extension of the embargo lists and the stance the United States delegate should take. Later pages weigh how Far Eastern countries outside the Paris organisation might join or cooperate with it, without swelling membership so much that its work slows. The paper shows Washington preparing its case before facing allied delegates.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200110006-3:
Japanese security export controls on trade with China from 1945 to 1952 are traced in a working paper sent out on 28 January 1953 as background for current China Committee problems. The paper was prepared for officials dealing with how tightly Japan should control its China trade. Its period runs from Japan's surrender through the early occupation years.

The opening section covers export controls under the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. Washington held that trade between Japan and China, then non-communist, was vital to Japan's economic welfare. Later pages reach the point where Japan expected its control level to be debated at a conference, was told it would not be. Asked for bilateral talks instead, where it was urged to keep its existing controls in place.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000100020030-3:
Geographic support for war is planned in Annex C, dated 15 May 1959, to the Global War Plan for the DD/I area. The annex states a main mission: providing geographic intelligence, cartographic work, and measurement services if global war came. Its assumptions are those of the war plan it belongs to, and its wartime duties are then set out in order.

Support would flow to Agency action components working on national policy and strategic war planning, with weight on regional questions and broad strategy. Other duties cover area analysis and targeting studies for unconventional warfare, plus detailed support for tactical intelligence and field operations. Evacuation arrangements appear too, with mapping work to move to San Antonio, Texas, and geographic work to Fort Lee, Virginia, if the Washington plant had to be left.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200050009-3:
Reports finished by the Geography Division during March 1959 are listed in a 6 April 1959 memorandum. Each line gives a report number, project and control numbers, a title, its classification, the hours of work spent, and who asked for it. Some jobs took over a thousand man-hours, while others were short memoranda.

Titles show the range of the division's work that month. Studies cover northeast Thailand, a map and chart appraisal, Soviet satellite tracking activities in the Antarctic, and Soviet penetration into North Atlantic waters. Other entries serve the National Intelligence Survey program for Pakistan and Hungary. Requesters include the Special Warfare School at Fort Bragg, a guided missile branch, and offices across the Agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200260015-3:
April 1959 brought the Cartography Division its heaviest intake on record, its monthly report states. New requests for maps and charts totalled one hundred ninety, up sharply over March, and total workload at month's end stood at five hundred thirty-six jobs. The rise is linked to the usual build-up near the end of the fiscal year, stronger this year than in past years.

Overtime reached two hundred forty-seven man-hours in April, most of it planned to stay capped in the month ahead. Much effort went to support of operational work for the plans directorate, spread over three major projects. Technical notes describe work on a substitute for large, bulky light tables used in compilation, where a glowing panel design had reached a stage needing outside skill to perfect.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000100070017-3:
Results of an Inspector General survey of the Office of Central Reference are sent to the Director of Central Intelligence on 25 April 1956. The covering memorandum is signed by Lyman B. Kirkpatrick, the Inspector General. In general, the survey found the Agency's central reference system, run by that office for the intelligence directorate, efficient and effective.

Responses reached the research offices of the Agency and other parts of the United States intelligence community in good time, the survey reports. Major problems and minor flaws were still found, and the report proposes specific fixes for the Director's approval. A draft letter to the deputy director for intelligence is attached, asking for his comments on the report by 15 June 1956.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000500040025-3:
Origins and conduct of the Agency's Reserve Officer Training Program are examined in a study drawn from an Inspector General survey. Before 1949, Agency staff who held reserve commissions took part on an individual basis. Within the Second Army area alone, one hundred thirty-eight Agency employees with Army Reserve commissions were scattered among nineteen different reserve organisations.

Senior officials who held commissions themselves saw the risk: in a general mobilisation, these citizen soldiers might be pulled away from the Agency. Deals with the Army and Air Force created reserve units for staff with a mobilisation assignment to the Agency. The Korean War sped recruitment. The study lists the program's aims, from a smooth shift from peacetime to wartime roles to training as one unit so teamwork and mutual confidence could grow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200030025-3:
Joint running of Project OILSTONE by the Agency and the Air Force is organised in a paper dated 29 July 1955 on organisation and the division of duties. At the top, the Director of Central Intelligence and the Air Force Chief of Staff share the making of broad policy. They weigh what the project's operations mean for national and world policy and settle disputes passed up from below.

Project directors on each side direct work inside their own organisations, exchange information freely, and report progress upward. The paper then assigns duties element by element, from the joint project headquarters downward. Work is phased, with an early phase under the project director's control covering planning and recruiting, and a final phase of active operations from overseas bases once readiness is declared.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200040015-3:
Legal ground for the Agency buying goods and services for the Air Force and Navy under Project AQUATONE is set out in a 16 July 1957 memorandum. The Agency had been acting as procurement agent for both services for material developed under the project. Before taking that role on, it weighed the legal basis carefully with the Air Force general counsel and fiscal officials.

Two legal authorities are offered as sound footing, the first being a section of federal law that lets one executive department procure for another. A second memorandum in the file, dated 25 October 1957 and sent to the Director of Central Intelligence, records that the deputy director had reviewed the legal views and concurred in them. The file shows secret buying being fitted, clause by clause, inside ordinary government law.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200080011-3:
Five special projects hidden inside a financing memorandum are identified for the Director of Central Intelligence in a 13 August 1958 paper. The financing paper had named no tasks, because the projects were so sensitive and its recommendations might circulate to unwitting readers. This companion paper supplies the identities under tight control.

CHALICE is named first: it is Project AQUATONE under a new name. Its work covers the two overseas detachments, the home base at Edwards Air Force Base, most of the Development Projects Staff, and the thirteen U-2 aircraft still in Agency hands. A later project covers a satellite program: launching reconnaissance satellites that would photograph the Soviet bloc during overflight, store the film in a capsule. Drop it over a chosen ocean area for recovery.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200110107-3:
Field findings from visits to two overseas detachments fill memorandum DPS-4135, dated 11 September 1958. Dr. R. Scott and the writer spent 12 to 15 August at Detachment B and 21 to 29 August at Detachment C. Scott's own report would cover quality control, tracker and drift sight problems, and judging of camera configurations, while this paper gives the writer's parallel observations.

Quality control at Detachment B draws sharp words. Much detail was being lost while mission film was processed, blamed on high and uneven solution temperatures, uneven processing speeds, and thin technical know-how among some machine operators. Maintenance records draw fire too: test breakdowns often went unrecorded, and serviced parts came back with a blanket stamp instead of itemised records, until the maker, Hycon, clarified expected shutter life.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100050042-3: A declassified CIA file marked Requirements. The needs. The document holds the marking. The file remains. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100050114-3:
Further information is requested from a source who worked from January 1957 at Aircraft Engine Plant No. 45 in Moscow. The paper, dated 13 January 1959 in the file, states that the source appears to hold information indicating the plant produced some article for guided missiles. Finished articles were reportedly shipped to another plant, possibly Plant No. 456 at Khimki.

Questions put to the source are exacting. What technical aviation school in Moscow did he attend, and where does it stand? Does he know others who attended it or worked at either plant? On what authority does he claim that Plant No. 45 made parts for guided missiles, and did he actually see or work on them? Precisely which missile parts were made, with drawings, and a layout sketch of Plant No. 45 showing where each kind of work was done, are also requested.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100060041-3:
Costing the Soviet military effort is the purpose of a general requirement paper on military economic information. The desired information covers the field of military economics. Its use is to work out what Soviet military programs and activities cost, and to measure their impact on the Soviet economy and on single sectors of it.

A stated goal is to be able to cost alternative Soviet military programs against their military aims, so that the economic feasibility of undertaking or continuing a program becomes visible. The basic approach takes each program or activity in as much detail as the data allow. One section that follows deals with manpower: how the Soviet armed forces draw conscripts, how long they serve, and how pay is set by class and rank.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120071-3:
General comments on a draft study of Soviet machine building begin with iron ore. Supplies of iron ore have been short of late. Yet the growth of machine building has not been much affected. Gross output rose by about fourteen per cent a year through the 1950s. Shortages of some metal types and shapes are blamed in the main on poor timing. The timing of making and of shipping was at fault.

The comments warn of a gap in the draft. It does not always make clear one point. Does new capacity mean net gains, or gross gains? A further route to growth should be named. Capacity can be raised by swapping old gear for new. That path needs no big building work. Since 1955, worn gear had been swapped out even before it was fully written off.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100150069-3: A solicited requirement in the Agency's files, its scan badly garbled, asks for information on Czechoslovakia and the Soviet Union bearing on guided missiles. Legible passages report sites near Prague: one on the road leading north into the city, and a Soviet-restricted area. Another item places military installations on the Vltava River. The paper also asks whether Czechoslovakia is producing missile fuels. Most lines cannot be read with confidence, so this rests only on the passages that survive clearly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00346a000100050018-3:
Views of the Intelligence Advisory Committee's ad hoc committee on exchanges are sent to the State Department on 27 September 1957. The subject is a Soviet proposal for long-term exchanges of three to six months in stated fields. The committee weighs gain to the United States against gain to the Soviet Union, counting the technological gain on the Soviet side, using terms set in a February 1956 paper.

Longer stays change the balance, so the paper first judges the general effect of a three-to-six-month basis against the four-to-six-week exchanges run before. It then takes the suggested fields one by one. Assessments rest only on what each side could gain by overt observation; the covert side was being judged separately by the Director of Central Intelligence. One industrial exchange is judged a substantial net advantage to the United States on a two-month opening basis.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090013-3:
Additional material for the Director's testimony before the Joint Economic Committee's subcommittee on economic statistics is forwarded on 4 November 1959. One copy and a carbon of material on Soviet economic penetration are enclosed, for possible inclusion in the testimony to be given to the subcommittee.

The material argues that the challenge of Soviet economic growth is not confined to statistics, and that the Soviets are not passively letting internal achievements speak for themselves. Over the past five years the whole Sino-Soviet bloc has cultivated economic contacts with the underdeveloped countries, taking every opportunity offered and creating more. The weapons of this economic offensive are named as trade, credits, and grants. Offers of steel mills, oil prospecting parties, refineries, machine tools, and pharmaceutical chemicals are listed. The bloc is said to have extended more than three billion dollars in military and economic aid since 1954.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090022-3:
The Soviet challenge is the theme of an address by Allen W. Dulles to the National Association of Manufacturers. He spoke in New York on 4 December 1959, to the group's Congress of American Industry. Twelve years earlier, on 3 December 1947, he had addressed the same congress on the same subject. The challenge, he said then, was to prove that the system of free men under law can survive.

That is still the challenge, he says. Weeks before, Khrushchev had amiably advised Americans, as he left the United States, that Communism would in time take them over. In 1947 the Soviets had based their hopes on a forecast of collapse of free enterprise. Stalin, Molotov, and Vishinsky had dismissed the Marshall Plan as a device to unload excess goods and capital. The old leaders and their arguments are gone, the address goes on, but the objectives remain.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090040-3:
William J. Donovan and national security are the subject of an address by Allen W. Dulles to the Erie County Bar Association at Buffalo, 4 May 1959. Dulles had known Donovan as a lawyer, then served under him in the Office of Strategic Services in the Second World War, and recalls his courage warmly.

The early career of Buffalo's son is retraced: born in the First Ward on New Year's Day 1883, schooled at St. Joseph's Institute and Niagara University. At Columbia he took his arts degree in 1905 and his law degree in 1907, and starred as a football quarterback, before returning to Buffalo in 1907 to practise law. The war years follow. Inside wartime information work there was a split. The Office of War Information told the enemy the magnitude of the American war effort. One branch of the Office of Strategic Services worked to confuse the enemy and break their will to resist.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090059-3:
Cold War Problems — Economic Penetration is a declassified Agency study dated 25 September 1958. It asks six set questions about Bloc trade and aid. They cover Bloc capacity, motives, and organization. They also cover data sources, arms deals, and the effect of Western trade controls.

Seven sections answer those questions in turn. One weighs how far Agency figures on Bloc aid can be trusted. It judges trade totals sound within a small margin, while aid delivery figures rest on firmer ground only at the lowest amounts. Arms sales to free world buyers get a section of their own, as do the limits of export controls.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090121-3:
Communist Economic Penetration is a declassified Agency outline on Soviet trade and aid under Khrushchev, in rough scanned type. It calls peaceful competition, built on trade and development aid, the newer and subtler Soviet line. The goals of world Communism, it states, had not changed.

Figures carry much of the case. Soviet trade with poorer areas had risen 500 percent since 1954, while trade with the West had more than doubled. Soviet exports in 1957 are put at about four billion dollars, against 18 billion for the United States. Aid is described as chiefly political in motive, and Bloc programs are broken into credit, training, and trade parts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100011-3:
Presentation to PRC on ERA FY '60 Research Program is a declassified Agency paper that lays out a year of economic research work. It states that the Cold War was being fought more and more in the economic field. The office held the major share of analysts in the government who worked on the Sino-Soviet Bloc.

Part of the program answers direct demands from users of intelligence. The rest, about 30 percent of the man-hours, came from the office's own choice. Those studies aimed to sharpen future national estimates, with work on Soviet output and industrial growth near completion. A project on Bloc gold reserves shows the forward look the office prized.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100020010-3:
Comments dated 1 April 1955 in declassified Agency files review a planned outline for a study of economic defense problems. The writer calls the outline of vital importance and asks for careful treatment. The study was to rest on security needs and to link with international controls acceptable to COCOM nations.

Much of the comment weighs how to measure what a cut in Bloc imports would do. Ruble-dollar ratios are named as one gauge of relative production costs. The writer warns that the work would be slow and might end without a firm result, given thin and doubtful data. Parts of the outline itself are called illogical and at odds with themselves.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100110001-3:
Use of Inducements or Pressures on Free World Countries in Support of the U.S. Economic Defense Program is Staff Study No. 11 of the CFEP Drafting Group, revised June 7, 1955. It catalogs the tools the United States could use to win allied backing for trade controls on the Bloc. A check list of methods fills an appendix.

Worked cases show the tools in action. An American technical advisory group in the Helmand Valley of Afghanistan helped with farm work, health, and training under a development program. School and demonstration farms backed that effort. Stockpile buying from allied nations is given as one more lever the United States could pull. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100200001-3:
Political Impact of Free World Controls on Trade with the Sino-Soviet Bloc is Staff Study No. 20 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 17, 1955, contributed by the Defense Department. It asks what free world trade controls do to each side in political and strategic terms. Conclusions lead the study.

The core finding favors controls. Free world controls are judged to impose a greater strategic cost on the Sino-Soviet Bloc than on the free world itself. Raising the level of controls would raise that relative cost, and a total embargo would impose the highest possible cost. The system as built, the study notes, rested mainly on selectivity rather than a full ban. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000200060006-3:
Strategic Materials Transiting Yugoslavia to the Bloc is a declassified Agency case paper on goods routed through Yugoslavia. It sets its limits first: goods of Yugoslav origin and deals that never touch Yugoslav soil are left out. The base source is a Belgrade Embassy summary, D-733 of 29 April 1954.

That summary judges Yugoslav controls sound on paper if properly used. The real problem lay in re-export and switch trading by a few Yugoslav firms, using goods that began in other nations. Cases follow, among them locomotives and electrical gear from Liverpool meant for Hungary via Rijeka. Goods from two United States firms, marked for a single name, appear in a second case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000200100029-3:
DCP Case Summaries, filed as Enclosure 2 under number CA-2276, collect short accounts of suspected diversions of strategic goods. Case 368 covers metal working machines and diamond drills. Five boring tools and eight hollow drills of West German make, valued at 2,330 dollars, were said to have been diverted to Communist China at Rotterdam.

Case 369 takes up bearings across several nations. A later case follows Chilean copper sold to a Dutch metals broker. Informants suspected that part of it reached the Bloc: 5,250 tons were set for delivery from August to December 1955. Shipments of 1,500 tons in May 1955 are listed with dates and vessel names. The summaries survive in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100030037-3:
A memorandum dated 31 July 1959 sends a proposed contingency force training program to the Director of Training. A meeting on 16 July 1959 had agreed that manpower study proposals go to the training office for study and a recommendation. Tab A is sent for information, and Tab B for action.

Tab A sketches the range of operational specialists a ready force might need. The range is drawn from the Limited Warfare concept paper. Set job titles carry their own descriptions of duties and tests for each post. The training part of the proposal then takes up timing and frequency: how soon such a program could start, and how often it should run. The memorandum survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200010010-3:
CIA Presentations at Senior War Colleges is a declassified Agency memorandum that tracks a 1960 effort step by step. At a February meeting, Mr. Matthew Baird proposed set orientation lectures at the senior war colleges. The lectures would state, with authority, what the Agency is and does.

The Defense Department carried the idea forward in a March memo to service leaders. Replies were mixed. The National War College and the Armed Forces Staff College judged their coverage of the Agency already sound. The Industrial College, by contrast, wanted more. A July date was set for talks before the combined faculties of the Air University, with Lyman Kirkpatrick among the speakers.
cicero-letters-shuckburgh-vol-3:
Civil war between Caesar and Pompey fills the third volume of Cicero's letters, in Shuckburgh's 1899 version. The great orator is caught between two giants. He writes in anguish to friends as Rome tears itself apart.

Each letter weighs flight, loyalty, safety, and shame anew. Cicero's brilliance and worry stand bare on every page. He knows the Republic he loves is dying either way. The volume gives history in its raw state. Outcomes have not yet hardened into fate, and a gifted man tries, letter by letter, to keep his honor intact. Few sources let a reader watch a republic die so closely.
cinq-mars-volume-3:
Alfred de Vigny drives his hero toward conspiracy in Cinq-Mars, Volume 3 of the English edition. Henri de Cinq-Mars, favorite of Louis XIII, now sickens of favor bought by submission to Richelieu. He sits weary, turning over combinations of events he desires and dreads. De Vigny pauses the plot to study a restless mind.

Court life at Paris and the Louvre presses in as the cardinal's spies multiply. Cinq-Mars calculates chances, measures himself against men of history, and finds his path wanting. Marie de Gonzague, the princess he loves, stays barred to a subject who serves two masters. Friends urge caution while recruiters for revolt test his pride in secret. The Spanish party, France's enemy, waits at the edge of the intrigue. Readers mid-novel feel the trap being built, board by board, out of honor, love, and the wish to strike one blow for France.
clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-a-you:
Clarissa Harlowe — Volume 3 of Richardson's novel in letters turns on Clarissa's removal from her father's house. The detailed contents are blunt: she was terrified out of her fixed resolution and tricked away. Her grief and compunction on waking to the fact fill her letters to Miss Howe.

Lovelace's own letters lay open his contrivance. One to his agent Joseph Leman shows the whole scheme, and one to Belford exults in its success. Clarissa lodges meanwhile with her sister Sorlings, attended by Mrs. Greme, Lord M.'s housekeeper. She writes to her sister for her clothes. Blame, in her own account, falls first on her early correspondence with Lovelace against her father's ban.
conscience-volume-3:
A sister pleads for her brother in Conscience, Volume 3, the third English portion of Hector Malot's French novel of 1893. Phillis comes to Saniel, now a successful Paris doctor, because her brother Florentin stands accused and needs a great man's help. Saniel's past has made him careful of other people's ruin. The request forces the murderer to weigh a stranger's innocence against his own safety.

Inside, a paralyzed widow appears who witnessed an assassination and cannot speak what she saw. Malot builds the volume on blocked testimony: truth present in the room, unable to reach the court. Saniel treats patients, builds his practice, and argues with the conscience he thought he had buried with Caffie. Every success raises the price of confession higher. Readers in the third volume feel the net drawn by other hands than the police, as the people Saniel helps become the people who can destroy him.
cosmopolis-volume-3:
Paul Bourget deepens his Roman society study in Cosmopolis, Volume 3 of the English edition. The set now knows each other's secrets too well for safe flirtation. Marquis de Montfanon still argues faith against the age with laughter in his blue eyes. His scarred face hides a fanatic's zeal under genial manners.

Salon talk turns sharper as love affairs cross lines of nation, class, and belief. A vanquished Catholic and discontented socialists discover hatreds they hold in common. Bourget follows motives down into childhood, family pride, and wounded vanity. Rome's churches and ruins stand behind the intrigue as a standing rebuke. Duels of honor hang over the young men. Readers in the third volume watch the design tighten. A whole city of drifting modern souls appears here. Each soul feels sure the others are the lost ones. Faith waits at the edge of every conversation.
curtius-history-greece-vol-3:
Persia invades in the third volume of Curtius's History of Greece, in Ward's 1868 version. Marathon, Thermopylae, and Salamis form its blazing core. Small Greek cities face the might of the Persian Empire and win.

Curtius tells the heroic age with a scholar's care and a poet's pulse. Leonidas falls, Themistocles schemes, and free men outfight a host. The stakes, he insists, were the future of the West itself. Readers get the full sweep of the wars that saved Greek freedom. A master tells the tale, one who knew the ground and the sources well. His love for Greece glows on every page of the wars.
dialogues-of-the-buddha-vol-3:
The third volume of the Dialogues of the Buddha, from 1921, completes the Rhys Davids translation of the Digha Nikaya. T. W. Rhys Davids died the next year; his wife Caroline carried the Pali Text Society's work onward. The final long discourses of the collection stand here.

Late suttas take up the marks of a great man, the chanting of the teaching in council, and the Buddha's instructions for the order after his death. One discourse lists the points of doctrine in numbered sets, built for memory and recital. Read across three volumes, the Digha gives the fullest picture of the Buddha as a teacher among rivals. The set remains a standard English Nikaya.
dialstone-lane-part-3:
Chapters nine to thirteen of W. W. Jacobs's novel fill this third part of Dialstone Lane. Mr Vickers comes home from a stroll with Mr William Russell and a couple of ferrets, as the church bells ring for morning service. Breakfast is gone but for a cold herring and the dregs of a tea pot.

A strange squeaking overhead puzzles him, like several pairs of new boots at once. It is new boots, worn by Charles, and the household turns upside down. Captain Brisket, caught out, tries to finish a hard word with a cough before Mr Chalk. Asked how he knows a certain lady, he says it is because she cannot whistle. This file holds part three only.
diana-of-the-crossways-volume-3:
The third volume of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways spans chapters eighteen to twenty-six. Diana appears as the authoress, earning her living by her pen in London. Drives in sunlight and moonlight carry her between city and country friends. She keeps a night-watch in the chamber of death beside Emma's household.

The young minister of state, Percy Dacier, becomes her intimate counsellee and secret love. Once more the crossways, and a change of turnings, warns of a fateful choice. A disappointed lover receives a multitude of lessons in her drawing room. Meredith builds the volume from visits, letters, and talk. Diana's influence over a statesman feeds the scandal that will accuse her of selling secrets, the charge toward which everything moves.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-3:
With books thirty-six through forty, the Roman History of Dio Cassius starts to survive in full, not just in scraps. Earnest Cary's Loeb translation fills this third volume. Dio wrote around 230 CE, and from here his story of the late republic runs without large gaps.

Pompey rises on his eastern victories, and Catiline plots against the state. Caesar then marches through Gaul while the senate and the great men pull Rome toward civil war. Dio tells these years with a senator's eye for power and pride. The volume lands the reader at the edge of the war that ended the republic.
dionysius-halicarnassus-roman-antiquitie:
Edward Spelman's 1758 translation of Dionysius of Halicarnassus reaches books six through eight in this third volume. The Roman Antiquities, written around 7 BCE, now covers the hard early years of the republic. Debt, hunger, and pride set the orders of Rome at odds.

The struggle of the orders fills these books: plebeians walk out of the city, tribunes rise to guard them, and war with the Volscians presses from outside. Coriolanus, exiled and turned enemy, marches on Rome and is turned back by his mother. Dionysius gives the fullest surviving tale of these fights. His speeches show how Greeks of his age read Roman virtue.
donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-egypt-v:
Donovan Pasha and Some People of Egypt, Volume 3, by Gilbert Parker, holds two tales of British officers in Egypt. Parker opens The Man at the Wheel with a verdict on Wyndham Bimbashi. His career, we are told, was a series of mistakes. He was opinionated. He had no luck. Worst of all, he did grave things on his own responsibility. He also held the native mind in supreme contempt.

Riots followed his high handed actions. Villagers attacked him between the sugar cane fields. His bravery was never in doubt. His tact was another matter. The climax comes in an unauthorized sortie against an Arab tribe he had offended. A Tyrant and a Lady completes the volume. Parker's Egypt keeps one lesson ready. In a country ruled by foreigners, character is administration, and a fool with power makes enemies wholesale.
droll-stories-volume-3:
Honoré de Balzac's third volume of Droll Stories delivers the third ten tales from the abbeys of Touraine. Balzac's prologue boasts that virtuous ladies read his bawdy book in secret and defends its mirth as a public benefit. The tales include Perseverance in Love, Bertha the Penitent, the monk Amador who became a glorious abbot, and the Fair Imperia married at last.

Provosts who fail to recognize things, pretty maids who convince judges, and three pilgrims' odd sayings fill out the ten. The mock-chronicle language, the clerical settings, and the twist endings match the earlier volumes. Balzac planned a hundred of these tales in the manner of Boccaccio and Rabelais; the thirty gathered across three volumes are the surviving monument.
embers-volume-3:
Embers, Volume 3, by Gilbert Parker, gathers the later songs of his verse collection. Parker opens in London with In Camden Town. The poem counts the years of sun and snow that have passed over Camden Town. Jean and A Memory follow. Then the ground shifts to Canada. In Camp at Juniper Cove and Juniper Cove Twenty Years After make a pair, the same shore at two ages of a life.

Listening, Nevertheless, and Ishmael keep the reflective key. An Arab Love Song and The Camel-Driver to His Camel recall Parker's Egypt. A Son of the Nile and A Farewell from the Harem stand near them. The Australian Stockrider and The Bridge of the Hundred Spans close the volume's travels. Parker's embers are banked fires: old places, old faiths, and old loves, still warm enough to sing over.
ethics-part-3:
Benedict de Spinoza turns in part three of his Ethics, in Elwes's translation, to the origin and nature of the emotions. He complains that earlier writers treated man as a kingdom within a kingdom, disturbing nature's order instead of following it. Spinoza instead studies feelings as natural phenomena with definite causes, like lines and planes.

Love, hatred, envy, ambition, and the rest are derived from three primary affects: desire, pleasure, and pain. The ambitious man who desires glory and fears shame, and the envious man delighted by another's misfortune, illustrate the system in the middle propositions. This psychology, built without moral scolding, prepares his account of human bondage and the freedom reason can win.
euclid-elements-heath-vol-3:
Heath's third Euclid volume covers Books Ten through Thirteen, completing the Elements. The 1908 edition closes with geometry's most demanding ancient material. Book Ten alone classifies irrational lengths at enormous length.

That classification was antiquity's hardest mathematics, filling a quarter of the whole work. Books Eleven through Thirteen turn to solid geometry and its figures. The five Platonic solids close the Elements in a famous finale. Euclid proves that exactly five regular solids can exist. Geometry here climbs into philosophy's own country, as Plato had hoped. Heath's notes guide readers through the densest proofs with patience.
euripides-plays-way-loeb-1912-vol-3:
Way's third Loeb volume of Euripides, first printed in 1912, holds the Bacchanals, the Madness of Hercules, the Children of Hercules, the Phoenician Maidens, and the Suppliants. The scan staged here is a 1930 reprint of the edition. The Bacchae, often ranked Euripides' greatest play, stands first here.

In it the god Dionysus returns to Thebes and drives its king to a gruesome death. Hercules, struck mad by Hera, kills his own wife and children in his hall. The remaining plays plead for Athens as protector of the weak and the dead. Way's complete verse set lets readers follow Euripides' darkening view of gods and war. No other English Euripides of the age attempted all nineteen plays.
evan-harrington-volume-3:
The third volume of George Meredith's Evan Harrington spans chapters fourteen to eighteen. The Countess de Saldar describes her field of action in a long, brilliant letter. She has seen her brother Evan pointed out as the tailor-fellow, yet fights on. Her star, she insists, will win him an heiress.

A capture and a small skirmish between Rose and Evan sharpen the love plot. Evan, pressed by debt and honour, writes himself tailor in a fatal document. In the next chapter he calls himself gentleman and rejects the shame. Meredith builds these chapters on letters and confrontations. The volume's heart is Evan's war with himself, torn between the shears of his father's shop and the drawing rooms his sisters covet for him.
eve-s-diary-part-3:
Twain's Eve's Diary, Part 3 shifts to an extract from Adam's diary. Mark Twain lets Adam answer Eve's bright, restless voice. Adam asks for patience, since Eve is young and new to the world. Her delight in each flower and color both charms and tires him.

Adam lists her loves: rocks, sand, moss, sky, dawn, and sunset seas. None has practical value, he notes, yet color alone enthralls her. He admits she is beautiful, recalling her on a sunlit boulder watching a bird. A Monday noon entry shows her taking to every animal without reserve. A brontosaurus in camp reads to her as gain and to him as calamity.
falkland-book-3:
Lytton's Falkland, Book 3 is told through Lady Emily Mandeville's journal. Edward Bulwer-Lytton shifts the early novel into her private voice here. Her friend Julia visits, and tears confess what words cannot. No letter from Falkland for days leaves Emily in dread.

A note then arrives: he has come back, dangerously near. She has seen him, and the moment atones for all suffering, she writes. He urged her to fly with him, mixing happiness with guilt. She feels the sophistry of his arguments yet cannot resist them. A dinner and ball at the Mandevilles' will force a meeting. The journal form shows a conscience arguing with a spellbound heart. Days are dated Friday through Monday.
following-the-equator-a-journey-around-t:
Australia fills Following the Equator, Part 3, by Mark Twain, in diary form with a dinner table anecdote. Twain opens Chapter XX with a calendar maxim praising free speech and free conscience, paired with the prudence never to practice either one. Then a visitor, Mr G, recalls meeting Twain years before at Nauheim in Germany, when cholera had broken out at Hamburg and everyone was hurrying for trains.

The talk turns to an earl and a remarkable Californian the earl had met, and to a small surprise in how Twain greeted his lordship. It is a fair sample of this book's method: a shipboard or hotel conversation unfolds, a character emerges in three exchanges, and a continent gets judged by the company it keeps. Part 3 covers the Australian colonies in that diary form, mixing public questions with private comedy.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-3:
Conquest turns brutal in the third volume of Freeman's History, from 1867, covering the years 1066 to 1070. William subdues the north in the harrying, a winter of fire and famine. Castles rise to lock down a sullen, broken land.

Freeman spares nothing in telling conquest as catastrophe. Rebellions flare and are crushed with methodical cruelty. His thoroughness as a scholar matches his passion as a partisan. The volume shows what invasion really cost ordinary folk. Pageants of kings often skip that side of 1066. It is the darkest book of his great set, and among the most powerful.
fromont-and-risler-volume-3:
Alphonse Daudet spends his factory capital in Fromont and Risler, Volume 3 of the English edition. Sidonie Risler reigns over balls and bills that the house of Fromont absorbs. Her husband dreams of profits while cashier Sigismond keeps the true accounts in silence. Frantz Risler, the brother who loved Sidonie first, suffers at the edge of the household.

Claire Fromont watches her playmate's caprices cool into calculation. Georges Fromont, partner and lover in one, lets the business drift toward crisis. Daudet alternates ballroom shimmer with counting-house dread in this volume. Thefts of money and truth grow harder to hide from clerks and kin. Risler's trust, the firm's real capital, is spent by everyone but him. Readers in the third volume see the end approaching: the honest man's house filling with gaiety, debt, and a brother's despair.
froude-english-ireland-vol-3:
Rebellion and Union close Froude's Irish history in this third volume, from 1872. Wolfe Tone's rising of 1798 fails in blood and reprisal. The Act of Union then folds Ireland's parliament into Westminster's for good.

Froude calls these years the tragic end of Ireland's darkest century. French fleets, pike charges, and scaffold speeches crowd his climax. His account was controversial then and remains so now. Few histories of the period match its narrative power, whatever readers make of its verdicts. The volume completes a trilogy that still shapes debate on England's rule in Ireland today. Its force explains why Irish readers still argue with it fiercely.
froude-history-england-vol-3:
Later Henrician years fill the third volume of Froude's History, in the 1870 printing. Thomas Cromwell falls from power and goes to his death. The king's six wives meet their varied, often tragic fates as his rule hardens into tyranny.

Froude does not flinch from his hero's dark side in this book. Executions, forced oaths, and fear mark the court he describes. Yet he still defends the Reformation as a needful break with Rome. The volume shows Tudor power at its most ruthless, and it tests the reader's sympathy for both the king and the cause he served.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-3:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 16, 1945, record the Allied military chiefs' afternoon session at Potsdam. The top secret record is an unnumbered item following document 710 in volume two. Much of it turns on the wording of surrender terms for Japan.

After approving the conference program paper, the chiefs took up an estimate of the enemy situation. Sir Alan Brooke pointed to a line in it touching the survival of Japan's imperial institution. He asked if the U.S. chiefs had weighed how to interpret unconditional surrender for the Japanese. From a military view, he argued, explaining the term could shorten the war in outlying areas. If the throne survived, the Emperor could order far-flung garrisons to cease fire. If the dynasty were destroyed, those garrisons might fight on for months or years.
gao-gaoreports-b-290452-3:
In companion files B-290452.3 through B-290452.5, dated May 23, 2005, GAO ruled on protests by VSE Corporation and Johnson Controls World Services, Inc. The target was a sole-source bridge contract for seized property services, awarded to EG&G Technical Services, Inc. The buyer was Customs and Border Protection. GAO sustained VSE's protest and dismissed the Johnson Controls protest. The agency had made the sole-source award with no justification and approval on file. It had also failed to plan the purchase in a sound way ahead of time.

A first digest point sets a filing rule: a protest of a planned sole-source award must come within 10 days of the notice on FedBizOpps.
gao-gaoreports-b-293925-3:
Poly-Pacific Technologies, Inc., is the protester in GAO decision B-293925.3, dated May 16, 2005. The firm challenged an Air Force award to U.S. Technology Corporation. The contract covered leasing and recycling of abrasive blast media. GAO denied the protest. The agency had fairly judged that the winner's product met the terms of the solicitation. The protester's rival reading of those terms was not a fair one.

At most, the digest says, the protester's reading showed a patent ambiguity in the document. Such a flaw must be protested before award, not after. The solicitation had been a total small business set-aside.
gao-gaoreports-b-294420-3:
Envirosolve's bid for its protest costs is the matter of GAO file B-294420.3, dated February 17, 2005. The Drug Enforcement Administration had sought bids for disposal of hazardous waste seized at clandestine drug laboratories. Envirosolve protested its exclusion from the competitive range. The agency then cancelled the solicitation soon after a supplemental protest was filed. GAO denied the costs. The first protest, it held, was not clearly meritorious.

That finding closed the door under the cost rules. A quick cancellation by the agency does not, on its own, prove that a protest was well founded when it was brought.
gao-gaoreports-b-294572-3:
In GAO files B-294572.3 and B-294572.4, dated October 20, 2005, a protest by Spherix, Inc., is sustained. The Forest Service had awarded ReserveAmerica NY, Inc., the contract for the National Recreation Reservation Service. GAO found that several key points said to justify the award on a cost and technical tradeoff lacked a sound basis. It also found that the agency had misled Spherix on a basic point of compliance. The winner had been praised for offering an alternate start-up plan that broke the stated terms. Spherix had been told the stated plan was required.

This was the second round of the same fight. GAO had sustained Spherix's protest of an earlier award under the same solicitation.
gao-gaoreports-b-294777-3:
Patriot Contract Services is the subject of an advisory opinion in GAO file B-294777.3, dated May 11, 2005. The Navy had awarded American Overseas Marine Corporation a contract to run nine large roll-on and roll-off cargo ships for the military. The solicitation required letters of commitment for key staff. Those letters had to reflect agreed position, salary, and benefits. The record showed that the winner had not in fact discussed salary, benefits, or work location with some of the staff it proposed. On that ground GAO found the protest meritorious.

Because the case came as an advisory opinion, the finding guides the forum that asked for it rather than binding the parties.
gao-gaoreports-b-294867-3:
Manassas Travel, Inc., protested an Army travel contract in GAO file B-294867.3, dated May 3, 2005. The Army had awarded Alexander Travel Ltd. one of six contracts for official travel management. The deals ran two years, with three one-year options. Manassas offered a lower price but drew a weaker risk rating. GAO denied the protest. The award rested fairly on the winner's higher rating under the most heavily weighted technical factor. Named strengths in the record backed that rating.

At a hearing, the agency gave a credible account of those strengths. It matched the written record made at the time. That match let the award stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-294986-3:
Knoll, Inc., and Steelcase, Inc., are the protesters in GAO files B-294986.3 and B-294986.4, dated March 18, 2005. The Air Force had awarded Trade Products Corporation its Total Office Package and Relocation Effort contract. Both furniture makers attacked the scoring of the technical offers. Knoll added a claim about the winner's current schedule contract term. GAO denied the protests. The digest states the ground in one sentence: the record showed that the agency's evaluation was reasonable.

Furniture and office moves may sound minor beside weapons work. The same rules of fair scoring applied, and the same deference to a sound record.
gao-gaoreports-b-295352-3:
Requests by the Department of State and Wackenhut International, Inc., are decided in GAO files B-295352.3 and B-295352.4, dated April 19, 2005. Both sought a second look at a ruling that had sustained Inter-Con Security Systems' protest. The contract covered guard services at the embassy in Abidjan, Ivory Coast. GAO denied the requests for reconsideration. The preference for U.S. persons had been applied without the data the rules required, and nothing showed the agency had that data in time.

The agency's fallback plea fared better. GAO granted a change to its remedy, which had ordered the contract ended at once. Security needs at the embassy and changed needs drove the softer course.
gao-gaoreports-b-295455-3:
In GAO ruling B-295455.3 and B-295455.4, dated August 10, 2005, OTI America, Inc., was the protester. The Government Printing Office was running a limited contest among firms holding parallel contracts for electronic passport book covers. The State Department worked with the printing office on the program. OTI was cut from the contest. GAO denied the protest. A first point confirms that GAO may hear such a case, since the use of options here ran a limited competition.

On the merits, the covers OTI delivered for testing failed material contract terms. That failure gave the agency a sound basis to drop the firm.
gao-gaoreports-b-295496-3:
Poly-Pacific Technologies Inc. returns in GAO file B-295496.3, dated January 18, 2006. The National Guard Bureau had awarded Opti-Blast Inc. a contract for plastic and glass media used to strip paint from Army vehicles, plus recycling of the used media. Poly-Pacific attacked the scoring of the winner's past performance. GAO denied the protest. The digest is one sentence: the agency fairly judged that the contracts cited in the winner's offer were relevant to the work.

Relevance is the hinge of past performance scoring. Work of like kind and scale counts; the agency's call on that point gets deference where the record supports it.
gao-gaoreports-b-296194-3:
TMC Design protested its cut from an Army contest for a jammer system in GAO decision B-296194.3, dated August 10, 2005. The system blocks radio signals that set off roadside bombs. Its name is the CREW System. The firm was cut before field tests of its gear.

GAO denied the protest. The written bid had flaws that field tests could not cure. GAO found that view sound on the record. A bid with deep flaws on paper can be cut early. It need not go to field tests first. The case helps firms see why the written bid must stand on its own.
gao-gaoreports-b-296358-3:
DOR Biodefense and Emergent BioSolutions protested a change to a vaccine deal in GAO decision B-296358.3, dated January 31, 2006. The holder was DynPort Vaccine Company. The work was research on a botulinum vaccine. The Army made the change. The firms said it went past the scope of the first deal.

GAO denied the protests. The change did not shift the type of work in a large way. Cost and time also stayed in the range firms could have seen at first. That kept the change in scope. A change in scope must be large and stark to force a fresh contest. That bar was not met here.
gao-gaoreports-b-296490-3:
Johnson Controls again protested the Treasury guard systems award in GAO decision B-296490.3, dated March 23, 2007. The winner was again Quanta Systems. The site was the currency plant in Washington. This round hit past work marks and staff claims. The agency had missed a key fact on past work.

GAO sustained the protest. The call required past work review. The agency knew how the winner, as the old holder, had done. It failed to weigh that known record. A staff edge claimed for the winner was also weak. The record did not show the agency weighed the firm's own staff plan, which cut the claimed edge.
gao-gaoreports-b-296511-3:
Triad Logistics protested an Air Force award for transient support work in GAO decision B-296511.3, dated October 20, 2005. The winner was M1 Support Services. The site was Mountain Home Air Force Base in Idaho. The buy was set aside for firms owned by disabled veterans. The firm hit past work marks.

GAO denied the protest. The marks fit the scheme in the call. They were also sound on the record. Best value here weighed price and past work. The firm did not show the marks broke that scheme. Past work fights need proof of a flaw in the scheme or the facts. That proof was not made here.
gao-gaoreports-b-296699-3:
BAE Technical Services sought its protest costs in GAO decision B-296699.3, dated August 11, 2006. GAO had backed the firm in its Eglin range fight. The firm sought 488,988.40 dollars. The fight had mixed won and lost points. Proof of how costs split was thin.

GAO backed pay of 463,902.58 dollars. Costs for lost points that stand alone can be cut. Here most cost proof did not split the points well. A page count of the briefs was a sound split tool. That tool set the sum due. The case shows how cost claims are split when briefs mix won and lost claims.
gao-gaoreports-b-296860-3:
Honeywell Technology Solutions sought protest costs in GAO decision B-296860.3, dated December 27, 2005. The first fight was over a Navy award for tech and design support.
