Great crises test Rome in the third volume of Niebuhr's History, in the 1837 Hare and Thirlwall version. The Punic Wars and the republic's fall are rebuilt from the sources. Niebuhr's critical method reaches its full, revolutionary rigor in these chapters on Rome's hardest centuries of war and change.

He taught historians how to read ancient evidence with new eyes. Every claim must show its root in a source he trusts. The book's influence spread far beyond Roman studies into all history writing. Epoch-making in its day, it stays foundational now: the work that proved the past could be reconstructed, not merely retold, by strict and honest method.
night-and-morning-volume-3:
Book the Third of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning fills volume three of this copy. A verse from Thomson's Castle of Indolence heads its first chapter. The scene shifts to Paris, in a popular and respectable quarter that is not quite fashionable.

A curious building juts from the shops on the Rue, built like an ancient Roman temple. Green pilasters and gilded cornices dress its front. Three small statues above stand, by rumour, for Hymen, Cupid, and Fortune. A brass plate on the door names Monsieur Love. Lytton sets love, marriage, and luck over a Paris shopfront as his tale resumes.
no-defense-volume-3:
Volume three of Gilbert Parker's No Defense holds Book the Third, which closes the novel. A letter opens the book, then strangers arrive at Salem. Lord Mallow intervenes, and a clash of race follows. Sheila has her say, Noreen comes, and a talk with the governor leads toward what happened.

The first chapter shows a planter at his table on Christmas Day. His lands lie on the Thomas River, a few hours from Spanish Town. He has given presents and kept the feast with his people. A rich table of boar, pigeon pies, and barbecued hog marks the day. Parker sets the close amid plantation life.
normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its-anci:
Part three of Gordon Home's Normandy opens at chapter seven, concerning Mont St Michel. Verses from Tennyson's Gareth and Lynette head the chapter, about a royal mount flashing through mist. Home quotes an older book on the mount's majestic gulf and its strategic weight in war.

Readers had glimpsed that gulf already from Avranches, in an earlier chapter. Home warns that many miss the rock's best sides by taking the straight national road. The winding coast road from Pontaubault shows more, he says. A tramway now runs along the causeway to the mount itself. Old spell and new ease meet at the famous rock.
northern-lights-volume-3:
Volume three of Gilbert Parker's Northern Lights holds When the Swallows Homeward Fly, George's Wife, and Marcile. The first tale opens as the sun stalks away into evening. Banners of gold and crimson trail behind it, and swift twilight streams over the land. Two men on a high hill watch it go.

One man's look is like a light in a window to a lost traveller. He has made a journey few attempt and fewer finish. On foot and alone, save for dogs and Indian guides, he reached the far northwestern Arctic seas. Ice hummocks housed him, and pemmican and seal fat fed him. Parker honours endurance in the far North.
one-of-our-conquerors-volume-3:
George Meredith's third volume opens with book three. Chapter nineteen pits Nature against Circumstance in men's hearts. Active men feel the two forces split apart, he writes. Soldiers and heroes know that wild moment well, he says. They march on while praising Nature's topping wisdom.

A great assembly at Lakelands follows in chapter twenty. Dartrey Fenellan and an intruder named Jarniman enter. A ladies' lapdog causes momentous effects from minor causes. Nesta's engagement closes this part of the novel. Meredith blends satire, romance, and moral debate. The balance of nature and duty is his lasting theme.
orderic-vitalis-ecclesiastical-history-f:
Thomas Forester's third volume of the Ecclesiastical History of Orderic Vitalis came out in 1855. Orderic wrote at Saint Evroul in Normandy, an English-born monk watching two kingdoms at once. His history is the fullest Norman chronicle of his century.

Crusaders' tales from the Holy Land, the wars of Henry I, and the affairs of Norman churches and courts fill this stretch of the work. Orderic gathers reports from returning knights and pilgrims, and he marks marvels beside hard fact. His cast runs from kings to hermits and robber saints. Readers who want the feel of the Anglo-Norman world, not just its wars, come to Orderic.
pahlavi-texts-west-vol-3:
West's third volume of Pahlavi Texts appeared in 1885 in the Sacred Books of the East. He continued rescuing Zoroastrian literature from Middle Persian originals. Priestly writings from Persia under Islamic rule fill the volume.

The contents include the Sad Dar, a popular summary of religious duties. Other pieces offer hymns, legends, and moral counsel for the faithful. Such writings kept an endangered tradition alive across hard centuries. West translated with patience and supplied full scholarly notes. His five-volume project remains a monument of preservation. Readers meet Zoroastrianism here as a living community's faith. The tradition's refusal to disappear gives these pages their quiet power.
palfrey-history-new-england-vol-3:
John Gorham Palfrey's History of New England reached Volume 3 in 1858. The founding fathers give way here to their children and heirs. A second generation takes up the Puritan errand in the wilderness.

Churches, schools, and town meetings fill the middle movement of the work. Sons are tested against the high vision their fathers brought over. Faith cools for some, while towns grow rich and sure of themselves. Palfrey writes as a proud heir of the people he studies. The volume shows a holy mission hardening into a settled, lasting society over time. Strain between old ideals and new habits runs through it.
pappus-collection-hultsch-vol-3:
Friedrich Hultsch finished his edition of Pappus of Alexandria in 1878 with this third volume. It holds the fragments of book eight of the Mathematical Collection, on mechanics, with supplements and full indexes. The Greek text comes with Hultsch's Latin version. Pappus wrote around 320 CE.

Book eight treats centers of gravity, inclined planes, and the machines of the engineer. Even in scraps it shows Greek mechanics at its most exact. The indexes open the whole Collection to study, name by name and term by term. With this volume the richest source for lost Greek geometry stands complete in its classic edition. No public domain English version exists.
pausanias-description-greece-frazer-vol-:
Frazer's third Pausanias volume carries the commentary south into the Peloponnese. Pausanias's route runs through Sparta, Olympia, and Argos in this section. Frazer's 1898 edition matches the traveler against the landscape itself.

Olympia's games and statues receive especially full archaeological treatment. Spartan customs and Argive legends get tested against stones and inscriptions. Frazer sets each legend against its landscape with tireless learning. His method shows readers how to verify an ancient author. The old heartland of Greek myth becomes a mapped, walkable country. Scholars still consult these volumes when excavating the sites Pausanias described two millennia ago.
pentagon-papers-vol-3:
The Pentagon Papers were a classified history of the Vietnam War written inside the Defense Department in the late 1960s. Volume 3 of the Senator Gravel edition, issued in 1971, covers the years when the United States took over the fighting. Gravel's edition put the leaked record before any reader who wanted it.

These pages hold the memos, cables, and studies behind the bombing campaigns and the huge troop build-up of 1965 to 1968. They show leaders weighing wider war against the risk of Chinese or Soviet entry, and doubting their own strategy as casualties rose. Read beside the era's public statements, the volume documents the gap between what officials said and what they believed.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-volume-:
Part 3 of volume 1 of Sheridan's memoirs opens at Chattanooga in September 1863, just after Chickamauga. His troops take position inside the entrenchments while the enemy fortifies Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge. The army sits in partial siege, its supplies dragged sixty miles over mountain roads from Bridgeport.

Sheridan describes headquarters under the shadow of Lookout Mountain, shells dropping into camp, and the loyal Mr. Crutchfield feeding him information. The chapter builds toward Grant's arrival and the battles for the heights. It shows Sheridan waiting, exposed and shelled, on the eve of his famous charge up Missionary Ridge.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-3:
Part 3 of Grant's memoirs opens at chapter twenty-seven, in 1862, with Grant chafing at Corinth. He holds a nominal command and yet no command under Halleck, and asks again and again to be relieved. Sherman calls as he is packing and urges him so strongly not to go that he stays.

Granted removal of his headquarters to Memphis, Grant rides west with a tiny escort through unguarded country. He dines at La Grange with a secessionist host who proudly feeds soldiers' families from his plantations. Grant listens, and files the man away. The part shows a general waiting for his chance.
pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-far-n:
Volume 3 of Gilbert Parker's Pierre and His People collects four far north tales: Shon McGann's Tobogan Ride, Pere Champagne, The Scarlet Hunter, and The Stone. Pretty Pierre, the figure who links the whole set, moves through a world of mountain huts, buffalo robes, and Hudson's Bay men.

Shon McGann's Tobogan Ride opens in a mountain hut, where Shon sings of Farcalladen Rise with his pipe between his teeth. Around him sit Pretty Pierre, Jo Gordineer, the Honourable Just Trafford, and their host Prince Levis, a French Canadian whose princely name was a Rocky Mountain joke. Talk turns to the ghost of Guidon Mountain while a drink called ginger-tea is made under the eye of prohibition law.
plato-dialogues-jowett-vol-3:
Benjamin Jowett's third volume of Plato holds three works, and the first of them is the giant: the Republic. In ten books, Socrates and his friends build a just city in speech to learn what justice is in a single soul. The volume's other works reach even higher.

The Republic gives Plato's theory of the ideal state, ruled by philosopher kings, and his allegory of the cave. Timaeus then tells how a divine craftsman shaped the cosmos, and Critias begins the tale of Atlantis and its war with ancient Athens. No other volume of Plato has shaped Western thought more. Jowett's translation keeps its Victorian polish.
poems-volume-3:
George Meredith's Poems conclude in the third volume of the Surrey Edition, issued by the Times Book Club in London in 1912. A frontispiece shows the South Wester, the storm wind of his Surrey hills. By this volume the selection reaches Meredith's earthier, folk-touched manner: the Stave of Roving Tim opens the contents with a wind that blows east and west. Jump-to-Glory Jane follows, the tale of a servant girl's religious ecstasy.

The Sage Enamoured and the Honest Lady offers a longer narrative, while short pieces ask whether love is divine and warn that joy is fleet. A Lesson of Grief begins the closing movement. Across three volumes the Surrey Edition gave Edwardian readers the complete Meredith as poet. Philosopher, storyteller, singer of wind and weather, his work still rewards the patient reader it demands.
pretiosa-margarita-novella-de-thesavro-a:
A second digitized copy of the 1546 Venice Pretiosa Margarita Novella survives in this record. Its title page reached through the Internet Archive with funding from the Getty Research Institute's research library. The same bibliographic facts stand on the page: the new precious pearl on the treasure and most precious philosophers' stone, the art collected from Arnold. Raymond, Albertus, and Michael Scotus by Janus Lacinius, the ten-year privilege of the Venetian Senate, and the date in Roman numerals, M.D.XLVI.

Duplicated digitizations matter for a book like this one, since copies differ in their plates, their completeness. The sharpness with which a reader can study the woodcut apparatus of an alchemical classic. The underlying work, the Margarita tradition descending from Petrus Bonus, argues the antiquity and dignity of alchemy from its authorities. Having the Getty copy beside the Wellcome copy lets scholars compare impressions across two great collections.
prince-zilah-volume-3: Only the front matter of the file survives for the third volume of a French novel in English dress. Its header names Jules Claretie as author and places the book in a series of French writers crowned by the French Academy. Because the pages after the header are missing here, nothing can be said about this volume's plot or people. Readers get the publishing facts only: the title, the author, the series, and the volume number.
prose-masterpieces-from-modern-essayists:
Five Victorian men of letters share the third volume of a Putnam anthology printed at New York and London in 1891. The book gathers long essays and lectures that editors of the day counted as models of English prose.

James Anthony Froude opens with The Science of History, a lecture given at the Royal Institution in 1864. Edward A. Freeman writes on race and language, William Ewart Gladstone on kin beyond sea, John Henry Newman on private judgment, and Leslie Stephen closes with a plea for plain speaking. Readers get five strong voices on history, faith, and speech.
quintilian-institutio-butler-loeb-vol-3:
The third Loeb volume of Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria, in H. E. Butler's English, holds books six through eight. The Roman teacher's great course on speaking now turns from the bones of a case to its life. Style, feeling, and the handling of a jury come to the front.

Book six treats the closing appeal, the rousing of pity and anger, and the use of laughter. Book seven orders the arguments, and book eight opens the study of style: clarity, ornament, and tropes. Quintilian quotes poets and orators on every page to make his points live. These books show rhetoric as an art of moving minds.
ranke-history-england-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Ranke's History, in the 1875 Oxenford translation, swings with England's faith. The boy king Edward rules first, then Mary drives a Catholic return. Elizabeth's early years close the book's span of fierce change.

Each reign reverses the last one's church settlement in turn. Ranke follows the swings with his usual depth and calm control. He shows how faith, fear, and foreign threats shaped each choice. Protestants burn under Mary, then Catholics suffer under her sister. The nation's soul seems at stake in every parliament and pulpit. Ranke gives the struggle the weight of great European history.
ranke-reformation-germany-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Ranke's German Reformation history appeared in Austin's version in 1844. The Schmalkaldic War tests the new faith by force of arms. The Peace of Augsburg then secures it by treaty and law.

Ranke closes with the famed rule that ends the long struggle. Each prince's faith, the treaty says, shall be his land's faith. That harsh bargain shaped Germany for a hundred years to come. Dissenters must yield, move, or hide under the new settlement's terms. Ranke judges the deal with his master's calm and distance. The volume ends an age and explains the map it left.
reymont-the-peasants-vol-3:
Spring wakes the land in the third English volume of Reymont's The Peasants. Fields thaw, work resumes, and passions rise with the sap in the trees. The struggle for land, the peasant's endless obsession, pushes the Boryna drama toward open tragedy.

Lust, jealousy, and pride break through the village's strict customs. Reymont matches the season's surge of life with rising heat in his tale. Every planting and festival carries a charge of hope or menace. Many readers find this the most intense of the four volumes, where the great Polish village saga presses hardest on its people.
rhoda-fleming-volume-3: For the third volume of Rhoda Fleming, by George Meredith, the front pages consist solely of a publisher's header. From it a reader learns the title, the author's name, and that the text is in English. The header also numbers the item twenty-ninth in a series of Meredith's works. No opening chapter, contents page, or preface follows in what is shown. Which stretch of the Fleming sisters' story falls in this third part is a question the front pages leave open.
roughing-it-part-3:
Part 3 of Mark Twain's Roughing It, in an 1880 printing, opens at Chapter XXI on the twentieth morning of a long stage trip. By noon the party would reach Carson City, capital of Nevada Territory, and the narrator is sorry, not glad. The riders had grown fond of stage life and its daily wonders. Settling down to a dull life in a village felt flat and sad by contrast with the road.

The new home, as it comes into view, is a desert walled in by bare, snow-clad hills, with no tree in sight. Sage-brush and greasewood stretch through deep, powdery alkali dust that coats riders, coach, mules, and mail-bags one dull color. Dead beasts of burden lie along the route, and a lone raven now and then watches the coach pass.
sacred-books-east-vol-20-vinaya-texts-3:
Volume twenty of the Sacred Books of the East closes the Vinaya Texts with the Cullavagga, in the 1885 translation by T. W. Rhys Davids and Hermann Oldenberg. The Cullavagga, the Lesser Series, finishes the Pali rule book for monks and nuns. Parts one and two stand in volumes thirteen and seventeen.

The Cullavagga rules daily life in fine grain: dwellings, furniture, bathing, and the duties of teacher and pupil. It also tells of the first council after the Buddha's death, where the teaching was recited and fixed. The founding of the order of nuns appears here too. With it, the Vinaya set stands complete in English.
samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-3:
Part 3 of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren, written as Josiah Allen's Wife, opens at Chapter VII in the middle of the fifth week of a trying visit. Lodema had been uncommonly provoking, and Samantha expected she would set Josiah going. Samantha groaned in spirit at the job ahead of parting their two tongues. Then, all of a sudden, she saw a curious change come over her partner's face. She remembers the very date the change became visible. It was the morning the invitation came to old Mr. and Miss Pressley's silver wedding, on the fifteenth day of the month, about the middle of the forenoon.

Not half an hour after Elnathan Pressley came to the door with the invitations, Samantha saw the change in Josiah's manner. When she asked him afterward what that strange look meant, he did not hang back a mite from telling her.
sandra-belloni-volume-3: George Meredith's Sandra Belloni, Volume 3, appears here only as Project Gutenberg header matter, marked v3 and listed as number 21 in a series by the author. Meredith is named as author, with a release date of September 2003. The file was first posted on January 4, 2002, as Etext number 4415, in Edition 10, in English and ASCII. Pat Castevans and David Widger are credited with producing the electronic text. No title page, contents list, or chapter passage is present in the portion shown here.
satapatha-brahmana-eggeling-vol-3:
Eggeling's third volume of the Satapatha Brahmana appeared in 1894. The Sacred Books of the East series carried it as volume forty-one. Creation stories and a great flood legend appear within its ritual exposition.

Later Indian epics would retell several myths preserved in these books. Readers meet the gods as working priests knew them, inside sacrifice itself. The volume shows myth living inside ritual rather than in storybooks. Eggeling's notes guide readers through the dense ceremonial detail. Ancient India's imagination survives here in prose of great age. The flood tale of Manu, ancestor of humanity, is among its treasures for comparative mythology.
self-help-sailor-s-knots-part-3:
W. W. Jacobs published this dockside tale in 1909 as part three of his Sailors' Knots set. A night-watchman sits on the jetty nursing a sore corn and a bad liver, sunk in gloom. A passing waterman raps his bare foot with an oar, and the old man takes it as proof of a sour rule of life.

Kindness, the watchman holds, never wins thanks: help a man and he tries to borrow from you. He spins yarns to prove the point, in broad dock speech full of dry humor. Jacobs turns a grumble on a jetty into a small comic study of human nature.
sherman-memoirs-vol-2-part-3:
Part Three of Sherman's memoirs, in Volume Two, covers his most famous campaign: the March to the Sea. In late 1864 Sherman cut loose from Atlanta and marched across Georgia to Savannah. His 1875 account tells it as he planned it.

Sherman explains why he tore up rails, lived off the land, and aimed at the South's will to fight. The Carolinas campaign follows, harder and wetter than Georgia. His memoirs defend the march as humane in the long run, since it shortened the war. Critics in the South never agreed, and the argument still runs. His men called the march bumming, and Sherman does not hide the foraging.
sketches-new-and-old-part-3:
Mark Twain's sketches new and old continue in this third part, opening with a disgraceful persecution of a boy. In San Francisco a well-dressed boy, bound for Sunday school, was arrested and jailed for stoning Chinamen, the papers reported. Twain purports to weep over this blow at human justice.

Hear the defense first, Twain urges. The boy's schooling came from daily papers all week, not Sunday lessons alone. California taxed the foreign Chinese miner while letting the Irish foreigner dig free, the sketch notes with acid calm. Twain's irony defends the boy to indict the grown-ups who taught him.
strabo-geography-hamilton-falconer-vol-3:
Volume Three of Strabo's Geography, in the Hamilton and Falconer version, holds Books Fourteen through Seventeen. The survey moves east and south to finish the known world. Asia, Egypt, and Libya close the great tour.

Strabo describes ports, rivers, and peoples at the edge of Roman rule. Egypt gets a long, rich account of its land and temples. His sources thin out here, and wonders grow more common. The volume completes a work of vast scope. With it, readers hold the fullest picture the ancient world ever drew of itself.
stubbs-constitutional-history-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Stubbs's Constitutional History of England appeared in 1878. The Tudor age transforms the old order across this final book. Henry's break with Rome and his Reformation Parliament lead the change.

Royal supremacy over the church bends the old constitution to new ends. Stubbs shows how medieval forms survived while their meaning shifted fast. Councils, courts, and parliaments serve a stronger, more central crown. His three volumes close with the modern state coming into view. Generations learned from Stubbs where England's freedoms first took root. The work's scale and care have kept it in print ever since.
sylvia-s-lovers-volume-3:
Volume III of Elizabeth Gaskell's Sylvia's Lovers, printed at London in M.DCCC.LXIII, or 1863, holds the novel's last chapters, from XXX to XLV. It opens on Happy Days, but the contents quickly turn: evil omens, rescued from the waves, an apparition, and a reckless recruit.

Things unutterable, mysterious tidings, and bereavement follow, then the recognition and confidences, in which the truth hidden since the press-gang days comes out at last. An unexpected messenger, the bedsman of St. Sepulchre, a fable at fault, and the unknown lead to first words and the closing chapter, Saved and Lost. Gaskell ends Sylvia's story in the key of its motto, with redress coming only behind the veil and too late to restore what was taken.
symonds-renaissance-italy-vol-3:
Fine arts fill Volume 3 of Symonds's Renaissance in Italy, from 1875. Painters, sculptors, and builders from Giotto to Michelangelo pass in review. Churches, palaces, and frescoed halls rise across his glowing chapters.

Symonds writes of pictures and buildings with rare grace and feeling. His lives of the great artists rank among the finest in English. He shows how patrons, cities, and rival masters drove art upward. Technique serves beauty, and beauty serves civic pride in his tale. Readers gain a full map of the age's visual glory here. Prose worthy of its subject carries the whole splendid survey.
tales-from-the-arabic-payne-1884-vol-3:
Payne's Tales from the Arabic closes with Volume III, printed in 1884 alongside the end of his Nights. The last Breslau and Calcutta stories take their place in English, in the translator's full and faithful style. With this volume, John Payne's double project stands whole: the great cycle and its overflow, both complete.

The supplement's tales reward the reader who wants more of the world the Nights opened. Their plots turn on wit, luck, and the thin line between beggar and king. Volume III finishes a set that scholars use to trace how Arabic story collections grew beyond any single book.
talleyrand-memoirs-vol-3:
In Volume Three, Talleyrand tells of Napoleon's fall and the Bourbon Restoration that followed. The French diplomat had bet against his old master and helped shape what came next. Beaufort's translation keeps his dry voice intact.

The volume covers the collapse of the Empire, the return of the Bourbon kings, and France's uneasy peace. Talleyrand defends his dealings with the allies and his role at the settlement of Europe. Old scores are settled in smooth, polite prose. For students of diplomacy, this is a master class in surviving defeat. Paris crowds, allied armies, and a nervous court crowd these chapters.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-volume-: George Meredith wrote The Adventures of Harry Richmond. For volume three, only the Gutenberg front wrapper stands here. No novel text follows it. The wrapper lists the part as number 52 in the Meredith set. It gives file 4446. First posting was January 31, 2002. A September 2003 release date is given. David Widger is credited with the file's making.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-3:
Part three of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer opens at chapter eight, with Tom in flight from school and in a black mood. He dodges through lanes till he is clear of the returning scholars, then falls into a moody jog.

Tom crosses a small branch stream two or three times, trusting the boyish belief that crossing water baffles pursuit. Past the Douglas mansion on Cardiff Hill, he plunges into dense wood and sits on a mossy spot under a spreading oak. Noon heat stills even the birds, and a far woodpecker's taps deepen the hush. Readers follow Tom's gloom toward play at Robin Hood and a clash with Joe Harper in the woods.
the-amazing-marriage-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's 1895 novel fills this third volume, from Studies in Fog, Gout, an Old Seaman to a descent into a steamer's engine room. Gower Woodseer stays at the center, seen now as a philosopher and man of action.

The first chapter sends Gower by coach on his father's hard-earned gold, bound on an errand of help. At Chinningfold a butler doubts his rough dress and glib speech, then fetches Mrs. Carthew. She rises in alarm at news from the bride she had lately seen married and sent off with her lordly young husband, fearing what a messenger's arrival may mean.
the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-of-tw:
Volume three of Gilbert Parker's romance opens at chapter sixteen, the morning after Guida's marriage. Guida works with feverish unrest and will not go where she might see Philip's ship, the Narcissus, before its fixed sailing hour. From her kitchen door she can see Noirmont Point.

Her grandfather watches her spin and sing for his afternoon sleep and suddenly sees her as a grown woman. He takes snuff, forgets it, and recalls that she was born the day he sold a blue enamelled watch to the Duc de Mauban. Affection, pride, and a sense of time passing fill a quiet household scene before departure.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-3:
August 1885, volume three, number three, carries a portrait of John Albion Andrew, called the war governor of Massachusetts. Andrew, the twenty-first governor of the state, was born on May 31, 1818, at Windham, near Portland, Maine. His father Jonathan was a small trader there.

His mother Nancy Green Pierce, of New Hampshire, had taught at Fryeburg Academy, where Daniel Webster once taught. She died on March 7, 1832, and the family later moved to a farm in Boxford. Andrew entered Bowdoin College in 1833, studied hard, ranked low in his class, yet was popular for his genial temper among fellow students.
the-complete-poetical-works-of-percy-bys: Volume 3 of Percy Bysshe Shelley's complete poetical works, in the Oxford Edition of 1914 edited by Thomas Hutchinson, is shown here by its title page and contents alone. The volume is given to translations. Homer's hymns come first, addressed to Mercury, Castor and Pollux, the Moon, and the Sun. Hymns to the Earth, Minerva, and Venus follow. Then comes The Cyclops, a satyric drama from the Greek of Euripides. Epigrams from Plato also appear. No translated text follows.
the-complete-writings-of-charles-dudley-: Charles Dudley Warner's complete writings, volume 3, came to Project Gutenberg in June 2001 as etext 2673. What is present is the header alone: copyright cautions, the rule that the header be seen first on opening the book, and an appeal for donations. The volume's own pages never begin in what is given, so its contents cannot be listed here.
the-confession-of-a-child-of-the-century: Volume 3 of Alfred de Musset's Confession of a Child of the Century, in the French Immortals series, reached Project Gutenberg as etext 3941. The header alone stands here, giving an April 2003 release date and a September 2001 first posting, with David Widger as producer.The chapters themselves remain out of view. David Widger produced the etext.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum: Volume 3 of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer, printed at Dublin in 1839, is shown here by front matter alone in this record. A note repeats that the title page names no author, the work being generally attributed to Lever. The plates listed include The Inn at Munich and Mr. Burke's Enthusiasm for the Duke of Wellington, plus a passport office scene. No contents or chapter text follows here, and a second record also called Volume 3 carries chapters XVIII to XXIII.
the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-arblay: Volume III of The Diary and Letters of Madame d'Arblay (Frances Burney) covers 1792 to 1840. It has notes by W. C. Ward and Macaulay's essay, and a portrait of General d'Arblay. The contents open on the French emigrants at Juniper Hall in 1792-3: the Duke de Liancourt's flight, Madame de Genlis's retreat, Madame de Stael, and Talleyrand. The execution of Louis XVI follows, and at last Miss Burney's marriage to M. d'Arblay. Only the title page and contents synopsis are present here; the year is omitted because its pages disagree on it.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-p:
Part three of Paradise in Dante's Vision, in the Rev. H. F. Cary's verse, opens at canto twenty-two. Dante turns in awe to his guide, as a child runs to the one it trusts most. She soothes him, asking if he forgets he stands in heaven, where all is holy and done with zeal. Then she bids him look on the famed spirits around them.

A hundred small spheres shine, each fairer from the light they share. One great, bright soul draws near to grant his wish. Ahead lie the fixed stars, the highest sphere, and the final sight of God.

Part three of Purgatory in Dante's Vision spans cantos eleven through eighteen, in Cary's verse. Proud souls open canto eleven with a slow, bent recital of the Lord's Prayer, reshaped for those still on earth. They walk under great stones like weights they bore in life, and pray as they go.

Sloth, wrath, and envy fill the ledges ahead. Carved scenes teach humility, and smoke blinds the wrathful. Dante learns how love, bent or straight, drives each soul. The middle of the mountain tests the will as much as the body.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-3:
Deborah's song of triumph opens volume three of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations. The text prints her chant from Judges, praising God for Israel's revenge and blessing Jael, who drove a tent nail through Sisera's head. Next comes Jephthah met by his daughter, a tale of a rash vow and its sad price.

Each entry pairs a Bible passage with one of Doré's engravings and a brief head note. The volume moves through the age of the judges, where songs, vows, and wars mark Israel's loose, fierce youth. Doré draws crowds and storms with bold force.
the-dwelling-place-of-light-volume-3:
Volume three of Winston Churchill's The Dwelling-Place of Light opens at chapter fifteen on Hampton Common. A crowd of sixteen nations packs the snow-dusted green to hear speakers preach Syndicalism from the bandstand, each in his own tongue. Janet pushes through to watch a tall Italian orator whose face burns like a house on fire.

Strike fever grips the mill town, and Janet must choose her side. Love, class, and revolt meet in her choice. Churchill closes his tale of the Chippering Mill with crowds, speeches, and a young woman's hard-won stance.
the-forsyte-saga-volume-3: John Galsworthy wrote this Forsyte volume, holding Awakening and To Let. Only the front matter and start of contents are present here. The heads for To Let name a meeting. They name a fine fleur Forsyte and scenes at Robin Hill. A mausoleum stands in the list. Figures called Jon and Fleur appear, with parts named idyll, trio, duet, and caprice. No page of the tale itself can be read in what is present. So its scenes cannot be stated from this front matter alone.
the-french-revolution-volume-3:
Hippolyte A. Taine wrote this third volume on the French Revolution, covering the rule of the revolt at its height. Five books move from the setting up of the new government to its end.

The preface mocks false gods: as Egypt's priests hid a crocodile behind gold cloth, so France, Taine says, hid a beast behind fine words. Books take up the Jacobin plan, the minds of its chiefs, the rulers of town and country, and the ruled: the oppressed and the hungry. Taine closes his tale of the revolt with the fall of the men who had ruled by the guillotine.
the-gilded-age-part-3:
Part 3 of The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today is dated 1873. Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote the novel. This part opens with Chapter XIX. Harry Brierly draws pay as an engineer. He stays at the City Hotel in Hawkeye. He keeps putting off his return to the rail line. He writes long letters to Philip instead.

Harry shines in Hawkeye society. He deals in land and knows bankers and public men. He plays guitar and banjo. Laura Hawkins turns her charm on him, and he thinks of winning her. Colonel Sellers warns him off. The Hawkins blood is good blood from Tennessee, he says. Hard luck, not low worth, has brought the family down.
the-great-conspiracy-volume-3:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record is Part 3. It opens with Chapter XI, The Causes of Secession. Logan sums up his case so far. From the very hour the Republic was born, some of its own citizens hated it. When they could not rule it, they worked to weaken and destroy it. They used conspiracy, sedition, mutiny, nullification, and secession.

He quotes Edward McPherson's history of the rebellion to the same effect. In the slaveholding states, a body of men was always disaffected to the Union. They resisted the Constitution. They sought to refine away the powers of the general government. Over years they perverted the sentiments of large masses. They prepared them for revolution. Logan sets out to sift the true causes of secession. He works from the proofs laid out for that claim.
the-home-book-of-verse-volume-3: Burton Egbert Stevenson edited The Home Book of Verse, Volume 3, by various poets. The pages present repeat the shared contents of Volumes 1 through 4 of the etext editions, the same contents that stand at the front of the Volume 1 record. Part I, Poems of Youth and Age, opens with The Human Seasons by John Keats, then a section called The Baby lists poems by Matthias Barr, William Blake, George MacDonald, and others. Only the title page and shared contents are present here.
the-ink-stain-tache-d-encre-volume-3: The third volume of René Bazin's The Ink-Stain closes a three-record split. The pages present here hold only an old etext header. The novel's ending does not appear. The header lists the file as etext 3974. Release came in April 2003. The volume stands sixty-first in the French Immortals series. It stands third among Bazin's works in that series. What can be stated is the volume's place in the set. How Bazin ends his romance of scholarly life stays unread here.
the-lane-that-had-no-turning-volume-3:
Gilbert Parker opens volume three of his Pontiac tales with the tragic comedy of Annette. Her trousseau of linen, bedding, and yarn has waited for months while Benoit, a singing river driver, fails to return for their wedding at St Saviour church. Her large family pities her and abuses him in equal measure.

They press her toward Farette, the old miller they owe for flour. Other tales in the volume include Mathurin, Parpon the Dwarf, and the marriage of the miller. Parker shows village love and debt pulling against each other in plain, tender scenes.
the-legends-of-the-jews-volume-3:
Louis Ginzberg devotes volume three of his legend gathering to the Exodus and the death of Moses. Paul Radin translated this volume from the German manuscript, a change from the translator named in the first two volumes. His preface calls Moses both the greatest religious guide of Israel and its first national leader.

The preface links Sabbath, sanctuary, and commandments closely to Moses life and work. Legend, he argues, kept that life woven into daily national practice rather than distant past. Readers get stories of manna, law giving, and desert years told through later Jewish tradition.
the-letters-of-horace-walpole-earl-of-or: Horace Walpole letters fill four volumes, and volume three covers 1759 to 1769. Only the title page and a detailed contents list are present here, naming letters to George Montagu, William Pitt, and Sir Horace Mann. Early entries promise Hawke victory over Conflans, tumults in Ireland, and a visit to Princess Emily. Newly collected letters are marked in the list. The correspondence itself, covering the Seven Years War era and London social life, stays beyond the pages held in this record.
the-life-of-jesus-christ-for-the-young-v: Richard Newton wrote his life of Jesus Christ for young readers, and this record holds volume three, called the gallery of the life. Only the title page, contents, and illustration list are present here, naming lessons on the apostles chosen, teaching by parables and miracles, liberality, humility, children, and the Transfiguration. A colored map of Palestine and forty numbered illustrations support the lessons. The text itself is not included in this record.
the-literary-remains-of-samuel-taylor-co:
Volume the Third of The Literary Remains of Samuel Taylor Coleridge appeared in 1838, collected and edited by Henry Nelson Coleridge. The third and fourth volumes are inscribed to John Hookham Frere. Contents here include a Letter to a Godchild and a Latin-titled statement of faith on the Trinity from 1830, the Formula Fidei de Sanctissima Trinitate.

The opening pages present Coleridge's dense theological reasoning in his own terms. Under headings like The Identity and The Ipseity, he defines God as the absolute subject, essentially causative of all true being, and as the self-affirming "I Am." Greek phrases and references to the Gospel of John run through the argument, showing Coleridge working out doctrine with close, demanding logic.
the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1620-m: For volume 3 of The Mayflower and Her Log by Azel Ames, the record holds the Project Gutenberg header and nothing further. The header dates the release to June 2003 and assigns the etext number 4103. David Widger is named as the file's producer. Readers looking for Ames's account of the Pilgrim voyage will find only boilerplate here: remarks on changing copyright laws, the welcome to free electronic texts, and the foundation's employee identification number.
the-money-master-volume-3:
Volume 3 of Gilbert Parker's The Money Master contains Epoch the Third, chapters XIII to XV, and opens at Chapter XIII, The Man from Outside. A young singer performs at the Manor Cartier before a small group around a bright wood fire. Applause and cries of encore greet her last note.

The stranger who answers her question is the Man from Outside, a man of about thirty-three with fluent French spoken in a slight English accent. The singer is Zoe Barbille, and the visitor's marked liking for her concerns M. Fille, who coined the stranger's nickname in sarcasm. Zoe's mother had vanished alone seven years earlier, and M. Fille has stood to Zoe almost as an elder brother ever since.
the-nest-egg-captains-all-book-3:
W. W. Jacobs's story The Nest Egg, from his Captains All collection, is told by the familiar night-watchman. Artfulness, he begins, is a gift, but it does not always pay. He has met plenty of artful ones, he says. None was the better for meeting him. His trick was to pretend to be more stupid than they thought he looked. Then he let them run on until he turned on them.

His proof case concerns Charlie Tagg, a steady young shipmate who saved nearly every penny for marriage. His girl kept the money for him: seventy-two pounds of his and seventeen shillings and sixpence of her own, held toward setting up housekeeping. Something then happened, the watchman warns, that he has known happen to sailormen before.
the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volume-3: Volume 3 of George Meredith's novel The Ordeal of Richard Feverel is represented here only by its Project Gutenberg header. The header names title and author. It gives the etext number 4408 and dates the first posting to December 28, 2001. No title page or chapter text appears in what is present. Pat Castevans and David Widger produced the etext, the fourteenth Meredith item in the Gutenberg series. The rest is legal notice about copyright and distribution.
the-physiology-of-marriage-part-3:
Third part of Honoré de Balzac's The Physiology of Marriage bears the heading Relating to Civil War. It opens at Meditation XXIII, Of Manifestoes, under a motto from Diderot. The motto pairs Klopstock's seraphs with Milton's devils. The husband now stands in open contest with his wife. Religion and law are on his side, and her native craft plus the usages of society are on hers.

Rather than argue at length, the opening pages hand down numbered maxims. One warns that anything may be expected from a woman in love. Another holds that a wife who means to deceive acts from study, never from reason. A third compares such women to fleas moving by erratic leaps. They stay inside a narrow area that a cool-headed husband can make still narrower. The tone is comic, dry, and frankly one-sided.
the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-3:
Part 3 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens at Chapter VIII, The Question of the Seal. Henry VIII wakes from an unrefreshing nap near five o'clock, muttering that his end is at hand. A wicked light flames in his eye. He vows he will not die until another man goes before him. The Lord Chancellor is admitted, kneeling by the couch.

The Chancellor reports that the peers have confirmed the Duke of Norfolk's doom and wait the King's pleasure. Henry's face lights with fierce joy, and he demands to be lifted up. He will seal the warrant himself before Parliament. His voice fails, and an ashen pallor sweeps his cheeks. Robbed of the chance, he orders the Great Seal put in commission so the head can be brought before another sunrise. Then comes the hitch: the Chancellor asks who keeps the Seal, if not himself.
the-purcell-papers-volume-3: Volume three closes the 1880 London set of Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu's tales. Richard Bentley and Son issued the set. A memoir by Alfred Perceval Graves heads the work, as in the earlier volumes. Library data on the title page records the reprint history. It also names the Chicago copy behind the reprint. Only the title and publication pages are present here. The start of the contents list appears with them. The tales themselves do not appear.
the-reign-of-henry-the-eighth-volume-1-o: James Anthony Froude's history is presented with an introduction by W. Llewelyn Williams in a Dent edition first published in 1909, opening with a Carlyle motto on history as a true epic poem. Volume one lists three chapters covering the social condition of England in the sixteenth century, the last years of Wolsey's administration, and the parliament of 1529. Here only the title pages and that short chapter list are present, so the history itself does not appear.
the-seaboard-parish-volume-3:
Volume three of George MacDonald's The Seaboard Parish begins with a walk with the narrator's wife. Its contents promise a last shore-dinner and a pastoral visit. A gathering storm and a gathered storm follow. Shipwreck, a funeral, and a sermon come after. Changed plans, a studio, and home again close the list.

Autumn was creeping up on the earth, the narrator writes. Winter held by its skirts behind. Rain had fallen during the day, then the air cleared by evening. The moon shone out near the full. His wife Ethelwyn came into his study and gazed out a moment. She called the night lovely and agreed to a little turn. She went to put on her bonnet at once.
the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-3:
Volume three of Gilbert Parker's The Seats of the Mighty holds chapters fourteen to nineteen of Captain Robert Moray's memoirs. Its headings include In the Chamber of Torture and Be Saint or Imp. A danseuse and the Bastile close the list.

Chapter fourteen, Argand Cournal, finds Moray still a prisoner. Gabord has been withdrawn and a new jailer substituted. Sentinels outside his door refuse all information. For months he has heard nothing of Alixe. He knows little of Doltaire or Bigot, and sees no sign of Voban. Guards at his door talk seldom, and then with brutal jests. Yet Moray gathers that all is not well between Bigot and Doltaire. The Governor also schemes against Doltaire, he learns.
the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-entert: A Project Gutenberg header is the whole of what this record shows for volume three of George Meredith's The Shaving of Shagpat. It identifies the e-text as number 4403, released in September 2003. A first posting date of December 21, 2001 is also given. The producers named are Pat Castevans and David Widger. Beyond the header lie only the project's usual legal and fundraising notices. No page of the story, no contents list, and no title page survives in the portion at hand. The third volume's contents are thus undescribed here.
the-sisters-volume-3:
Volume three of Georg Ebers's The Sisters opens at chapter twelve, during a feast. In a vast peristyle, cups were still being emptied, Ebers writes. Carousers grew merrier and noisier while Cleopatra abused her maids for clumsiness. Every touch hurt her as they undressed her, the scene says. No translator is named in the pages shown for this volume.

Meanwhile a Roman and his friend Lysias paced their tent in violent agitation. Lysias warned Publius to speak lower, fearing listeners in the thin walls. He reported an intruder slipping from their tent in a black robe sprinkled with gold. He swore the stealthy figure was Eulaeus. Publius demanded why he had not had the man caught. Lysias answered that their tent was pitch-dark, and the villain was slippery as a badger.
the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-volume-:
The third day of Zola's Lourdes, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, begins at seven on a bright August Sunday morning. M. de Guersaint rises fresh and gay in the Hotel of the Apparitions and bursts in on Pierre. The young priest, home past one in the morning, sleepless and fevered, has only just dropped off at daybreak. His scattered cassock and garments testify to his weariness and agitation of mind.

De Guersaint teases the lazybones, points to the ringing bells, and demands breakfast before they fetch Marie from the hospital by eight. Two cups of chocolate are ordered. Zola contrasts the father's breezy faith with Pierre's exhausted doubt, and the happy chiming town outside sharpens the difference. The day's processions and judgments at the grotto lie ahead for both men.
the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volume-3:
Book Three of Zola's Paris, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, opens on the Wednesday before mid-Lent Thursday at the Duvillard mansion. A great charity bazaar for the Asylum of the Invalids of Labour fills three Louis Seize salons. Five thousand admission cards have gone out across Parisian society. Whispers note that police agents guard the surrounding streets, since this is the mansion lately bombarded by an anarchist attack.

The bazaar was Duvillard's own idea, his wife presiding with distinguished nonchalance over stalls still being decorated at noon. The Globe newspaper praises her generosity as the answer of the spheres above to hateful passions below. Zola stages high society's charity as theatre, with real suffering used as scenery and Pierre watching the performance.
the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volume-3:
Part Three of Zola's Rome, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, finds Pierre before the Vatican, whither a harassing attraction ever leads him. There he meets Monsignor Nani, fresh from his weekly audience with the Pope. Nani, smiling with civility over a faint irony, offers the waiting priest a diversion: cards for the international pilgrimage's reception and for the Pope's mass at the Basilica on Sunday. People fight for such cards, he says.

Nani reports the Holy Father looking yellow and feverish, yet living by force of soul. Pierre accepts while insisting he is only losing time in waiting; Nani replies that he is looking, reflecting, and enlightening himself. Zola shows Vatican power as smooth management, where access is currency and a doubting priest is being carefully handled.
the-tragedy-of-the-chain-pier-everyday-l:
Charlotte M. Braeme's Tragedy of the Chain Pier, issued as number three of the Everyday Life Library of Chicago, opens by slighting its own setting. Most visitors to Brighton prefer the new West Pier, larger, more fashionable, and always crowded with beautiful women and celebrities. The narrator describes its library, shops, refreshment rooms, and music, then looks down at the emerald water washing the wonderful network of poles below the jetty.

Standing there with only a rail between watcher and deep water breeds dreams born of the sea, she says, and the pier is a famous place for studying human nature and flirtation. This lush, lingering scene-setting promises a sensation novel of love and disaster. Braeme, a hugely popular Victorian romancer, lets Brighton sparkle before her tragedy darkens it.
the-tragic-comedians-a-study-in-a-well-k:
Volume three of George Meredith's Tragic Comedians, dated 1892, opens at Book Three, chapter twelve, with Clotilde reading a letter in the shade of the garden walls. Her own fervent letter to the baroness rises in combative retort as she reads. The baroness's answer strikes chill as a glacier cave: she has come to arrange an unfortunate, impracticable affair, chiefly in Clotilde's interest. Clotilde must end her relations with Dr. Alvan discreetly, using the baroness's intervention, and call tomorrow afternoon.

Clotilde scribbles one line in receipt and signs her initials, then tells her father the woman is hateful. Meredith shows an innocent girl discovering cynicism in a scandalous old woman's polished cruelty. The duel of letters drives his study of Lassalle's romance toward its appointed tragedy.
the-trail-of-the-sword-volume-3:
Volume three of Gilbert Parker's Trail of the Sword opens Epoch Three, 'As Water unto Wine,' three months after the last events. George Gering joyfully prepares for two voyages, one to marriage with Jessica and one with William Phips to the Spaniards' country. His return to New York with news of captured Hudson's Bay posts brought consternation, and no man was angrier than Colonel Richard Nicholls. Jessica, a guest at Government House, was more agitated than anyone.

Her father, the Honourable Hogarth Leveret, likes the now less-Puritan Gering and awaits the marriage cheerfully. He has long suspected his daughter's interest in Iberville, the French Catholic enemy, but not that she treasures two unanswered letters from him. Parker builds his love triangle on treason's edge, where a daughter's keepsakes could ruin a governor's house.
the-translation-of-a-savage-volume-3:
Volume three of Gilbert Parker's Translation of a Savage opens with chapter nine, The Faith of Comrades, in a library at night. Francis Armour has left his wife's room and sits alone, face to face with his conscience, which Parker calls the loneliest tête-à-tête in the world. The little dwarf conscience perches on every hillock of remembrance, making slow signs in the language of the soul. Armour waves the butler away and reviews his whole life in fantastic panorama, like a drowning man's illumination.

The room of his boyhood, tutorship, and ambitious youth stands unchanged, yet he feels no part of it, wrapped in the strangeness of crisis. Parker's final volume turns inward, weighing the Armour family's debts to Lali. The remaining chapters run to The End of the Trail, where her story and theirs must settle.
the-trespasser-volume-3:
Volume three of Gilbert Parker's Trespasser opens with chapter twelve, He Stands Between Two Worlds, at the family solicitor's office. Gaston has spent weeks among old family papers, fishing out ancient documents from curiosity and presentiment. A clerk brings a small box found locked inside another, the property of a distant branch, the Belward-Staplings. It was probably shut away generations ago, after some family conference. Gaston takes out parchments with broken seals and faded tape.

One parchment bears his own name outside: 'Sir Gaston Robert Belward,' with 'Bart.' added, and he laughs at the thought of completing the reproduction, an M.P. turned baronet. The papers show him his heritage yet pull him toward the distant past and the land of the heathen. Parker's final volume turns on what a found name does to a man already divided.
the-understudy-night-watches-part-3:
W. W. Jacobs tells The Understudy through his night-watchman narrator, who opens by cursing dogs aboard ship. A mongrel has just chased him off the Henry William, and the skipper expects him to guard a vessel guarded already by teeth. His grumbling leads into a tale told in broad riverside dialect.

The story proper concerns Sam Small, Ginger Dick, and Peter Russet drinking in a little Commercial Road public house. A big black dog walks in, licks Sam's hand and biscuit, and adopts him on the spot. Jacobs builds the comedy slowly, letting the watchman's yarn-spinning voice carry sailors' superstitions, friendship, and the trouble one devoted dog can cause.
the-unpopular-review-volume-ii-number-3:
Henry Holt and Company issued The Unpopular Review quarterly from New York, and volume two, number three covers July to September 1914. The contents mix economics, politics, and lighter pieces. Contributors include A. S. Johnson, Hugh H. Lusk, Arthur J. Todd, Fabian Franklin, Clayton Hamilton, Paul Elmer More, and David Starr Jordan.

Johnson's opening essay attacks the new social conscience as a class phenomenon wearing a universal mask. It shows, he argues, special care for one social group and quiet hostility toward another, siding with labour against capital before facts are established. Other pieces treat syndicalism, immigration and labour supply, disfranchisement of property, academic leadership, and hypnotism, giving the number a combative, argumentative flavour.
the-works-of-edgar-allan-poe-volume-3: Volume three of the Raven Edition of Edgar Allan Poe's works is represented by a contents list alone. The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym fills most of the volume, in twenty-five chapters. Tales follow, including Ligeia and Morella. King Pest and The Spectacles also appear. Notes to the third volume are listed last. The stories themselves do not appear in the pages present.
the-works-of-guy-de-maupassant-volume-3: For volume three of Maupassant's works, The Viaticum and Other Stories, the pages present stop at the contents. Seventeen stories are listed, from The Viaticum to A Mesalliance. Ghosts, The Thief, and An Honest Ideal appear among them. The National Library Company of New York published the volume. Its copyright page dates to 1909. None of the stories themselves are included among the pages given.
the-world-for-sale-volume-3:
Volume three of Gilbert Parker's The World for Sale begins with book three, chapter twenty, Two Life Pieces. Fleda speaks with Ingolby, who has lost his sight. She marvels that he knows the day is fine. Ingolby explains that blindness sharpened his other senses. A light wind, fresh air, and warm sun told him plenty. His hands smooth the coverlet as he talks.

Parker renders disability as heightened perception rather than helplessness. Ingolby remains commanding even in bed. The final chapters build toward The Sleeper and the title chapter. Old rivalries and loves move toward resolution. Readers finish a frontier saga of ambition and endurance.
the-writings-of-samuel-adams-volume-3: Volume three of The Writings of Samuel Adams is represented here by a Project Gutenberg header alone. Harry Alonzo Cushing edited the collection. The header dates this electronic text to March 1999. Names of the volunteers who prepared it are given. Adams's own writings do not appear in the pages present in this record, so nothing of his arguments can be read from them.
their-silver-wedding-journey-volume-3:
Part III of William Dean Howells's novel opens at chapter XLVIII on a train journey toward Ansbach. The Marches fall into talk with a young German railway architect riding on official business. He defends Nuremberg's enforced Gothic style as part of new imperial patriotism.

Ansbach promises relief in its calmer classical facades and an old mansion hotel facing a sycamore square. A prince is expected there, and the Marches must sup elsewhere. The passage rewards readers who enjoy travel writing mixed with fiction, where manners, architecture, and national feeling all get noticed.
thirlwall-history-greece-vol-3:
Persia's great invasion fills Volume 3 of Thirlwall's History, from 1845. Marathon, Thermopylae, and Salamis stand as the book's famed set pieces. Small Greek cities face the vast empire of the Great King.

Thirlwall tells the heroic age with a scholar's care for proof. He praises courage without inflating it past what sources allow him. Athens and Sparta, rivals at home, stand as one against Persia. The wins that saved Greek freedom get neither bombast nor cold doubt. His warmth stays quiet, his facts stay firm, page by page. The volume remains a model of how to write patriotic history honestly.
to-win-the-love-he-sought-the-great-awak: E. Phillips Oppenheim's To Win the Love He Sought, also titled The Great Awakening, reaches volume three in a Collier edition copyrighted in 1912. Oppenheim also wrote The Mischief-Maker, Berenice, and Havoc. A contents list begins under the heading Adrienne Cartuccio. Chapter titles promise a meeting, a singer, treachery, and bitter springs of anger and fear. One title quotes going down into hell to win the love he sought. The title pages and opening contents are what is shown in this record, so Oppenheim's chapters themselves do not appear.
un-ga-res-3:
War criminals still at large haunted the victors of the Second World War. Resolution 3 of the General Assembly was passed on 13 February 1946. It recalls the Moscow Declaration of 1943. In it, Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill had pledged that enemy crimes would be judged. It also cites the war crimes terms of the Nuremberg Charter of August 1945. Some guilty men, the text says, still dodge justice in the lands of some states.

Member states are urged to act at once. They should arrest the war criminals who bore blame for these crimes, or who took a consenting part in them. The men are to be sent back to the lands where their deeds were done, to be judged and punished under the laws of those lands.
un-ga-res-a-69-3: West Africa's Ebola outbreak forced the UN to build an emergency mission in 2014, and Resolution A/69/3 deals with its budget. The Assembly had read the Secretary-General's report on the United Nations Mission for Ebola Emergency Response. The report also covered the Office of the Special Envoy on Ebola. It takes note of the report and backs the views of its budget advisers, with a warning that the vote settles nothing about the mission's shape or staffing for good.
un-ga-res-es-11-3:
Russia lost its seat on the UN Human Rights Council under Resolution ES-11/3, passed by the General Assembly in emergency session in April 2022. The text recalls the 2006 rule that set up the council. Under it, the Assembly may suspend a member that commits gross and steady breaches of human rights. Grave reports from Ukraine, under Russian attack since February 2022, fill the grounds.

The Council itself had voiced grave concern in March 2022 at reports of such breaches by Russian forces. The Assembly cites its own March votes on the war, then acts: Russia's rights of membership in the council are suspended. Few states have ever drawn that penalty.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 3, adopted on 13 February 1946, called for the arrest and return of war criminals. The Assembly cited the Moscow Declaration of 1943 on enemy cruelty. It cited the laws of war in the Hague Convention of 1907. It cited the war crimes definitions in the charter of the International Military Tribunal. It held that some offenders were still dodging justice in certain lands.

Members were urged to act at once to arrest those who had ordered or willingly joined in such crimes. They were urged to send them back to the countries where the deeds were done. There they were to be tried and punished under those countries' laws. Governments outside the United Nations were called on to do the same.

Resolution 69/3 of the General Assembly is a short budgetary note on the United Nations Mission for Ebola Emergency Response, the emergency mission created during the 2014 West African outbreak. The Assembly acts on the Secretary-General's report and the advice of its Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions. It takes note of the report and endorses the Advisory Committee's conclusions. It stresses that this step does not prejudge its later review of the mission's budget, structure, staffing, and operations. That review comes once a detailed budget is submitted.

UN General Assembly Resolution ES-11/3 — the 2022 emergency-session resolution suspending Russia from the Human Rights Council. It punished Moscow over Ukraine atrocities. The 2022 Council suspension is the Moscow punishment: the Russian Council membership formally revoked over Ukraine atrocities here.
un-sc-res-3:
Security Council Resolution 3 dealt with the Iranian crisis of 1946, one of the first disputes the young council faced. The catalog year of 1942 predates the UN itself and is wrong. Iran had charged that Soviet troops stayed on its soil past the agreed date for leaving after the war, and Tehran brought the complaint to the council in New York.

The resolution noted talks between Iran and the Soviet Union and asked both sides to report back on their progress. It kept the matter on the council's list in case talks failed. Soviet forces withdrew that spring. The case showed both the promise and the limits of the new body's reach.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: UN Security Council Resolution 3 — the 1946 resolution addressing Soviet troops remaining in Iran after World War II. It was among the very first crises the new Security Council ever handled. The 1946 Iran crisis is the first: the new Council’s earliest handled disputes.
uncle-robert-s-geography-uncle-robert-s-:
Uncle Robert's Visit, by Francis W. Parker and Nellie Lathrop Helm, belongs to a Home-Reading series about farm life. An editor's preface introduces Colonel Parker, president of the famous Cook County Normal School in Chicago. Teachers across the country, it says, already owe him classroom methods that arouse a child's interest and self-activity.

The preface ties Parker to the Pestalozzian movement, which links daily experience to school study. Rural schools suffer most from dry teaching, since one teacher faces ten or thirty children at every level at once. Home reading and practical experiments are Parker's remedy. The visit narrative that follows puts an educator's holiday to work teaching country children through their own farm world.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s10-3: Section 10.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations is a one-line format rule in the part on presidential papers. It concerns the Daily Compilation of Presidential Documents. The rule states where the Compilation appears. It is published online, on the Government Printing Office access system. No other format, schedule, or content rule is stated in the section.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s11-3:
Section 11.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations gives subscription facts for the Code itself. The rule sits in a part on subscriptions, under Title 1 on general provisions. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. It is aimed at buyers who order the bound paper set from the government.

The subscription price for a complete set is stated for one year in bound paper format. That price does not include postage, the rule notes. Postal rates in force at the time are applied to orders based on the delivery method the buyer requests. The Government Publishing Office handles those orders. Price and postage are kept as separate charges.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s15-3: Section 15.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers staff assistance from the Office of the Federal Register. It sits in Part 15, on services to federal agencies. The rule states what the staff of that office is to provide. The staff is to give informal help and advice to officials of the various agencies. The help covers broad and specific programs of rule drafting. It also covers procedures and the practices of issuing rules. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s16-3: Section 16.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with the duties of a man who certifies documents. It sits in Part 16, on the men who act for agencies with the Federal Register. The officer of an agency who certifies is in charge of two tasks. The first is to fix to each first document the count of true copies that the rules call for. The second is the act of certification set by two named sections.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s17-3:
Section 17.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets criteria for emergency publication in the Federal Register. It sits in Part 17 of Title 1, on filing for public inspection and publication schedules, in the electronic Code as of October 2026. The issuing body is the Administrative Committee of the Federal Register.

The text shown turns on the design of the emergency route. Emergency publication is designed to give the fastest possible publication of a document. That speed is tied to a stated end: the document must involve an emergency situation. The ends named are the prevention of such a situation, its alleviation, its control, or its relief. The section thus ties the fast track to pressing public need rather than to routine business.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s18-3:
Section 18.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers submission of documents to the Federal Register. The rule sits in a part on preparation and transmittal of documents generally, under Title 1. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. Letters of transmittal that go with the documents are also covered.

Each document that law requires or allows to be filed for public inspection and published must be sent to a named officer. That officer is the Director of the Federal Register, the rule states. Exceptions for set cases are flagged in the next part of the rule. The section is the front door rule for the daily journal of federal actions.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s19-3:
Section 19.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with the path of orders of the President. It sits in Part 19, on Executive orders and proclamations of the President. If the order or the proclamation is signed by the President, a set step is to be made. The first form of the text, and two copies of it, are to be sent on. They are to go to the Director of the Federal Register, for print in the Federal Register.

A second clause deals with a note to be put on the copies. The Office of the Federal Register is to have a set note placed on the copies of all such orders. That note is to be signed by the Director, or by a man the Director lets sign in his place.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s2-3:
Section 2.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations gives the location and hours of the Office of the Federal Register. That office publishes the government's daily journal of rules and notices. It is a component of the National Archives and Records Administration.

The office sits at 732 North Capitol Street, North West, in Washington, in suite A-734. A mailing address follows for the same office. Office hours run from a quarter to nine until a quarter past five. The days are Monday through Friday, official federal holidays excepted. The section is pure directory information, written into the Code so any citizen can find the office.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s20-3:
Section 20.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers organization statements for the United States Government Manual. It sits in Part 20, on the handling of Manual statements. The rule tells agencies how to show their lines of authority and structure. A chart may be used if it shows the structure with clarity. Charts must stay legible when shrunk to the size of a Manual page.

Charts that fail that test will not be put in the Manual. Lists of the heads of working units should be set out so as to show how units relate to each other where that can be done. A narrative part of the rule follows in the text. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026, an unofficial compilation.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s3-3: Section 3.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations concerns copies of official acts and documents. It sits in a part on services to the public, under the Federal Register system. This section does not set the copying rules itself. It points readers to the National Archives regulations for public use of records. Those rules, in parts 1252 through 1258 of Title 36, govern the furnishing of reproductions and certificates of authentication. One cited rule requires advance payment of the fees for copying and certifying.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s301-3:
Section 301.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations describes the organization of the Administrative Conference of the United States. The rule sits in a part on organization and purpose for that body under Title 1. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. The Conference studies and improves federal agency process.

The Chairman is appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate for a five year term, the rule states. The Council consists of the Chairman and ten other members appointed by the President. Those members serve three year terms, with a mix of public and government members as the rule goes on to set. Leadership structure is fixed before purpose is stated.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s304-3:
Section 304.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets the terms for making a records request to the Administrative Conference of the United States. It sits in Part 304, on disclosure of records or information. A request may be made with the online form on the agency web site, or by a written letter sent by post or fax.

For the fastest handling of a mailed request, both the letter and the cover should be marked as a freedom of information request. A request for records about the requester carries added terms set out in a later section. A request about an other person goes more smoothly with that person's signed leave, or with proof that the person has died. The request counts as received when the agency liaison logs it in.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s425-3:
Section 425.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations tells people how to see records about themselves held by the President's Commission on White House Fellowships. Privacy law gives individuals access to their own files. This section gives the address and the door.

Any person may request review of records pertaining to him. He may appear in person at Room 1308, 1900 E Street, North West, in Washington. The hours are work days between half past eight and five. Or he may write to the Commission on White House Fellowships Administrative Officer in Washington. The section points to its next paragraph for identification requirements. Reviewing one's own file starts, in this rule, with showing up or writing in and proving who one is.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s5-3:
Section 5.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with the printing of documents in the Federal Register. It sits in Part 5, a general part of the title. A first section, 5.2, names the documents that are covered by the rule as of course. This section deals with all the rest. When the Director of the Federal Register holds that the printing of such a document would be in the public good, a path is set.

On that view, the Director may let the document be filed for public view with the Office of the Federal Register. The Director may also let it be printed in the Federal Register. The rule is short and turns on the call of the Director in each case.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s51-3:
Section 51.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations explains when the Director of the Federal Register will approve a publication for incorporation by reference. It sits in the part that lets agency rules point to outside material instead of reprinting it.

Approval comes in two stages. Informal approval follows when the preamble of a proposed rule meets the part's requirements, and a preamble that falls short is sent back to the agency. Formal approval in a final rule needs an eligible publication, a proper preamble, proper wording of incorporation, the publication on file with the office, and a written request from the agency. The Director must answer within twenty working days once the agency has met every requirement.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s6-3: Section 6.3 of Title 1 of the federal rules deals with lists in the Federal Register. Each daily issue must carry a list by number for its readers. The list names the parts of the federal rule book hit that day. The hits come from documents printed in that same day's issue. A second rule adds a running list as the month goes on. From the second issue of a month, the list is kept up to date. It then shows all parts hit by that month's documents so far.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s601-3:
Section 601.3 of Title 1 of the federal rules gives the terms used in its part. The part is how a capital planning body meets environmental law. The terms set here hold for that part in all its rules. Each term is given a full sense in the body of the text.

One term is Administrative Record, the whole file of an agency's act. It joins all matter, writ or digital, that was before the agency. The file shows how the choice was made and what it rests on. A second term is Categorical Exclusion, short CATEX in the text. It names a class of acts with no big effect on man's surroundings. For such acts no assessment or impact statement is a must. More terms, like Central Area, are set in the same list.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s602-3:
Section 602.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets the definitions used in the Freedom of Information Act rules of the National Capital Planning Commission. It sits in Part 602, the part that governs how the Commission handles requests for its records. Each defined term controls how the rest of that part is read.

Among the terms fixed here, Act and FOIA both mean the Freedom of Information Act. An adverse determination covers a decision to withhold records in whole or part, a failure to answer all parts of a request, and denials of fee waivers or of expedited processing. Agency record is defined broadly, reaching books, papers, maps, plans, photographs, and machine-readable materials alike.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s603-3:
Section 603.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets Privacy Act program duties for one commission. The body is the National Capital Planning Commission. The rule sits in its Privacy Act regulations under Title 1. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six.

The Commission must name a Senior Agency Official for Privacy to set up and oversee its Privacy Act program. That official must ensure the Commission follows privacy laws, rules, and its own privacy policies. Listed duties for the official begin with reporting duties. The rule thus places clear ownership of privacy work on one senior official, rather than leaving it diffuse.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s8-3:
Section 8.3 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with the fresh state of the Code. It sits in Part 8, on the Code of Federal Regulations. Each book of the Code is to be made fresh at least once in each year of the calendar. If no change has been made in the book in the year, a plain note of that fact may serve as the new part for the year. More rounds of fresh work may be made at any time.

The Director of the Federal Register is to call for such rounds. The call can rest on the fact that the facts in the unit have been put out of date in the main. It can also rest on the view that the step fits the aim and the end of the Committee, as a named section states.
vedanta-sutras-thibaut-vol-3:
Thibaut completed his Vedanta Sutras translation with a third volume in 1904. It appeared as volume forty-eight of the Sacred Books of the East. The volume finishes Ramanuja's commentary on Badarayana's aphorisms in English.

With both great commentaries now fully translated, readers could compare the systems whole. Sankara's non-dualism and Ramanuja's qualified monism stand side by side. Thibaut's own introductions judge between the rivals with scholarly care. The set became a landmark of English Indology on publication. Later translators refined details, but Thibaut's architecture endured. Anyone studying Vedanta seriously still reckons with his three volumes and their arrangement.
vittoria-volume-3: The third volume of Vittoria by George Meredith, number 43 in the Gutenberg series of his works, opens in this file with the standard old Project Gutenberg license pages. Those pages are all that is present here. They warn that copyright laws change across the world and tell readers to check their own country's law before passing the file on.
