No part of Meredith's novel of love and revolt in Italy appears in these pages, and the volume's own chapter list is not given.
vyse-operations-gizeh-vol-3:
Volume Three of Howard Vyse's Operations serves as the appendix to his Gizeh work. It gathers the papers, letters, and plates that back the main journals. The volume appeared in 1842, after the dig ended.

Findings are set out with lists, notes, and views of the sites. Other scholars' letters weigh in on the results. The plates show chambers and objects as the team found them. Thorough readers get the proof behind the story here. The set closes a record that, for all its flaws, still anchors study of the pyramids.
wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-conspirac:
Volume three of John Richardson's Wacousta, or The Prophecy, opens at sea, aboard a schooner. A night without event, and full of dread, has just passed. Old habits of superstition weigh on the sailors, too strong to shake off. Many of them believe the silent steersman who appeared among them was no living man at all. He was a spirit, they think, sent from the world of the dead to warn them of evil to come.

Their shipmate Fuller swore all through the sleepless night that what he saw was a ghost. Captain de Haldimar's own shaken state, after the same visit, settles the matter for men whose faith in marvels runs in the blood. Richardson carries his frontier tale onto the lakes, where fear does the work of an enemy. The mystery of the steersman hangs over the closing volume from its first page.
wanda-vol-1-of-3: Ouida's Wanda appeared in three volumes from Chatto and Windus at London. This first volume bears the year 1873. She inscribed the book to Walpurga, Lady Paget, born Countess von Hohenthal, in admiration and affection. A line of Pope, about a perfect woman nobly planned, heads the dedication. A motto from Goethe's Faust heads the title page. Pages present here hold the title page, that dedication, and the heading of a proem only, so the novel itself is not shown.
wanda-vol-2-of-3:
Volume two of Ouida's Wanda, from Chatto and Windus at London with its title page dated 1883, opens at chapter eleven. Wanda has come back from a round of visits. She reports to the Princess on her royal friends, her cousins, and society at large. She speaks of her fears for the peace of Europe, and her doubts about the strength of the empire. One name she never speaks: that of her late guest, the one person Madame Ottilie burns to hear of.

Pressed at last, Wanda allows that he called once. She heard him speak in the Chamber, she says. He spoke well in public, and sent the Princess tender, grateful messages. All the while, the scent of white lilac pursues her, and the memory of its giver. Ouida writes high-society love as a war between duty and a heart that betrays itself.
wanda-vol-3-of-3:
Volume three of Ouida's Wanda, dated 1883 on its Chatto and Windus title page, opens at chapter twenty-nine in deep autumn. Wanda and Sabran have come home from a tour among the mines of Galicia and the plains of Hungary. A warm welcome in restored Idrac is behind them. The October rains are up, and every brook is a torrent. News from Paris waits for her: an old friend of her father's is dead. The Duc de Noira was her godfather.

The duke was a Legitimist hermit who never married. He has left her his famous gallery of pictures and his collection of eighteenth-century art. Her presence in Paris is requested. Wanda sees that the news pleases Sabran, who wants the journey. In an unselfish impulse she tells him to go alone in her place. The final volume turns on art, inheritance, and parting.
what-s-mine-s-mine-volume-3:
George MacDonald closes What's Mine's Mine in volume three. The first chapter finds Mercy well enough to leave her room for the drawing room. Evenings there feel new to her, and her days give time for thought. Her mother and Christina visit often. Mercy has entered a part of life far from all she knew before.

The contents promise a dread find, love in gloom, and a generous dowry. Night scenes, a peat moss, and a bold visit build toward the end. Later chapters bring a move, a new village, one more expulsion, and a farewell. Love and loss, tested by pride, reach their close here.
yoga-vasistha-mitra-vol-3:
The third volume of Mitra's Yoga-Vasistha continues the immense dialogue between the sage Vasistha and Prince Rama. Vihari-Lala Mitra issued his four-volume English version in the 1890s. By this stage the teaching has moved from the world's unreality to the state of the liberated soul.

Vasistha describes the man who is free while living: calm in gain and loss, acting without bondage to the act. More tales unfold, of worlds nested in atoms and lives relived in dream. The doctrine is radical idealism: consciousness alone is real, and all else its play. The volume holds the epic's most sustained philosophy. Mitra's notes help readers through the Sanskrit terms.
